questions.question: Your brother-in-law calls you during one of your night duties and tells you that your sister just delivered a baby girl and that both the mother and the child are doing well following the cesarean delivery. The next morning, however, you get a call that the baby started having trouble breathing and has been shifted to the NICU. He also sends you a photo of her chest X-ray via WhatsApp. On the radiograph, you note streaky, perihilar linear densities and fluid in the horizontal fissure. Which of the following is true regarding the given clinical condition?
options: Only observation and supportive therapy is needed
It can predispose to bronchopulmonary dysplasia
questions.answer: A. Only observation and supportive therapy is needed
questions.explanation:
Benign respiratory distress in a newborn with a chest X-ray showing fluid in the interlobar fissure is indicative of transient tachypnoea of newborn (TTN), also known as retained fetal lung liquid syndrome. The management of TTN is supportive oxygen therapy and observation.

It is more common after a term, cesarean delivery and is due to the delayed clearance of the lung fluid from the interstitium into the pulmonary lymphatics.

Other findings of chest x-ray imaging are prominent (perihilar) pulmonary vascular markings, increased interstitial markings, and a “wet silhouette” around the heart.

Chest radiograph (A) on day 1 at 6 hours shows a bilateral diffuse ground-glass appearance and fine granularity due to interstitial opacities.

Chest radiograph (B) of the same patient at the age of 2 days (B) shows that the pulmonary parenchymal opacities have decreased, though perihilar streaky markings are still present.

Treatment is supportive and minimal oxygen treatment (< 40%) is often adequate; infants usually recover within 3 days.

questions.question: A preterm, extremely low birth weight baby, delivered by emergency caesarian section was admitted to the NICU and treated for respiratory distress syndrome. She responded to treatment and was discharged. At 6 months of age, she is still having recurrent respiratory distress and requires supplemental oxygen at home. The baby was diagnosed with bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Which of the following does not cause this clinical complication?
questions.explanation:
Inhalation of nitrous oxide (N2O) is not associated with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). Inhaled NO is a pulmonary vasodilator approved for the treatment of hypoxic respiratory failure in term and near-term infants with pulmonary hypertension. It may have a role in preventing BPD.

BPD is a pathologic process leading to clinical features of chronic lung disease that originates in the neonatal period and is defined by an oxygen requirement for 28 days postnatally. Inflammatory injury to the developing lungs due to barotrauma and oxygen toxicity resulting from prolonged mechanical ventilation is the key factor driving the pathogenesis of BPD. Together with other antenatal and postnatal factors, it results in aberrant tissue repair, dysregulated vascular and arrested alveolar development, which is the basis of the pathology seen in BPD.

questions.question: A female newborn was delivered at 40 weeks of gestation by emergency C-section, following signs of severe fetal distress. Greenish amniotic fluid was noted. Immediately following delivery, the baby was shifted to the NICU and had to be intubated. Her chest X-Ray is as below. What does it show?
questions.answer: D. Patchy infiltrates and coarse streaking
questions.explanation: The image shows patchy infiltrates and coarse streaking, which are characteristic findings in the chest X-ray image of infants with meconium aspiration syndrome.

questions.question: A newborn infant, delivered at home, at 42 weeks of gestation, became cyanotic and started breathing rapidly. The child was immediately taken to the nearby primary health centre. As the medical officer prepares to intubate, she notes greenish staining on the vocal cords. Which of the following is this baby likely to develop?
questions.explanation:
Respiratory distress in a post-term neonate with a history of greenish (meconium-stained) amniotic fluid during delivery is suggestive of meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS). The aspirated meconium can block the large and small airways, causing patchy atelectasis and emphysema. This produces a ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Severe overinflation can lead to air leak syndromes such as pneumothorax.

Meconium consists of water, desquamated GIT cells, skin, lanugo hair, vernix, bile salts, pancreatic enzymes, lipids, and mucopolysaccharides. The bile salts and pancreatic enzymes can cause chemical pneumonitis. Meconium can also cause surfactant inactivation by displacing it from the alveolar surface and inhibiting its surface tension-lowering ability. Severe MAS is associated with remodelling and thickening of the muscular walls, resulting in pulmonary hypertension.

Infants who develop MAS typically present in the first 12 hours after birth with varying degrees of respiratory distress. On inspection, many affected infants have 'barrel chests'; crackles (rales) and rhonchi often can be heard on auscultation. In severe cases, the entire lungs can be involved resulting in a total “whiteout” of the lungs on the radiograph.

Listeriosis is an infection that is acquired from the mother and is reported to be rarely associated with meconium-stained amniotic fluid.

questions.question: Which of the following is false about apnea of prematurity (AOP)?
options: Usually resolves by 37 weeks post conceptional age
Gentle tactile stimulation is often adequate for mild to moderate episodes
Recurrent AOP can be treated with caffeine or theophylline
AOP is a risk factor for Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)
questions.answer: D. AOP is a risk factor for Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)
questions.explanation:
Apnea of prematurity (AOP) is not a risk factor for sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

It is defined as cessation of breathing for longer than 20 seconds or for any duration if accompanied by cyanosis or bradycardia. It is a diagnosis of exclusion. It is seen in preterm infants and usually resolves by the 37th week of gestation. Recurrent apnea of prematurity may be treated with caffeine or theophylline. It does not predict the future occurrence of SIDS.

Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) is the sudden death of an infant under one year of age, which remains unexplained after a thorough case investigation, including the performance of a complete autopsy, examination of the death scene, and review of the clinical history.

questions.question: While monitoring the respiratory rate of the infants in the NICU, you notice one baby which suddenly stops breathing. Which of the following statements is true in this regard?
options: Primary apnea is characterized by labile BP and tachycardia
Caffeine therapy should be given in primary apnea
Secondary apnea responds to stimulation by establishing normal breathing.
Central asphyxia can cause secondary apnea
questions.answer: D. Central asphyxia can cause secondary apnea
questions.explanation:
Secondary apnea can occur as a central CNS meditated asphyxia or due to neuromuscular disorders.

Apnea is the cessation of breathing for >20 seconds or for any duration if accompanied by bradycardia and cyanosis.

Primary Apnea
Secondary Apnea

Failure to initiate respiratory effort at birth
Apnea developing in an infant who has initiated a respiratory effort

There may be bradycardia and decreased tone. BP remains normal

Can originate in CNS due to asphyxia or peripherally due to neuromuscular disorders

Respond to tactile stimulation
Require ventilatory assistance and drugs- caffeine or theophylline

questions.question: A 15-day-old infant had conjunctivitis, which later developed into respiratory distress and pneumonia. Chest X-ray examination revealed bilateral lung infiltrates. Peripheral smear count showed 14,300/dL (N 43, L 54, E3). Which of the following is the most likely pathogenic organism?
questions.explanation:
The organism most likely to cause the mentioned infections is Chlamydia trachomatis.

Pneumonia caused by C. trachomatis can develop in 10–20% of infants born to women with active, untreated chlamydial infection. Only approximately 25% of infants with nasopharyngeal chlamydial infection develop pneumonia.

C. trachomatis pneumonia of infancy has a very characteristic presentation. It usually occurs between 1-3 months of age and is insidious, with a persistent cough, tachypnea, and absence of fever. Auscultation reveals rales; wheezing is uncommon.

The absence of fever and wheezing helps to distinguish C. trachomatis pneumonia from respiratory syncytial virus pneumonia.

A distinctive laboratory finding is the presence of peripheral eosinophilia (>400 cells/µL).
The most consistent finding on chest radiograph is hyperinflation accompanied by minimal interstitial or alveolar infiltrates.

questions.question: The radiologist calls and confirms a Bochdalek hernia in a baby born with multiple congenital anomalies. The baby had been placed under an oxygen hood in the NICU, in view of postnatal respiratory distress. On repeat evaluation, he continues to have sternal retractions and is not maintaining saturation. Which of the following would be your initial clinical intervention in this case?
options: Intubate and insert a nasogastric tube
Insert a central venous pressure line
questions.answer: A. Intubate and insert a nasogastric tube
questions.explanation:
Once the diagnosis of congenital diaphragmatic hernia is made or suspected, all patients are intubated. Also a nasogastric tube, connected to continuous suction, is placed in the stomach to reduce lung compression.

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a birth defect of the diaphragm. The most common type of CDH is a Bochdalek hernia (postero-lateral diaphragmatic hernia); other types include Morgagni hernia (anterior-parasternal), diaphragm eventration, and central tendon defects of the diaphragm. Malformation of the diaphragm allows the abdominal organs to push into the chest cavity, hindering proper lung formation and expansion.

Immediate steps of management:

Endotracheal intubation → Placement of a nasogastric tube → Administration of fluids and inotropic agents → Administration of surfactant therapy to only preterm infants with findings suggestive of respiratory distress syndrome.Other options:

Option B: Bag and mask ventilation is to be avoided as they lead to gastric/abdominal distension and compression of the lung.

Option C: Both arterial and central venous lines are inserted; however, this is not the first line of intervention.

Option D: To support respiratory failure, the first modality to be used is conventional ventilation, and if there is no improvement, then high-frequency ventilation is used.

questions.question: A newborn delivered vaginally, at term, was diagnosed with congenital diaphragmatic hernia. The most important limiting factor for survival in this condition is ________.
questions.explanation:
Pulmonary hypoplasia is a very poor prognostic factor in congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

Poor prognostic indicators in CDH:

• The presence of liver in the thoracic cavity

• Pulmonary hypoplasia, pulmonary hypertension

• Early respiratory distress, within 24 h after birth

• Need for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation

• Herniation to the contralateral lung (right-sided hernia)

questions.question: You are doing a quick pre-op evaluation of a 2-day-old baby shifted for emergency pediatric surgery. Parents had brought him with a history of sudden, noisy breathing. He appeared cyanotic with decreased breath sounds on the left side of the chest. Chest X-ray taken in the casualty is given below. Which of the following is not true about the underlying condition?
options: Most commonly seen on the left side
Mortality is usually associated with pulmonary hypoplasia
Pulmonary dilators markedly improve the survival
questions.explanation:
The given clinical picture of neonatal respiratory distress, absent breath sounds in the left side of the chest, and an X-ray image showing bowel loops in the thoracic cavity is diagnostic of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Though less commonly documented, dextrocardia is seen in association with CDH.

A diaphragmatic hernia is defined as a communication between the abdominal and thoracic cavities with or without abdominal contents in the thorax. It is mostly congenital, with a defective formation of the pleuroperitoneal membrane. Females are affected twice as often as males.

Bochdalek hernia accounts for up to 90% of the hernias seen in the newborn period, with 80-90% occurring on the left side. So, the heart will be pushed to the right side (dextroposition).

Predictors of a poor prognosis include an associated major anomaly, symptoms before completion of 24 hours since birth, severe pulmonary hypoplasia, herniation to the contralateral lung, and the need for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO).

Nitric oxide is a selective pulmonary vasodilator. It reduces ductal shunting and pulmonary pressures, resulting in improved oxygenation.

questions.question: Which of the following gross motor milestone would you expect to see in a 3-year-old child?
questions.answer: C. Walk upstairs with alternate foot
questions.explanation: A three-year-old should normally be able to walk upstairs with alternate feet.

questions.question: You notice a child pulling to the standing position and then shuffling around by holding onto furniture. At what age is this milestone typically attained?
questions.explanation: Cruising is an activity in which a child pulls to the standing position and then shuffles around holding onto a piece of furniture. Cruising is attained by 10-11 months.

questions.question: In the pediatric wards, you notice a baby, totally occupied with his little game and a mother trying hard to spoonfeed him. He is busy stacking toy cubes on top of each other and starts gleefully clapping once he makes a tower of 6. What is the likely age that this milestone corresponds to?
questions.explanation:
A child can usually make a tower of 6 blocks by 24 months.

A child makes a tower of:

• 2 blocks by 15 months

• 3 blocks by 18 months

• 6 blocks by 2 years

• 9 blocks by 3 years

questions.question: By what age is the milestone shown in the image typically attained?
questions.explanation:
The milestone shown in the image is a mature pincer grasp, which is seen at the age of 12 months. It is identified as a mature pincer grasp as the object is secured between the opposed thumb and the tip of the index finger.

Developmental progression of the grasp:

• At 6 months, the infant reaches and holds a larger object in a crude manner using the ulnar aspect of his hand (Ulnar palmar grasp). At 8-9 months, the object is grasped by the radial side of the palm (radial palmar grasp).

• At 9 months, the immature pincer grasp develops. The object is secured between the adducted thumb and the extended index finger.

• At 12 months, the mature pincer grasp develops. The object is secured between the opposed thumb and the tip of the index finger.

questions.question: A final-year medical student is examining a baby in the ward. As the infant is pulled to sit, he notices a head lag. By what age should this infant ideally start to hold his head steady without any bobbing motion?
questions.explanation:
An infant can hold his head steady when pulled to sit, without head bobbing, by the age of 4 months.

Regarding head steadiness:

• Up till 2 months of age, there is a significant head lag when the infant is pulled to sit.

• At 3 months, head lag is partially compensated but still present; the infant attains early head control with bobbing motion and sits with back rounded.

• At 4 months, there is no head lag when pulled to sit and the infant sits with full truncal support.

questions.question: Your sister tells you that your nephew has now started using his crayons. He easily copies circles, but still has trouble with squares. Other than a minor ASD noted incidentally at birth, he is a perfectly healthy child. Which of the following would you expect him to be able to do at this stage?
questions.answer: D. Know his name and gender
questions.explanation:
Normally, a child is able to copy a circle at 3 years and a square at 4 years. This child is a 3-year-old, and he should be able to know his name and gender.

• A child is able to tell a story at 4 years.

• Asks meaning of words at 5 years.

• A child can skip at 5 years.

questions.question:
Match the following milestones with corresponding age.

Milestone
Age

A) Handedness
1) At Birth

B) Taste perception
2) 24-36 months

C) Monosyllabic babble
3) 1.5 months

D) Smiles in response to voice
4) 6 months

E) Creeps upstairs
5) 15 months
questions.explanation:
Handedness is established during the 3rd year (24 to 36 months).

Taste perception is present since birth.

Monosyllabic babble is seen at 6 months.

Response to faces and voices with a smile is seen at 1.5 months.

The child creeps upstairs by 15 months.

questions.question: You are taking a detailed history from the parents of a child with a suspected autism spectrum disorder. Parents are worried that their child does not smile or maintain eye contact and is not interested in toys. At what ages should a typical child exhibit "social smile" and "stranger anxiety"?
questions.explanation:
Social smile is typically seen at 2 months and stranger anxiety at 6 months.

Social smile: At 1 month of age, a child smiles involuntarily. At 2 months of age social smile develops; that is, the child smiles voluntarily and reciprocally, in response to someone else’s smile.

Stranger anxiety: Before 6 months, the child is sociable and friendly even with strangers. At 6 months, there is an onset of stranger anxiety; infants look back and forth between an approaching stranger and parent and may cling or cry anxiously.

questions.question: A pediatrician is evaluating a toddler for mental retardation. She hands a bright red ball to the baby and lets him play with it. She then takes the ball and hides it under a blanket in front of him. The child confusedly stares at the blanket and cries instead of searching for it. What is being tested here?
questions.explanation:
Understanding that objects continue to exist even when not seen is called object permanence. This is due to an ability to form a mental representation of the object. It is attained at the age of 8–9 months.

Option A: Separation anxiety begins at about 9 months of age. Children wake up crying from their naps as they realize that their parents are not in the same room as them. This is different from stranger anxiety displayed by the child at the age of 6-7 months, wherein they react to approaching strangers by crying or clinging to their parent.

Option B: A transitional object is an object, such as a blanket or a stuffed toy, that is used by many children as a symbol of the absent parent. It is seen at around 18 months.

Option C: Symbolic transformations in play:

• At 12 months - make-believe (symbolic) play centres on the child’s own body, e.g., the child pretends to drink from an empty cup.

• At 18 month - symbolic transformations in play are not limited to the child's body, e.g., a doll can be fed from a plate.

questions.question: Parents of 9-month-old infant, with a history of preterm delivery and prolonged NICU stay, are concerned that child is lagging behind in his milestones. You would suspect a developmental delay in this child if his developmental quotient (DQ) is below _______ %?
questions.explanation:
A developmental delay should be suspected if the development quotient (DQ) is below 70%.

It is calculated as:
DQ = Developmental age x 100⁄Chronological age

From the highest milestones achieved by the child, the developmental age in a particular domain is calculated. The chronological age is the actual age in term babies. However, in preterm infants, a corrected age rather than postnatal age is used till two years of age. This is used to account for the small gap in neurological development that premature children have yet to catch up. For example, a child born at 32 weeks gestation (gestational age) seen at 12 weeks of age (postnatal age), should be considered as a 4-week-old (corrected age) child.

If there is a delay (DQ<70%) in more than 2 domains, then global developmental delay (GDD) is suspected.

questions.question: Which of the following milestones is expected to be seen in a child at 5 years of age?
options: Riding a tricycle and making a tower of 9 blocks
Establishment of handedness and parallel play
questions.explanation:
Developmental milestones at the age of 5 years include:

• Motor - skips

• Adaptive - Draws a triangle

• Language - Asks meaning of words

• Social - Dresses and undresses

Undressing is easier and hence learned before dressing.

• 2 years - Helps to undress

• 3 years - Helps in dressing (if helped with buttons)

• 5 years - Dress and undress fully (without any help)

questions.question: Which of the following is not a definitive test for developmental surveillance?
questions.explanation:
Denver-II is a developmental screening test (not a definitive test) that assesses child development in 4 domains:

• Gross motor

• Fine motor adaptive

• Language and

• Personal social behaviour

 Tests for the developmental quotient

Definitive Tests

Screening tests

(Bayley-II)

Stanford–Binet Intelligence Scale

Wechsler Intelligence Scale

questions.question: A child was able to count 4 pennies but was unable to name 4 colors. The probable age of the child is ______.
questions.explanation:
A 4-year-old child can count 4 pennies but cannot name 4 colours. A child can name 4 colours at 5 years of age.

Note:

An easy way to remember this:

• No. of objects counted = age

• No. of colours identified = age - 1

questions.question: A term, 4-month-old infant, is developing normally. By what age do you expect her to walk without support and use polysyllabic jargon?
questions.explanation:
A 15-month-old child can walk without support and use polysyllabic jargon.

Walking: A child begins to cruise at 10 months, walk with support at 12 months, and walk without support at 15 months.

Jargon is seen around 15 months of age. It is a pre-linguistic vocalization in which the child babbles using strings of word-like sounds and produces words that do not make much sense to others.

questions.question: One of the kids has scribbled all over a newly painted wall inside an Anganwadi. You notice there are some triangles and squares as well, in this "drawing". This child must be older than _______
questions.explanation:
The milestones at 5 years of age are:

• Motor - skips

• Adaptive - draws triangle

• Language - asks meaning of words, names 4 colors

• Social - dresses and undresses

questions.question: After assessing a young child treated for unilateral retinoblastoma, you note significant delays in the cognitive and fine motor domains. The baby can stand without support and creep well. Normally, the highest fine motor skill a baby of this age is expected to have is ________
questions.explanation:
A baby that stands without support is most likely to be 12 months. The highest fine motor skill she is expected to have is mature pincer grasp (12 months).

Bidextrous reach is seen at 4 months and unidextrous reach at 6 months. Immature pincer grasp is seen at 9 months. Child begins to scribble after 15 months.

Fine motor development is critically linked with hand-eye coordination. Children who have disease-related loss of vision in early infancy develop difficulties in visuomotor integration and lags behind in fine motor milestones.

questions.question: You are a pediatrics resident handling the well-child clinic for the week and you are teaching undergraduates how to do a simple developmental assessment. A preterm baby born at 32 weeks, is brought in for a follow-up visit at 6 months. What is the age you would ask the students to assume when undertaking developmental assessment in this child?
questions.explanation:
The corrected age (in weeks) to be assumed while undertaking developmental assessment is 16 weeks.

Corrected age (in weeks) = (Gestational age + postnatal age) - 40 weeks

In this case, since the baby is born 8 weeks preterm, the 8 weeks of intrauterine growth and development she missed, is accounted for post-natally. Thus, for assessing the correct developmental age, 8 weeks has to be subtracted from the chronological age.

In babies born preterm, corrected age is used for their developmental assessment until 2 years of age.

questions.question: All of the following statements are true regarding principles of development except?
options: It is dependent on the functional maturation of the nervous system
Specific responses replace mass activity as the child matures
In the extremities, development occurs distal to proximal
questions.answer: D. In the extremities, development occurs distal to proximal
questions.explanation:
In the extremities, development occurs proximal to distal.

Growth
Development

Denotes a net increase in size/mass of tissues
Denotes maturation of functions

Cephalocaudal

Head ⇒ Neck ⇒ Trunk & upper limbs ⇒ Lower limbs

Distal ⇒ Proximal

Hands increase in size before upper arms

 Proximal ⇒ Distal

Hand use is learnt before the use of fingers

Rules of development:

• It is a continuous process

• It depends on the functional maturation of the nervous system

• The sequence of attainment of milestones is the same in all children

• It progresses in a cephalocaudal direction and proximal to distal.

• Certain primitive reflexes have to be lost before relevant milestones are attained

• The initial disorganized mass activity is gradually replaced by specific actions.

questions.question: A young infant is brought to you with a suspected developmental delay. The child is intently looking at his own hands. You would consider referring this child to a specialist if this milestone persists after ______.
questions.explanation:
Between 12 and 20 weeks, the child observes his own hands very intently. This milestone is called hand regard and it should disappear by 20 weeks. Its persistence after 20 weeks is considered abnormal.

In a blind child, however, it may persist beyond 20 weeks normally and is called apparent hand regard.

questions.question: Which of the following fetal hormones does not play any role in fetal growth?
questions.explanation:
Growth hormone does not play any role in fetal growth, although it is present in high levels during the fetal period. However, it does have a role in the postnatal period.

Insulin and thyroxine hormones are required for normal growth and development during late gestation. Glucocorticoid has a role in the prepartum maturation of organs such as liver, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract.

questions.question: A child is brought to the pediatrician for vaccination. The child is able to speak in	2-3 word sentences and is able to make a tower of 6 cubes. What is the expected weight of the child, if his development is normal and birth weight was 3 Kgs?
questions.explanation:
The child is able to make a tower of 6 cubes and speaks in 2-3 word sentences which indicates the child is of 2 years of age. Birth weight quadruples by the age of 2 years. Hence the child's weight should be 3 kgs x 4= 12 Kgs.

Infants may lose up to 10% of their birth weight in the 1st week of life and regain it by their 2nd week.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false?
options: Head circumference should be measured within 24 hours after birth
Head circumference equals chest circumference at 1 year of age
A boys height at 2 and half years is half of his adult height
A girls height at 2 years is half of her adult height
questions.answer: A. Head circumference should be measured within 24 hours after birth
questions.explanation:
Head circumference should not be measured within 24 hours because the head is subjected to molding during delivery, which makes the measurements unreliable.

The maximum circumference of the head from the occipital protuberance to the supraorbital ridges on the forehead is recorded using the cross-tape method.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements regarding the eruption of teeth is false?

1. The first primary tooth to erupt is the lower central incisor

2. All primary teeth erupt earlier in the lower jaw than their counterparts in the upper jaw.

3. The first secondary tooth to erupt is the first molar.

4. No teeth till 12 months of age is called delayed eruption.

5. Teething is manifested as gingival hyperemia and sucking fingers.
questions.explanation:
Primary teeth in the upper jaw erupt earlier than their counterpart in the lower jaw, except for lower central incisors and second molar. No primary teeth till the age of 13 months is called delayed eruption.

As seen in the image below, the first primary tooth to erupt is the lower (mandibular) central incisor, at 5-7 months. All primary teeth erupt by 1.5–2.5 years of age.

The first secondary tooth to erupt is the first molar (maxillary or mandibular), at 6-7 years, followed by the lower central incisor.

Causes of delayed eruption:

• Idiopathic: Most common

• Hypothyroidism

• Hypoparathyroidism

• Familial

• Mechanical blockage of individual teeth

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy presented to the clinic for a missed vaccination. His routine anthropometric measurements were noted. He was found to be 90 cm tall with a lower segment of 45 cm. Which among the following is the most likely diagnosis in this child?
questions.explanation:
The upper segment to lower segment (U/L) ratio in this child is 1. The U/L ratio is low for his age which makes spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia most likely among the given options.

The lower segment is defined as the length from the symphysis pubis to the floor. The upper segment is measured by subtracting the lower segment from the height.

The U/L ratio is

• 1.7 at birth

• 1.3 at 3 years

• 1 after 7 years

• 0.9 in adults

High U/L ratio:

• Rickets

• Achondroplasia

• Untreated congenital hypothyroidism

Low U/L ratio:

• Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia

• Vertebral anomalies

Arm span:

• Length between the tips of the middle finger of the outstretched hands is the arm span.

• It is shorter than the length by 2.5 cm at birth; it equals height at 11 y and thereafter is slightly greater than height (usually<1 cm).

options: Head reaches 90% of adult size at 1 year
Lymphoid growth follows a sigmoid-shaped pattern
Perinatal period is between 28 weeks of gestation to 7 days after birth
Growth of child is cephalocaudal and distal to proximal
questions.answer: D. Growth of child is cephalocaudal and distal to proximal
questions.explanation:
Growth of child is cephalocaudal and distal to proximal.

During fetal life, the growth of the head occurs before that of the neck, and arms grow before legs. The distal parts of the body such as hands increase in size before the upper arms.

Growth rate of different tissues:

• Brain growth: At age of 1 month, the head size is about 36% of the expected head size in adults. It doubles in the first year of life to 72% and becomes 83% of adult size at 2 years.

• Lymphoid growth: It is prominent in mid-childhood. It peaks at 4–8 years and regresses subsequently.

• Gonadal growth: It stays dormant during childhood and shows a rise with the onset of puberty.

• Somatic growth: General body growth shows an S-shaped curve. It is rapid during the fetal period and the first 3–4 years. It is steady in the following period, followed by a growth spurt during puberty. Later, it slows down considerably.

Note: WHO defines the perinatal period from 22 weeks of gestation (or ≥500 g) up to 7 days after birth.

questions.question: A young boy is brought to the clinician by his parents with complaints of impulsive behavior and decreased levels of attention at school and everyday activities. The clinician is suspecting a case of ADHD. Which of the following is not included in the criteria for diagnosis of ADHD?
options: Symptoms begin before 7 years of age
Symptoms should be present for at least 6 months
Should be reported by independent observers
Behaviour must be developmentally inappropriate in two or more settings
questions.answer: A. Symptoms begin before 7 years of age
questions.explanation:
Attention-deficit hyperactive disorder (ADHD) must begin before 12 years of age, according to DSM-5 criteria. It was 7 years as per the previous DSM-4 criteria.

DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria for attention-deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)-

1. A persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity/impulsivity present for at least 6 months, that interferes with functioning or development.

2. Several inattentive or hyperactive/impulsive symptoms were present before 12 years of age.

3. Several inattentive or hyperactive/impulsive symptoms are present in 2 or more settings (e.g., at school [or work] or at home) and is documented independently.

4. There is clear evidence of clinically significant impairment in social, academic, or occupational functioning.

 5. Symptoms do not occur exclusively during the course of schizophrenia, or another psychotic disorder, and are not better accounted for by another mental disorder (e.g., mood disorder, anxiety disorder, dissociative disorder, personality disorder, substance intoxication or withdrawal).

Treatment: Presynaptic dopaminergic agonists, commonly called psychostimulant medications, including methylphenidate, dexmethylphenidate, amphetamine, and various amphetamine and dextroamphetamine preparations are used.

questions.question: In the image given below, the weight and height of a child are plotted against his age in years. Identify the correct statement.
options: WHO growth charts used now are developed by National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS).
Short stature is defined as a height below 5th percentile.
Puberty in this child will be normal.
Bone age of this child is less than chronological age.
questions.answer: D. Bone age of this child is less than chronological age.
questions.explanation:
Bone age of this child is less than chronological age, as seen in cases of constitutional delay.

As seen in the graph, the child was short initially, but the final height is within normal range. Hence, this child has constitutional delay.

Other options:

• The WHO growth charts are based on Multicentre Growth Reference Study (MGRS). National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) developed growth charts that were used in the past.

• Short stature is defined as a height below the third percentile or more than 2 standard deviations below the median height for age and gender (<-2 SD) according to the population standard.

• Puberty will be delayed in this child.

questions.question: Identify the correct statement from the following.
options: Children with pica are at increased risk of megaloblastic anemia
Breath-holding spells are associated with hypertonia
Thumbsucking in a child is a way of discharging tension
Bedwetting after a period of 3 months of dryness at night is called secondary enuresis
questions.answer: C. Thumbsucking in a child is a way of discharging tension
questions.explanation:
Thumbsucking in a child is a way of discharging tension. It is a self-limiting habit disorder, usually seen between 6 months to 2 years.

Option A: Pica is persistent ingestion of non-nutritive substances for at least 1 month. It hampers the development of the child and requires clinical attention. Children with pica are at an increased risk of lead poisoning, iron-deficiency anemia, and parasitic infections.

Option B: Breath-holding spells: It is preceded by a provocative event such as anger. Crying stops at full expiration. Child may have apnoea, cyanosis, pallor, hypotonia, or even loss of consciousness, and generalized tonic–clonic seizure (GTCS). Subtypes include cyanotic, pallid, and mixed episodes. Seizures and cardiac causes should be ruled out. Parents should be reassured that breath-holding spells are self-limiting.

Option D: Enuresis:

• When the child has never been dry, it is called primary enuresis.

• When the bedwetting starts after a minimum period of six months of dryness at night, it is termed as secondary enuresis.

• Nocturnal enuresis is caused due to maturational delay. In a normal individual, antidiuretic hormone (ADH) levels usually peak between 4 am and 8 am. This circadian rhythm is impaired in nocturnal enuresis, leading to bedwetting.

• Treatment - Behavioural therapy with positive reinforcement, bladder alarms, and desmopressin reserved for cases resistant to behavioural therapy.

questions.question: As part of the annual school health check-up camp, the visual acuity of a 6-year-old girl is being tested by the optometrist. What is the expected visual acuity in this age?
questions.explanation:
According to Parson's diseases of the eye, visual acuity of 20/20 is attained by the age of 6 years. Nelson's Textbook of Paediatrics mentions that by the age of 5 or 6 years most children attain 20/20 vision.

Generally accepted visual acuity according to age:

• Visual acuity of 20/40 at 3 years of age

• Visual acuity of 20/30 at 4 years of age

• Visual acuity of 20/20 at 5 or 6 years of age

Which of the following screening tools can be used to detect the boy’s condition?

questions.question: Identify the correct statement.
options: Macrocephaly is defined as an occipitofrontal circumference greater than 3 SD above the mean for age and sex
Microcephaly is defined as an occipitofrontal circumference more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex
Infants with benign familial megalencephaly have normal head circumference at birth
questions.answer: C. Microcephaly is defined as an occipitofrontal circumference more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex
questions.explanation:
Microcephaly is defined as an occipitofrontal circumference more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex.

Macrocephaly is defined as an occipitofrontal circumference more than 2 SD above the mean for age and sex.

Monosomy 1p36 is associated with microcephaly.

Infants with benign familial megalencephaly have increased head circumference at birth.

Important causes of macrocephaly:

• Megalencephaly (enlargement of the brain parenchyma)

• Benign familial

• Neurocutaneous syndromes such as neurofibromatosis, tuberous sclerosis

• Lysosomal storage diseases: Tay–Sachs, mucopolysaccharidosis, gangliosidosis

• Increased cerebrospinal fluid

• Hydrocephalus

• Benign enlargement of subarachnoid space

• Hydranencephaly (absence of cerebral hemispheres; the cranial cavity is filled with cerebrospinal fluid [CSF])

• Enlarged vascular compartment

• Arteriovenous malformation

• Subdural, epidural, subarachnoid, or intraventricular hemorrhage

• Increase in the bony compartment

• Bone disease: Achondroplasia, osteogenesis imperfecta

• Bone marrow expansion: Thalassemia major

• Miscellaneous causes

• Intracranial mass lesions: Cyst, abscess, or tumor

• Raised intracranial pressure: Idiopathic pseudotumor cerebri

questions.question: A mother brings her baby of 14 months to the clinic after being concerned about the shape of the baby’s head. You are suspecting a case of craniosynostosis. The premature fusion of which of the following suture is seen in this child?
questions.explanation:
The picture is suggestive of a child with left posterior plagiocephaly (as the left side of the head is flattened) which involves the premature fusion of the left lambdoid suture.

In the case of a left anterior plagiocephaly, the premature fusion of the left coronal suture is seen.

• Primary craniosynostosis: It results from a primary defect of ossification.

• Secondary craniosynostosis: It results from the failure of brain growth.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy was found to have a height for age 2 standard deviations below the median. Furthermore, his bone age was found to be equal to chronological age. Which of the following is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Familial short stature is most likely as bone age is equal to chronological age.

Bone age is more than chronological age in precocious puberty.

Bone age is less than chronological age in all other causes of short stature such as constitutional delay, undernutrition, genetic diseases, and endocrine causes.

questions.question: The most calorically dense macronutrient is _______
questions.explanation:
Fat is the most calorically dense macronutrient providing approximately 9 kcal/g.

The nutrients that provide energy intake in the child’s diet are referred to as macronutrients. They include the following:

1. Fats (∼9 kcal/g)

2. Carbohydrates (4 kcal/g)

3. Proteins (∼4 kcal/g)

The main dietary sources of fat are as follows:

• For infants: human milk/formula

• For older children: fat from animal products, vegetable oils, and margarine.

questions.question: The mother of a school-going child is worried that he eats a lot of junk food. She is anxious to learn about the healthy diet to be followed in the child. You would ideally advise the mother to restrict the dietary intake of saturated fat to less than ______ percentage of total energy intake.
questions.explanation:
According to current dietary guidelines for children, energy from saturated fats should be <10% of total energy intake.

Current dietary guidelines for children and adolescents:

• Total fat should account for <30% of total daily energy

• Saturated fat less than 10% of total daily energy

• Dietary cholesterol <300 mg/day

• No trans-fat

questions.explanation:
Margarine and other hydrogenated oils are trans fat. Trans fat is not recommended in children according to current dietary guidelines.

questions.question: A newborn baby is ready to be discharged. As a part of your discharge advice, for how many months would you recommend exclusive breastfeeding?
questions.explanation:
Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for 6 months.

Complementary foods rich in iron and other micronutrients should be introduced at about 6 months of age. Breastfeeding should continue for at least the first year.

questions.question: You are taking a neonatal case for presentation during your postings. The mother tells you that the child is exclusively breastfed. Which of the following is least likely to corroborate with this history of being exclusively breastfed?
questions.explanation:
Exclusively breastfed infants are least likely to have evening colic. The incidence of diarrhoea, allergy to bovine milk, and atopic eczema are least reported in exclusively breastfed infants.

Option A: Vitamin K content of milk is low and may contribute to hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

Option B: Breast milk contains inhibitors of glucuronyl transferase and enhances absorption of bilirubin from the gut. This leads to the development of breast milk jaundice.

Option C: During the first few days, the breastfed infant has a black-green coloured stool. It changes to golden yellow by the end of the first week.

questions.question:
Which of the following mothers can initiate breastfeeding?

1. A mother with an active infection of herpes on both her breasts.

2. A mother with positive serology for hepatitis B infection.

3. A mother with active tuberculosis.

4. A mother who is on treatment with chemotherapeutic agents for leukaemia.

5. A mother with a history of chronic smoking.
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is 2 and 5 only. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated if the mother has hepatitis B infection or if she is a chronic smoker.

Infants born to an HbsAg positive mother routinely receive hepatitis B immunoglobulin and hepatitis B vaccine. So, a delay in the initiation of breastfeeding is not required.

Contraindications of breastfeeding:

Do not Breastfeed

Do not give expressed breastmilk

Infant factors:

• Classic galactosemia

Maternal factors:

• Human T-cell lymphocyte virus (HTLV) infection

• Ebola virus infection

• PCP/cocaine abuse

Do not Breastfeed (Temporarily)

Do not give expressed breastmilk (Temporarily)

Maternal factors:

• Brucellosis

• undergoing diagnostic imaging with radiopharmaceuticals

• Active herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection with lesions on the breasts

Do not Breastfeed (Temporarily)

Can give expressed breastmilk

Maternal factors:

• Untreated, active Tuberculosis

• Active Varicella infection

Alcohol consumption and smoking are NOT contraindications of breastfeeding. However, smoking and alcohol consumption should be discouraged.

Note: In a mother with untreated, active tuberculosis:

• Temporarily withhold breastfeeding but can feed with expressed breastmilk

• Resume breastfeeding once she has been adequately treated for 2 weeks and is no longer contagious.

questions.question: As a part of your neonatal rotation, you are asked to assess the adequacy of breastfeeding and breastfeeding techniques in a primi mother. Which of the following would be an indicator of inadequate breastfeeding in the neonate?
options: Baby sleeping for 2-3 hours after feed
questions.answer: B. Weight loss >10% of birth weight
questions.explanation:
Weight loss of >7-10% of birth weight is an indicator of inadequate breastfeeding in a neonate.

Indicators of inadequate breastfeeding in the newborn:

• Weight loss >7-10 % of birth weight

• Lethargy (sleeping longer than 2–3 hours)

• Delayed passage of stools (Less than 4 times/day)

• Decreased urine output (urinating less than 5–7 times/day)

• Hypernatremic dehydration

• Inconsolable crying and increased hunger

Insufficient milk intake may be caused by insufficient milk production, failure of established breastfeeding, and health conditions in the infant that prevent proper breast stimulation.

Breastfed neonates usually feed 8–12 times a day, with a minimum of 8 times per day. However, the neonate should be breastfed only on demand.

questions.question: A 2-month-old child is brought to your OPD with complaints of diarrhoea. The mother wants to know if she should continue breastfeeding. Which of these components in breast milk, beneficial in intestinal cell maturation and repair, prompt you to advise her to continue breastfeeding?
questions.explanation:
The epidermal growth factor present in breastmilk helps in intestinal cell maturation and repair. This is why mothers are advised to continue breastfeeding in an infant affected with diarrhoea. It is also beneficial in luminal surveillance.

questions.question:
A young working mother wants to add formula feeds to the diet of her 5-month-old child as she would be unable to breastfeed her baby frequently and satiate her. Which of the following fatty acid should the mother look for in the formula to ensure optimal brain development in the child?

1. Eicosapentanoic acid

2. Docosahexaenoic acid

3. Arachidonic acid

4. Linolenic acid
questions.explanation:
Docosahexenoic acid (DHA) and arachidonic acid (ARA), both play an important role in the growth and CNS development in babies.

DHA and ARA are essential poly unsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) present in breast milk.

Both are essential for cognition functions, visual acuity, and immune responses. They have optimal effects on brain development when included together, in efficacious levels, in an infant's diet.

Almost all infant formulae are now fortified with pre-formed DHA and ARA.

It is advisable that all infants upto 6 months of age are to be exclusively breastfed and not formula fed. However, in unavoidable situations such as lactation failure or maternal infections where breastfeeding is contraindicated, the use of a formula feed that contains both DHA and ARA is recommended.

Other options:

• Eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and Linolenic acid are other essential fatty acids that are present in breast milk.

• These are required for the overall protection of the cardiovascular system as well as to reduce systemic inflammation.

questions.question: Breast milk is superior to cow’s milk because ________
options: Casein is 60% of the protein content
Whey is 70% of the protein content
questions.answer: D. Whey is 70% of the protein content
questions.explanation:
Whey constitutes 70-80% of breast milk's protein content. The Whey: Casein ratio in human milk fluctuates between 70:30 and 80:20. This ratio is 20:80 in cow's milk. The high fraction of soluble whey protein in breast milk makes it easily digestible.

The predominant whey protein is α-lactalbumin in human milk and β-globulin in cow milk. Human milk contains amino acids like taurine and cysteine (lacking in cow’s milk), which are necessary for neurotransmission and neuromodulation.

Breast milk is rich in polyunsaturated fat (not saturated fat), which is necessary for myelination. Human breast milk is generally rich in oleic acid and linoleic acid.

Sodium concentration is not high in breast milk. It has a low osmolality, and hence, the solute load on the kidneys is low.

questions.question: An exclusively breastfed neonate in his 4th week of life was found to be jaundiced. His stools are yellow and urine appears pale straw, he is otherwise well. A provisional diagnosis of breastmilk jaundice is made. Which of the following is false about this condition?
options: Some babies need treatment with phototherapy
It is common in the second week of life
questions.explanation:
Breastfeeding is not contraindicated in breast milk jaundice. Mothers are advised to continue breastfeeding at frequent intervals.

Breastmilk jaundice is seen in about 2–4% of exclusively breastfed babies. There is significant unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia after the 7th day and may last for 2–3 weeks. This may be caused by the breast milk that might contain β-glucuronidase, which deconjugates intestinal bilirubin and promotes its absorption and other inhibitors of glucuronyl transferase. Persistently high bilirubin levels may require changing from breast milk to infant formula for 24–48 h and/or treatment with phototherapy, without cessation of breastfeeding.

Breastfeeding jaundice (BFJ)

It is an early-onset, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia of breastfed infants. Occurs in the 1st week after birth (usually appears after 24 - 72 hours of birth). It is due to decreased milk intake with dehydration and/or reduced caloric intake. The treatment would include continuing breastfeeding and supplementation with formula feeds if needed.

questions.question: A 26-year-old nursing mother presents with fever and pain in her left breast. She has had difficulty with breastfeeding previously, and now examination reveals her left breast is warm, red, swollen, and painful to palpation. She was started on dicloxacillin. What advice should be given to the mother regarding breastfeeding?
options: Continue feeding from both the breasts
Continue feeding from only right breast
Continue feeding from only left breast
questions.answer: B. Continue feeding from both the breasts
questions.explanation:
Lactational mastitis is not a contraindication to breastfeeding and the mother should continue feeding on both breasts.

It is most commonly caused due to Staphylococcus aureus present in the infant's nasopharynx. Dicloxacillin is safe to be given in nursing mothers.

questions.question: Which of the following statements are true with respect to the WHO Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative for small, sick, and preterm newborns (2020)?
options: Paladai feeding is indicated in very preterm infants with no suck-swallow-breath coordination
Finger-feeding is optimally indicated for short-term use and may improve breastfeeding rates at discharge
Feeding tubes are indicated only in neurologically compromised infants for long-term use
Bottle feeding can lead to overfeeding but has a reduced risk of aspiration in infants with immature suck-swallow-breathe reflex
questions.answer: B. Finger-feeding is optimally indicated for short-term use and may improve breastfeeding rates at discharge
questions.explanation:
Finger-feeding is optimally indicated for short-term use and may improve breastfeeding rates at discharge. It is indicated in neurologically compromised and preterm infants for a short period of time.

Paladai feeding is indicated in preterm, late preterm, and term infants for supplementation. It is economic, cheap, and is easy to use and clean. It has a risk of aspiration and is a slower method of feeding.

Feeding tubes- orogastric or nasogastric tubes are an efficient way of measuring intake. It is optimally used in very preterm infants with no suck-swallow-breathe coordination for long-term use. It requires frequent replacement.

Bottle and teat feeding, though not recommended is an efficient way to feed. Slow-flow teats mimic breastfeeding and are preferred to rapid-flow teats. They allow overfeeding and there is a risk of aspiration.

questions.question: A 9-month-old boy was brought to the well-baby clinic for routine immunization. He has a weight for height less than 2 standard deviations below the median. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A low weight-for-height, or wasting, indicates acute malnutrition.

Nutritional status is often assessed in terms of anthropometry

• Low weight-for-height, or wasting, indicates acute malnutrition.

• High weight-for-height indicates overweight.

• Low height-for-age, or stunting, indicates chronic malnutrition. This is the best indicator of long-term nutritional status in the pediatric population.

• Low weight for the age indicates acute or chronic malnutrition. It does not differentiate between wasting and stunting. Hence, it has limited clinical significance.

Note:

Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is an age-independent parameter used for screening wasting in children.

questions.question: A child is brought to the OPD for regular follow-up. Which of the following anthropometric record would prompt you to suspect a diagnosis of moderate malnutrition?
options: Weight for height < -2 SD to > -3 SD
Weight for height +2 SD to +3 SD
questions.answer: B. Weight for height < -2 SD to > -3 SD
questions.explanation:
An anthropometric score of Weight for height < -2 to > -3 SD indicates moderate malnutrition.

The indicators of undernutrition include:

questions.question: Which of the following is an age-independent index?
questions.explanation:
All the indices listed, namely, Kanawati and Mclaren index, Jellife ratio, and Rao and Singh index, are age-independent indices.

Age-independent indices:

• Kanawati and Mclaren index: Mid-arm circumference/Head circumference

• Jellife Ratio: Head circumference/Chest circumference

• Rao and Singh Index: Weight (kg) × 100/height2 (cm)

• Dugdale Index: Weight (kg)/height1.6 (cm)

questions.question: You are an intern evaluating a 2-year-old girl child for malnutrition. The measurement with the WHO standard mid-upper-arm-circumference (MUAC) tape shows yellow. This reading would correspond to?
questions.explanation:
The yellow colour on the new WHO standard mid-upper arm circumference of (MUAC) tape correlates to a MUAC of 11.5 to 12.5 cm.

MUAC tape cut-offs:

Colour
Measurements
Indication

< 11.5 cm
Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM)

 Yellow
11.5 to 12.5 cm
Under-nourished

Normal

Mid-upper arm circumference is used in children between 6 to 60 months. It is measured between the acromion and olecranon process and is an age-independent parameter.

Alternative methods for evaluating malnutrition:

Bangle Test - It has an internal diameter of 4 cms. Normally, it should not cross the elbow.

QUAC stick test - It is given by the formula - Mid-upper arm circumference/ Height of child

Skinfold thickness: It is an age-independent parameter. Routinely, we measure the triceps skinfold thickness. It is measured with the help of Harpenden calliper.

• Normal: 10 mm

• Severe malnutrition: < 6 mm

questions.question: A young child is brought to you for a general check-up. The physician is examining as shown below in the image. What would be the cut-off to label the child as malnourished?
questions.explanation:
The image shows the measurement of skinfold thickness using Harpenden calipers. The cut-off to label the child as malnourished would be the triceps skinfold thickness value of less than 6mm. This is an age-independent parameter.

Alternative methods for evaluating malnutrition:

Bangle Test - It has an internal diameter of 4 cms. Normally, it should not cross the elbow.

QUAC stick test - It is given by the formula - mid-upper arm circumference/ height of child.

questions.question: You are sent for active field surveillance of malnourished children to a rural district in central India. Which of the following specific finding would prompt you to make a diagnosis of marasmus?
questions.explanation:
Children with marasmus have a voracious appetite, whereas children with kwashiorkor often refuse to eat.

Marasmus is a calorie deficit state and kwashiorkor is a protein deficit state. The signs of low protein manifesting as hypoalbuminemia and edema are characteristically seen in kwashiorkor.

questions.question: Sheila, a widowed maid brings her youngest child to your OPD with complaints of cough and cold. She has not been able to feed her kids after the lockdown affected her work. The image of the child is shown below. Which of the following is least likely to be seen in this case?
questions.explanation: The image shows a child with marasmus which is not associated with apathy. Apathy is a psychomotor change seen in kwashiorkor.

Wasting of buccal pad of fat is classified as grade 4 marasmus.

questions.question: A child from an urban slum area is admitted to your unit and is receiving treatment for Kwashiorkor. Which of the following is not true regarding the treatment?
options: Suspect primary treatment failure if appetite is not regained by day 4
Suspect secondary treatment failure if oedema reappears after 4 weeks
questions.answer: A. Start iron therapy on admission
questions.explanation:
In a child with kwashiorkor, iron therapy (3 mg/kg/day) should be started only once the child starts gaining weight. Iron should not be given in the stabilization phase because excess iron can lead to free radical formation.

The image below explains the treatment protocol to be followed in the case of PEM.

The following should strike a suspicion of treatment failure in PEM:

Inpatient cases:

Primary Failure
Secondary failure

Failure to regain appetite by day 4.

Failure to start losing oedema by day 4.

Presence of oedema on day 10.

Failure to gain at least 5 g/kg/day by day 10.

Failure to gain 5 g/kg/day for 3 consecutive days during rehabilitation.

Reappearance of oedema after 4 weeks.

Outpatient cases:

Primary failure
Secondary failure

Failure to gain any weight by 2 weeks

Failure to lose oedema in 4 weeks

No weight gain in two visits

questions.question:
A 20-month-old child diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) is receiving treatment in your clinic. Given below are five statements regarding the treatment. Pick out the incorrect statements.

1. Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be started from day 1 of admission.

2. The stabilization phase would ideally include the first seven days of treatment.

3. Vitamin A is given daily to overcome micronutrient deficiency.

4. F-75 feeds can be initiated in split portions.

5. Promote skin to skin contact with mother to avoid hypothermia.
questions.explanation:
Vitamin A is not given daily in the treatment of SAM. It is given on day 1, day 2 and day 14.

The general treatment involves 10 steps in 2 phases:

Initial stabilization phase: It focuses on restoring homeostasis and treating medical conditions and requires 2-7 days of inpatient treatment.

Mnemonic: SHIELDED

• Sugar deficiency(hypoglycemia)

• Hypothermia

• Infection

• ELectrolyte imbalance

• DEhydration

• Deficiency of nutrients

Rehabilitation phase: It focuses on rebuilding wasted tissue and generally takes several weeks.

Steps:

• Treat hypoglycemia (blood glucose level <54 mg/dl): if symptomatic, give 10% Dextrose IV at 5ml/kg. Feeding should be initiated with starter F-75 (formula with 75 kcal/100 ml of feed)

• Treat hypothermia (axillary <35°C or 95°F): Skin-to-skin contact with care called “kangaroo technique” or dress in warmer clothes, cover head, wrap in a warmed blanket, and provide indirect heat.

• Treat dehydration: Hydrate with ReSoMal (45 mmol Na/L). It is a low-sodium rehydration solution for malnutrition.

• Correct electrolyte imbalance: There is a deficit of potassium and magnesium and excess sodium. Give extra potassium (3 to 4 mEq/kg/day) and magnesium (4 mEq/ kg/day) for at least 2 weeks.

• Treat an infection: Starting on the first day, give broad-spectrum antibiotics to all children.

• Correct micronutrient deficiencies:

• Do not give iron in the stabilization phase, because excess iron leads to free radical injury. Give iron 3 mg/kg/day once the child starts gaining weight after the stabilization phase.

• Give vitamin A on day 1. Repeat on day 2 and day 14.

• Folic acid 1 mg (5 mg on day 1)

• Zinc (2 mg/kg/day)

• Copper (0.3 mg/kg/day)

• Start cautious feeding: Give 8 to 12 small feeds of F75 feeds. It is low-lactose milk that contains 75 kcal and 0.9 g protein per 100 mL. After 3 days, transition to F100 feeds is made which is called a catch-up diet. This provides 100 kcal and 2.9 g protein per 100 mL. After 1 week, calories are further increased to 150–200 kcal/kg/day and protein to 4–6 g/kg/day.

• Rehabilitation: The indications of entry to this phase are reduced/minimal oedema and the return of appetite.

• Beginning of feeding.

• After 3 days, the transition to energy-dense feeding

• Stimulation of emotional and sensorial development

• Transfer to home-based diet

questions.question: A 3 year old child is brought to the hospital with complaints of multiple episodes of loose stools and progressive weight loss. She was found to have a mid-upper arm circumference of 10.5 cm. Which of the following is true regarding the management of this child?
options: Administer 10 mL of 50% glucose IV, if unconscious
Continue aggressive hydration, even after dehydration resolves
Use ReSoMal for rehydration 5 mL/kg every 30 min for the first 2 hours
questions.answer: D. Use ReSoMal for rehydration 5 mL/kg every 30 min for the first 2 hours
questions.explanation:
Progressive weight loss and mid-upper arm circumference of <11.5 cm denote severe acute protein-energy malnutrition (PEM). When accompanied by loose stools, management includes the use of low sodium ORS for rehydration of 5ml/kg every 30 min for the first 2 hours.

Management of fluid/electrolyte status in SAM:

1. Do not give IV fluids unless the child is in shock.

2. Give ReSoMal (low-sodium rehydration solution for malnutrition) 5 mL/kg every 30 min for the first 2 hr orally or NG tube.

3. Then give 5-10 mL/kg in alternate hours for up to 10 hour. The amount depends on stool loss and eagerness to drink. Feed every other alternate hour.

4. Give ReSoMal after each watery stool as a prevention strategy.

5. Do not continue aggressive hydration even after dehydration resolves.

Treatment of hypoglycemia in malnutrition:

• If conscious: 10% glucose (50 mL) orally or 1 teaspoon sugar under the tongue, whichever is the quickest.

• If unconscious: Immediately give sterile 10% glucose (5 mL/kg) by IV.

Note:

50% glucose is never used in children as it is extremely viscous and concentrated. This could lead to injection site pain, severe thrombophlebitis, and irritation. Also, this can cause osmotic overload in a three-year-old.

questions.question: A young girl who was grossly emaciated and undernourished was started on partial parenteral nutrition together with enteral nutrition via a nasogastric tube. In the first week, which among the following would be the hallmark for the development of refeeding syndrome?
questions.explanation:
The hallmark of refeeding syndrome is the development of severe hypophosphatemia.

Refeeding syndrome is a complication of the acute nutritional rehabilitation of children who are undernourished from any cause, and it may follow overly aggressive enteral or parenteral alimentation.

When excessive carbohydrates are administered, the resultant increase in serum insulin levels may produce the following:

1. Hypophosphatemia (hallmark)

2. Hypokalemia

3. Hypomagnesemia

A controlled transition over 3 days from F-75 to F-100 is recommended by the WHO for treating malnutrition, to prevent refeeding syndrome.

questions.question: Which of the following is an 'Anti-infective' vitamin?
questions.explanation:
Vitamin A is required for the maintenance of epithelial functions, creating an effective barrier against pathogens; hence, it is called as an anti-infective vitamin. So, vitamin A deficiency can lead to changes in the epithelia of all mucosal surfaces, leading to increased chances of infections.

Vitamin E (Tocopherol) helps is an anti-oxidant. Deficiency manifests as skin changes and hair loss.

Vitamin D maintains calcium and phosphorus homeostasis. Deficiency can lead to rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

Vitamin C helps in the formation of connective tissues and collagen in the skin, bone, and blood vessels. Deficiency leads to their fragility and causes scurvy.

questions.question: What would be the ideal dose of vitamin - A that you should prescribe to a 9-month-old infant along with the measles vaccine?
questions.explanation: For a child aged 9 months, the dose of vitamin A given is 100,000 IU.

questions.question: A 2-year-old unvaccinated girl is brought to the OPD with high-grade fever and maculopapular rashes for 2 days. On examination, she has blue-white spots on her buccal mucosa as shown in the image attached below. Which of the following vitamin deficiency is associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
The girl is suffering from measles. It is associated with vitamin A deficiency.

Vitamin A deficiency is associated with an increased risk of infection and increased mortality with a variety of infectious diseases particularly measles. Hence, vitamin A therapy is indicated in all patients with measles.

The main functions of vitamin A are as follows:

• Maintenance of vision, especially night vision

• Maintenance of epithelial tissues

• Differentiation of various tissues, particularly during reproduction and gestation, by regulating gene expression.

Features of vitamin A deficiency:

• Eyes: Defective dark adaptation is a characteristic early clinical feature, resulting in night blindness (earliest manifestation). This can further progress to xerophthalmia, Bitot's spots, conjunctivitis, or keratomalacia, leading to blindness.

• Poor overall growth, anaemia

• Diarrhoea, susceptibility to infections

• Increased intracranial pressure

• Keratinization of mucous membranes and skin (hyperkeratosis)

questions.question: A young girl of class 4 complains of a burning sensation in the eye. Clinical examination of eyes reveals the finding shown below. What could be the mechanism for the development of such lesions?
options: Deposition of calcium in the conjunctiva
questions.answer: D. Keratinization of the conjuctival epithelium
questions.explanation:
The given clinical image is showing Bitot spots, which occur due to keratinization of the conjunctival epithelium. Bitot spots are triangular, frequently bilateral, and present on the bulbar conjunctiva.

Normally, bulbar conjunctiva is a stratified, columnar, non-keratinized epithelium. In vitamin A deficiency, there is squamous metaplasia of the conjunctival epithelium and tangles of keratin admixed with gas-forming bacteria producing a dry, scaly patch with a foamy appearance called Bitot spots.

Option A: Deposition of calcium in the conjunctiva is termed conjunctival concretions, which usually occurs over the palpebral conjunctiva, in chronic inflammatory conditions of the eye.

Option B: Scarring of the conjunctiva is seen in chlamydial infection of the eye.

Option C: Excessive growth of conjunctival tissue is seen in the pterygium of the eye.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy with complaints of dry, itchy eyes and night blindness had the following ophthalmic finding as given in the image. What is the stage of vitamin A deficiency as per WHO classification?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a corneal ulcer occupying <1/3rd of the cornea under a slit lamp with a fluorescein stain. This corresponds to stage X3A of vitamin A deficiency.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the OPD with complaints of headache, desquamation of the skin, and bone pain. Pathological examination revealed lysosomal rupture within the cells, prompting a suspicion of hypervitaminosis A. Which of the following statement is false about the principle vitamin that is excess in the given condition?

1. All-trans retinoic acid is the most bioactive form of vitamin A.

2. Protein Energy Malnutrition (PEM) can cause vitamin A deficiency.

3. Excess vitamin A causes hyperostosis.

4. Raised Intracranial Pressure (ICP) can be seen in hypervitaminosis but not deficiency of vitamin A.

5. 11-trans retinal is required for vision.
questions.explanation:
Both hypervitaminosis A and deficiency of vitamin A cause raised intracranial pressure (ICP) (not just hypervitaminosis A). 11-cis retinal(not trans) is required for vision.

Hypervitaminosis A causes headache, vomiting, desquamation of the skin, and hyperostosis of long bones. Rupture of lysosomes in the cells is the pathological feature of hypervitaminosis A.

All-trans retinoic acid is the most bioactive form of vitamin A, and it is required for cell differentiation and the regulation of transcription. On the other hand, 11-cis retinal is required for vision. Protein-energy malnutrition can cause vitamin A deficiency because of the impaired synthesis of retinol-binding protein (RBP).

questions.question: Your best friend is recently worried that she has a lot of hair fall. Which of the following vitamin capsules if added to her diet can help prevent free radical injury and thus be beneficial for her??
questions.explanation:
Vitamin E/ Tocopherol is a potent antioxidant and is helpful in preventing hair fall. It promotes hair growth and prevents hair roots from getting damaged by free radical injury.

Alpha-tocopherol is the active component of vitamin E and it is mainly located within cell membranes, preventing lipid peroxidation and the formation of free radicals.

Deficiency of this can also lead to neurological defects, hemolysis, and posterior column defect.

Treatment includes vitamin E supplementation (25–50 units/day for a week).

Note:

The other vitamins having antioxidant properties are vitamins A, C, and E (vitamin E is the most important).

The other vitamin beneficial in the treatment of hair fall is biotin.

questions.question: An anxious mother brings her 6-month-old child with concerns about not gaining weight and height. On examination, stunted growth, craniotabes, frontal bossing, and craniosynostosis are noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Craniotabes (soft skull), frontal bossing, stunted growth, and craniosynostosis are clinical features of rickets.

General features include failure to thrive, listlessness, protruding abdomen, proximal muscle weakness, and fractures.

Head to toe-examination would include the following features:

Head examination would include craniotabes, frontal bossing, delayed fontanel closure, delayed dentition, and craniosynostosis.

Chest examination would reveal rachitic rosary, Harrison's sulcus, and repeated respiratory infections and atelectasis.

Spinal deformities could include kyphosis, scoliosis, lordosis.

Limb examination and extremities may show windswept deformity, anterior bowing of tibia, coxa vara, and enlargement of wrists and ankles. Bowings of legs (genu varum) or knock knees (genu valgum) may be noted. These changes can be seen only in children of the weight-bearing age group/ toddlers.

The image shows frontal bossing:

The image below shows the rachitic rosary:

The image below shows craniotabes:

questions.question: The X-ray image of a child with muscle weakness and failure to thrive is attached below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The clinical vignette with the above X-ray image shows fraying and cupping of the metaphysis, suggestive of rickets.

Radiological features in rickets:

• Fraying (Widening and irregularity of the growth plate)

• Cupping (Concavity of the metaphysis)

• Splaying at metaphysis (widening of metaphyseal ends)

• Generalized rarefaction

questions.question: An 8-year-old child from a rural slum area is brought to your OPD with deformity as shown in the image. Which of the following conditions is characteristically associated with this deformity?
questions.explanation:
Windswept deformity (combination of valgus deformity of one leg with varus deformity of the other leg) is seen in rickets. It is also seen in rheumatoid arthritis but characteristically seen in rickets.

Other deformities of extremities seen in rickets:

• Enlargement of wrists and ankles

• Valgus or varus deformities of limbs

• Anterior bowing of the tibia and femur

• Coxa vara

questions.question:
Your school friend brings his 5-year-old son to your OPD with small swellings on the chest that he had felt while giving the child a bath. On examination, you note swellings at the costochondral junctions. Which of the following conditions would be your differentials to this clinical presentation?

1. Scurvy

2. Rickets

3. Tietze syndrome
questions.explanation:
Swelling of the costochondral junctions is seen in all the 3 conditions mentioned above.

Rachitic rosary
Scorbutic rosary

Beaded (rounded) in appearance
Angulated in appearance

Non-tender
Tenderness on palpation (subperiosteal haemorrhage)

Due to metaphyseal widening
Due to epiphyseal separation

Note:

Tietze syndrome is the benign inflammation of the costochondral junction.

Image: Given below is a photo of the chest cage with pectus excavatum.

Image: The above image shows a rachitic rosary type of appearance.

questions.question: A 22-month-old girl presents with failure to thrive and delayed achievement of motor milestones. On examination, she seems irritable and is noted to have bowed legs, thick wrists, and dental caries. Which of the following is not a radiographic sign of this condition?
options: Increase in the width of the growth plate
questions.explanation:
The child is suffering from rickets. Subperiosteal hemorrhage is not a radiographic sign of rickets. On the contrary, it is seen in scurvy.

Radiographic features of rickets:

• Widening of the growth plate: Decreased calcification leads to reduced bone density

• Fraying: The edge of the metaphysis loses its sharp border.

• Cupping: The edge of the metaphysis changes from a convex or flat surface to a more concave surface.

• Splaying: Weight-bearing and stress on the uncalcified bone gives rise to the widening of the metaphyseal end.

• Enlargement of the wrists and ankles due to the widening of the distal end of the metaphysis.

• Coarse trabeculation of the diaphysis

• Generalized rarefaction

questions.question: A 2-year-old child from an urban slum is diagnosed with nutritional rickets. Which of the following biochemical markers can be seen in this child?
questions.explanation:
In nutritional rickets serum, alkaline phosphatase levels are increased.

Biochemical findings in nutritional rickets (nutritional vitamin D deficiency):

1. Normal or low calcium (since due to low calcium and vitamin D deficiency, PTH increases which will try to normalize the low calcium)

2. Parathyroid hormone levels are elevated (in order to increase the serum calcium)

3. Hypophosphatemia (because of increased parathyroid hormone [PTH])

4. Metabolic acidosis (secondary to PTH induced renal bicarbonate wasting)

questions.question: A child in your unit is admitted with alopecia, oligodontia, and features of rickets with elevated serum levels of alkaline phosphatase activity and 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D. What could be the pathology?
questions.answer: D. End-organ resistance to vitamin D
questions.explanation:
Alopecia and oligodontia (reduced number of teeth) with features of rickets in a child is classically seen in vitamin D-dependant rickets type 2 where the pathology is end-organ resistance (receptor hyposensitivity) to vitamin D.

Rickets causes

• Nutritional vitamin D deficiency

• Secondary vitamin D deficiency

• Vitamin D-dependant rickets, type 1 (defect in 1-alpha hydroxylase)

• Vitamin D-dependant rickets, type 2 (end organ resistance)

• Chronic kidney disease

• Hypophosphatemic rickets

• X-linked dominant hypophosphatemic rickets (PHEX gene mutation)

• Autosomal dominant (fibroblast growth factor [FGF] resistance to endopeptidases)

• Oncogenous rickets (increased FGF 23)

Note:

Vitamin D antibodies are found in most patients of systemic sclerosis.

questions.question: Stoss therapy is used in the treatment of which of the following micronutrient deficiencies?
questions.explanation:
Stoss therapy is used in the treatment of vitamin D deficiency.

There are 2 strategies for the administration of vitamin D:

• Stoss therapy: Here, 300,000-600,000 IU of vitamin D are administered orally or intramuscularly as 2 or 4 doses over 1 day.

•

The alternative strategy is daily vitamin D with a minimum dose of 2,000 IU/day for a minimum of 3 months.

Both strategies should be followed by a daily vitamin D intake of 400 IU/day if the child is < 1-year-old or 600 IU/day if the child is >1-year-old. Children must also receive adequate dietary calcium and phosphorus.

questions.question: A child with rickets not responding to treatment is being evaluated. Investigations show serum calcium level of 9 mg/dL, low phosphate level of 2 mg/dL, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and normal parathyroid hormone levels with normal arterial blood gas levels. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario of a child with a history of treatment-resistant rickets, normal levels of calcium (9 to 11 mg/dL), parathyroid hormone, arterial blood gas (ABG), with decreased phosphate (normal, 2.5 to 4.3 mg/dL), and elevated levels of alkaline phosphatase (normal, 33 to 96 U/L) is suggestive of hypophosphatemic rickets.

Hypophosphatemic rickets:

X-linked dominant hypophosphatemic rickets is the most common genetic cause of rickets while the most common, overall is nutritional vitamin D deficiency. PHEX gene (phosphate-regulating endopeptidase on x chromosome) products are responsible for the inactivation of phosphatonin. Mutation of this PHEX leads to increased phosphatonin (FGF 23) levels, and hence, the excretion of phosphorous is increased. This is also associated with impaired renal tubular reabsorption of phosphate leading to its excess excretion.

The chart attached below summarizes the evaluation of hypophosphatemic rickets.

Treatment-resistant rickets :

Patients respond well to a combination of oral phosphorus and 1,25-D (calcitriol). Frequent dosing helps prevent prolonged decrements in serum phosphorus levels because there is a rapid decline after each dose. In addition, frequent dosing decreases diarrhea, which is a complication of high-dose oral phosphorus.

questions.question: A concerned mother of an infant, known case of cystic fibrosis, presents to your OPD with complaints of abdominal pain, loose stools not settling with antibiotics, and other medications.
