questions.question: Venkatesh decided to present a rare case report of maternal disomy of chromosome 15 at a scientific conference. He collected the following image representing the disorder's features. What is this disorder?
questions.explanation:
Maternal disomy of chromosome 15 is seen in Prader–Willi syndrome. The image shows the characteristic features of truncal obesity, short stature, and small hands and feet.

Uniparental disomy: Offspring receives both copies of a chromosome from 1 parent and no copies from the other parent.

Prader-Willi syndrome
 AngelMan syndrome

Deletion

Paternal chromosome 15

Maternal chromosome 15

Uniparental Disomy
Maternal disomy (duplication) seen in 25% of cases
Paternal disomy (duplication) seen in 5% of cases

Clinical features

Elevated Ghrelin levels: Loss of appetite control, obesity

Severe hypotonia

Short stature

Small hands and feet

Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism

Cognitive impairment

Short stature

Severe mental retardation with lack of speech

Stiff arm movements

Spastic, uncoordinated walk

Seizures

An inappropriate outburst of laughter (Happy puppets)

Chromosome 15 diseases: Chromosome 15 has its own MAP (mnemonic),

• M: Marfan syndrome

• A: Angelman syndrome

• P: Prader Willi syndrome

questions.question: Triangular facies is indicative of which of the following diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Triangular facies is indicative of Russell–Silver syndrome.

Russell–Silver syndrome:

• Clinical features: Short stature, triangular face (small jaw and pointed chin), microcephaly, limb and facial asymmetry, 5th finger clinodactyly.

• A few cases are due to genomic imprinting disorder involving chromosome 11.

Note: Triangular facies is also seen in Alagille syndrome.

The image given below shows a child with Russell–Silver syndrome.

questions.question: During an intersectoral collaborative event, an award-winning geneticist from the National Human Genome Research Institute is invited for an endowment oration. He presents his lecture on an experimental form of treatment that uses the transfer of genetic material to cure diseases known as 'Gene Therapy'. Which of the following techniques does he mention for this therapy?
questions.explanation:
Electroporation is used in gene therapy.

Gene therapy is a technique that uses genes to treat or prevent disease through the delivery of DNA into a patient's cell by using recombinant viruses/naked DNA/DNA complexes. The methods used include intranuclear injection, electroporation, gene-gun, sonoporation, and magnetofection.

Gene therapy was first used for severe combined immunodeficiency disorder (SCID), which is due to adenosine deaminase enzyme deficiency.

questions.question: The following is the finding noted in a 12-month-old baby who is growing well and developing normally since birth. Which of the following is a true statement regarding this finding?
options: Maternal history of phenytoin intake during pregnancy should be suspected
Chromosomal analysis should be done to rule out other chromosomal abnormalities
questions.explanation:
The picture depicts a Simian crease – a single transverse palmar crease. It is a normal finding in about 3% of the population. In a child with simian crease and normal growth and development, reassurance should be provided.

• A simian crease is one of the findings of Down's syndrome however presence of only this finding should not lead to a diagnosis of Down's syndrome.

• Maternal history of phenytoin intake during pregnancy does not lead to this finding. However, maternal alcohol intake can be associated with this condition.

• Chromosomal analysis in an otherwise well child is not indicated.

questions.question: Non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPS) is particularly useful in the modern era of diagnosis in clinical genetics. Which of the following statements is not true regarding this test?
options: Evaluates maternal blood for fetal abnormalities
Positive test need confirmation by invasive testing
questions.explanation:
Non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPS) has a high negative predictive value.

NIPS:

• Useful in screening high-risk pregnancies for aneuploidies.

• Done after 10 weeks of gestation.

• Evaluates maternal blood for screening.

• Positive tests need confirmation by invasive testing (like amniocentesis, chorionic villous sampling).

questions.question: A mother reports to the OPD with the complaint that her child smells funny. On examination, you notice that the child has a global developmental delay and smells mousy. What is your probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Mousy odor is characteristically seen in phenylketonuria due to excess phenylacetate (phenyl ketone) formed in the body.

In the absence of phenylalanine hydroxylase, phenylalanine enters into alternate metabolic pathways which result in the formation of phenyl lactate, phenylacetate, and phenylacetylglutamine.

questions.question: A boy who attends school is sent to the principal's office as he often distracts others by rhythmically rocking back and forth on his seat. His mother worried about his behavior brings him to you. She also gives you a history of seizures. On examination, you notice he has blonde hair, fair skin, microcephaly, prominent maxillae with widely spaced teeth, and growth retardation. His urine changes its color transiently to blue-green on the addition of 1ml ferric chloride solution. What is the cause of CNS symptoms in this child?
questions.explanation:
The clinical vignette describes a case of phenylketonuria. CNS damage in patients with phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by hyperphenylalaninemia in brain tissue.

High blood levels of phenylalanine saturate the transport system across the blood-brain barrier causing inhibition of the cerebral uptake of other large neutral amino acids such as tyrosine and tryptophan impairing brain protein synthesis.

Microcephaly, prominent maxillae with widely spaced teeth, enamel hypoplasia, and growth retardation are other common findings in untreated children. Low bone mineral density and osteopenia have been reported in affected individuals of all ages.

Excess phenylalanine is metabolized to phenyl ketones (phenylpyruvate and phenylacetate) that are excreted in the urine. However, these metabolites have no role in the pathogenesis of CNS damage; their presence in body fluids simply signifies the severity of the condition.

Hypotyrosinemia can be partially responsible for the signs and symptoms but the primary cause is hyperphenylalaninemia.

Laboratory diagnoses of phenylketonuria include:

• Guthrie's test: growth of bacillus subtilis is seen

• Ferric chloride urine test: transient blue-green color

• Blood phenylalanine levels: elevated

• Enzyme studies

• Genetic mutation studies

• Tandem mass spectrometry: Gold standard screening method for all metabolic disorders.

questions.question: An infant with severe vomiting who was misdiagnosed as a case of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is being screened for metabolic disorders. Screening reveals hyperphenylalaninemia. On ordering an enzyme study, you would include all of the following enzymes except:
questions.explanation:
Defects of either phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) or tetrahydrobiopterin(BH4) can cause hyperphenylalaninemias.

PAH deficiency is diagnosed as phenylketonuria.

Malignant hyperphenylalaninemias include three enzyme defects, dihydropteridine reductase,pyruvoyl tetrahydropterin synthase, and GTP cyclohydrolase which help in BH4 synthesis. The deficiency of BH4 impairs three hydroxylase(phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan), and severe neurological symptoms develop because of the lack of neurotransmitters.

Dihydropteroate synthase is present only in bacteria and this makes it a useful target for sulfonamide antibiotics, which compete with the PABA precursor.

questions.question: As a physician treating a 2-month-old baby with phenylketonuria what will be your mainstay of treatment?
questions.explanation:
A low-phenylalanine diet is the mainstay of treatment of PKU.

The goal of therapy is to reduce phenylalanine levels in the plasma and brain. Because phenylalanine is not synthesized endogenously, small amounts of phenylalanine should be added to the diet to prevent phenylalanine deficiency. Dietary deficiency of this amino acid is manifested by lethargy, failure to thrive, anorexia, anemia, rashes, diarrhea, and even death; moreover, tyrosine becomes an essential amino acid in this disorder and its adequate intake must be ensured.

Sapropterin dihydrochloride , a synthetic form of BH4, which acts as a cofactor in patients with residual PAH activity, is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to reduce phenylalanine levels in PKU.

questions.question: An infant born out of a second-degree consanguineous marriage presents with jaundice, irritability, and vomiting. His mother gives a history of fever for the past 4 days. On examination, petechiae are present, he has hepatomegaly and extensor hypertonia of the neck and trunk. Labs reveal elevated serum transaminases, hypophosphatemia, and elevated levels of succinylacetone in serum and urine. Which of the following enzymes is deficient?
questions.explanation:
The clinical vignette describes a case of Hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 is caused by the deficiency of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase (FAAH).

Elevated levels of succinylacetone in serum and urine are diagnostic for tyrosinemia type I.

Liver(jaundice, acute hepatic crisis, elevated serum transaminases), kidney(hypophosphatemia), and nerve damage(extensor hypertonia of neck and trunk) are caused by metabolites of tyrosine degradation, especially fumarylacetoacetate and succinylacetone, and is usually precipitated by minor infections.

A diet low in phenylalanine and tyrosine can slow but does not halt the progression of the condition. The treatment of choice is nitisinone (NTBC), which inhibits 4-HPPD and reduces the flux of tyrosine metabolites to FAH, thus decreasing the production of the offending compounds, fumarylacetoacetate, and succinylacetone.

questions.question: A father while changing his child's diaper observes a boiled cabbage odor emanating from it. Curious about the smell, he calls you. As a pediatrician, you investigate the child thoroughly and conclude that the child is suffering from Type 1 Tyrosinemia. As the child grows all of the following complications can occur except:
questions.explanation:
Corneal ulceration is not a feature of hereditary tyrosinemia type 1. In fact, ocular manifestations are a feature of hereditary tyrosinemia type 2 which presumably occur due to tyrosine deposition.

Boiled cabbage odor may be present in tyrosinemia resulting from increased methionine metabolites (sulfur-containing compounds).

Features of hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 (hepatorenal tyrosinemia):

• An acute hepatic crisis commonly heralds the onset of disease, which may progress to liver failure, hepatocellular carcinoma, and death.

• Episodes of acute peripheral neuropathy resembling porphyrias often triggered by a minor infection, such crisis can be associated with paralytic ileus

• Renal involvement, which is manifested as a Fanconi-like syndrome with hyperphosphaturia, hypophosphatemia, normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, and vitamin D–resistant rickets

The treatment of choice for HT Type 1 is nitisinone, which blocks early steps in the tyrosine degradation pathway and limits the formation of toxic tyrosine metabolites.

Note:

Boiled cabbage odor can also be found in cases of Hypermethioninemia.

questions.question: A 2-year-old girl presented with photophobia and speech delay. On examination, she had bilateral herpetiform corneal ulcers and painful hyperkeratotic plaques on the palms and soles. Which among the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Palmar and plantar hyperkeratosis, herpetiform corneal ulcers, and intellectual disability are seen in hereditary tyrosinemia type 2 (Richner–Hanhart syndrome/ oculocutaneous tyrosinemia)

Treatment with a diet low in tyrosine and phenylalanine aiming to achieve plasma tyrosine levels <500 µmol/L improves skin and eye manifestations.

The image below shows herpetiform corneal ulcer:

questions.question: A child who was being evaluated for hypertyrosinemia is diagnosed with Richner-Hanhart syndrome. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is the likely cause of hypertyrosinemia in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Oculocutaneous tyrosinemia/Richner-Hanhart syndrome (type II) is caused by the deficiency of tyrosine aminotransferase.

It is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by palmar and plantar hyperkeratosis, herpetiform corneal ulcers, and intellectual disability.Untreated patients have marked hypertyrosinemia. In contrast to tyrosinemia type I, liver and kidney function are normal, as are serum concentrations of other amino acids and succinylacetone.

questions.question: A 15-month-old baby who presented with seizures and self-injurious behavior has increased plasma tyrosine levels. Urine metabolic screening reveals the presence of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid and its metabolites 4-hydroxyphenyllactic and 4-hydroxyphenyl acetic acids. Which of the following in-born errors of metabolism is the child suffering from?
questions.explanation:
Primary deficiency of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (4-HPPD) causes hereditary tyrosinemia type 3. The diagnosis is suspected in children with sustained moderate increases in plasma levels of tyrosine (typically 350-700 µmol/L on a normal diet) and the presence of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid and its metabolites 4-hydroxyphenyllactic and 4-hydroxyphenylacetic acids in urine.

Asymptomatic infants with 4-HPPD deficiency have been identified by neonatal screening for hypertyrosinemia. In symptomatic patients, developmental delay, seizures, intermittent ataxia, and self-injurious behavior have been reported. Liver and renal abnormalities are absent.

Note:

Transient tyrosinemia of the newborn is the most common acquired cause for increased plasma tyrosine levels. Seen in premature infants receiving a high protein diet and due to the immaturity of 4-HPPD enzyme. Mostly asymptomatic, but sometimes manifested by lethargy, poor feeding, and decreased motor activity. Hypertyrosinemia usually resolves
spontaneously in the first 2 months of life. Treatment includes a low protein diet and vitamin C.

questions.question: A 4-month-old infant who was started on a high-protein diet after weaning from breastfeeding developed severe metabolic acidosis, ketosis, failure to thrive, mild hepatomegaly, and an unusual swimming pool odor. A history of similar illness was noticed in his siblings and his father. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The clinical vignette and the characteristic swimming pool odor describe Hawkinsinuria.

Hawkinsinuria is an autosomal-dominant condition caused by mutations in the gene for 4-HPPD.

In infants, this disease causes severe metabolic acidosis, ketosis, failure to thrive, mild hepatomegaly, and swimming pool odor. Mental development is usually normal. Affected individuals excrete hawkinsin (4-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid), and its metabolites.

Treatment consists of a low-protein diet during infancy. Breastfeeding is encouraged. A trial with large doses of vitamin C (up to 1,000 mg/24 hour) is also recommended.

questions.question: The following findings in an 18-year-old are characterized by a deficiency of _________
questions.explanation:
The following condition is characterized by the deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase.

The image represents ochronosis: Bluish-black pigmentation of the ear cartilage and/or sclera due to deposits of accumulated homogentisic acid.

This is characteristically seen in alkaptonuria. It is a rare autosomal-recessive disorder is caused by the deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase. Large amounts of homogentisic acid are formed, which are excreted in urine or deposited in tissues. Clinical manifestations of alkaptonuria consist of ochronosis and arthritis in adulthood. Arthritis predominantly involves the spine, hip, and knee. Radiologically, it is characterized by intervertebral calcifications. In children, blackening of the urine on standing is observed; it is caused by the oxidation and polymerization of homogentisic acid.

questions.question: A patient presented to the OPD with complaints of pigmentation of the face and severe backache and stiffness. The X-Ray image of the spine is as shown. Her urine color changes to brownish-black on standing. Which of the following drugs can be used in her treatment?
questions.explanation:
The clinical image shows the accumulation of alkapton bodies in connective tissues on the face and urine turning brownish-black on standing are associated with alkaptonuria. X-ray shows calcification of intervertebral discs called ochronotic spondyloarthropathy also seen in alkaptonuria. Nitisinone can be used in the treatment of alkaptonuria.

Nitisinone, formerly known as NTBC, inhibits 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPPD) (early step in the tyrosine degradation pathway) and efficiently reduces homogentisic acid production in alkaptonuria. Treatment of arthritis is symptomatic. In presymptomatic individuals, treatment using a combination of nitisinone with phenylalanine and a tyrosine restricted diet can be tried.

The patient’s urine contains elevated levels of homogentisic acid, which is oxidized to a dark pigment on standing as shown below in the image:

questions.question:
A 10-year-old boy presented with right-sided weakness and deviation of angle of mouth to the left is diagnosed to have a metabolic disorder. Diffusion-weighted MRI reveals diffusion restriction along the left middle cerebral artery. Which of the following defects can be responsible for the boy's condition?

1. Cystathionine β-Synthase deficiency

2. Defects in methylcobalamin formation

3. Deficiency of methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase

4. Pyridoxine deficiency

5. Vitamin C deficiency
questions.explanation:
The clinical vignette describes a thrombotic stroke in the left MCA territory. Elevated levels of serum homocysteine lead to a hypercoagulable state.

Homocystinuria is caused by the following:

• Cystathionine β-Synthase deficiency: This is classic homocystinuria. The most common inborn error of methionine metabolism.

• Defects in methylcobalamin formation: Methylcobalamin is the cofactor for the enzyme methionine synthase, which catalyzes the remethylation of homocysteine to methionine.

• Deficiency of methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase: This enzyme reduces 5,10 methylenetetrahydrofolate to form 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, which provides the methyl group needed for remethylation of homocysteine to methionine.

• Pyridoxine deficiency: B6 is the co-factor for the enzyme cystathionine β-synthase

Metabolic disorders which can cause stroke include:

• Homocystinuria

• MELAS (metabolic encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes)

• Leigh syndrome

• Fabry's disease

• Propionic acidemia

• Glutaric aciduria

 Vitamin C deficiency increases the risk of hemorrhagic stroke.

questions.question: An 8-month-old boy presented with lethargy, failure to thrive, and developmental delay. On investigation, he had elevated levels of homocysteine in blood and homocystinuria. As the child grows, which of the following features is least likely to develop?
questions.explanation:
The above findings support a diagnosis of homocystinuria. Short stature is not a manifestation of homocystinuria.

Manifestations of homocystinuria:

• Ectopia lentis - downward and inward subluxation (inferonasal).

• Intellectual disability and psychiatric and behavioral disorders

• Thromboembolic episodes like stroke and MI

• Skeletal abnormalities resembling those of Marfan syndrome: They are tall and thin, (NOT short) with elongated limbs and arachnodactyly.

questions.question: A 16-year-old boy with frequent episodes of photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhea, and depression is diagnosed to have a metabolic disorder. Metabolism of which of the following amino acids is affected?
questions.explanation:
Pellagra-like symptoms- photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhea, and episodic depression are seen in the deficiency of tryptophan.

Niacin is not strictly a vitamin, since it can be synthesized in the body from the essential amino acid tryptophan; deficiency of tryptophan causes pellagra-like symptoms.

Treatment with nicotinic acid or nicotinamide (50-300 mg/24 hr) and a high protein diet results in a favorable response in symptomatic patients with Hartnup disease.

The image below shows Casal's necklace, a lesion seen around the neck which is caused due to the deficiency of niacin or nicotinic acid.

questions.question: Which of the following is false regarding Hartnup disease?
options: Defect in the transport of monoamino-monocarboxylic amino acids, including tryptophan, is seen
Defect in the B0AT1 protein occurs in the intestine and renal tubules
Pellagra-like rash may develop in symptomatic patients
Treatment is with supplementation of tryptophan
questions.answer: D. Treatment is with supplementation of tryptophan
questions.explanation:
The treatment of Hartnup disease is not with the supplementation of tryptophan.

Hartnup disease

• It is caused by a defect in the transport of monoamino-monocarboxylic (neutral) amino acids, including tryptophan, by the intestinal mucosa and renal tubules.

• There is a defect in B0AT1 protein in the intestine/ renal tubules or both, which is caused by a mutation in SLC6A19.

• Tryptophan is an essential amino acid and a precursor for nicotinic acid (niacin) and serotonin. Decreased intestinal absorption of tryptophan in conjunction with its increased renal loss causes reduced availability of tryptophan for niacin synthesis in affected individuals.

• A pellagra-like rash may develop in symptomatic patients, and some patients may have intermittent ataxia.

• Diagnosis is based on aminoaciduria and increased excretion of indole compounds detected by Obermeyer test.

• Treatment is with nicotinic acid or nicotinamide and a high-protein diet.

questions.question: An infant with poor feeding is suspected to have an inborn error of metabolism. Further evaluation reveals hyperammonemia +, acidosis +, ketosis +. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
In this case, hyperammonemia +, acidosis +, ketosis +. This is seen in organic aciduria.

Organic acidemias most commonly present in infancy with poor feeding, vomiting, hypotonia, high anion gap metabolic acidosis, hepatomegaly, seizures. Organic acid accumulation inhibits gluconeogenesis and inhibits the urea cycle leading to hyperammonemia.

Common organic acidurias:

• Methylmalonic aciduria

• Propionic aciduria

• Isovaleric aciduria

• Maple syrup urine disease

• Glutaric aciduria type I

• Multiple carboxylase deficiency

questions.question: A 10-day-old male infant presented with poor feeding, and recurrent generalized convulsions. On examination, the pediatrician notices repetitive movements of the extremities –appears to be boxing and bicycling and a peculiar burnt sugar odor was present in urine. What is the deficient enzyme in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The diagnosis is maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) which is due to deficiency of branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKDH).

Leucine, isoleucine, and valine are the 3 essential amino acids, which are branched-chain amino acids. Their decarboxylation is accomplished by BCKDH using thiamine (vitamin B1) pyrophosphate as a coenzyme.

Leucine is metabolized by BCAA aminotransferase to α-ketoisocaproic acid, which leads to the disrupted metabolism of neurotransmitters and amino acids (glutamate, GABA, glutamine, alanine, and aspartate). α-Ketoisocaproic acid can reversibly inhibit oxidative phosphorylation and result in cerebral lactic acidosis. Collectively, these processes are detrimental to the normal function of neurons and glia, clinically manifesting as encephalopathy and brain edema and referred to as leucinosis.

Treatment options include hemodialysis, restricting dietary substances, thiamine for milder forms, and orthotopic liver transplant.

questions.question: While doing your morning rounds in the pediatrics department, you notice a peculiar rancid cheese odor emanating from a six-month-old girl who was admitted for respiratory distress. Second-degree consanguinity was documented between the parents. Urine organic acid analysis by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry showed marked excretion of 3-hydroxybutyric acid along with moderate excretion of 3- hydroxy-isovaleric acid. What is the most likely condition is she suffering from?
questions.explanation:
The clinical vignette suggests a diagnosis of isovaleric acidemia. Sweaty-feet odor or rancid cheese odor may be present.

Isovaleric acidemia is caused by the deficiency of the enzyme isovaleryl CoA dehydrogenase, which affects the breakdown pathway of leucine leading to the accumulation of intermediates.

questions.question: A mother brings her 3-year-old boy with the complaints that her child's urine smells like her tomcat's urine. She also gives a history of generalized seizures and perioral desquamating lesions. On examination, the child has global developmental delay and diffuse thinning of the scalp. Investigations reveal multiple carboxylase deficiency. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation:
Biotin is the treatment of choice for multiple carboxylase deficiency.

Multiple carboxylase deficiency refers to one of two inherited defects of biotin metabolism. Tomcat urine is characteristically seen in multiple carboxylase deficiency.

• Neonatal/infantile form is caused by a deficiency of holocarboxylase synthetase and presents in the first week of life with lethargy, poor muscle tone, and vomiting.

• Juvenile/late form is caused by biotinidase deficiency and is associated with a slow but progressive loss of biotin in the urine, leading to organic aciduria. It is characterized by alopecia, ataxia, ketoacidosis, dermatitis, seizures, myoclonus, and nystagmus.

Both infantile and late-onset multiple carboxylase deficiency can be treated with pharmacological doses of biotin.

It is called multiple carboxylase deficiency because biotin is a water-soluble vitamin that is a cofactor for all 4 carboxylase enzymes in humans:

• Pyruvate carboxylase

• Acetyl CoA carboxylase

• Propionyl CoA carboxylase

• 3-methylcrotonyl CoA carboxylase

Note:

Acquired deficiency of biotin may occur in infants receiving total parenteral nutrition without added biotin, in patients with prolonged use of antiepileptic drugs (phenobarbital, phenytoin, primidone, carbamazepine), and in children with short bowel syndrome or chronic diarrhea who are receiving formulas low in biotin. Excessive ingestion of raw eggs may also cause biotin deficiency because the protein avidin in egg white binds biotin, decreasing its absorption. Infants with a biotin deficiency may develop dermatitis, alopecia, and candidal skin infections. This condition readily responds to treatment with oral biotin.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common acquired cause of increased plasma tyrosine levels?
questions.answer: D. Transient tyrosinemia of the newborn
questions.explanation:
Transient tyrosinemia of the newborn is the most common acquired cause for increased plasma tyrosine levels. Seen in premature infants receiving a high protein diet and due to the immaturity of 4-HPPD enzyme. Mostly asymptomatic, but sometimes manifested by lethargy, poor feeding, and decreased motor activity. Treatment includes low protein diet and vitamin C.

Options A and B, i.e., hepatorenal tyrosinemia and oculocutaneous tyrosinemia, are hereditary causes of increased tyrosine levels.

Option C: Tyrosine levels are normal in alkaptonuria.

questions.question: Richner-Hanhart syndrome is _____.
questions.explanation:
Richner–Hanhart syndrome is hereditary tyrosinemia type 2 (oculocutaneous tyrosinemia).

• It is a rare autosomal-recessive disorder is caused by the deficiency of tyrosine aminotransferase.

• It is characterized by ocular manifestations, skin lesions, and mild to moderate intellectual disability in ~50% of the patients.

• It is diagnosed by an assay of plasma tyrosine concentration.

• Treatment includes a diet low in tyrosine and phenylalanine.

questions.question: In phenylketonuria, which of the following phenyl ketones is excreted in urine?
questions.explanation:
In phenylketonuria, phenylpyruvate is excreted in the urine.

In phenylketonuria (PKU), excess phenylalanine in the blood is metabolized to phenyl ketones, namely, phenylpyruvate and phenylacetate, which are excreted in the urine, giving rise to the term phenylketonuria (PKU).

Acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate are keto-acids but are not phenyl ketones. These are not excreted in phenylketonuria.

questions.question: A 2-month-old infant presented with abdominal distention and increased irritability for 10 days. Physical examination showed jaundice, hepatomegaly, and a boiled cabbage odor. Which among the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The clinical vignette is in favor of tyrosinemia. Boiled cabbage odor may be present in tyrosinemia resulting from increased methionine metabolites (sulfur-containing compounds).

Note:

Boiled cabbage odor can also be found in cases of Hypermethioninemia.

questions.question: A neonate born out of a second-degree consanguineous marriage is suspected to have an inborn error of metabolism. He can present with all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Irritability and incessant crying are not classical features of inborn errors of metabolism (IEM).

Clinical clues suggesting IEM in a neonate are:

• Unexpected deterioration after a normal initial period.

• Nonspecific, unexplained features such as poor feeding, lethargy, vomiting, hypotonia, failure to thrive, respiratory abnormalities, apnea, bradycardia, and hypothermia.

• Family history of similar illnesses, unexplained sibling deaths, or progressive neurological disease.

• Parental consanguinity: Most acutely presenting metabolic disorders are autosomal recessive.

questions.question: A worried mother brings her 2-year-old child with the complaints that he hasn't begun walking or talking. On examination, there is microcephaly, fair hair, light-colored skin, and blue eyes. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical manifestations point to the diagnosis of Phenylketonuria (PKU).

Characteristic clinical findings in Phenylketonuria:

• Mental retardation

• Failure to walk or talk

• Seizures

• Hyperactivity

• Tremor

• Microcephaly

• Failure to grow

• Deficiency of pigmentation (fair hair, light skin color, and blue eyes)

Oculocutaneous albinism (OCA) is a group of inherited disorders characterized by a reduction or complete lack of melanin pigment in the skin, hair, and eyes.

Its symptoms are albinism with vision problems, which include:

• Strabismus

• Photophobia

• Nystagmus

• Impaired vision or blindness

• Astigmatism

Neuropsychiatric manifestations are not seen.

chapters.chapter: Metabolic Disorders Of Urea Cycle, Complex Molecules, And Carbohydrates

questions.question: A 3-day-old child is suspected to have an inborn error of metabolism. Further evaluation reveals elevated blood ammonia in the presence of normal blood pH and bicarbonate levels. There are no ketone bodies in the urine. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In this case, hyperammonemia is +ve; acidosis is -ve; and ketosis is -ve: This is consistent with the urea cycle defect.

questions.question: A young infant started seizing in his cradle. He was immediately rushed to the casualty. On investigation, blood ammonia was markedly elevated. Which of the following is used to lower the ammonia levels?
questions.explanation:
All of the above agents are used in the treatment of acute hyperammonemia in an infant.

Treatment of acute hyperammonemia in an infant:

• Provide adequate calories, fluid, and electrolytes intravenously.

• Minimal amounts of protein as a mixture of essential amino acids during the first 24 hours of therapy.

• Give priming doses of the following compounds: Sodium benzoate, Sodium phenylacetate, Arginine hydrochloride.

• Initiate peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis if the above treatment fails to produce an appreciable decrease in plasma ammonia levels.

Benzoate forms hippurate with endogenous glycine in the liver. Each mole of benzoate removes 1 mole of ammonia as glycine.

 Phenylacetate conjugates with glutamine to form phenylacetylglutamine, which is readily excreted in the urine. One mole of phenylacetate removes 2 moles of ammonia as glutamine from the body.

Arginine administration supplies the urea cycle with ornithine. It is effective in all patients, except those with arginase deficiency.

Note:

Phenylbutyrate which is metabolized to phenylacetate in our body can also be used as it scavenges nitrogen.

questions.question: An infant's mother is distressed that her baby refuses her feeds and starts vomiting immediately when fed and becomes lethargic. After thorough investigations, the baby is diagnosed with HHH syndrome. Which of the following is least likely to be found?
questions.explanation:
Hyperuricemia is not a component of HHH syndrome

HHH syndrome is a rare autosomal-recessive disorder caused by a defect in the transport system of ornithine from the cytosol into the mitochondria (deficiency of ornithine permease/translocase), resulting in the accumulation of ornithine in the cytosol leading to hyperornithinemia and a deficiency of this amino acid in mitochondria results in the disruption of the urea cycle and hyperammonemia. Homocitrulline is formed from the reaction of mitochondrial carbamyl phosphate with lysine, which can become a substrate for the OTC reaction when ornithine is deficient.

Components of HHH syndrome:

• Hyperammonemia

• Hyperornithinemia

• Homocitrullinemia

questions.question: As a geneticist studying the familial inheritance of porphyrias, which of the following is likely to show the inheritance pattern given below?
questions.explanation:
The given pedigree chart shows X-linked dominant inheritance. X-linked protoporphyria is inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern.

All porphyrias are autosomal dominant except the following :

• Congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP) (autosomal recessive)

• δ-Aminolevulinic acid dehydratase porphyria (ADP) (autosomal recessive)

• Protoporphyria - X-linked protoporphyria (X-linked dominant)

• Erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) (autosomal recessive)

questions.question: The most common porphyria which manifests in childhood is ______
questions.explanation:
Erythropoietic protoporphyria (autosomal recessive) is the most common porphyria to manifest in childhood.

Porphyria cutanea tarda (option A) manifests in adults.

Congenital erythropoietic porphyria (option B) also known as Günther disease presents itself in utero or in infancy. It is a rare autosomal-recessive disease.

Hereditary coproporphyria (option D) presents itself in the post-pubertal age.

questions.question: Which of the following is also known as plumboporphyria due to its clinical similarity to lead poisoning?
questions.explanation:
δ-Aminolevulinic acid dehydratase porphyria (ALAD) is also called plumboporphyria/Doss porphyria due to its clinical similarity to lead poisoning, although it is not related to lead exposure.

ALAD catalyzes the condensation of 2 molecules of ALA to form the pyrrole porphobilinogen (PBG). The enzyme is subject to inhibition by lead because ALAD is the principal lead-binding protein in erythrocytes, and lead can displace the zinc atoms of the enzyme, thus inhibiting it. Therefore, both lead poisoning and ALAD porphyria produce similar signs and symptoms. Symptoms resemble those of other acute porphyrias, including acute attacks of abdominal pain and neuropathy.

questions.question: A 16-year-old girl was admitted for severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. She developed generalized seizures in the hospital for which she was given phenytoin. Her symptoms worsened, she developed muscle weakness which progressed to quadriparesis. Urinary porphobilinogen was found to be high. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is acute intermittent porphyria which presents as a neurovisceral syndrome with no cutaneous manifestations and no phototoxicity.

Acute Intermittent Porphyria:

• Autosomal dominant

• Deficiency of the enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase

• Presents at post-pubertal age

• Present with hepatic and neurologic manifestations

• Exacerbated by P450 inducing drugs like phenytoin, progesterone and dietary restriction

questions.question: You are reading an article titled, ' Dark age vampires or our patients', which describes an 18-year-old man who has had an intolerance to sunshine since the age of 6. When playing cricket he suffered intense burning, redness, swelling, and crusting of knees unprotected by shorts, with similar changes on cheeks and bridge of the nose. His labs showed elevated concentrations of total erythrocyte protoporphyrin. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies can explain this boy's condition?
questions.explanation:
Symptoms of cutaneous photosensitivity beginning in childhood and a substantially elevated concentration of total erythrocyte protoporphyrin supports a diagnosis of erythropoietic protoporphyria. The enzyme deficient in erythropoietic protoporphyria is ferrochelatase (FECH).

Symptoms consist of acute pain and itching often occurring within minutes of sunlight exposure and followed by redness and swelling with continued exposure. Swelling may resemble angioneurotic edema and solar urticaria. Symptoms are usually worse in the spring and summer. Chronic changes may include lichenification, leathery pseudovesicles, labial grooving, and nail changes, but changes in pigmentation and pronounced scarring are unusual.

Life-threatening protoporphyric hepatopathy is characterized by greater increases in erythrocyte and plasma protoporphyrin levels, increased photosensitivity, and either chronically abnormal liver function tests or rapidly progressive hepatic failure.

questions.question: A 6-month-old baby boy has coarse facial features, cloudy corneas, and gingival hypertrophy. He has no neck control and is unable to roll over. Laboratory investigations reveal markedly reduced activity of N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase activity in WBCs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This clinical vignette is strongly suggestive of I-cell disease or inclusion cell disease. It is also known as type II Mucolipidosis.

It is an autosomal recessive inherited as a lysosomal storage disorder. It is caused due to a defect in N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase required for the Golgi to phosphorylate mannose residues on glycoproteins. This leads to defective mannose-6-phosphate, an important cell signaling molecule required for trafficking of the lysosomal enzyme from the site of its production in the endoplasmic reticulum to the lysosome. Due to this defect, the lysosomal enzymes are secreted out of the cell and there is an increased serum concentration of the same. Intracellularly, there are abnormal inclusion bodies and vacuolizations, thus earning the disease its name.

Clinically, these patients present with symptoms either at birth or early in life with growth retardation, failure to thrive, delay of developmental milestones, coarse facial features with a cloudy cornea and gingival hypertrophy, and other non-specific findings such as hip dislocations, inguinal hernias, hepatomegaly, joint limitation, and skin changes.

Investigations to establish a diagnosis may include measuring N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase activity in WBCs or in cultured fibroblasts and estimating serum levels of lysosomal enzymes.

Option B: Galactosemia is caused due to the complete absence of galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase. The deficiency of this enzyme leads to an inability to convert galactose-1-phosphate (galactose-1-P) to uridine diphosphate galactose. It is characterized by typical clinical features such as jaundice, vomiting, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, poor feeding, lethargy, diarrhea, E.Coli sepsis. Infants may also have edema, ascites, full fontanelle, encephalopathy, and excessive bruising and bleeding. They tend to develop cataracts due to the accumulation of galactitol.

Option C: Adrenoleukodystrophy is an X-linked recessive disorder of β-oxidation of fatty acids. There is a very large chain fatty acids buildup in the adrenal glands, the white matter of the brain, and testes. It is a progressive disease that can lead to adrenal gland crisis, coma, and death.

Option D: Hurler syndrome is an important diagnosis in a patient presenting with clinical features given in this clinical vignette. But it is a mucopolysaccharidosis type 1-H caused due by the defect in the α-L Iduronidase leading to the accumulation of heparin sulfate and dermatan sulfate. It is characterized by skeletal abnormalities, hepatosplenomegaly, and severe intellectual disability. Infants develop characteristic coarse facial features, a wide nasal bridge, and a flattened midface. Features such as hepatosplenomegaly, umbilical or inguinal hernias, and typical skeletal abnormalities, known as dysostosis multiplex laos are also seen. They also have developmental delays and recurrent sinopulmonary diseases. Failure to thrive and growth restriction are also seen.

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy is brought with complaints of severe pain in his right thigh which has progressively worsened over the last few months. He is unable to walk because of the same. His mother also says he has had repeated nose bleeds in the last few months and the child has stopped playing with his friends as he gets easily tired for a month. Physical examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly. Lab reports show thrombocytopenia and anemia. An assay of peripheral blood leucocytes shows low levels of beta-glucosidase. What is the inheritance pattern of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of bone pain, epistaxis, hepatosplenomegaly, and low levels of β-glucosidase suggests a diagnosis of Gaucher's disease that is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

Gaucher's disease:

• It is an inborn error of metabolism due to the deficiency of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase (β-glucosidase) that leads to the accumulation of glucocerebroside in the lysosomes of cells.

• It is the most common lysosomal storage disorder.

• The clinical features result from the accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the spleen, liver, bone marrow, bone, and other tissues.

• There are 3 clinical subtypes, delineated by the absence or presence and progression of neurologic manifestations: type 1, or the adult, nonneuronopathic form; type 2, the infantile or acute neuronopathic form; and type 3, the juvenile or subacute neuronopathic form

• Typical clinical features include delayed puberty, painless hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, liver cirrhosis, hypersplenism and pancytopenia, bleeding tendencies, bone pain due to avascular necrosis, osteoporosis, pathological fractures.

• Neurological symptoms such as developmental delay, hypertonia, strabismus, supranuclear gaze palsy (seen in type 3).

• Bone marrow examination usually reveals the presence of Gaucher cells (have a characteristic wrinkled-paper appearance)

• Enzyme replacement therapy for Gaucher's disease: imiglucerase, velaglucerase alfa, taliglucerase alfa,eliglustat

questions.question: A 6-month-old infant with progressive failure to thrive and milestone regression is being evaluated for an inborn error of metabolism. On examination, hypotonia, apathy, deafness, hepatosplenomegaly, and generalized lymphadenopathy are present. Fundus examination is shown below. A liver biopsy shows foamy hepatocytes loaded with sphingomyelin. Electron microscopy reveals zebra bodies. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The clinical vignette along with the cherry-red spot on fundus examination suggests a diagnosis of Niemann-Pick disease type A- Lysosomal storage disorder due to an inherited deficiency of sphingomyelinase

Type A is a severe infantile form with extensive neurologic involvement (hypotonia, milestone regression, apathy), marked visceral accumulations of sphingomyelin (hepatosplenomegaly, foamy hepatocytes, zebra bodies on EM), and progressive wasting and early death within the first 3 years of life.

In contrast, patients with Niemann-Pick disease type B have organomegaly but generally no CNS involvement.

questions.question: A case series reviews children with lysosomal storage disorders who usually present with dysmorphic facies, organomegaly, milestones regression, and failure to thrive. Which of the following disorders does not have enzyme replacement therapy as a therapeutic option?
questions.explanation: Enzyme replacement therapy is not available for Sanfilippo syndrome (MPS type III).

questions.question: A 3-month-old female child was brought to the clinic with a history of failure to thrive. On examination, generalized hypotonia and hepatomegaly were present. A chest X-ray image shows massive cardiomegaly. A muscle biopsy is performed and the findings are attached in the image below. Which of the following is the most likely enzyme that is involved in the suspected condition?
questions.explanation:
The muscle biopsy shows the presence of large vacuoles. This along with the clinical vignette is strongly suggestive of Pompe's disease or type II glycogen storage disease. It is caused due to the deficiency of the enzyme lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase.

Clinically, the child presents with hypotonia, hepatomegaly, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The affected child usually dies around the age of 2 years due to heart failure.

Investigations include chest X-ray imaging which shows cardiomegaly. The muscle biopsy showing vacuoles further aids the diagnosis.

Treatment includes enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant enzyme a-glucosidase alfa (Myozyme).

questions.question: A 6-month-old is brought by his parents with a history of decreased weight gain. On examination, you find that the baby has hepatosplenomegaly, muscle weakness and atrophy, hypotonia, and decreased deep tendon reflexes. Blood tests reveal normal glucose levels. Biopsy of the liver reveals initial stages of cirrhosis due to the accumulation of abnormal glycogen with few branch points, whose structure resembles amylopectin. The clinical and laboratory results are indicative of which glycogen storage disease?
questions.explanation:
The clinical and laboratory features indicate Andersen's disease in the baby. Inability to gain weight, hepatosplenomegaly, muscle weakness, and accumulation of abnormal glycogen resembling amylopectin point towards the diagnosis.

Andersen's disease is type IV glycogen storage disease. It is transmitted in an autosomal recessive pattern and occurs due to a deficiency of glycogen branching enzyme because of pathologic variants in the GBE1 gene. This leads to accumulation of of an abnormal structure of glycogen known as polyglucosan. It is characterized by

• Growth delay

• Hepatomegaly due to the accumulation of polysaccharides with few branch points

• Myopathy

• There might be fasting intolerance and ketosis in the initial stages. Hypoglycemia usually appears late in the disease when it is associated with cirrhosis, esophageal varices, and ascites.

• Biopsy of the liver will show the presence of abnormal glycogen which resembles amylopectin. Amylopectin is found in plants and has very few branches. Since there is a defect in the branching of the glycogen, the abnormal glycogen appears like amylopectin.

The diagnosis is confirmed by absent branching enzyme activity in skin fibroblasts, muscle, or liver and analysis of the DNA mutation.

Von Gierke's disease (Option A) has features of lactic acidosis, hypoglycemia, hyperuricemia, impaired growth, and bone thinning. It occurs due to a defect in the glucose 6-phosphatase.

McArdle disease (Option C) usually manifests as exercise intolerance, muscle cramping with exercise. It is usually a benign chronic condition. It occurs due to a defect in the muscle glycogen phosphorylase.

Tarui disease (Option D) also presents similar to the McArdle disease. Patients may have developmental delay, and hemolytic anemia in addition to exercise-induced muscle cramps. It occurs due to a defect in the muscle phosphofructokinase.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy develops hypoglycemia and muscle weakness with moderate activity. On examination, he had hepatomegaly and growth restriction. Investigations revealed the accumulation of limit dextrins and increased glycogen deposits in the liver. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is Cori disease.

Glycogen debrancher deficiency (Glycogen Storage Disease III) is also known as Cori disease, Forbes disease, and limit dextrinosis.

Cori’s disease may be clinically indistinguishable from von Gierke’s disease in infancy and childhood as hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, hyperlipidemia, and growth retardation is common. Accumulation of limit dextrins is unique to Cori's disease. Definitive diagnosis is through enzyme assays in the liver, muscle, or both.

questions.question:
A 5-day-old neonate is brought to the emergency room with vomiting and poor feeding. Breastfeeding was initiated soon after birth. On examination, the child is lethargic and has hepatomegaly. Labs reveal increased plasma galactose and increased urine galactitol levels. Examination of the mother shows the presence of skin lesions on the breast with the histopathological appearance showing characteristic 'Cowdry Type A' inclusions as shown below. Choose the correct statements from those below:

1. The child's condition is an absolute contraindication to breastfeeding

2. The mother's condition is an absolute contraindication to breastfeeding

3. The child is prone to E.coli sepsis

4. The child is prone to sepsis caused by S. aureus

5. The mother has a risk of recurrence of her condition
questions.explanation:
The given clinical complex describes a case of classic galactosemia in the infant (increased plasma galactose and urine galactitol levels) and herpes simplex of the breast in the mother (histopathology shown in the image has large multinucleate virus-infected cells with typical eosinophilic Cowdry Type A inclusions).

Galactosemia is an absolute contraindication to breastfeeding and the child is at risk for E.coli sepsis. Herpes lesions on the breast are a relative contraindication to breastfeeding and she is at risk for recurrence.

 Deficiency of galactose-1-uridyltransferase leads to the accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate and galactitol causes classic galactosemia.

Infants show vomiting, diarrhea, and poor weight gain within 3-4 days of breastfeeding.Jaundice and liver dysfunction appear in the first or second week of life. Untreated children may show nuclear cataracts (oil-droplet cataract), vitreous hemorrhage, hepatic failure, cirrhosis, ascites, splenomegaly, or intellectual disability. The proximal renal tubular disease may also manifest as metabolic acidosis, galactosuria, glucosuria, and aminoaciduria. The most common cause of death is E.coli sepsis.Acute galactose toxicity is manifested by neurological symptoms

Diagnosis is made by genetic or mutational analysis. There will the presence of reducing substances in the urine. Elimination of galactose from the diet along with adequate calcium supplementation reverses growth failure and renal and hepatic dysfunction.

questions.question: A father has noticed that whenever his daughter drinks fruit juice she has multiple episodes of vomiting. He reports to you that his daughter is allergic to fruit juice. Which of the following enzyme deficiency is likely?
questions.explanation:
Aldolase B deficiency is likely in this child.

In the given case scenario, the child becomes symptomatic after ingesting fruit juice that contains fructose; this indicates that she has hereditary fructose intolerance, which is caused by the deficiency of aldolase B.

Deficiency of fructose-1,6- bisphosphate aldolase (Aldolase B hereditary fructose intolerance): Fructose aldolase B is present in the liver, kidney, and intestine. It catalyzes the hydrolysis of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into triose phosphate and glyceraldehyde phosphate.

Clinical features: Patients are asymptomatic until fructose or sucrose is ingested (usually from fruit, fruit juice, sweetened cereal, or table sugar). Clinical features include jaundice, hepatomegaly, vomiting, lethargy, irritability, and convulsions. It resembles galactosemia. Acute ingestion causes symptomatic hypoglycemia. Chronic intake results in failure to thrive and hepatic disease. The persistence of fructose intake can lead to liver failure, kidney failure, and death.

Diagnosis: Reducing substance is seen in the urine during an episode (Benedict's test +). An assay of fructaldolase B activity in the liver gives a definitive diagnosis.

Treatment: Complete elimination of all sources of sucrose, fructose, and sorbitol from the diet. With age, symptoms become milder even after fructose ingestion. The long-term prognosis is good.

Note:

The deficiency of fructokinase is not associated with any clinical manifestations. Fructosuria is an accidental finding usually made because the asymptomatic patient's urine contains a reducing substance. No treatment is necessary, and the prognosis is excellent.

questions.question: "Tomcat urine" is characteristically seen in ________
questions.explanation:
Tomcat urine is characteristically seen in multiple carboxylase deficiency.

It is named so because of its peculiar odour.

questions.question: The enzyme deficient in hereditary coproporphyria is ________
questions.explanation:
The enzyme deficient in hereditary coproporphyria is coproporphyrinogen oxidase (CPOX).

Hereditary coproporphyria (HCP):

• Autosomal-dominant hepatic porphyria is caused by the deficiency of CPOX.

• Acute attacks of HCP are treated as in acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), which includes intravenous hemin and identifying and avoiding precipitating factors. Cholestyramine may be of some value for photosensitivity occurring with liver dysfunction.

• Gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogs can be effective for the prevention of cyclic attacks.

questions.question: Deficiency of the enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase causes _____________
questions.explanation:
Deficiency of the enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase causes acute intermittent porphyria.

Other options:

• Porphyria cutanea tarda: Deficiency of Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD)

• Variegate porphyria: Deficiency of Protoporphyrinogen oxidase (PPOX)

• X-Linked protoporphyria: Gain of function mutation of δ-aminolevulinate synthase 2 (ALAS2)

questions.question: A mother who is a hairstylist has noted that her baby's hair looks dull, breaks off easily, and is tufted. She brings the child to you and informs you about the past history of seizures. Investigations reveal elevated plasma ammonia levels and argininosuccinate levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is argininosuccinic aciduria due to argininosuccinate lyase deficiency.

It is accompanied by high levels of argininosuccinate levels in blood, CSF, and urine. It is also associated with friable, tufted hair known as trichorrhexis nodosa.

Image showing Trichorrhexis nodosa:

questions.question: Accumulation of ______ takes place in Farber’s disease.
questions.explanation:
Accumulation of Ceramide is seen in Farber’s disease due to ceramidase deficiency.

 Clinical features of Farber’s disease :

• Painful joint swelling, nodules, progressive joint deformity

• Hoarse cry

• Breathing difficulty

• Failure to thrive

questions.question: A child is found to have paralysis due to poliovirus infection. Which of the following is false regarding the paralysis seen?
options: It is an upper motor neuron type
Strenuous physical exercise during the onset exaggerates the paralysis
It can be caused by polio vaccination
questions.answer: A. It is an upper motor neuron type
questions.explanation:
Poliovirus mainly affects the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord and medulla oblongata (cranial nerve nuclei), causing lower motor neuron (LMN) type of paralysis. It damages motor and autonomic nerves; sensory nerves are not involved.

Poliovirus is a non-enveloped, positive-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Picornaviridae family. Three antigenically distinct serotypes (types 1, 2, and 3) are known. Ages 6 months to 5 years are most commonly affected. The virus is transmitted via the fecal-oral route and has an incubation period of 8-12 days. Humans are the only known reservoir for the polioviruses.

The virus colonizes and replicates in the GI mucosa (M cells), followed by entry into the blood via regional lymph nodes. In blood, it causes viremia and gets access to the CNS via the peripheral nerves, finally reaching the anterior horn cells in the spinal cord.

Most cases are subclinical. Some have minor illnesses like fever, sore throat, headache, and malaise. It can present as non-paralytic polio (aseptic meningitis) or paralytic polio (flaccid paralysis with absent deep tendon reflexes). Most frequently, the completely affected muscle is the tibialis anterior. It is asymmetric paralysis which is more severe if strenuous physical exercise occurred during the onset of paralysis. Death usually occurs due to respiratory paralysis.

Vaccination schedule for polio:

• Live attenuated: oral polio vaccine (OPV) (Sabin) at birth (day 0); then boosters at 6, 10, and 14 weeks and at 15-18 months; additional doses till 5 years

• Inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) (Salk) given intradermally; two fractional doses at 6 and 14 weeks as well as 9 months of age.

questions.question: An outbreak of paralytic polio has occurred in Nigeria. Which of the following is the most likely type to cause such outbreaks?
questions.explanation:
Most of the outbreaks of paralytic polio are caused by the type 1 virus.

Three antigenically distinct serotypes (types 1, 2, and 3) of poliovirus are known. Poliovirus type 1 has historically been the predominant cause of poliomyelitis worldwide and continues to be transmitted in endemic areas.

Most infections with poliovirus are asymptomatic. Rarely, patients can have the following presentations:

• Abortive poliomyelitis - a minor illness, manifested by fever, malaise, sore throat, or headache.

• Non-paralytic poliomyelitis - manifested by aseptic meningitis.

• Paralytic poliomyelitis - aseptic meningitis followed by severe back, neck, and muscle pain with rapid/gradual onset of motor weakness. It is the least common presentation of poliovirus infection.

Wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999. Until 2015, over 90% of cVDPV (circulating vaccine-derived polioviruses) cases were due to the type 2 component in OPV.

Bivalent oral polio vaccine (OPV) contains serotypes 1 and 3. Serotype 2 has been removed, as it is implicated in the pathogenesis of cVDPV and occasionally vaccine-associated paralytic polio (VAPP).

Note:

On 25 April 2016, India switched from trivalent oral polio vaccine (OPV) to bivalent OPV; this day is called the National switch day.

questions.question: Which of the following signs may be seen in a child with polio?
questions.explanation:
All of the above signs may be seen in a child suffering from polio.

• Tripod sign - When the child is asked to sit up unassisted, the child assumes the tripod posture.

• Kiss the knee sign - The child cannot kiss the knee due to spine stiffness.

• Head drop sign - A hand is placed under the patient's shoulder and the trunk is raised. Usually, the head will also raise, but in the case of poliomyelitis, the head drops backward.

questions.question: You have been appointed as a member of the acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) surveillance team. What age groups would you target for surveillance?
questions.explanation:
Acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) surveillance is done in children from 0-15 years.

Every case of acute flaccid paralysis in any child under 15 years is to be reported promptly. Fecal samples of all these cases are obtained (2 samples) and transported to the laboratory within 72 hours of collection at 4–8 degree Celcius or frozen at -20 degree Celcius. This process is known as the reverse cold chain.

The differential diagnosis for acute flaccid paralysis include the following:

• Non-polio enteroviruses

• West Nile virus

• Guillan–Barre syndrome

• Other neurotropic viruses: rabies, varicella-zoster, and Japanese encephalitis

questions.question: When was India declared polio-free by WHO?
questions.explanation:
India was certified polio-free on March 27, 2014.

• The last case of polio reported in India was in January 2011.

• Type 2 virus was declared eradicated in September 2015.

• Switch from trivalent to bivalent vaccine was done in India in April 2016.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a component of Polio Endgame Strategy 2019-2023 by WHO?
options: Stop all circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV) outbreaks within 120 days of detection
Separation of polio surveillance and vaccine preventable disease surveillance
Interrupt transmission of all wild poliovirus (WPV)
questions.answer: B. Separation of polio surveillance and vaccine preventable disease surveillance
questions.explanation:
Integration, not separation, of polio surveillance with vaccine-preventable disease (VPD) surveillance, is a part of Polio Endgame Strategy 2019-2023.

Goals of the Polio Endgame Strategy 2019–2023

Goal One: Eradication

• Interrupt transmission of all wild poliovirus (WPV)

• Stop all circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV) outbreaks within 120 days of detection and eliminate the risk of emergence of future VDPVs

Goal two: Integration

• Contribute to strengthening immunization and health systems to help achieve and sustain polio eradication

• Ensure sensitive poliovirus surveillance through integration with comprehensive vaccine-preventable disease (VPD) and communicable disease surveillance systems

• Prepare for and respond to future outbreaks and emergencies

Goal Three: Certification & Containment

• Certify eradication of WPV

• Contain all polioviruses

questions.question: At your vaccination center, you have noticed increased reporting of vaccine-associated paralytic polio (VAPP). Which of the following statement is true regarding this adverse effect of the vaccine?
options: It occurs mostly after the first dose of oral polio vaccine
It is more likely to occur if the first dose was parenteral inactivated polio vaccine
It Is most likely to occur if given on the same day as yellow fever vaccine
It is more likely to occur if multiple parenteral injections have been given at the same time
questions.answer: A. It occurs mostly after the first dose of oral polio vaccine
questions.explanation:
Vaccine-associated paralytic polio (VAPP) occurs mostly after the first dose of oral polio vaccine (OPV).

VAPP is said to occur if:

• Acute flaccid paralysis occurred 4 to 40 days after receiving OPV, and residual weakness lasted for more than 60 days after the onset of paralysis.

• Isolation of vaccine-related poliovirus in any stool samples and no isolation of wild poliovirus from any stool samples.

Note:

• VAPP: Vaccine-associated paralytic polio

• VDPV: Vaccine-derived polio virus. A very rare strain of polio virus, genetically changed from the original strain contained in OPV.

• cVDPV: circulating vaccine-derived polio virus. In areas of low vaccination coverage, a VDPV strain may revert to a form that can cause cases of paralytic polio, leading to an outbreak. This form is called a cVDPV.

questions.question: While volunteering in an orphanage that takes care of disabled kids, you notice the typical hand-knee gait of polio in a child. He walks by putting his right hand on his right lower thigh while stepping forward. Which of the following muscle weakness is responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation:
Polio commonly affects the quadriceps, and weakness of the quadriceps leads to the buckling (bending) of the knee while walking or bearing weight on the leg. So, in order to walk, the person has to prevent the buckling of the knee by supporting with the hand, producing a hand-knee gait.

Examination findings in paralytic polio:

A. In the early stage

• Asymmetric motor paralysis - involvement of affected muscles is haphazard. No associated sensory loss.

• Commonly affects the lower limbs

• Most common muscle affected - Quadriceps, although it is most often partially paralyzed

• Most common muscle to undergo complete paralysis - Tibialis anterior

• The most affected muscle in the hand - Opponens pollicis

• Bulbar/bulbospinal polio - It is a rare but life-threatening disease affecting the motor neurons of the medulla and resulting in the involvement of the respiratory and cardiovascular centers, which may cause death.

B. In the late-stage

• Weakness, wasting, and deformity of the limbs

• At the hip-flexion-abduction-external rotation

• At the knee, flexion deformity is common; in severe cases, there is triple deformity: flexion, posterior subluxation, and external rotation

• At the foot, the commonest deformity is equino-varus. Other deformities - equinovalgus, calcaneo-valgus, and calcaneo-varus

• In the upper limb: affects the shoulder and elbow, hand muscles are spared.

questions.question: Serological testing of a neonate born to an HIV-infected mother turned out positive. Which of the following is the most likely route by which the newborn might have acquired the infection?
questions.explanation:
The most common cause of HIV infection in an infant is the intrapartum transmission.

The mechanism of intrapartum transmission appears to be mucosal exposure to infected blood and cervicovaginal secretions in the birth canal. The intrauterine contractions during active labor/delivery could also increase the risk of late microtransfusions.

Routes of HIV transmission in an infant:

• Intrauterine

• Intrapartum - most common

• Breastfeeding - least common

Risk factors for vertical transmission:

• High maternal viremia (most important)

• Preterm delivery (<34 weeks)

• Vitamin A deficiency

• Prolonged rupture of membranes (>4 hours)

• Low birth weight

• Low maternal CD4 count

questions.question: You are evaluating children infected with HIV in a village, where there is little awareness about HIV and its treatment. Which of the following will be the most common presenting feature in these children?
questions.explanation:
Failure to thrive is the universal finding in children with HIV.

Important features in HIV-infected children include the following:

• Presenting features - failure to thrive, lymphadenopathy, oral thrush, chronic diarrhea, or respiratory symptoms.

• Most common AIDS-defining illness (opportunistic infection) in children - Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia

• Most common fungal infection - oral candidiasis

• Recurrent and chronic bacterial infections (especially, Streptococcus pneumoniae)

• Most common GI disease - chronic/recurrent diarrhea with malabsorption

• Most common renal disease - nephrotic syndrome

• Most common hematological manifestation - anemia

• Most common neoplasms - non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, primary CNS lymphoma, and leiomyosarcomas

questions.question:
Match the following HIV cases with their respective stages.

Clinical case
Stage

1. A 5-year old child with persistent diarrhea for 20 days.
a. Stage 3

2. An asymptomatic 2-year-old with persistent generalized lymphadenopathy.
b. Stage 4

3. A 7-year-old with recurrent oral ulcers and persistent parotid enlargement
c. Stage 1

4. A 4-year-old with HIV-associated cardiomyopathy
d. Stage 2
questions.explanation:
Correct match is: 1-a, 2-c, 3-d, 4-b.

A 5-year old child with persistent diarrhea for 20 days - Stage 3

An asymptomatic 2-year-old with persistent generalized lymphadenopathy - Stage 1

A 7-year-old with recurrent oral ulcers and persistent parotid enlargement - Stage 2

A 4-year-old with HIV-associated cardiomyopathy - Stage 4

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman in labor comes to the emergency department at 37 weeks gestation. She never had a prenatal checkup. The routine screening revealed she is HIV-positive. Which of the following method is least likely to prevent the perinatal transmission of HIV?
options: Administration of ART prophylaxis to baby after birth
questions.explanation:
Vaginal cleansing before delivery is least likely to prevent the perinatal transmission of HIV.

Methods to prevent perinatal transmission of HIV include the following:

• Antiretroviral therapy (ART):

• Single-dose nevirapine at the onset of labor followed by a single dose to the newborn within 72 hours of birth.

• Zidovudine can also be used from the 2nd trimester onwards throughout pregnancy and for 6 weeks after birth to infancy.

• Breastfed infants should receive NVP for 6 weeks if the mother is receiving cART, or NVP for the duration of breastfeeding if the mother is not on therapy. Formula-fed infants in resource-limited countries should receive ZDV bid or NVP qd for 6 weeks.

• Elective cesarean section*

• Breastfeeding: Usually contraindicated, except in developing countries where breastfeeding may be continued for 6 months.

*Note:

Maternal cART is documented to decrease the rate of perinatal HIV-1 transmission to <2%, and <1% if the mother’s viral RNA level is <1,000 copies/mL at delivery. Thus, elective C-section at 38 weeks of gestation should be considered only for women whose viral load is >1,000 copies/ mL in late gestation, to further reduce the risk of vertical transmission.

Guidelines for the use of antiretroviral drugs during C-section are as follows:

• For elective (planned) C-section, ART should be given prior to the operation.

• Women on lifelong ART should continue their standard ART regimen.

• In case of emergency C-section in pregnant women who are not on ART, the three-drug regimen should be started before the surgery and continued thereafter.

questions.question: A patient is started on HAART treatment for HIV. Her CD4 count is 150 cells/μl. She developed a fever and her symptoms worsened during her first week of treatment. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) is characterized by an increased inflammatory response to subclinical opportunistic infections after initiating retroviral therapy.

Features seen are fever, worsening of opportunistic infections, new manifestations like lymphadenopathy, pulmonary infiltrates. It typically occurs within 1st few weeks of starting therapy. It commonly occurs in patients with progressive disease, or severe CD4 + T-lymphocyte depletion.

questions.question: Which of the following is an indication to start ART in children, as per the WHO guidelines?
options: <11 months infant of CD4 count < 1500 cells/mm3
questions.explanation:
Antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated in all children with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 cell count, as per the latest WHO recommendations 2016.

Also, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for infants, children, and adolescents with HIV, irrespective of their clinical and immune conditions.

questions.question: A mother brings her 6-week old infant to your PHC for immunization. The baby was not administered the BCG vaccine as he is HIV positive. His recent CD4 counts were 13%. Which of the following vaccines should you not administer in this child?
questions.explanation:
The live attenuated oral polio vaccine (OPV) should be avoided in severely immunocompromised infants (CD4 cell percentage <15%) because of an increased risk of paralytic polio.

Vaccine
Recommendation

Oral polio vaccine (OPV)

Yes, if CD4% ≥15%
No, if CD4% <15%

Varicella and MMR

Yes, if CD4% ≥15%
No, if CD4% <15%

Pentavalent (Hep B, DPT, Hib)
Yes

Inactivated polio vaccine (IPV)
Yes

BCG
No

Live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV or nasal spray)
No

Injectable influenza vaccine (flu shot)
Yes

questions.question: Which of the following is not a part of the 2025 HIV targets of Global AIDS Strategy 2021-2026?
options: 95% of women of reproductive age have their HIV and sexual and reproductive health service needs met.
90% of people living with HIV recieve preventive treatment for TB
95% of pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV have suppressed viral loads.
75% of HIV-exposed children are tested by two months of age and again after cessation of breastfeeding
questions.answer: D. 75% of HIV-exposed children are tested by two months of age and again after cessation of breastfeeding
questions.explanation:
95%(not 75%) of HIV-exposed children are tested by two months of age and again after cessation of breastfeeding is part of the High level 2025 targets of Global AIDS Strategy 2021-2026

High-level 2025 targets

• 95% of people at risk of HIV infection have access to and use appropriate, prioritized, person-centered, and effective combination prevention options.

• 95% of women of reproductive age have their HIV and sexual and reproductive health service needs met.

• 95% of pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV have suppressed viral loads.

• 95% of HIV-exposed children are tested by two months of age and again after cessation of breastfeeding

• 75% of all children living with HIV have suppressed viral loads by 2023 (interim target)

• 95–95–95 testing and treatment targets are achieved within all subpopulations, age groups, and geographic settings, including children living with HIV.

• 90% of people living with HIV receive preventive treatment for TB.

• 90% of people living with HIV and people at risk are linked to people-centered and context-specific integrated services for other communicable diseases, noncommunicable diseases, sexual health and gender-based violence, mental health, drug and substance use, and other services they need for their overall health and wellbeing.

The Strategy keeps people at the center and aims to unite countries, communities, and partners across and beyond the HIV response to take prioritized actions to accelerate progress towards the vision of zero new HIV infections, zero discrimination, and zero AIDS-related deaths.

This Strategy lays out a framework for transformative action to reduce the inequalities by 2025 and to get every country and every community on track to end AIDS by 2030.

questions.question: A 26-year-old pregnant labourer who is HIV-positive delivers a healthy male baby. She was advised ART previously but has been non-compliant with her treatment. What is recommended by NACO with regards to feeding the baby?
questions.explanation:
NACO recommends exclusive breastfeeding as the infant feeding choice in the first 6 months. This is irrespective of the fact that the mother is on ART or the infant is provided with ARV prophylaxis for 6 weeks.

Breast-feeding and replacement feed simultaneously (mixed feeds) in the first 6 months should not be done, as it leads to mucosal abrasions in the gut of the baby, thereby facilitating HIV entry.

Breast-feeding should not be stopped abruptly. Only in situations where breastfeeding cannot be done (maternal death, severe maternal illness) or individual mother’s choice (at her own risk), then exclusive replacement feeding which is safe, sustainable, affordable and feasible can be started.

In resource-rich settings/developed countries, exclusive alternative formulations are recommended.

questions.question: You are an intern posted in the postnatal ward of a hospital. You receive an HIV-positive patient on PND-1. Which of the following tests would you use to detect HIV in the baby?
questions.explanation:
HIV in a baby born to an HIV-infected mother is diagnosed using HIV DNA PCR.

NACO recommends the use of a qualitative HIV-1 DNA PCR (NAT) in children aged <18months

Antibody assays (e.g., ELISA) that are commonly used for HIV testing in adults and older children are not reliable in infants and young children because of the persistence of transplacentally acquired maternal antibodies until 18 months after birth. For this reason, HIV virologic testing (PCR) must be performed using tests that detect HIV DNA or RNA. Scheduled repeated testing is necessary because test sensitivity increases with time from HIV virus exposure. Also, a very recent infection will not be detectable by PCR.

Cord blood should not be used for testing because of the possibility of contamination of the sample with maternal blood.

questions.question: The image given below depicts the mode of infection with which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows, infection through fecal oral route, colonization of the organism, and replication in the GI mucosa (M cells), followed by entry into blood via regional lymph nodes. In blood, it causes viremia and gets access to the CNS via the peripheral nerves, finally reaching the anterior horn cells in the spinal cord. The pathogenesis expalined above is that of polio infection.

Option A: Infection with Campylobacter jejuni is implicated in the pathogenesis of Guillain–Barre syndrome, where the antibodies against C. jejuni cross-react with the gangliosides (GM1) in the peripheral nervous system.

Option B: Hepatitis A infection occurs through the fecal-oral route, and the virus replicates in the GI mucosa and is then transported to the liver.

Option D: Rotavirus causes diarrhea by causing malabsorption.

questions.question: Kenny packs are used in the treatment of ________
questions.explanation:
Kenny packs are used in the treatment of poliomyelitis.

Treatment of poliomyelitis includes the following:

• Symptomatic and supportive treatment: Analgesics, bed rest, and physiotherapy

• Sister Kenny’s treatment: Hot moist packs applied to muscles to relieve pain and spasm

• Optimum positioning of limbs to prevent deformity

• Management of pure bulbar poliomyelitis consists of maintaining the airway and avoiding the risk of aspiration.

questions.question: Which of the following is not commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus?
questions.explanation:
Acute pharyngitis or sore throat is most commonly caused by group A Streptococcus (GAS) - not staphylococcus.

Staphylococcus aureus causes localized infections like furuncle, carbuncle, bullous impetigo, pyomyositis, and folliculitis (skin and soft tissue infections). It may cause bloodstream infections if there is a breach in the skin.

questions.question: Anu, a pre-school student presented with a fever and sore throat. She also had an acute onset generalized erythematous rash with pastia lines over the antecubital fossa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of scarlet fever.
