The child with lactose intolerance generally has perianal excoriations. The condition is diagnosed by using stool examination which shows acidic stool positive for reducing substances. Treatment is by diet control using a diet devoid of lactose. It can be congenital due to lactase deficiency or acquired after post-viral gastroenteritis. In secretory diarrhoea, the epithelial cells’ ion transport processes are turned into a state of active secretion. The most common cause of acute-onset secretory diarrhoea is a bacterial infection of the gut.

Chronic diarrhoea is, in many cases, the result of an intestinal infection that persists longer than expected.

Dysentery/Shigellosis is a type of food poisoning caused by infection with the Shigella species. It is spread by means of faeco-oral transmission.

questions.question: Ramya, a 6-year-old child with acute diarrhoea is admitted and started on fluid therapy with reduced osmolarity Oral Rehydration Solution . Which of the following statement is false about reduced osmolarity ORS?
questions.explanation:
The total osmolarity of reduced osmolarity ORS is 245 mOsm/L (not 311 mOsm/L)

Reduced osmolarity ORS is now the global standard of care in the management of acute gastroenteritis.

questions.question: Sathish, your gym partner and father of a 12-month-old child, calls you for a teleconsult. His child has been passing loose watery stools without fever. He wants to know the medications to be given to his child. What dose of oral zinc would you prescribe to this child?
questions.explanation:
All children older than 6 months of age with acute diarrhoea should receive oral zinc (20 mg/day) for 10-14 days during and after diarrhoea.

Most of the cases of under-five acute diarrhoea are infectious in aetiology with more than 50% due to the Rotavirus, which is self-limiting. Treatment will include fluid and electrolyte correction and zinc supplementation.

questions.question: In a child admitted with viral enteritis along with signs of dehydration, which type of acid-base imbalance is likely to be seen?
questions.explanation:
Isotonic dehydration with acidosis is the most common finding in children with severe viral enteritis.

Viruses that cause human diarrhoea selectively infect and destroy the villus tip cells in the small intestine.

In the small intestine, the upper villus enterocytes are differentiated cells, which have absorptive functions, such as the transport of water and electrolytes. On the other hand, the crypt enterocytes are undifferentiated cells and are net secretors of water and electrolytes.

Selective viral infection of intestinal villus tip cells thus leads to decreased absorption of salt and water (proportionate loss of water and salt—isotonic dehydration) and an imbalance in the ratio of intestinal fluid absorption to secretion.

Metabolic acidosis may be a result of stool bicarbonate losses in children with diarrhoea. These can also be seen due to secondary renal insufficiency or lactic acidosis as a sequelae to diarrhoea.

questions.question:
The intestinal biopsy report of a 7-year-old boy evaluated for chronic watery diarrhoea revealed a flat intestinal mucosa. Which of the following conditions would you suspect in this child?

1. Tropical sprue

2. Giardiasis

3. Amoebiasis

4. HIV enteropathy

5. Neutrophilic gastroenteritis
questions.explanation:
Chronic diarrhoea with a flat intestinal mucosa can be seen in conditions Tropical sprue, giardiasis, and HIV enteropathy.

Causes of the flat intestinal mucosa (subtotal or total villous atrophy):

1. Celiac disease

2. Tropical sprue

3. Giardiasis

4. Bacterial overgrowth

5. HIV enteropathy

6. Eosinophilic gastroenteritis

7. Cow’s milk or soy protein enteropathy

8. Graft versus host disease

9. Chemo or radiotherapy

10. Protein-energy malnutrition

11. Tuberculosis or lymphoma

Amoebiasis and neutrophilic gastroenteritis may also rarely have villous atrophy but the presentation is generally acute. Amoebiasis is characteristically associated with dysentery and biopsy would reveal a flask-shaped ulcer.

questions.question: Suyash, a 10-year-old boy presented to the clinic with a history of malabsorption, diarrhoea, and poor appetite after having his favourite white sauce pasta. His mother adds that he develops such symptoms only when he takes pasta or roti. The duodenal biopsy revealed crypt hyperplasia and CD8+ cells in lamina propria. Which of the following tests is least likely to be used for the diagnosis of the condition?
questions.explanation:
The clinical vignette is suggestive of celiac disease and an anti-nuclear antibody test is not used in the diagnosis of celiac disease.

Symptoms are pre-dominantly seen after consuming a diet rich in gluten (Wheat pasta or roti). Diagnosis of celiac disease is made based on lab and histopathological findings.

Celiac disease-specific antibodies are as follows:

• Anti-tissue transglutaminase (Anti-TG2) IgA antibodies

• Anti deaminated - IgG forms of gliadin peptides antibodies

• Endomysial antibodies (EMA)

The duodenal biopsy will show crypt hyperplasia, villous atrophy and CD8+ cells in lamina propria

questions.question: A 9-year-old boy presented with vomiting for 5 days. His sister, who has coeliac disease had similar symptoms. IgA-tissue transglutaminase titre is 5 times the upper limit of normal. Which of the following is not an extraintestinal manifestation of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The boy is suffering from coeliac disease. Polycythemia is not an extraintestinal manifestation of coeliac disease.

On the contrary, the most common extraintestinal manifestation of celiac disease in the paediatric age group is iron-deficiency anaemia that is refractory to iron therapy, and not polycythemia.

Celiac disease is an immune-mediated systemic disorder triggered by the ingestion of wheat gluten and related prolamines from rye and barley.

The intestinal symptoms are caused by the atrophy of the small bowel mucosa and malabsorption. The symptoms include diarrhoea, vomiting, anorexia, weight loss, failure to thrive, rectal prolapse, and intussusception.

The extraintestinal manifestations are caused due to malnutrition and autoimmunity and they include the following:

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of pancreatic insufficiency in childhood?
questions.explanation:
Cystic fibrosis is the most common cause of pancreatic insufficiency in children, which, if untreated, will lead to malnutrition.

Other rare causes include:

• Shwachman–Diamond syndrome

• Isolated enzyme deficiencies

• Chronic pancreatitis

• Protein-energy malnutrition

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with fever, severe epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting for 6 hours. He feels comfortable when he bends forward and assumes a knee-chest position. Which of the following tests is not useful in the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?
questions.explanation:
Serum elastase is not used for the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis. The measurement of faecal elastase is used as a screening test for pancreatic insufficiency.

The criteria for the diagnosis of pancreatitis in children is defined as 2 of 3 of the following:

1. Epigastric abdominal pain;

2. Serum amylase and/or lipase activity at least 3 times greater than the upper limit of normal; and

3. Imaging findings characteristic of, or compatible with, acute pancreatitis.

Serum lipase is now considered the test of choice for acute pancreatitis as it is more specific than amylase.

CT scan has a major role in the diagnosis and follow-up of children with pancreatitis. Other useful investigations are USG, ERCP, and MRCP.

questions.question: Anwesha, an orator preparing for her international debate finale presents to your clinic with lesions on her lower lip as shown below. She is concerned as these lesions are painful, recurrent and hamper the flow of her speech. Which of the following points about this condition is incorrect?
options: They are seen in Gluten-sensitive enteropathy
questions.explanation:
The lesions given in the above image are aphthous ulcers, and they are not contagious. All the other points are true.

Aphthous ulcers are painful, recurrent, and non-contagious oral lesions. They are well-circumscribed, ulcerative lesions with a white necrotic base surrounded by a red halo. They heal in 10–14 days without scarring. Their aetiology is unclear but the following factors have been implicated:

1. Allergic or immunologic reactions

2. Emotional stress

3. Genetics

4. Injury to soft tissues in the mouth

5. Inflammatory bowel disease

6. Gluten-sensitive enteropathy

7. Behcet disease

8. Sweet syndrome

9. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection

10. Cyclical neutropenia

Treatment generally includes local anaesthetic to relieve pain and B-complex supplementation to enhance healing.

questions.question: The nanny of a 3-year-old boy brings the child to the ER after he had accidentally ingested button batteries from the mobile phone toy that he was playing with. What would be the next best step in the management of this child?
options: Observation and follow up in 24 hours
Observation until the foreign body passes out in faeces
questions.explanation:
Button batteries and sharp objects in the oesophagus and foreign bodies associated with respiratory symptoms all mandate urgent endoscopic removal.

Button batteries, in particular, are very dangerous foreign bodies, which must be expediently removed because they can cause:

• Mucosal injury in 1-hour contact time

• Involve all layers of the oesophagus in 4 hours

Injury is thought to be secondary to electrochemical burns from electrical discharge. Chemical burns from electrolyte alkali leakage and pressure necrosis also may contribute to mucosal injury.

Asymptomatic blunt objects and coins lodged in the oesophagus can be observed for up to 24 hr in anticipation of passage into the stomach.

questions.question: A mother observed unusual redness on the palms of her young child while putting him to sleep. She brings him to your OPD and on examination, you find mild abdominal distension, splenomegaly, and pedal edema. You admit the child for further evaluation, but on the night of admission, he suddenly starts vomiting fresh blood. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A child presenting with hematemesis and splenomegaly is presumed to have variceal bleeding unless proved otherwise. Bleeding from oesophagal varices is the most common presentation of portal hypertension.

Palmar erythema(redness of the palms) and ascites (swelling of the abdomen) are features of liver failure seen in this patient.

Upper GI endoscopy is the preferred diagnostic test for oesophagal varices.

The management of acute variceal bleeding-

• Attain hemodynamic stability through blood transfusion/fluids

• Vasoactive drugs (e.g., octreotide)

• Endoscopy to perform ligation or sclerotherapy

• Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt should be considered for variceal bleeding refractory to medical and endoscopic therapy.

Secondary prophylaxis to reduce the recurrence of bleeding includes-

• Nonselective β blockade (propranolol, nadolol)

• Obliteration of varices through serial treatment via ligation or sclerotherapy

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy was brought by his mother to the ER after having a sudden episode of vomiting blood. On examination, splenomegaly is detected with engorged superficial veins around his umbilicus. Which is the investigation of choice in this patient?
questions.explanation:
A child presenting with hematemesis and splenomegaly is presumed to have variceal bleeding and hence, upper GI endoscopy is the investigation of choice.

The upper GI endoscopy provides a definitive diagnosis and an option to treat via band ligation or sclerotherapy.

Capsule endoscopy, ultrasound, CT, MRI, and elastography are not recommended because of their suboptimal accuracy compared to endoscopy. Capsule endoscopy is used to investigate an occult/obscure gastrointestinal bleed mostly suspected to be in the small intestine.

questions.question: A 14-year-old boy was brought to the OPD by his father who observed a yellowish tinge to his skin and eyes. He gives a history of recent onset fatigue after playing football for a few minutes and cannot stay active on the playground for a long time like before. Investigations revealed isolated conjugated hyperbilirubinemia but are normal otherwise. Liver histology revealed a black pigment. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The presence of fatigue, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and black pigment on liver biopsy, termed as "black liver" is suggestive of Dubin–Johnson syndrome.

Dubin-Johnson syndrome is an autosomal recessive inherited defect in hepatocyte secretion of bilirubin glucuronide. Disease results from absent function of multiple drug-resistant protein 2, an ATP dependent canalicular transporter.

The most commonly reported symptoms are abdominal pain and fatigue, jaundice, dark urine, and slight enlargement of the liver.

Inherited conjugated hyperbilirubinemia-

Dubin–Johnson syndrome
Rotor syndrome

Autosomal recessive
Autosomal recessive

Absent function of multiple drug-resistant protein (MRP-2)
Defect in anion transport

Black liver on biopsy (due to accumulation of epinephrine metabolite)
Black liver is not seen

Normal levels of coproporphyrin in urine
Increased levels of coproporphyrin in urine

Gall bladder is not visualized on oral cholecystography
Gall bladder is visualized on oral cholecystography

questions.question: You are an intern posted in the paediatrics department and a child with Dubin-Johnson syndrome is admitted to your unit. During rounds, the attending paediatrician asks you which molecular defect causes liver disease in this patient. Your answer would be
questions.explanation:
Molecular defect causing liver disease in Dubin–Johnson syndrome is ABCC2 (codes for canalicular protein with ATP-binding cassette), it leads to the mutation of multiple drug-resistant protein 2 (MRP2) receptor. Hence, there is a defect in the transfer of conjugated bilirubin from the liver to bile in Dubin–Johnson syndrome.

Important diseases and their molecular defects:

ATP7A
Menke’s disease

ATP7B
Wilson disease

CFTR
Cystic fibrosis

SERPINA 1
α-1 antitrypsin deficiency

ABCC2 (MRP2 protein defect)
Dubin Johnson syndrome

questions.question: All are true about transient familial neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, except:
options: Occurs due to maternal antibody against fetal UGT1A1
It is also known as Lucey Driscoll syndrome
Stop breast feeding when jaundice sets in
questions.answer: D. Stop breast feeding when jaundice sets in
questions.explanation:
Lucey Driscoll syndrome or transient familial neonatal hyperbilirubinemia is a self-limiting condition and there is no need to stop breastfeeding.

Lucey Driscoll syndrome is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder affecting enzymes involved in bilirubin metabolism. It causes transient familial neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and jaundice occurs during the first 4 days of life. It is due to maternal antibodies against fetal UGT1A1 (UDP glucuronosyltransferase family 1 member A1).

questions.question: Lately, a teacher observed that an anxious young girl had started drooling saliva from her mouth while listening in the classroom. She had also developed a deterioration in her handwriting while taking down notes. Her mother was informed and she brought her child to your clinic. On examination, she had tremors and mild hepatomegaly. A slit-lamp examination was done and showed the following picture. The right statement about this disease is -
options: Coombs-positive hemolytic anaemia may be present.
Patient can be treated with triethylenetetramine
questions.answer: D. Patient can be treated with triethylenetetramine
questions.explanation:
The image shows the Kayser-Fleischer ring, which is characteristic of Wilson's disease. It is an autosomal recessive disorder, characterised by low serum ceruloplasmin levels. Coomb's negative hemolytic anemia may be present. The patient can be treated with triethylenetetramine also known as trientine.

Wilson’s disease is caused due to a loss-of-function mutation in the ATP7B gene on Chr.13q. The gene encodes a copper transporting ATPase (ATP7B) which has 2 functions:

• Maintains copper in bound form by binding copper to apoceruloplasmin

• Helps excrete free copper in bile.

Thus, an ATP7B deficiency leads to excess deposition of free copper within tissues.

Lab markers
Change in Wilson's disease
Reason

Serum ceruloplasmin
↓↓
ATP7B deficiency results in reduced bound copper

24h urinary copper
↑↑
Excess free copper excreted in urine

Total serum copper
↓
Due to marked reduction in ceruloplasmin

The drugs used in the management of Wilson's disease include:

• Chelating agents as first-line drugs

• D-penicillamine

• Trientine or triethylenetetramine

• Elemental zinc as maintenance therapy.

questions.question: A mother observed deterioration in her young child's academic performance and loss of interest in everyday activities for the last few weeks. She has also lost the ability to play catch with her brother and complains of muscle weakness. There is mild hepatomegaly noted on examination. Her serum ceruloplasmin levels were reduced. All of the following manifestations can occur in a patient with this disease except?
questions.explanation:
The presence of reduced ceruloplasmin levels, motor incoordination, and hepatomegaly suggest the patient is suffering from Wilson’s disease. Sparse depigmented hair is not a feature of Wilson's disease. It is a feature of Menke's disease.

Wilson's disease is caused due to a mutation in the ATP7B gene that leads to excess deposition of free copper within tissues.

It has the following clinical features:

(most common)

Note: Wilson's disease may also present as cirrhosis and hepatic failure, where shrinkage of liver occurs.

questions.question: In Wilson Disease, hepatic copper content usually exceeds____ μg/g dry weight.
questions.explanation:
In Wilson disease, hepatic copper content usually exceeds 250 μg/g dry weight.

Hepatic copper accumulation is the hallmark of Wilson disease. It is measured using neutron activation analysis/atomic absorption spectrometry.

questions.question: A male infant was born to a mother with chronic hepatitis B infection. The infant is suspected to have been exposed at the time of delivery. At 4 months, which of the following viral markers signifies ongoing viral replication in the infant?
questions.explanation: HBeAg signifies the ongoing viral replication in case of hepatitis B infection.

questions.question: A 9-year-old boy was brought to the OPD by his mother with a history of fatigue and myalgia for a few days, associated with rashes that started a week before it. On examination, coppery-red coloured skin lesions were seen on the face and limbs including palms and soles. His serology was positive for HBsAg. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The coppery-red colored papules along with a positive HBsAg are suggestive of Gianotti-Crosti syndrome, also known as papular acrodermatitis.

It is an immunologic reaction to viral infections. The most common associations are Epstein-Barr virus, hepatitis B virus, Coxsackievirus A16, and parainfluenza virus, as well as with many childhood immunizations.

Skin lesions are monomorphic, firm, coppery red papules sized 1-10 mm. They occur in crops and may become profuse and coalesce into plaques, forming a symmetric eruption on the face, ears, buttocks, and limbs, including the palms and soles. The trunk, scalp, and mucous membrane are relatively spared.

The image given below shows the coppery red papules seen in Gianotti-Crosti syndrome.

questions.question: Which of the following drugs are not used in the treatment of hepatitis B?
questions.explanation:
Ribavirin is a drug used in the treatment of hepatitis C, not hepatitis B.

Indications for starting antiviral therapy in chronic hepatitis B are:

• Patients without cirrhosis

• HBeAg + with HBV DNA >20,000 IU/mL and ALT level >2 times the upper limit of normal

• HBeAg -ve with HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL and ALT level >2 times the upper limit of normal

• Patients with compensated cirrhosis and an HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL

• Patients developing acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis.

Drugs used in the treatment of hepatitis B are:

• First-line treatment: Entecavir or tenofovir

• Other drugs:

• Pegylated interferon-alpha

• Telbivudine

• Lamivudine

• Adefovir

questions.question: A young child developed sudden bouts of vomiting and was brought to the ER. Her condition rapidly worsened as she developed seizures. She had a history of influenza infection one week ago. The patient's liver biopsy will show ______.
questions.explanation:
Severe vomiting in a 5-year-old child, rapidly worsening to seizures, with a history of viral infection (influenza) is suggestive of Reye's syndrome. Hence, liver biopsy will show marked microvesicular steatosis.

Reye's syndrome is a secondary mitochondrial hepatopathy. It is precipitated due to

• Viral infection (influenza, adenovirus, herpes, coxsackievirus A, Epstein–Barr virus)

• Salicylate or antiemetic use

• Inborn error of metabolism such as single enzyme defects of ß oxidation.

• Toxins

There is an acute onset of vomiting and encephalopathy, rapidly progressing to seizures, coma, and death. There is no jaundice.

Investigations

• ↑ ALT and AST

• ↑ Ammonia

• normal bilirubin

• Hypoglycemia

• PT prolonged

• INR increased

• Liver biopsy: marked microvesicular steatosis. Necrosis is not seen.

questions.question: A 12-year old girl was rushed to the ER by her parents due to hematemesis. They gave a history of weakness and fatigue for the last few weeks. On examination, the patient had spider telangiectasias and mild palmar erythema. Liver function tests showed the following results- AST-1100IU/L, serum bilirubin- 8mg/dl, albumin- decreased, globulin- elevated, PT- prolonged along with Anti-Nuclear Antibody positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The symptoms of liver failure and portal hypertension along with a positive anti-nuclear antibody(ANA) is suggestive of Type 1 autoimmune hepatitis. It is associated with-

• Elevated serum aminotransaminase concentrations.

• Liver-associated serum autoantibodies.

• Hypergammaglobulinemia.

questions.question: A 2-week-old low-birth-weight neonate presents with jaundice. Stools are pale/clay coloured. Liver biopsy shows loss of architecture. The most likely diagnosis is_______.
questions.explanation:
Neonatal jaundice in a low-birth-weight (LBW) neonate with consistently pale/clay coloured stools with liver biopsy finding of loss of architecture is suggestive of neonatal hepatitis.

Wilson disease and hereditary hemochromatosis will not present with jaundice in the neonatal stage. Hence, they can be excluded. Injury to liver cells can present the clinical and histologic picture of “neonatal hepatitis.”

Differentiation between Neonatal hepatitis and EHBA

Neonatal hepatitis
Extrahepatic biliary atresia (EHBA)

Definition

It implies intrahepatic cholestasis which includes

• Hepatic injury due to metabolic, viral, or idiopathic causes

• Intrahepatic bile duct injury

• Obliteration of the entire extrahepatic biliary tree at or above the porta hepatis(85% cases) OR

• distal segmental bile duct obliteration with patent
extrahepatic ducts up to the porta hepatis(uncommon)

Clinical features

Family history is present

Premature or LBW baby

Clay-coloured stools

Family history absent

Normal appearance, without looking sick

Persistent acholic stools

Investigations
Liver biopsy: Loss of liver architecture

HIDA scan: screening test

USG: triangular cord sign

Liver biopsy: bile duct proliferation

questions.question: A mother is concerned about her 3-week-old baby having yellowish discolouration of skin and eyes. On examination, the baby is chubby and playful. Stools are pale in color. Further evaluation with USG shows triangular cord sign and liver biopsy shows bile duct proliferation. The most likely diagnosis is ______.
questions.explanation:
Neonatal jaundice in a neonate without a sick-looking appearance and with acholic stools, USG showing triangular cord sign, and liver biopsy showing bile duct proliferation is suggestive of biliary obstruction, which may be seen in biliary atresia.

Wilson disease and Hallervorden Spatz disease (neurodegeneration with iron accumulation in the brain) do not present with jaundice in the neonatal stage. Hence, they can be excluded.

Differentiation between neonatal hepatitis and EHBA

Neonatal hepatitis
Extrahepatic biliary atresia (EHBA)

It implies intrahepatic cholestasis which includes:

Hepatic injury due to metabolic, viral, or idiopathic cause

Intrahepatic bile duct injury

Obliteration of the entire extrahepatic biliary tree at or above the porta hepatis(85% cases) OR

Distal segmental bile duct obliteration with patent
extrahepatic ducts up to the porta hepatis (uncommon)

 Clinical features

Family history is present

Premature or LBW baby

Pigmented stools

Family history absent

Normal appearance, without looking sick

Persistent acholic stools

Investigations

Liver biopsy: Loss of liver architecture

USG: triangular cord sign

HIDA scan: screening test

Liver biopsy: bile duct proliferation

Liver biospy:

• Biliary atresia is characterized by proliferation of the bile ductule, presence of bile plugs, and portal or perilobular edema and fibrosis, with the basic hepatic lobular architecture intact.

• In neonatal hepatitis, there is severe, diffuse hepatocellular disease, with distortion of lobular architecture, marked infiltration of inflammatory cells, and focal hepatocellular necrosis.

questions.question: A mother leaves her 3-year-old son unattended for 20 mins and later finds him holding a blue coloured empty strip of tablets with a few tablets scattered on the floor. A few hours later he is rushed to the ER with nausea and vomiting. As an intern taking the history, you suspect accidental ingestion of paracetamol tablets. The pattern of liver injury you would expect in this case is
questions.explanation:
The pattern of liver injury caused by paracetamol (acetaminophen) is centrilobular necrosis.

Acetaminophen toxicity results from the formation of a highly reactive intermediate metabolite, N -acetyl-p -benzoquinone imine (NAPQI). In therapeutic use, only about 5% is metabolized by the hepatic cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP2E1 to NAPQI, which is then immediately joined with glutathione to form a nontoxic mercapturic acid conjugate.

In overdose, glutathione stores are overwhelmed, and free NAPQI is able to combine with hepatic macromolecules to produce hepatocellular necrosis. Single acute toxic dose of APAP is generally considered to be >200 mg/kg in children.

Patterns of hepatic drug injury:

Disease
Drug

Centrilobular necrosis
Acetaminophen, Halothane

Microvesicular steatosis
Valproic acid

Acute hepatitis
Isoniazid

Methotrexate

Cholestasis
Chlorpromazine, Erythromycin, Estrogen

Veno occlusive disease
Busulphan, Cyclophosphamide

Portal and hepatic vein thrombosis
Estrogen, Androgen

Biliary sludge
Ceftriaxone

Hepatic adenoma/hepatocellular carcinoma
Oral contraceptive pills, Anabolic steroids

questions.question:
You are examining a young child who presented to the ER with a high fever and abdominal pain. The patient winces on abdominal palpation of the right upper quadrant. USG showed hydrops of the gallbladder. All of the following conditions are associated with hydrops of the gallbladder except
__________.
questions.explanation:
Hydrops of the gallbladder is not associated with cystic fibrosis.

Hydrops of gallbladder is the acute acalculous non-inflammatory distension of the gallbladder, which occurs in infants and children. It is characterized by the absence of calculi, bacterial infections or congenital anomalies of the biliary system.

Hydrops is distinguished from acalculous cholecystitis by the absence of a significant inflammatory process and a generally benign prognosis.

Conditions associated with hydrops of GB:

• Infections: Streptococcal pharyngitis, staphylococcal infection, ascariasis, leptospirosis, typhoid fever, and viral hepatitis

• Kawasaki disease

• Total parenteral nutrition, prolonged fasting

• Sickle cell crisis, thalassemia

• Sepsis

• Mesenteric adenitis, necrotizing enterocolitis

Note: In cystic fibrosis cholelithiasis, cholecystitis, micro gallbladder is seen.

questions.question: A young boy was admitted with complaints of fever and abdominal pain for 2 days. ESR and CRP were elevated and CT Abdomen obtained was as shown in the picture. Which of the following is not a common feature in the given condition?
questions.explanation:
The symptoms of fever and abdominal pain and a hypodense lesion on the CT are suggestive of a Liver abscess in this patient.

Signs and symptoms of a liver abscess include fever, chills, night sweats, malaise, nausea, hepatomegaly, as well as pain and tenderness in the right upper quadrant. They also show elevated inflammatory markers, hypoalbuminemia and leukocytosis. However, jaundice is uncommon.

questions.question: A mother brought a healthy-looking, 3-month-old infant for routine immunization. As you were giving the shot, you noticed some noisy breathing in the baby, which became worse once he started crying. However, it decreased, as you held him in a prone position. There were no clear signs of distress. According to his mother, he had been feeding well at home and has not had any episodes of apnea or cyanosis. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A clinical picture of inspiratory stridor that worsens on crying and relieves in a prone position in a newborn without respiratory distress is suggestive of laryngomalacia.

Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital laryngeal anomaly and the most common cause of stridor in infants and children. Stridor is exacerbated by any exertion: crying, agitation, or feeding. In the prone position, the stridor disappears.

On laryngoscopy, an omega-shaped epiglottis is visualized.

In most children, only expectant observation is required as the condition resolves secondary to nervous system maturation, within 18 to 24 months of birth. However, neonates with severe laryngomalacia may develop marked upper airway obstruction resulting in cor pulmonale, life-threatening apneic episodes, feeding difficulties, obstructive sleep apnea, and failure to thrive. In such cases, surgical resection of supraglottic tissues and supraglottoplasty has been the favoured approach.

questions.question: A senior casualty nurse informs you that a 5-year-old girl with severe respiratory distress might require intubation. You just finished stabilising and placing an ET tube in Mohan, a 57-year-old man with head trauma and a GCS of 7. Which of the following is not a feature of child's airway?
options: The larynx being located higher in the neck at the level of C3-C4
The narrowest part being the subglottic region
questions.explanation:
The pediatric airway is funnel shaped. In comparison, the adult airway is cylindrical.

In newborns, the larynx is situated at the level of C3-C4, where it facilitates simultaneous respiration and swallowing during feeding.

questions.question: During a night shift, you get a call from the ER to come and see a toddler, who presented with complaints of fever, drooling, and a muffled voice since evening. On examination, the child has a stridor and you pick up a "thumb sign" on the lateral x-ray of his neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Thumb sign on lateral x-ray of neck is pathognomonic for acute epiglottitis (AE). It is seen due to epiglottic enlargement.

AE is an inflammation of the epiglottis. The arytenoids, false cords, and posterior tongue may also be involved.

In children, Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) is the most common cause. This has decreased dramatically since the widespread availability of immunization (pentavalent). Streptococcus pyogenes, S. pneumoniae, and S. aureus have also been implicated. Non-infectious causes can be foreign body ingestion and trauma from thermal or caustic agents.

It has a progressive and potentially fulminating course, characterised by high fever, sore throat, dyspnea, and rapidly progressing respiratory obstruction.

AE is a clinical diagnosis and a true emergency, X-ray soft tissue neck is not necessary to confirm it. It may be used to rule out differentials such as laryngotracheobronchitis, foreign body obstruction, retropharyngeal abscess or congenital anomalies. The time taken for X-rays should be avoided in a critically ill child due to the risk of sudden complete airway obstruction.

The definitive diagnosis of AE is made during direct laryngoscopy. However, since manipulation can induce a laryngospasm, it is generally avoided.

The image below shows thumb sign:

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common etiological agent associated with epiglottitis in children, overall in the world?
questions.explanation:
The most common etiological agent, overall in the world, of acute epiglottitis in the pediatric age group, now is Streptococcus.

In the past, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) used to be the most commonly identified cause of acute epiglottitis. But, since the widespread use of the H. influenzae type b vaccine, invasive disease caused by H. influenzae type b in pediatric patients has been reduced by 99%.

Therefore, other organisms, such as Streptococcus pyogenes (GAS), Streptococcus penumoniae, non-typeable H. influenzae, and Staphylococcus aureus, have become the common causes of acute epiglottitis in pediatric age group, overall in the world.

Lateral X-ray of the neck shows the thumb sign in acute epiglottitis.

questions.question: A 5 year old boy was suffering from low grade fever, inspiratory stridor and barking cough for past 5 days. His chest X-ray is given below. What is the cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Barking cough is a feature of laryngotracheobronchitis, which is caused by the parainfluenza virus. The X-ray finding is the 'Steeple sign' due to subglottic narrowing.

The age of presentation of laryngotracheobronchitis ranges from 6 months-6 years. The clinical features include barking cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, low-grade fever.

Management:

• Racemic epinephrine nebulization leads to the rapid improvement of upper airway obstruction. Epinephrine constricts pre-capillary arterioles in the upper airway mucosa and decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure, leading to fluid resorption and improvement in airway edema.

• Dexamethasone-by the least invasive route (Oral>IV>IM ). It is indicated in all the grades of croup.

• Oxygen should be administered to children who are hypoxemic (SpO2 <92 %)

Antibiotics are not indicated in laryngotracheobronchitis.

questions.question: 2-year-old Neha has been having fever since yesterday and is refusing food. Parents became alarmed when she developed an abnormal barking cough today morning and have brought her to the casualty. On examination, the child looked exhausted and had visible chest retractions and stridor. The temperature was 39.6 degrees and SpO2 was 93% on room air. Chest X-ray reveals a 'steeple' sign. What is the treatment of choice in this child?
options: Send a throat swab and start IV antibiotics
questions.explanation:
Fever, barking cough, inspiratory stridor and a steeple sign on chest radiograph are suggestive of acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup). The treatment of choice in this child is nebulization with racemic epinephrine.

Epinephrine acts rapidly and provides immediate relief. It constricts pre-capillary arterioles in the upper airway mucosa and decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure. This increases fluid resorption and reduces airway edema.

• 0 to 2- mild

• 3 to 7- moderate

• 8 to 11- severe

• 12 to 17- impending respiratory failure

Treatment of moderate to severe croup :

• Racemic epinephrine nebulization

• Dexamethasone is indicated in all grades of croup and is given by the least invasive route (Oral>IM>IV)

• Oxygen should be administered to children who are hypoxemic (SpO2 <92 %)

• Antibiotics are not indicated in croup

questions.question: A child in your unit is admitted with acute bronchiolitis. Which of the following is the most common etiological agent responsible for this condition during infancy?
questions.explanation:
Acute bronchiolitis is predominantly a viral disease in children younger than 2 years. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the most likely etiological agent and is responsible for more than 50% of cases.

Acute bronchiolitis refers to airway inflammation and obstruction of the lower respiratory tract.

Clinical features of bronchiolitis include fever, cough, fine inspiratory crackles, expiratory wheezes, and breathing difficulty. Cyanosis may be seen in severe cases.

Radiographs may be normal in some patients. In the majority of them, there will be interstitial infiltrates, hyper-expansion of the chest, and peribronchial thickening.

Management is mainly conservative. Hypoxemic children should receive cool, humidified oxygen. Rarely, a child might develop respiratory failure and require hospitalization and invasive ventilation.

questions.question: 10-month-old Ishaan was presented to the OPD with a 3-day history of lower respiratory tract symptoms and an expiratory wheeze. Chest X-ray showed mild peribronchial thickening. Which of the following statements is false regarding the condition described?
options: The risk is higher for infants with young mothers or mothers who smoked during pregnancy.
It is more common in children who have not been breastfed.
The mainstay of treatment is antibiotics.
There is a higher incidence of wheezing and asthma in children with a history of bronchiolitis.
questions.answer: C. The mainstay of treatment is antibiotics.
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute bronchiolitis. The treatment is mainly supportive. Hypoxemic children should receive cool, humidified oxygen. Rarely, a child might develop respiratory failure and require hospitalization and invasive ventilation.

It is more common in boys, in those who have not been breastfed, and in those who live in crowded conditions. The risk is higher for infants with young mothers or mothers who smoked during pregnancy.

Acute bronchiolitis is predominantly a viral disease caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and antibiotics are not indicated.

There is a higher incidence of wheezing and asthma in children with a history of bronchiolitis.

questions.question: The pediatric intensivist is contemplating whether to start aerosolized ribavirin in a young boy with a severe respiratory infection. There would be a clear indication to start the drug if _________.
options: The child has not received any immunization
There is a history of severe atopy
There is a history of recurrent infection
questions.explanation:
Ribavirin is the only specific antiviral therapy available for the treatment of severe bronchiolitis caused by RSV infections. It is reserved as a last-line agent for life-threatening bronchiolitis in patients who are immunocompromised or who have hemodynamically significant cardiopulmonary disease. In otherwise healthy children, the management of acute RSV bronchiolitis is typically supportive.

Ribavirin is a prodrug, which when metabolized resembles purine RNA nucleotides. In this form, it interferes with RNA metabolism required for viral replication.

MNEMONIC: (for indications of ribavirin)

• C-RIBAvirin:

• Hepatitis C

• RSV

• Influenza B

• Arenaviruses (Lassa, Bolivian, etc.)

Note - Ribavirin is also used in the treatment of hepatitis C and some viral hemorrhagic fevers.

questions.question: 3-year-old Sravya was referred with a one-week history of being unable to look upwards, constant neck flexion, and deviation to the right side. Parents also complained of feeding difficulty. On examination, the child was noted to have poor oral hygiene and the neck was tender on palpation. The X-ray is given below. Which of the following statements are false about the given condition?
options: It occurs mostly in children younger than 3-4 years
It is more common in boys
Examination shows unilateral bulging of the posterior pharyngeal wall
Trauma to the posterior pharynx is the most common cause
questions.answer: D. Trauma to the posterior pharynx is the most common cause
questions.explanation:
The history of progressive torticollis, neck pain and dysphagia in a young child along with a neck X-ray demonstrating a prevertebral soft-tissue swelling are all indicative of a retropharyngeal abscess. In young children, an antecedent upper respiratory tract infection is the most common cause of an RP abscess and not trauma.

It involves the suppuration of lymph nodes present in the RP space and is more common in children younger than 3-4 years since these lymph node chains involute after 5 years of age. Boys are affected more often than girls. In older children and adults, the cause is usually trauma to the posterior pharynx, which leads to inoculation of the retropharyngeal space.

Risk factors include poor oral hygiene, diabetes, an immunocompromised state, and low socioeconomic status.

Clinical manifestations are nonspecific and include fever, decreased oral intake, and drooling. Neck stiffness and torticollis may also be present. As the abscess grows in size, it can also lead to upper airway obstruction and asphyxiation. The physical examination can reveal unilateral bulging of the posterior pharyngeal wall.

Although lateral radiograph is used for initial imaging, CT of the neck with intravenous contrast is the best imaging study to evaluate patients with a retropharyngeal abscess. Treatment ranges from prolonged courses of intravenous antibiotics to surgical incision and drainage.

questions.question: The most common cause of bacterial pneumonia in children 3 weeks to 4 years of age is ______.
questions.explanation:
Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) is the most common bacterial pathogen in children 3 weeks to 4 years of age.

Aetiology of infectious pneumonia grouped by age of the patient:

Age group
Frequent pathogens (in order of frequency)

< 3 weeks
Group B Streptococcus, E.coli, gram-negative bacilli, S. pneumoniae, Hemophilus influenzae (type b)

3 weeks - 4 years
RSV, other respiratory viruses (rhinovirus, influenza, parainfluenza and adenovirus), S. pneumoniae, Hemophilus influenzae (type b), Mycoplasma pneumoniae

> 4 years
Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, S. pneumoniae, Hemophilus influenzae (type b)

questions.question: A 9-year-old boy presented with a 4-day history of high-grade fever and a productive cough with yellow sputum. Chest x-ray showed a consolidation in the right middle zone. According to WHO guidelines, which of the following is not an indication for hospital admission?
questions.explanation:
As per the revised 2014 WHO guidelines, it is safe to treat chest indrawing pneumonia at home.

However, a child who is HIV positive and has chest indrawing will need to be referred for inpatient treatment. Only those children who have general danger signs are classified as having “severe pneumonia” and need to be referred to a higher level (hospital admission).

Danger signs:

• Not able to drink

• Persistent vomiting

• Convulsions

• Lethargic or unconscious

• Stridor in a calm child

• Severe malnutrition

questions.question: A 5th standard girl is brought to the OPD with a high fever and cough with expectoration for 3 days. Her chest X-ray shows multiple pneumatoceles. Which of the following is the most common etiological agent implicated in this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia manifests as confluent bronchopneumonia, which is often unilateral and characterized by the presence of hemorrhagic necrosis and irregular areas of cavitation of the lung parenchyma, resulting in pneumatoceles, empyema, or at times, bronchopulmonary fistulas.

The following CT image shows cavitating pneumonia by S. aureus:

questions.question: A one-and-half-year-old child brought to the hospital with a history of breathlessness, fever, cough, and cold. On examination, respiratory rate was 46/min, and there were no chest retractions. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Give IV antibiotics and refer to higher centre
Oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home
No need of treatment only home remedies
questions.answer: C. Oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute respiratory illness. According to the IMNCI guidelines 2020, this child can be classified as having 'Pneumonia'. The treatment is oral amoxicillin, vitamin A and home care advice.

Fast breathing is defined as given in the table below:

Age of child
Fast breathing RR

<2 months
60 breaths/min

2-12 months
50 breaths/min

1-5 years
40 breaths/min

questions.question: An adolescent boy with a family history of asthma presented with intermittent wheeze and cough for 2 months. The onset of wheeze is triggered during exercise and while playing at school. Which of the following is preferred as regular therapy for the prevention of his symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Inhaled corticosteroids are recommended as regular therapy for the prevention of his symptoms of exercise-induced asthma.

According to GINA 2021 guidelines, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction can be prevented with daily treatment (regular therapy) with inhaled corticosteroids. SABA, LABA, or chromones may be used prior to exercise, along with warm-up before exercise.

Those who have mild exercise-induced asthma can use their regular inhaled corticosteroid before exercise and need not take SABA pre-exercise.

questions.question: A 17-year-old boy presented to the clinic with an acute respiratory tract infection. He has a history of asthma associated with recurrent respiratory tract infections and sinusitis. Genetic testing in childhood had revealed CFTR mutations. Which of the following is likely to be decreased in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of cystic fibrosis. In these patients, sperm count is most likely to be decreased.

Male patients with cystic fibrosis usually have infertility due to failure of development of Wolffian duct structures leading to congenital absence of bilateral vas deferens. There is defective sperm transport resulting in obstructive azoospermia.

The sexual function is generally unimpaired.

Option A: Sweat chloride levels are elevated (≥60 mEq/L) due to abnormalities in the CFTR protein leading to defective chloride transport.

Option B: Serum bicarbonate levels are increased due to excessive loss of salt in the sweat resulting in hypochloremic alkalosis.

Option D: Patients with cystic fibrosis have fat malabsorption secondary to exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, hence the increased stool fat.

questions.question: Which of the following has similar inheritance pattern as cystic fibrosis?
options: Accumulation of glycogen in the lysosome
Trinucleotide repeat expansion of CAG on chromosome 4
questions.answer: A. Accumulation of glycogen in the lysosome
questions.explanation:
Cystic fibrosis (CF), is an autosomal-recessive disorder. Accumulation of glycogen in the lysosome is seen in Pompe's disease which is another autosomal-recessive disorder.

Option B: Trinucleotide repeat expansion of CAG on chromosome 4 is seen in Huntington's disease, which is autosomal dominant.

Options C and D: Adult-onset polycystic kidney disease and retinoblastoma (RB gene mutation) are autosomal-dominant diseases.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about cystic fibrosis is not true?
options: Abnormality in CFTR gene leads to defective calcium transport.
Mutation in cystic fibrosis transport regulator is seen.
Males have infertility in adult life
questions.answer: B. Abnormality in CFTR gene leads to defective calcium transport.
questions.explanation:
In cystic fibrosis, abnormalities in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene lead to defective chloride channels and not calcium channels.

Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal-recessive disorder of children and adults. Dysfunction of the CFTR, the primary defect, leads to a wide and variable array of presenting manifestations and complications.

The most common CFTR mutation is F508 deletion.

More than 95% of males are azoospermic because of failure of development of Wolffian duct structures, but the sexual function is generally unimpaired.

questions.question: The most common organism causing pneumonia in cystic fibrosis among the pediatric age group is ________.
questions.explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common organism causing pneumonia in cystic fibrosis among the given options.

The most common organisms causing pneumonia in CF patients:

• The pediatric age group- S. aureus

• The adult population- P. aeruginosa (mucoid)

Pseudomonas aeruginosa-mucoid may also cause pneumonia in pediatric CF patients.

In cystic fibrosis, P. aeruginosa shows a special feature of developing a mucoid capsule. This complex polysaccharide generates a biofilm that provides a hypoxic environment and thereby protects Pseudomonas against antimicrobial agents.

Burkholderia cepacia pneumonia is associated with higher mortality, but it is not the most common. These patients are found to have severe pulmonary hypertension, possibly due to pulmonary inflammatory vascular response.

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy was evaluated for cystic fibrosis. Sweat chloride shows value of 38 and 44 mEq/L (normal<40). Which is the next best test to confirm the diagnosis of cystic fibrosis?
questions.explanation:
DNA analysis is used to confirm the diagnosis of cystic fibrosis in patients with equivocal (one normal and one abnormal value) or frankly normal sweat chloride values.

The diagnosis is confirmed if both of the following criteria are met:

• Presence of

• Clinical symptoms affecting at least one organ system (respiratory, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary) or

• Positive newborn screening or

• A sibling with cystic fibrosis

• Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by

• Two positive sweat chloride test results obtained on separate days or

• Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or

• An abnormal measurement of nasal potential difference

Options A and B: 72-hour fecal fat and chest CT are not used in the diagnosis of CF.

Option D: This testing is primarily used in research applications and has never undergone extensive validation as a clinical tool.

questions.question: A couple planning for pregnancy visits you for genetic counseling. They are both known to be heterozygous carriers of CFTR mutations. Which of the following is the most likely complication in an affected child at birth?
questions.explanation:
CFTR mutations are associated with cystic fibrosis (CF). Meconium ileus is a common complication associated with CF patients at birth.

Meconium found in the intestine of a neonate consists of succus entericus (bile salts, bile acids, and debris from the intestinal mucosa) and is normally evacuated within 6 hours of birth (or earlier).

Meconium ileus occurs in the first 24-48 hours of life when meconium becomes inspissated and obstructs the distal ileum causing abdominal distension and emesis. Abdominal radiographs show dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels and, frequently, a collection of granular, “ground-glass” material in the lower central abdomen.

Meconium ileus may also be seen with pancreatic atresia or pancreatic duct stenosis.

Radiological image shows contrast enema in a newborn infant with abdominal distention and failure to pass meconium. Several air–fluid levels in the small bowel are visible on the upright lateral view.

questions.question: A 9-year-old boy, diagnosed with cystic fibrosis shortly after birth has been having around 2-3 exacerbations per year, requiring hospital admissions. Infection by which of the following organisms has increased mortality in such patients?
questions.explanation:
Cystic fibrosis patients with Burkholderia cepacia pneumonia are found to have severe pulmonary hypertension, possibly due to pulmonary inflammatory vascular response, and have higher mortality.

Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (mucoid) are the most common pathogens causing pneumonia in CF patients. However, they have lower mortality compared to B. cepacia.

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy presents with a history of recurrent pneumonia and chronic diarrhea. His mother states that he has 6-8 foul-smelling stools per day. Physical examination reveals a low-grade fever and scattered rhonchi over both lung fields. Sweat chloride testing is elevated on 2 separate occasions. Which of the following drugs is used as a treatment option for this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of cystic fibrosis (CF). Ivacaftor is used in the treatment of cystic fibrosis.

Ivacaftor is a potentiator of the chloride channel and overcomes its defect. It activates the CFTR-G551D mutant protein.

Remember: IvaCaFToR (CFTR mutation in CF)

questions.question: A 4-year-old girl presented with cough and difficulty breathing following accidental inhalation of a peanut. On examination, there was localised wheezing and decreased breath sounds on the right side. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
In a child with a suspected foreign body in the lung, the next best step would be to do a rigid bronchoscopy as it is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

The rigid bronchoscope has a ventilation mechanism and a suction port making it easy for visualization and handling of the foreign body. However, it is pertinent to note that the initial investigation is usually a chest X-ray.

questions.question: All the following are true about Macleod syndrome except that _______.
options: It is also called Swyer-James syndrome.
It is not a true emphysema.
It is mostly linked to adenovirus.
Affected lung is larger in size compared to unaffected lung.
questions.answer: D. Affected lung is larger in size compared to unaffected lung.
questions.explanation:
Macleod syndrome refers to the inability of the lungs to grow after a severe obstructive bronchiolitis. Children with this condition often have chronic cough, recurrent pneumonia, and wheezing. On CT scan, the affected lung shows small size and decreased vascularity, hyperexpansion, and hyperlucency (false emphysema).

It is also called Swyer–James syndrome. It is mostly linked to adenovirus. Patients respond well to bronchodilators.

questions.question: A 15-year-old child has been recurrently hospitalized for infections, since 2 years of age. After a detailed evaluation, a diagnosis of Kartagener's syndrome was suspected. All of the following are components of the Kartagener triad except _____.
questions.explanation:
Male infertility is typical in Kartagener syndrome, but not a component of the triad.

Kartagener’s syndrome is primary ciliary dyskinesiacharacterized by the classical triad of:

• Situs inversus

• Chronic sinusitis

• Bronchiectasis

Primary ciliary dyskinesia (also called immotile cilia syndrome) is an autosomal recessive disorder affecting ciliary motility. It occurs due to ultrastructural defects in the dynein arm of cilia. This causes the retention of secretions due to a failed mucociliary clearance mechanism. Clinically, this manifests as chronic sinusitis and recurrent infections that ultimately lead to bronchiectasis.

As ciliary function is necessary to ensure proper rotation of the developing organs in the chest and abdomen. Its absence, will lead to situs inversus or a partial lateralizing abnormality.

Male patients with this condition tend to be infertile, due to asthenospermia (immotile spermatozoa due to impaired sperm flagella function).

questions.question: All the following are components of Young's syndrome except:
questions.explanation:
Asthma is not usually seen in Young's syndrome.

Young's syndrome is characterized by:

• Bronchiectasis

• Sinusitis

• Obstructive azoospermia

In contrast, Kartagener's syndrome is characterized by

• Bronchiectasis

• Sinusitis

• Situs inversus

questions.question: A term male neonate develops respiratory distress at birth, unresponsive to surfactant. Echocardiography is normal and chest X-ray shows a ground-glass appearance. Parents say that their first child died at 10 days of birth due to similar complaints. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The history and chest X-ray findings are suggestive of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP).

PAP is a rare, diffuse lung disease that is characterized by alveolar and interstitial accumulation of a periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain-positive phospholipoprotein (derived from surfactant).

Infants and children with PAP present with dyspnea, fatigue, cough, weight loss, chest pain, or hemoptysis. Boys are affected 3 times as often as girls.

Chest X-ray shows ground-glass opacity and HRCT shows crazy-paving pattern (as shown below).

Treatment options include total lung lavage, inhaled or subcutaneous granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF).

questions.question: A 3-month old previously healthy baby was brought to the casualty when the parents found that the baby was not breathing while asleep. Following resuscitative measures, the baby was still apnoeic, pulseless and asystolic. Which of the following is not a risk factor for sudden infant death syndrome?
options: Infants born to women aged >35 years
Infants of mother who smoked during pregnancy
questions.answer: B. Infants born to women aged >35 years
questions.explanation:
Higher maternal age is not a risk factor for sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

Risk factors for SIDS include

• Low socioeconomic status

• 3-4 months of age have the highest incidence

• Higher birth order irrespective of maternal age and low birth weight

• Cigarette smoking, alcohol, and drug abuse during pregnancy

• Sleeping prone, even side sleeping increases the risk

questions.question: A 6-month-old infant was admitted because of increasing stridor since birth, cough, pulmonary infections, and episodes of acute respiratory distress. On detailed evaluation using bronchoscopy and MRI imaging, a bronchial cyst was found to be the cause. The following are features of the lesion except that __.
options: It is usually confined to 1 lobe.
It is never associated with malignancy.
questions.answer: D. It is never associated with malignancy.
questions.explanation:
Bronchial cysts are associated with malignancy (pleuropulmonary blastoma).

Bronchial cysts are congenital malformations of the bronchial tree. It mainly presents as a mediastinal mass that may enlarge and cause local compression.

It is usually confined to a single lobe and is mostly multiloculated.

questions.question: In a child with yellow nail syndrome, you would expect to find all the following clinical features except _______.
questions.explanation:
Yellow nail syndrome is not associated with clubbing.

Yellow nail syndrome is characterized by respiratory manifestation (pleural effusion, bronchiectasis), lymphedema, and discoloured nails.

Yellow nail syndrome almost always occurs after 50 years of age, but a juvenile or familial form has also been observed.

questions.question: What is the most likely cause of a mediastinal mass in a 2-year-old child?
questions.explanation:
The most common mediastinal masses in young children are neurogenic tumours (50%-60%). In most cases (< 4 years of age), they are invariably malignant (neuroblastomas).

Anterior mediastinal masses:

• Thymoma - most common

• Malignant lymphoma (Hodgkin's and non-Hodgkin's)

• Teratoma

• Thyroid (retro- or sub-sternal extension)

• Thymic cyst

• Angioma

Middle mediastinal masses:

• Foregut duplication cyst (bronchogenic, enteric, and neurenteric) - most common

• Lymphadenopathy

• Vascular malformations

Posterior mediastinal masses:

• Neurogenic tumour - most common overall

• Foregut duplication cyst

• Vascular malformations

• Extramedullary hematopoiesis

questions.question: A junior radiologist performing a fetal doppler follows the direction of the flow of oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus to examine the fetal circulatory vessels. The sequence that he would follow is:
options: Umbilical artery → inferior vena cava → ductus venosus → right atrium → left atrium
Umbilical artery → superior vena cava → right atrium → ductus arteriosus → left atrium
Umbilical vein → ductus venosus → inferior vena cava → right atrium → left atrium
Umbilical vein → ductus arteriosus → superior vena cava → right atrium → left atrium
questions.answer: C. Umbilical vein → ductus venosus → inferior vena cava → right atrium → left atrium
questions.explanation: The sequence of oxygenated blood flow from the placenta to the fetal heart is umbilical vein → ductus venosus → inferior venacava → right atrium → left atrium.

questions.question: Oxygenated blood is carried to the fetus by ______.
questions.explanation:
Oxygenated blood is carried to the fetus by the umbilical vein.

The umbilical venous blood shunts via the ductus venosus into the inferior vena cava. Thus, the inferior vena cava, which also carries blood from hepatic veins, kidneys, and from lower extremities carries a mixture of deoxygenated and oxygenated blood. So, the highest percentage of oxygen in the fetal circulation is in the umbilical vein, followed by the inferior vena cava.

The umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta for oxygenation.

Note:

In the umbilical cord, there are a pair of umbilical arteries and a single umbilical vein.

Mnemonic: AVA- artery –vein- artery(2 arteries and a single vein).

questions.question: A final year student is asked to give a seminar on 'fetal circulation.' Which among the following statement told by him in the seminar is likely to be false?
options: Heart receives blood with high oxygen saturation
Pressure in right and left ventricles are equal
Liver receives blood with low oxygen saturation compared to the brain
Blood in inferior venacava has lower oxygen concentration compared to superior venacava
questions.answer: D. Blood in inferior venacava has lower oxygen concentration compared to superior venacava
questions.explanation:
Blood in the inferior vena cava has a higher oxygen concentration compared to the superior vena cava.

The superior vena cava carries the deoxygenated blood from the upper part of the body to the right atrium. The highly oxygenated blood is carried to the fetus from the placenta via the umbilical vein with 50% of the umbilical venous blood entering the hepatic circulation and the rest bypassing the liver and joining the inferior vena cava (IVC) via the ductus venosus. Hence, the blood in the inferior vena cava has a higher oxygen concentration compared to the superior vena cava. Also, relatively a larger percentage of oxygen-rich blood is perfused to the brain.

Pressures in both the right and left ventricles are equal in a developing fetus. The upper part of the body is perfused exclusively by the left ventricle while the lower extremities are perfused by the right ventricle.

questions.question: The total fetal cardiac output at term is estimated to be_________ per minute.
questions.explanation:
The total fetal cardiac output at term is approximately 450 mL/kg/min.

Approximately 65% of descending aortic blood flow returns to the placenta, and hence, only the remaining 35% perfuses the fetal organs and tissues.

The clinical relevance of this 65% blood flow being directed to the placenta comes in the context of delayed cord clamping vs early cord clamping after delivery. Delayed cord clamping entails the umbilical cord is clamped more than one minute after the birth or when cord pulsation has ceased. This delayed clamping allows the blood flow between the placenta and neonate to continue and helps improve the iron status in the infant.

questions.question: During the evaluation of a newborn, you hear a continuous machinery murmur. Where would the structure responsible for the murmur ideally be located?
options: Just proximal to the left common carotid
Just distal to the left subclavian
Just distal to the left common carotid
Just proximal to the left subclavian
questions.answer: B. Just distal to the left subclavian
questions.explanation:
Continuous machinery murmur in a newborn is characteristic of Patent ductus arteriosus. Most commonly, the ductus arteriosus is just distal to the left subclavian artery and the ductus enters the pulmonary artery at its bifurcation.

The image attached below shows the relations of ductus arteriosus.

questions.question: You assist the delivery of a 3.1 kg healthy term neonate by spontaneous vaginal delivery. As the baby transitions from the fetal circulation, what is the sequence of functional closure of the following structures?
options: Ductus venosus --> Foramen ovale --> Ductus arteriosus
Ductus arteriosus --> Foramen ovale --> Ductus venosus
Ductus venosus --> Ductus arteriosus --> Foramen ovale
Ductus arteriosus --> Ductus venosus --> Foramen ovale
questions.answer: A. Ductus venosus --> Foramen ovale --> Ductus arteriosus
questions.explanation:
Functional closure of the fetal circulatory adjustments occurs in the following sequence: Ductus venosus --> Foramen ovale --> Ductus arteriosus

 Fetal circulatory adjustment
 Functional closure
Anatomical closure

Ductus venosus
After removal of the placenta from fetal circulatory unit
7 days

Foramen ovale

At birth - after breathing is initiated

Months to years

Ductus arteriosus
10–15 hours
10–21 days

questions.question: During the examination of a neonate with documented hearing defects and bilateral zonular cataracts, you hear a continuous machinery murmur. The mother gives a history of viral exanthem during the first trimester of the pregnancy. By when should the underlying defective channel that is responsible for the murmur anatomically close?
questions.explanation:
The given vignette is suggestive of Patent ductus arteriosus in a child with congenital rubella syndrome. The anatomical closure of the ductus arteriosus occurs at 10-21 days.

Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is the most common congenital heart disease associated with rubella, followed by pulmonary artery stenosis (PS). PDA presents with a continuous machinery murmur.

Triad of congenital rubella syndrome

• Sensorineural deafness

• Congenital heart defects – MC is PDA

• Cataracts

Classical rubella syndrome consists of:

• Ocular defects: Congenital cataract, salt and pepper chorioretinopathy, microphthalmos, Glaucoma, and anterior uveitis

• Ear defects: Sensorineural hearing loss due to destruction of organ of Corti

• Heart defects: Patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary stenosis, and ventricular septal defects

 Fetal circulatory adjustment
 Functional closure
Anatomical closure

Ductus venosus
After removal of the placenta from fetal circulatory unit
7 days

Foramen ovale

At birth - after breathing is initiated

Months to years

Ductus arteriosus
10–15 hours
10–21 days

questions.question: A newborn infant develops respiratory distress 2 days after birth. On examination, she is mottled and has weak upper extremity pulses and absent femoral pulses. Investigations reveal the coarctation of the aorta. Which of the following drugs can you use to keep the ductus open medically before surgical repair?
questions.explanation:
Alprostadil, a prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) analogue, can be used to keep the ductus open medically in the coarctation of the aorta.

The ductus arteriosus (the fetal connection between the pulmonary artery and the descending aorta) is functionally closed at 10-15hrs after birth and anatomically closed at 10-21 days after birth.

Survival of newborns with certain heart lesions such as coarctation of the aorta, hypoplastic left heart syndrome and transposition of great vessels depends on the patency of ductus arteriosus. Closure of PDA in such conditions can lead to hypoperfusion, severe hypoxia and cyanosis.

PGE1 is a potent and specific relaxant of ductal smooth muscle. PGE1 analogues like alprostadil, misoprost and rioprostil can be used to keep the ductus open and support systemic blood supply.

In patent ductus arteriosus, the ductus is closed medically by NSAIDS (which inhibit prostaglandin synthesis) like ibuprofen trometamol/ ibuprofen lysine and indomethacin. Morphine can be used to manage respiratory distress but rarely preferred in a neonate.

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman with G2P1 and an Rh-negative pregnancy gave birth to a baby with an Rh-positive blood group. The direct Coomb's test is positive. Cord blood bilirubin level is more than 4 mg/dL. The team plans for an isovolumetric and simultaneous double set up exchange transfusion. But the preferred vessel seems obliterated. This obliterated fibrotic vessel would now be called as?
questions.explanation:
The umbilical vein is the preferred vessel for an isovolumetric and simultaneous double set up exchange transfusion. The obliterated remnant of the umbilical vein is the Ligamentum teres.

The vessels that are occluded soon after birth are in due course replaced by fibrous tissue and forms the following ligaments:

Fetal structure
Adult structure

Foramen ovale
Fossa ovalis

Umbilical vein
Ligamentum teres

Ductus venosus
Ligamentum venosum

Umbilical arteries
Medial umbilical ligaments

Ductus arteriosus
Ligamentum arteriosum

The median umbilical ligament or Xander's ligament represents the remnant of the embryonic urachus.

The lateral umbilical ligaments are folds of the peritoneum over the inferior epigastric arteries.

Note:

Cord blood bilirubin level more than 4 mg/dL is an indication for change transfusion in a neonate.

questions.question: The most common mode of inheritance of congenital heart disease is_____.
questions.explanation:
The most common mode of inheritance of congenital heart disease is multifactorial.

Multifactorial inheritance refers to traits that are caused by a combination of inherited, environmental, and stochastic factors.

questions.question: As a medical officer working under the RBSK scheme, the commonest congenital heart disease you would encounter is __________.
questions.explanation:
Ventricular septal defect(VSD) is the most common congenital heart disease.

The prevalence of congenital heart disease is estimated at 6-8 per 1000 live births.

The relative frequency of major CHD: VSD > ASD = PDA > CoA = ToF

NOTE:

Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cyanotic heart disease.

questions.question: As an intern posted in the pediatrics department, you notice a neonate with jaundice and a characteristic blueberry muffin rash. The mother gives an antenatal history of fever with a rash in her first trimester. On examination, he has bilateral cataracts, hepatosplenomegaly, and a murmur on auscultation. BERA reveals sensorineural deafness. On cardiac evaluation, which of the following is least likely to be found?
questions.explanation:
The classical triad of cataract, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart disease point towards congenital rubella syndrome. Atrial septal defect (ASD) is not found in congenital rubella infection.

Prenatal exposure to rubella increases the risk of congenital heart defects like:

• Patent ductus arteriosus (Most common)

• Peripheral pulmonic stenosis

• Ventricular septal defect (VSD)

• Myocarditis

Nonspecific signs of TORCH infections are hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, jaundice, and growth restriction.

questions.question: A mother reports to you that her baby is irritable and cries all the time. She has also noticed that her infant sweats excessively while feeding. Which of the following findings noted during the examination would you not include under NADA's major criteria?
options: Grade 2 mid-diastolic murmur at the mitral area
Grade 3 pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border
questions.explanation:
Wide and variable S2 (Abnormal S2) is not included under Nada's major criteria.

Features of congestive cardiac failure, a grade 3 pansystolic murmur with wide and variable S2, and an MDM at the mitral area suggest a diagnosis of large VSD in this baby.

NADA's criteria for clinical diagnosis of congenital heart disease:

Major criteria
Minor criteria

Systolic murmur grade 3 or more
Systolic murmur < grade 3

Any diastolic murmur
Abnormal second sound (S2)

Cyanosis
Abnormal ECG

Congestive cardiac failure

Abnormal chest X-ray findings

Abnormal BP

The presence of 1 major or 2 minor criteria indicates congenital heart disease.

Pansystolic murmurs are always pathological no matter their intensity.

Short, soft systolic murmurs of intensity <3 are often detected during febrile illnesses, after which they disappear. Such murmurs are called innocent murmurs. Before labeling any murmur as innocent, it should be reassessed after an interval.

questions.question: The most common type of ventricular septal defect is ______.
options: A and B have equal prevalence
questions.explanation:
Membranous is the most common type of ventricular septal defect (VSD) to occur.

VSD is the most common congenital cardiac malformation.

Types of VSD include membranous (most common), muscular, inlet/atrioventricular canal defects, and supracristal defects.

Swiss Cheese septum: a special type of muscular VSD with defects in the mid-portion or apical region of the ventricular septum.

Restrictive VSD -A small VSD where the size of the lesion is usually <5 mm. It is associated with normal right ventricular pressure.

Non-restrictive VSD -A large VSD where the size of the lesion is usually >10 mm leading to equalization of pressures in the right and left ventricle.

questions.question: An infant born to a diabetic mother was diagnosed with a ventricular septal defect. On examination of the baby, all of the following features can be found except:
options: Ejection systolic murmur at the pulmonary area
Holosystolic murmur at the left 4th intercostal space
Reverse splitting of second heart sound (S2)
A mid-diastolic murmur at the mitral area.
questions.answer: C. Reverse splitting of second heart sound (S2)
questions.explanation:
Wide, variable splitting of S2 is a feature of VSD and not reverse splitting.

The basic defect in VSD is a left-to-right shunt which occurs at the ventricular level. During systole, the left ventricle empties into the aorta and the right ventricle via the VSD, because of which the total amount of blood in the right side of the heart increases, and that on the left decreases. Due to this increase, the right ventricle takes a longer time to empty causing a delayed P2 and on the other hand, the left ventricle empties sooner causing an early A2. This explains the wide S2. Variations due to respiration still happen and hence, the second heart sound is widely and variably split.

Auscultatory findings of VSD include a pansystolic murmur also known as Roger's murmur/shunt murmur can be best heard in the fourth left intercostal space. Flow murmurs that can be heard include, an MDM at the mitral area and an ejection systolic murmur at the pulmonary area.

A hyperdynamic precordium, a palpable P2, parasternal heave, a laterally displaced apical impulse, and a systolic thrill can be detected on palpation.

questions.question:
A mother is worried about her 4-month-old infant's growth. She says that her infant feeds slowly and often requires periods of rest during feeding. On examination:

Anthropometry: the weight for age is less than the 5th percentile.

Vitals: RR = 62/min, SpO2 -95%,

Palpation: P2 is palpable and the precordium is hyperkinetic.

Auscultation: A grade 3 pansystolic murmur in the left 4th intercostal space and a mid-diastolic murmur in the mitral area.

On a chest x-ray of the baby which of the following is least likely to be seen?
questions.explanation:
The above findings are suggestive of a large VSD with congestive cardiac failure. On a chest X-Ray of such a patient pulmonary oligemia is not seen.

“Suck- rest-suck cycle “, failure to thrive, high respiratory rate are features suggestive of congestive cardiac failure. Acyanosis, hyperdynamic precordium, palpable P2,pansystolic murmur, and MDM in the mitral area suggest a large VSD.

In ventricular septal defect (VSD), there is left to right shunting of blood, and this large volume of shunted blood passes through the lungs, which is recognized in the chest X-ray as pulmonary plethora (increased pulmonary vasculature). Other findings seen on a chest X-ray include cardiomegaly with left ventricular apex.

If the defect is large, frank pleural effusion can be seen.

Significant cardiomegaly, prominence of the pulmonary arterial trunk, pulmonary plethora (increased vascular markings seen in the lung fields) can be seen on the X-ray image.

questions.question: A 6-week-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for immunization. She has a loud and harsh holosystolic murmur best heard over the lower left sternal border and is accompanied by a thrill. The chest radiographs and EKG are normal. Echocardiography reveals a small muscular VSD. What is the appropriate management?
options: Wait and watch till 5 years and then operate
Restrict physical activity and operate at 2 years
questions.explanation:
In patients with small VSDs, parents should be reassured of the relatively benign nature of the lesion, and the child should be encouraged to live a normal life, with no restrictions on physical activity. Surgical repair is not recommended.

Guidelines from the Council on Cardiovascular Disease in the Young of the American Heart Association (AHA) state that an isolated, small, hemodynamically insignificant VSD is not an indication for surgery. VSDs may get smaller or close completely without treatment, but they won't get any bigger.

Echocardiography is used to estimate pulmonary artery pressure, screen for the development of Left ventricular outflow tract pathology (subaortic membrane or aortic regurgitation), and confirm spontaneous closure.

questions.question:
A good surgeon knows when not to operate. As a pediatric surgeon, on which of the following cases of VSD would you operate?

Case 1- A child with large VSD showing transient improvement in symptoms with better exercise tolerance.

Case 2 - A child with the presence of a mid-diastolic, low-pitched rumble at the apex.

Case 3- A 14-month-old child in whom clinical symptoms and failure to thrive cannot be controlled medically

Case 4- A 6-month-old baby with moderate to large defect associated with pulmonary hypertension, even if the symptoms are controlled by medication

Case 5 - An infant with severe pulmonary vascular disease unresponsive to pulmonary vasodilators
questions.explanation:
Severe pulmonary vascular disease unresponsive to pulmonary vasodilators is a contraindication to the closure of a VSD - due to permanent remodeling of the pulmonary vasculature.

Indications for surgical closure of a VSD include:

1. Patients at any age with large defects in whom clinical symptoms and failure to thrive cannot be controlled medically;
