2. Infants between 6 and 12 mo of age with moderate to large defects associated with pulmonary hypertension, even if the symptoms are controlled by medication; and patients older than 24 mo with a Qp: Qs ratio greater than 2: 1.

3. Patients with a supracristal VSD of any size are usually referred for surgery because of their higher risk for developing aortic valve regurgitation

A child with large VSD showing transient improvement in symptoms with better exercise tolerance may be the first sign of developing pulmonary hypertension and indicates an urgent need for evaluation and immediate surgery - the increased pulmonary pressure reduces the amount of blood pushed into the lungs and thereby, congestion transiently.

The presence of a mid-diastolic, low-pitched rumble at the apex is caused by increased blood flow across the mitral valve and usually indicates a Qp: Qs ratio ≥of 2: 1. This murmur is best appreciated with the bell of the stethoscope.

Surgical risks are somewhat higher for defects in the muscular septum, particularly apical defects and multiple (Swiss cheese–type) VSDs. These patients may require pulmonary arterial banding if symptomatic, with subsequent de-banding and repair of multiple VSDs at an older age.

questions.question: Rahel, a 3-year-old girl who is a known case of congenital heart disease is admitted to your pediatric ward because of low-grade fever with afternoon elevations. On examination, she is febrile and has painless small erythematous lesions on her palms. Her echocardiography showed oscillating intracardiac vegetation. Which one of the following congenital defects is most likely associated with the above findings?
questions.explanation:
The above findings are suggestive of a diagnosis of infective endocarditis according to Modified Duke’s criteria. Patients with high-velocity blood flow lesions such as ventricular septal defect (VSD) and aortic stenosis are at high risk for infective endocarditis.

To make a diagnosis of IE,she has evidence of endocardial involvement (1 major) and fever, predisposing heart condition, Janeway lesions(a painless small erythematous lesion on palms)- 3 minor criteria.

In VSD, a high-pressure gradient across the defect → turbulent blood flow → traumatizes the vascular endothelium → predisposition for infective endocarditis. Important complications of VSD include infective endocarditis and Eisenmengerisation,

High-risk cardiac lesions for which endocarditis prophylaxis is advised before dental procedures and invasive procedures like tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy are prosthetic heart valves, prior endocarditis, post-cardiac transplant, congenital heart disease(6 months post repair and unrepaired).

questions.question: A mother brings her 4-year-old child to the OPD. She says that the child has recurrent chest infections, easy fatiguability, and poor growth. You notice a limb abnormality as shown in the image below and find the given X-ray of the child's arm in his medical history. Based on all the findings, you suspect a congenital heart disease. Which of the following conditions are you most likely to find on screening echocardiography?
questions.explanation:
The X-ray of the upper limb shows radial ray defects (absent radius and thumb) and the family history of heart disease suggest a diagnosis of Holt-Oram syndrome (aka hand-heart syndrome). Out of all the syndromes associated with cardiac defects, HOLT- ORAM has the strongest familial tendency - it is inherited in an Autosomal dominant manner.
Holt–Oram syndrome/cardiac limb syndrome is most commonly associated with atrial septal defect (ASD).

Features of Holt-Oram syndrome include:

• Hypoplastic or absent thumbs, radii

• Triphalangism

• Phocomelia

• 1st-degree heart block

• ASD

questions.question: A child born to a 35-year-old mother was found to have a round face, flat occiput, and a protruding tongue. Karyotyping of the child is as shown below. Which of the following is commonly associated with this disorder?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical findings and the karyotyping suggest a diagnosis of Trisomy 21 or Down syndrome. The most common cardiovascular lesion in Down’s syndrome is an endocardial cushion defect.

Other associated defects are atrial septum defects (ASD), ventricular septum defect (VSD), and patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), aberrant subclavian artery, and pulmonary hypertension.

Other congenital defects are seen in some syndromes:

Syndrome
Congenital defect

Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
Endocardial cushion defect, VSD, ASD

XO (Turner syndrome)
Bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of aorta

William's syndrome
Supravalvular aortic stenosis, peripheral pulmonic stenosis

Noonan syndrome
Pulmonic stenosis, ASD

Holt–Oram syndrome
ASD, 1st-degree heart block

Marfan's Syndrome
Mitral or Aortic Regurgitation

questions.question: Which among the following is the most common type of atrial septal defect?
questions.explanation:
Ostium secundum ASD (labelled as 3) is the most common type of atrial septal defect (ASD), located at the mid-inter-atrial septum, in the region of the fossa ovalis.

ASD is characterized by an abnormal opening in the atrial septum allowing communication between the right and left atria. There are four types based on their location within the septum:

• Secundum ASD - most common, usually an isolated abnormality

• Primum ASD - associated with abnormal mitral valve leaflet (partial AV septal defect)

• Sinus venous - is located at the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium. Associated with anomalous right pulmonary venous return to the SVC or RA

• Coronary sinus type ASD - also called unroofed coronary sinus

Ostium primum ASD: is located at lower atrial septum

Endocardial cushion defect/An AV septal defect/ AV canal defect consists of contiguous atrial and VSDs with markedly abnormal AV valves. The lesion is common in children with Down syndrome.

Congenital conditions associated with ASD include:

• Down's syndrome - usually an ostium primum defect

• Holt-Oram syndrome - autosomal dominant disorder with upper limb bony defects and cardiac septal defects, commonly secundum ASD

• Ellis-van Creveld syndrome - chondroectodermal dysplasia associated with postaxial polydactyly and ASD

• Lutembacher syndrome - combined ASD and mitral stenosis due to rheumatic valvulitis

• Mitral valve prolapse

questions.question: A 6-year-old child was brought to her pediatrician for routine well-child care. Her physical examination is normal except for a systolic murmur and a widely split second heart sound that does not vary with respiration. She has no family history of heart disease. Which among the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The age of the patient, normal physical findings except for a systolic murmur, and wide and fixed splitting of S2 are all in favor of a diagnosis of Atrial septal defect.

Most ASDs are asymptomatic and are picked up during routine physical examinations. A soft ejection systolic murmur best heard over the left upper sternal border is also commonly found.
The soft ejection systolic murmur is a flow murmur heard due to increased blood flow through the normal pulmonary valve. A delayed diastolic murmur can also be heard in the tricuspid area. As the right ventricle now receives more blood, the time required for its emptying is increased resulting in prolonged P2. Since the two atria are linked, inspiration does not produce any net pressure changes between them abolishing respiration-related changes in venous return hence causing fixed S2.

Causes of Wide and fixed splitting of S2 include,

1. Atrial septal defect

2. RBBB

3. TAPVC

Other options:

TAPVC - patients usually present with cyanosis and congestive cardiac failure around 4-10 weeks of age - this is when the fetal pulmonary vasculature regresses and there is increased pulmonary blood flow which results in early-onset cardiac failure. The physical findings are identical to ASD.

VSD - is an acyanotic heart disease and physical findings include a pansystolic murmur best heard in the left 4th parasternal area and a wide and variable split S2 which is usually masked by the pansystolic murmur.

PS - is an acyanotic heart disease and physical findings include an ejection systolic murmur and a thrill in the left second interface and a wide and variable split S2 because of delayed closure of P2.

questions.question: A child who used to play for hours together now comes back home and says he gets tired too easily, his concerned mother brings him to you. On auscultation, you find that there is a wide and fixed splitting of the second heart sound, ECG shows left axis deviation and features of left ventricular hypertrophy. What is your probable diagnosis?
questions.answer: C. Ostium primum atrial septal defect
questions.explanation:
Wide splitting of the 2nd heart sound with left axis deviation (LAD) and left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) points to the diagnosis of ostium primum atrial septal defect (ASD). Wide-fixed splitting of the 2nd heart sound is characteristic of ASD.

In ostium primum ASD, the basic abnormality is the combination of left-to-right shunt across the atrial defect and mitral insufficiency due to mitral valve clefts. Mitral valvular insufficiency increases the volume load on the left ventricle (seen as LAD & LVH on ECG). When mitral insufficiency is severe enough to cause clinical symptoms like fatigue on exertion, the left atrium enlarges as a result of the regurgitant flow, and the left ventricle becomes hypertrophied and dilated.

questions.question: An ECG finding of right ventricular enlargement in a 2-year-old child is most consistent with which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation:
In atrial septal defect (ASD), there is a left-to-right shunt, resulting in increased blood flow through the right side of the heart, which leads to enlargement of the right atrium and ventricle and dilation of the pulmonary artery, the left atrium may also be enlarged, but the left ventricle and aorta are normal in size.

Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA): There is shunting of blood from the aorta to the pulmonary trunk, which goes into the lungs and then again to the LA and LV. If the ductus is large, left ventricular or biventricular hypertrophy is present.

In ventricular septal defect (VSD), there is shunting of blood from the left ventricle to the right ventricle, but most of the blood is shunted directly to the inflow tract of the pulmonary trunk, so, there is no significant right ventricular hypertrophy. In VSD, the pulmonary artery left atrium, and left ventricle are enlarged.

In Tricuspid atresia, there is right to left shunting of blood through an ASD as the tricuspid valve is dysfunctional due to which the entire systemic venous return enters the left side of the heart using the foramen ovale or through an ASD, and hence, there is left ventricular hypertrophy.

questions.question: During an outreach program, you incidentally discover a child with an asymptomatic ASD. His parents are anxious as they had read on the web about transcatheter device closure and want to know if their child needs one. Your advice is he does not require it, for now, but needs regular follow-up. During the course of follow-up, you would take up the child for transcatheter device closure immediately in all of the following instances except:
options: If the size of the defect is <5mm at 2 years of age.
If the Qp: Qs ratio is > 2:1
questions.answer: B. If the size of the defect is <5mm at 2 years of age.
questions.explanation:
An ASD defect of size <5mm at 2 years of age does not need immediate transcatheter device closure.
Small ASDs (3 to <6mm in diameter) may grow smaller or close spontaneously. They do not cause symptoms and usually only need observation.

Transcatheter device or surgical closure is advised for:

1. All symptomatic patients

2. Asymptomatic patients with a Qp: Qs ratio of at least 2: 1

3. Those with RV enlargement.

4. ASD size >8mm

Closure (if indicated) is recommended before school entry. Repair is preferred during early childhood because surgical mortality and morbidity are significantly greater in adulthood.

questions.question: As an obstetrician, you discover an atrial septal defect incidentally in a 20-year-old primigravida. You will be watchful about all of the following complications, except:
questions.explanation:
Infective endocarditis is extremely rare in isolated atrial septal defect (ASD) and antibiotic prophylaxis for isolated ASDs is not recommended.

ASD is a low-pressure gradient defect whereas a high-pressure gradient across a defect is required to create a turbulent flow, which traumatizes the vascular endothelium, making the patient susceptible to endocarditis.

Patients with a small or moderate ASD are asymptomatic unless a complication occurs. Pulmonary hypertension, atrial dysrhythmias, tricuspid or mitral insufficiency, and heart failure may initially appear during the increased volume load of pregnancy.

questions.question: In a NICU you examine a preterm baby, who has a loud, harsh, continuous, machinery murmur in the Gibson area. All of the following can be found, except:
questions.explanation:
A preterm baby with the classical continuous machinery murmur in the Gibson’s area is in favor of patent ductus arteriosus as the diagnosis. Preterm babies with patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) have wide pulse pressure, hyperdynamic precordium, and bounding peripheral pulses with a continuous murmur.

If the PDA is large, it can cause overloading of the left ventricle leading to cardiomegaly and congestive heart failure. Retrograde aortic flow, decreased systemic blood flow, and moderate hypotension is common in premature infants with a PDA predisposing them to necrotizing enterocolitis.

questions.question: You are posted as an intern in the pediatrics OPD and your professor asks you to examine an interesting case of cyanosis. On examination, you notice the bluish discoloration of the lower limbs but the upper limb and head are pink and on examination of the chest you see a parasternal heave and a thrill is palpable. These findings can occur in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Differential cyanosis can be seen in patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) when there is a reversal of shunt.

Differential cyanosis is manifested as cyanosis of only the lower extremities while upper extremities are unaffected. It is a result of reduced arterial oxygen saturation in the distal aorta compared to that in the aorta proximal to the left subclavian artery.

 It is seen with:

• right-to-left shunting across a ductus arteriosus in the presence of coarctation or an interrupted aortic arch

• patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) with severe pulmonary artery hypertension (PAH)

The rest of the options cause cyanosis of all extremities. Among the options, PDA is the only condition that can manifest with differential cyanosis when there is a reversal of shunt.

Image: Right to left shunting of blood flow through a PDA between the aortic arch and pulmonary artery.

questions.question: During neonatal resuscitation of a baby delivered via Cesarean section, you hear a continuous murmur. Which of the following would you not include in your differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Small ventricular septal defect (VSD) characteristically produces a loud, harsh, or blowing holosystolic murmur (not continuous murmur) and is heard best over the lower left sternal border; it is frequently accompanied by a thrill.

Pansystolic or holosystolic murmurs begin almost simultaneously with the 1st heart sound and continue throughout systole (do not spill into diastole like a continuous murmur).

Continuous murmur is a systolic murmur that continues or “spills” into diastole and indicates continuous flow, such as in the presence of a patent ductus arteriosus or other aortopulmonary communication.

Other options:

Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA): The classic continuous murmur is described as being like machinery in quality.

Aortopulmonary window: The findings can mimic those of a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) (wide pulse pressure and a continuous murmur).

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations: Large fistulas are associated with dyspnea, cyanosis, clubbing, a continuous murmur, and polycythemia, commonly associated with Osler Weber Rendu disease.

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy starts seizing while playing catch with his father. He is immediately brought to the casualty. On examination, blood pressure in the upper extremity measured as 200/140 mm Hg and femoral pulses were not palpable. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Here, the diagnosis is coarctation of the aorta because the classic sign of coarctation of the aorta is a disparity in pulsation and blood pressure in the arms and legs (as seen in this patient). The femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses are weak (or absent in up to 40% of patients), in contrast to the bounding pulses of the arms and carotid vessels. Seizure is a complication secondary to systemic hypertension since untreated coarctation can increase the risk for intracranial hemorrhage and hypertensive encephalopathy.

The most common site of coarctation of the aorta is distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery near the insertion of ligamentum arteriosum (juxtaductal coarctation).

DDx: Takayasu arteritis is a chronic vasculitis of unknown etiology, predominantly affecting women with an age of onset that is usually between 10 and 40 years. The disease primarily affects the aorta and its primary branches.

questions.question: A chest X-ray of a patient shows inferior rib notching. Which of the following diseases would you include in your differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Notching of the inferior border of the ribs (four to eighth ribs) from pressure erosion by enlarged collateral vessels is a characteristic finding in the coarctation of the aorta by late childhood.

Causes of rib notching

Superior rib notching
Inferior rib notching

Poliomyelitis

Osteogenesis imperfecta

Neurofibromatosis

Marfan's syndrome

Connective tissue diseases

• Rheumatoid arthritis

• Systemic lupus erythematosus

• Scleroderma

• Hyperparathyroidism

Coarctation of the aorta

Blalock–Taussig shunt

Superior vena cava obstruction

AV malformation of chest wall

Schwannoma

questions.question: What’s your diagnosis and which is the most common anomaly associated with reference to the X-ray given below?
options: Transposition of great vessels , renal dysplasia
Coactation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve
Transposition of great vessels, bicuspid aortic valve
questions.answer: B. Coactation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve
questions.explanation:
The given X-ray demonstrates the “3” sign, which is pathognomic of coarctation of aorta. Bicuspid aortic valve is commonly associated with coarctation of the aorta.

3 sign: Indentation of the aorta at the site of coarctation, pre and post-stenotic dilatation along the left paramediastinal shadow

Other Chest X-ray features in coarctation of aorta:

• Dilated left subclavian artery

• Dilated ascending aorta

• Notching of 3rd and 9th ribs due to rib erosion by dilated collateral vessels

10% of individuals with CoA have a circle of Willis aneurysm.

questions.question: You are called to see a cyanotic neonate in the NICU. You note that the neonate has an oxygen saturation of 60%. Which of the following would not be in your differential diagnosis
options: Ventricular septal defect with pulmonic stenosis
questions.explanation:
Given clinical scenario is suggestive of cyanotic congenital heart disease. Isolated infundibular stenosis would not be in the differential diagnosis because it is an acyanotic congenital heart disease.

Time of onset of cyanosis in congenital heart disease:

Congenital cyanotic heart disease
Time of onset of cyanosis

• Tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary atresia

• Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum

• Tricuspid Atresia

• Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome

• Dextro - Transposition of Great Arteries (TGA) - with Intact Ventricular Septum

• Severe Ebstein’s anomaly

1st few hours or days of birth

Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection
 Neonatal period

• Tetralogy of Fallot

• TGA with VSD and pulmonic stenosis

1st few months of life.

(Not at birth)

Truncus arteriosus

Minimal cyanosis at birth

Moderate cyanosis in 1-2months.

Ebsteins anomaly

Mild: teenage or young adult.

Severe: at birth

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease?
questions.explanation:
The most common cyanotic congenital heart disease is tetralogy of Fallot (ToF).

Infants are often asymptomatic until later in life (beyond 1yr of life).

TOF has 4 components:

• Obstruction to right ventricular outflow (pulmonary stenosis)

• Malalignment type of ventricular septal defect (VSD)

• Dextroposition of the aorta so that it overrides the ventricular septum (overriding of the aorta), and

• Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)

questions.question: Below is an X-ray of an infant with cyanotic heart diease. Which is not a finding seen here?
questions.explanation:
Cyanosis and boot-shaped heart (cœur en sabot in French) points towards tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) and the atrial septal defect is not a finding seen in TOF.

Clinical findings in TOF:

• Right ventricular hypertrophy causing left anterior hemithorax bulge.

• Single S2 or soft P2 because of the stenotic pulmonary valve

• Systolic thrill in the left sternal border in 3rd and 4th parasternal spaces.

• The large 'a' wave in the jugular pulse is a reflection of the forceful contraction of the right atrium at the end of diastole as there is reduced distensibility of the hypertrophic right ventricle.

• There is a loud and harsh systolic murmur due to the right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction. It becomes louder, longer, and harsher as obstruction increases in severity from mild to moderate.

• However in severe obstruction, especially during tet spell, the murmur becomes less prominent as the blood is shunted towards the aortic valve and not through RVOT.

X-Ray in TOF showing boot shaped heart:

Acyanotic/pink tetralogy of Fallot: This occurs when obstruction to the right ventricular outflow is mild to moderate. The blood would flow more through the mildly obstructed RVOT and less through the VSD. Hence, there is less cyanosis.

questions.question: A mother brings her 2-month-old blue baby to your pediatric clinic for the first time. Neonatal records were not available but the mother says that the X-ray of the baby looked like that of a shoe. Which of the following wouldn't you expect in this baby?
options: Large "a" waves in jugular venous pulse
questions.explanation:
The given history of the shoe (boot) shaped heart in cyanotic baby is suggestive of tetralogy of Fallot and cardiomegaly is not a part of TOF presentation.

In the tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), we see concentric right ventricular hypertrophy without cardiac enlargement. It is because of pulmonary stenosis (PS) and the ventricular septal defect (VSD). Any build-up of pressure in the right ventricle due to PS is released through VSD to the left ventricle.

Option A: P2 is of low intensity and soft because the right ventricular outflow obstruction results in reduced pulmonary artery pressure.

Option B: The aortic root usually appears large because it overrides (straddling) the VSD, allowing deoxygenated blood shunted from the right ventricle mixed with blood from the left ventricle to exit the heart.

Option D: The large 'a' wave in the jugular pulse is a reflection of the forceful contraction of the right atrium at the end of diastole as there is reduced distensibility of the hypertrophic right ventricle.

questions.question: A primary school teacher notices a peculiar behavior in one of her pupils. Whenever he plays with his friends, she notices that her fingers and lips turn blue. The child then squats for sometime after which he feels better. Which of the following does not occur during squatting?
options: It increases the systemic vascular resistance
It increases the magnitude of right-to-left shunt
Leads to trapping of deoxygenated blood in lower limbs
questions.answer: B. It increases the magnitude of right-to-left shunt
questions.explanation:
Squatting decreases the magnitude of the right-to-left shunt in a child with tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) .

The child feels comfortable while squatting due to two compensatory mechanisms:

• Increasing systemic vascular resistance and, thus, decreasing the magnitude of the right-to-left shunt across the ventricular septal defect (VSD). Therefore, more blood goes to the lungs for oxygenation.

• Trapping deoxygenated venous blood in the lower limbs.

questions.question: While waiting for corrective open-heart surgery, you decide to manage a case of tet spells medically. Which of the following drugs would worsen the cyanosis?
questions.explanation:
Isoprenaline/isoproterenol should be avoided in tet or hypercyanotic spells. It will cause a decrease in total peripheral resistance (TPR) or systemic vascular resistance (SVR). So, more blood leaves the left ventricle leading to the increased right to left shunt. This results in the worsening of right ventricular outflow and causes worsening of cyanosis and the symptoms.

Treatment of hypercyanotic spell involves placing child in knee–chest position (or squatting), and use of:

• oxygen

• morphine - sedates the patient

• sodium bicarbonate - to counteract metabolic acidosis that develops when arterial Po2 <40 mmHg

• alpha-agonists (phenylephrine)- vasopressor used in severe cases

• beta-blockers (propranolol)- improves resting saturation and decreases the frequency of spells.

Drugs that increase SVR, such as IV phenylephrine (alpha-1 agonist) or propranolol (non-selective beta-antagonist/beta-2 block), can improve right ventricular outflow, decrease the right-to-left shunt, and improve the symptoms. This is same principle as squatting.

questions.question: Blalock-Taussig shunt is done between_________.
questions.answer: A. Subclavian artery to pulmonary artery
questions.explanation:
Blalock–Taussig shunt is done between subclavian artery to pulmonary artery

Name of the surgery
 Connects

Blalock–Taussig shunt (BS)
Subclavian artery to pulmonary artery

Waterston's shunt (WA)
Ascending aorta to right pulmonary artery

Pott's shunt (PD)
Descending aorta to pulmonary artery

Blalock–Taussig shunt is currently the most common aortopulmonary shunt procedure and consists of a Gore-Tex conduit.

Sometimes, the shunt is brought directly from the ascending aorta to the main pulmonary artery; in this case, it is called the central shunt.

Corrective open-heart surgery performed in critically ill newborns and early infancy is the preferred surgical treatment now.

questions.question: Which of the following is a component of the pentalogy of Fallot?
questions.explanation:
Pentalogy of Fallot consists of

• Tetralogy of Fallot: Ventricular septal defect + Pulmonic stenosis + Overriding of the aorta + Right ventricular hypertrophy

• Atrial septal defect

questions.question: An adolescent who is a known case of VSD is brought by his parents with complaints of breathlessness on exertion which is gradually progressive, bluish discoloration, and swelling of toes and fingers. Investigations showed features suggestive of pulmonary hypertension. Which of the following is not a part of the condition?
questions.answer: D. Predominant left to right shunt
questions.explanation:
Given clinical scenario along with the development of pulmonary hypertension is seen in Eisenmenger’s syndrome and predominant right to left shunt (not left to right shunt) is seen here.

Gradual onset of cyanosis, dyspnoea, fatigue, and in later stages, heart failure, chest pain, headaches, syncope, and hemoptysis in a setting of congenital acyanotic heart disease, are signs and symptoms of Eisenmenger’s syndrome.

Reversal of the shunt at the level of atria/ventricles/patent ductus arteriosus due to irreversible pulmonary vascular obstructive changes is defined as Eisenmenger’s syndrome.

Features of pulmonary hypertension in Eisenmenger physiology: Right ventricular heave, narrow split S 2 with a loud pulmonic component.

Chest X-ray showing prominent pulmonary artery and right ventricle, peripheral pruning of pulmonary vessels.

ECG shows features of right ventricular hypertrophy, with spiked P waves.

Treatment: Calcium channel blockers, prostacyclin, and it's analog treprostinil and lung transplantation.

questions.question: The most common type of total anomalous pulmonary venous connection is _________.
questions.explanation:
The most common type of total anomalous pulmonary venous connection (TAPVC) is supracardiac.

In TAPVC, pulmonary veins instead of draining into the left atrium drain into the right atrium directly or indirectly.

• Supracardiac (most common): Common pulmonary vein drains into superior venacava or left innominate vein.

• Cardiac: Pulmonary veins drain into right atrium or coronary sinus.

• Infracardiac (always obstructive and most dangerous): Pulmonary veins drain into the hepatic vein or portal vein or inferior vena cava.

questions.question: A neonate was noted to have cyanosis of the oral mucosa. Chest x-ray revealed a snowman appearance of the cardiac silhouette. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.answer: D. Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection
questions.explanation:
Snowman's appearance on the chest X-ray image is classically seen in total anomalous pulmonary venous connection (TAPVC).

The supracardiac variant can classically depict a snowman appearance/figure of 8/cottage loaf heart on the frontal chest radiograph.

The dilated vertical vein on the left, brachiocephalic vein on the top, and the superior vena cava on the right form the head of the snowman; the body of the snowman is formed by the enlarged right atrium.

The image given above shows a snowman or figure-8 configuration. Cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascularity are evident.

questions.question: You are examining a week-old male infant who was severely cyanotic at birth in the post-operative ward. He has undergone balloon atrial septostomy following prostaglandin E1 administration. Post-surgery there was a marked improvement in cyanosis. The most likely diagnosis is______.
questions.explanation:
Cyanosis at birth, prostagladin E1 administration, and septostomy to improve oxygenation are typical features of transposition of great vessels (TGA).

TGA is characterized by the aorta arising from the right ventricle and pulmonary artery from the left ventricle. Since systemic and pulmonary circulations are separate, survival depends on the mixing of oxygenated pulmonary blood and deoxygenated systemic blood which can occur:

• At atrial level: Through atrial septal defect (ASD)

• At ventricle level: Through ventricular septal defect (VSD)

• At great vessel level: Through patent ductus arteriosus

Chest X-ray image shows cardiomegaly, a narrow mediastinum (the classic “egg-on-string appearance”), and normal to increased pulmonary blood flow. The narrow pedicle of the heart is because of the malposition of the great vessels.

Treatment: Here, prostaglandin E1 administration and septostomy help initial stabilization by creating a communication between the right and left atria, thereby facilitating the mixing of systemic and pulmonary circulations.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman with bipolar disorder on lithium therapy expresses intent to conceive. She must be advised to stop the drug due to the risk of development of which of the following conditions in the fetus?
questions.explanation:
She must be asked to stop the intake of lithium as it can cause an Ebstein anomaly in the newborn.

Ebstein anomaly is characterized by the downward displacement of the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which results in a thin-walled, low-pressure, “atrialized” segment of the right ventricle due to the anomalous attachment of the tricuspid leaflets.

Lithium can also cause macrocephaly as a teratogenic effect.

questions.question: Akshay, a high schooler presents to you with swelling of fingers and toes. He said he gets palpitations while he is exercising and even when he hangs out with friends. An X-Ray of the patient is given below. ECG showed the presence of delta waves. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The diagnosis is Ebstein's anomaly.

The presence of clubbing and a box-shaped heart on chest X-Ray in the given case is suggestive of Ebstein’s anomaly. Clubbing develops secondary to cyanosis as ebstein's anomaly is a right to left shunt. Delta wave is observed in Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome. WPW and supraventricular tachycardia causing palpitations can be seen in association with Ebstein’s anomaly.

questions.question: In a 13-year-old child with Ebstein's anomaly, echocardiography would likely reveal:
questions.explanation:
Tricuspid regurgitation would be seen in a child with an Ebstein anomaly.

Mild cases develop cyanosis during adolescence or early adulthood. In severe cases, cyanosis manifests at birth.

Ebstein anomaly is characterized by the downward displacement of the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which results in a thin-walled, low-pressure, “atrialized” segment of the right ventricle due to the anomalous attachment of the tricuspid leaflets.

In Ebstein's, tricuspid valve tissue is dysplastic and results in tricuspid regurgitation.

The right ventricle is hypoplastic, which leads to decreased pulmonary outflow and there will be functional pulmonary atresia. As a result, blood shunts through the foramen ovale/atrial septal defect (ASD) results in cyanosis at birth.

Himalayan P wave (amplitude > 5 mm) is associated with tricuspid atresia, Ebstein anomaly, and combined tricuspid and pulmonary stenosis, where they indicate a dilated right atrium. Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome (WPW) and supraventricular tachycardia may be present in Ebstein anomaly.

Note:

In Ebstein anomaly, the malformed tricuspid valve is usually regurgitant, but may rarely be stenotic.

questions.question: A cyanotic newborn is suspected of having congenital heart disease. He has an increased left ventricular impulse and a holosystolic murmur along the left sternal border. ECG shows left axis deviation and left ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Clinical cyanosis in combination with left-axis deviation (LAD) and left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) noted on the electrocardiogram distinguishes tricuspid atresia from most other cyanotic heart lesions.

Other points in favor:

• Increased left ventricular impulse (in contrast to most other causes of cyanotic heart disease, in which an increased right ventricular impulse).

• Holosystolic murmurs audible along the left sternal border (due to associated ventricular septal defect).

Tricuspid atresia is the congenital absence of the tricuspid valve. So, blood cannot flow directly from the right atrium to the right ventricle, and the following associated defects are necessary for survival:

• Patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect: for the flow of blood from the right atrium to the left atrium

• Ventricular septal defect: for the flow of blood from the left ventricle to the right ventricle

• There is a hypoplastic right ventricle.

Option B and D: Truncus arteriosus and tetralogy of Fallot and - The ECG demonstrates right axis deviation (RAD) and evidence of RVH.

Option A: Transposition of great arteries- ECG is usually normal, showing the neonatal right-sided dominant pattern.

questions.question: You are examining a case of cyanosis in NICU as a resident. Which of the following cardiac features would make the diagnosis of tricuspid atresia unlikely?
questions.answer: D. Left ventricular hypoplasia on echo
questions.explanation:
Left ventricular hypoplasia would make the diagnosis unlikely as right ventricular hypoplasia is seen in tricuspid atresia.

Other features of tricuspid atresia:

• An increased left ventricular impulse is noted in contrast to an increased right ventricular impulse seen in most other cyanotic diseases.

• A VSD holosystolic murmur is audible along the left sternal border.

• The second heart sound (S2) is usually single.

• Left ventricular hypertrophy and left axis deviation on ECG.

• Tall, peaked P waves on lead II known as Himalayan P waves which are suggestive of an enlarged right atrium.

questions.question:
Which of the following cases could develop recurrent infections due to pulmonary congestion?

(1) A 12-year-old ventricular septal defect

(2) Tetrology of Fallot in a 3-year-old child

(3) A toddler with tricuspid atresia.

(4) A 17-year-old with an atrial septal defect on echocardiogram.
questions.explanation:
Patients with atrial and ventricular septal defects have increased pulmonary blood flow. This results in recurrent pulmonary infection due to congestion in the lungs.

Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) and tricuspid atresia (TA) are associated with reduced pulmonary blood flow (oligemic lung fields). They do not cause pulmonary congestion and do not predispose to infections.

Reduced pulmonary blood flow is due to

• Right ventricular outflow obstruction in tetralogy of Fallot

• Right ventricular inflow obstruction in tricuspid atresia

Cyanotic congenital heart diseases (CCHD) with decreased and increased pulmonary blood flow:

Decreased pulmonary blood flow
Increased pulmonary blood flow

Tetrology of Fallot

Pulmonary atresia

Ebstein's anomaly

Tricuspid atresia with an intact ventricular septum

Transposition of the great vessels with VSD and pulmonary stenosis

Transposition of the great vessels with VSD or PDA

Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVC)

Truncus arteriosus

Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS)

questions.question: A cyanotic baby at the 8th hour of life is being evaluated in NICU. Pulse oximetry shows 80 % not improving with 100 % O2. Records show that continuous machinery murmur was heard at birth but not anymore. Which of the following can be done?
questions.explanation:
This baby has a cyanotic congenital heart disease that is dependent on a patent ductus arteriosus. Prostaglandin E1 infusion prevents the closure of PDA in term neonates with duct-dependent congenital heart disease (CHD).

Cyanosis failing to improve with 100% oxygen suggests an underlying cyanotic CHD.

Functional closure of the PDA occurs soon after birth, usually within first week of life.

The open PDA acted as a conduit between systemic and pulmonary circulations, thereby preventing the onset of cyanosis.

Upon its closure, cyanosis manifested in the baby as the blood could not be pumped into the lungs for oxygenation. Deoxygenated blood is being shunted into the systemic circulation after the closure of PDA. Hence, you should maintain the patency of the duct with PGE1 infusion until surgery can be done.

Duct-dependent lesions: Anomalies, in a newborn with CHD, which are dependent on the patency of ductus arteriosus for survival.

• Right-sided lesions (Tetralogy of Fallot, PA/PS) cannot pump blood to the lungs. These patients are dependent on an open PDA for pulmonary circulation.

• Left-sided lesions (Hypoplastic left heart syndrome, Aortic stenosis, Coarctation of aorta) cannot pump blood into the systemic circulation. These patients are dependent on open PDA for systemic circulation.

questions.question: Below is the chest X-ray image obtained for a neonate on day 7 of life who developed heart failure later. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The classic "egg on end" appearance on this chest X-ray image is seen in the transposition of great arteries (TGA).

In the chest X-ray image, cardiomegaly with narrow mediastinum gives rise to the classic “egg-shaped heart.” The superior mediastinum appears narrow due to the anteroposterior relationship of the transposed great vessels and the radiologic absence of the thymus.

questions.question: Hematuria in children is defined as the presence of at least ______ RBCs per high power field in uncentrifuged urine.
questions.explanation:
Hematuria in children is defined as the presence of at least 5 RBCs/HPF (high power field) in uncentrifuged urine.

When using commercially available dipsticks (capable of detecting 3-5 RBCs / HPF of urine), the presence of 10-50 RBCs/μL suggests an underlying pathology.

False-negative results can occur in the presence of

• Formalin

• High urinary concentrations of ascorbic acid

False-positive results, on the other hand, may be seen

• With alkaline urine (pH > 8)

• Contamination with oxidizing agents such as hydrogen peroxide (used to clean the perineum before obtaining a specimen)

questions.question: An 11-year-old child was brought to the hospital by his mother with complaints of multiple episodes of passing blood in the urine. Which of the following condition is not associated with this symptom?
questions.explanation:
Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) presents with acute-onset microscopic hematuria not recurrent gross hematuria.

Causes of recurrent gross hematuria:

• Alport’s syndrome: hereditary nephritis

• Thin glomerular basement membrane disease

• IgA nephropathy: Berger’s disease

• Idiopathic hypercalciuria/hyperuricosuria

• Sickle cell nephropathy (papillary necrosis)

questions.question: A 6-year-old girl with urinary complaints was brought to the hospital by her parents. On further enquiry, they mention a history of skin lesions 5 weeks back. Low C3 levels are found during her investigations. Immunofluorescence microscopy reveals a “lumpy-bumpy” pattern of immunoglobulin and complement deposits on the glomerular basement membrane. Which of the following is not typically associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Urinary complaints with a history of skin lesions (pyoderma) point towards a likely diagnosis of glomerulonephritis. Results of complement study and immunofluorescence microscopy also correlate with this diagnosis. Frothy urine is due to proteinuria, which is a feature of nephrotic syndrome.

Classic features of nephritic syndrome/glomerulonephritis:

• Cola coloured urine (hematuria)

• Oliguria

• Hypertension

• Facial or body edema

questions.question: Akshay, accompanied by his father, presents to the OPD with complaints of cola-coloured urine and facial puffiness for 3 days. He has a history of fever with a sore throat that resolved 2 weeks back. Which of the following findings is consistent with the diagnosis of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
options: C3 level increases and ASO level increases
C3 level decreases and ASO level increases
C3 level decreases and ASO level decreases
C3 level increases and ASO level decreases
questions.answer: B. C3 level decreases and ASO level increases
questions.explanation:
C3 level decreases and ASO level increases in acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).

Acute PSGN is a classic example of an acute nephritic syndrome characterized by the sudden onset of gross hematuria, oedema, hypertension, and renal insufficiency. It follows infection of the throat or skin by certain nephritogenic strains of group A β-hemolytic streptococci-

• 1 to 2 weeks after an antecedent streptococcal pharyngitis or

• 3 to 6 weeks after streptococcal pyoderma

questions.question: Which of the following is not a characteristic feature of hematuria associated with glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation:
Hematuria associated with glomerulonephritis is typically painless.

Hematuria from within the glomerulus is often associated with brown-, cola-, or tea-colored urine. Urine analysis reveals RBC casts and deformed urinary RBCs (particularly acanthocytes).

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy presents with decreased urine output for 3 days. He has a history of sore throat 2 weeks back. On examination, he is hypertensive with pitting pedal oedema. The diagnosis is concluded as post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Which of the following is true about this condition?
options: Renal biopsy is indicated in severe impairment of renal function.
questions.answer: D. Renal biopsy is indicated in severe impairment of renal function.
questions.explanation:
The given clinical vignette of oliguria, pedal edema and hypertension point towards glomerulonephritis. Severe impairment of renal functions in a background of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is an indication for renal biopsy.

Indications for renal biopsy in glomerulonephritis:

• Presence of acute renal failure or nephrotic syndrome

• Absence of evidence of streptococcal infection

• Presence of normal complement levels

• Persistence of hematuria and proteinuria, diminished renal function, and/or a low C3 level for more than 2 months after the disease onset

Serum triglycerides (Option A) are elevated in nephrotic syndrome, not in nephritic syndrome.

The acute phase generally resolves within 6 to 8 weeks. Although urinary protein excretion and hypertension usually normalize by 4-6 wk after onset, microscopic hematuria (Option B) can persist for 1 to 2 years after the initial presentation.

The serum C3 level (Option C) is significantly reduced in >90% of patients in the acute phase, and returns to normal 6-8 weeks after onset.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old boy with a previously diagnosed renal disorder is brought to your OPD with the following reports for a second opinion. What is the likely diagnosis?

Light microscopy: Enlarged, pale glomeruli.
Electron microscopy: Subepithelial humps.
questions.explanation:
The findings mentioned are characteristic of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).

Findings in PSGN:

• Light microscopy: Enlarged, pale glomeruli with diffuse mesangial proliferation and an increase in the mesangial matrix. Polymorphoneutrophil (PMN) infiltration in the early stages.

• Immunofluorescence: “Lumpy-bumpy” deposits of immunoglobulin and complement on the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) and in the mesangium.

• Electron microscopy: Electron-dense deposits, or “humps,” are observed on the epithelial side of the GBM.

 The image given below depicts the microscopic picture of PSGN. It shows glomerular hypercellularity due to intracapillary leukocytes. Neutrophilic infiltration is present and is marked with purple hematoxylin stain (black arrows).

Other options:

Idiopathic rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis:

• Light microscopy: Crescents develop in several forms of glomerulonephritis (are a characteristic response to the deposition of fibrin in Bowman’s space)

• Electron microscopy: No deposits

Focal segmental glomerulonephritis:

• Light microscopy: Focal sclerotic lesions

• Electron microscopy: Foot process fusion

Minimal change disease:

• Light microscopy: Normal

• Electron microscopy Effacement of foot process

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy presented with cola-coloured urine, decreased urine output, and facial puffiness for 3 days. He had a history of skin infection 4 weeks back. On examination, he is found to be hypertensive. His serum C3 levels are low and ASO levels are increased. What is the appropriate step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
The features of hematuria, oliguria, facial oedema present with a history of skin infection points towards the diagnosis of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). Results of complement study and ASO levels also support this diagnosis. Supportive conservative therapy is the best step in the management of PSGN.

Management of PSGN is directed at treating the acute effects of renal insufficiency (sodium restriction and prescribing diuretics - usually with intravenous furosemide) and hypertension.

Although a 10-day course of systemic antibiotic therapy with penicillin is recommended to limit the spread of the nephritogenic organisms, antibiotic therapy does not aﬀect the natural history of acute PSGN.

Note: Steroids and cyclosporine are not used in the management of PSGN.

questions.question: Sarthak, a 7-year-old boy, was brought to the emergency department by his parents with complaints of blurred vision and severe headache since today morning. They mentioned an episode of fits 2 hours back following which they rushed him to the hospital. On further enquiry, it was elicited that the child had decreased urine output for 5 days with cola coloured urine. He was hypertensive with bilateral pitting pedal oedema. The doctor remembered that Sarthak has a glomerular disorder warranting him multiple prior ward admissions and his existing condition could be a possible complication of the same. All of the following are commonly seen as a complication of this disorder except-
questions.explanation:
The given features of oliguria, hematuria, pedal edema and hypertension are likely of glomerulonephritis. The complication of hypertensive encephalopathy is seen in this case due to symptoms of seizure, blurred vision and severe headache. Hyperkalemia and left ventricular failure are also common complications of glomerulonephritis while bleeding diasthesis is not a complication of glomerulonephritis.

Acute complications of glomerulonephritis result from hypertension and acute renal dysfunction-

• Hypertension is seen in 60% of patients and is sometimes associated with hypertensive encephalopathy and intracranial bleeding.

• Acute renal failure can occur, which may require treatment with dialysis.

Other potential complications include the following:

• Heart failure

• Hyperkalemia

• Hyperphosphatemia

• Hypocalcemia

• Hyponatremia

• Acidosis

• Seizures

• Uremia

questions.question: A 9-year-old boy presents with gross hematuria 2 days after an episode of diarrhoea. The serum C3 levels are normal. Light microscopy demonstrates focal and segmental mesangial proliferation and increased mesangial matrix in the glomerulus. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Gross hematuria following a gastrointestinal infection, associated with normal C3 levels, in a male patient is suggestive of immunoglobulin A nephropathy (Berger nephropathy).

• IgA nephropathy is the most common chronic glomerular disease in children.

• Focal and segmental mesangial proliferation and increased mesangial matrix are seen in the glomerulus.

• It is characterized by a predominance of IgA within mesangial glomerular deposits in the absence of systemic disease.

• It is seen more often in males.

• Gross hematuria occurs within 1-2 days of onset of an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection (in contrast to the long latency period observed in acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis).

• It can be associated with loin pain.

• Normal serum levels of C3 in IgA nephropathy (help to distinguish this disorder from PSGN).

• Serum IgA levels have no diagnostic value because they are elevated in only a few paediatric patients.

questions.question: A child developed dark coloured urine and flank pain 2 days after an upper respiratory tract infection. The physician suspects IgA nephropathy. What is the location of cellular injury in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The location of cellular injury in IgA nephropathy (Berger nephropathy) is the deposition of IgA antibodies in the mesangial cell.

Mesangial cells are directly exposed to the circulation; therefore, they are affected in diseases characterized by the deposition of immune complexes.

Mesangial cell diseases:

• IgA nephropathy

• IgM nephropathy

• Mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis

• Class II lupus nephritis

• Diabetic nephropathy

Note: In IgA nephropathy gross hematuria often occurs within 1-2 days of onset of an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection. In contrast, a longer latency period of about 1-2 weeks is observed in acute postinfectious glomerulonephritis.

questions.question: ANCA-positive , pauci-immune glomerulonephritis include-
questions.explanation:
Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA)-associated vasculitis is categorized into 3 distinct forms:

• Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA; formerly Wegener granulomatosis)

• Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA)

• Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, formerly called Churg–Strauss syndrome (CSS)

Kidney biopsies typically demonstrate crescentic glomerulonephritis with little or no immune complex deposition.

ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) comprises a group of multi-systemic diseases affecting small-to-medium-sized vessels. It is characterized by the presence of ANCA with specificity for either proteinase-3 (PR3) or myeloperoxidase (MPO).

Absence or paucity of immune complex deposits in vessel walls is very characteristic, hence the name “pauci-immune vasculitis.”

questions.question: An 8-year-old girl presented with complaints of cough, hemoptysis and swelling of both legs. Urinalysis was notable for hematuria and proteinuria. Serum anti-GBM antibodies were positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The diagnosis is Goodpasture disease (anti-GBM antibody disease). Anti–glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibodies are diagnostic.

"Goodpasture syndrome" is characterized by pulmonary haemorrhage and glomerulonephritis and "Goodpasture disease" is used for those patients with glomerulonephritis, pulmonary hemorrhage, and anti-GBM antibodies. It is caused due to autoantibodies directed against type IV collagen, which is present in the alveoli and glomerular basement membrane. Currently, the preferred term for both conditions is “anti-GBM antibody disease”.

Other options along with the pathogenesis of glomerular diseases:

• IgA nephropathy- mesangial cell disease due to immune complex deposition

• Minimal change disease- epithelial cell disease due to flattening of podocytes

questions.question: A 9-year-old boy has swelling of knee joints and non-blanching rashes as seen in the picture. Urine examination reveals hematuria +++ and proteinuria +. Microscopic analysis of his renal biopsy specimen is most likely to show which of the following finding?
questions.explanation:
The boy in this clinical scenario has characteristic features of Henoch–Schonlein purpura (HSP).

The renal biopsy in this patient will show mesangial proliferation with mesangial deposition of IgA

• HSP is a common small-vessel vasculitis in childhood.

• It is characterized by a purpuric rash and commonly accompanied by arthritis and abdominal pain.

• About half the patients with HSP develop renal manifestations, which vary from asymptomatic microscopic hematuria to severe, progressive glomerulonephritis.

• The nephritis associated with HSP usually follows the onset of the rash

• The pathogenesis of HSP nephritis appears to be mediated by the deposition of polymeric immunoglobulin A (IgA) in glomeruli.

questions.question: All are features of Alport syndrome except-
questions.explanation:
Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (not conductive hearing loss) is a feature of Alport syndrome (AS).

AS or hereditary nephritis is a genetic disease (most have X-linked inheritance) caused by mutations in the genes coding for type IV collagen, a major component of the basement membranes.

Clinical features of Alport syndrome:

• Hematuria: All patients have asymptomatic microscopic hematuria. Recurrent episodes of gross hematuria may be seen 1-2 days after an upper respiratory infection.

• Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (not conductive)

• Ocular abnormalities: anterior lenticonus, macular flecks, corneal erosions

• Proteinuria: Progressive proteinuria, often exceeding 1 g/ 24 hrs, is common by the 2nd decade of life.

questions.question: A 16-year-old boy presented with dark coloured urine. Urinalysis was notable for macroscopic hematuria and heavy proteinuria. His father is a known case of Alport syndrome. What defect is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
A defect in type IV collagen, a major component of the basement membrane, is responsible for Alport syndrome.

Alport syndrome is a genetically heterogeneous disease, 85% is X-linked and the rest may be autosomal recessive or autosomal dominant.

questions.question: All of the following syndromes are associated with renal disease except _______.
questions.explanation:
Sinding–Larsen–Johansson syndrome is an insertional periostitis at the inferior pole of the patella (not associated with Renal disease).

Lowe syndrome

Oculocerebrorenal syndrome: Hypotonia, renal disease

Denys–Drash Syndrome

Associated with Wilm's tumor:

Early-onset renal failure with renal mesangial sclerosis, male pseudohermaphroditism

Alport syndrome
Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, renal disease

Sinding–Larsen–Johansson syndrome
Periostitis at the inferior pole of the patella

questions.question: Microalbuminuria is defined as a urinary albumin excretion rate of _______.
questions.explanation:
Microalbuminuria is defined as a urinary albumin excretion rate of 30–300 mg/24 hrs.

Here, the presence of albumin in the urine is above the normal level but below the detectable range for the urine-dipstick methods. It is commonly associated with glomerular hyperfiltration and blood pressure elevation.

In adults, persistent microalbuminuria indicates diabetic nephropathy and is also a predictor of cardiovascular and renal disease.

In children, microalbuminuria is associated with obesity and predicts the development of diabetic nephropathy in type 1 diabetes mellitus.

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy presents with facial puffiness and frothy urine. Upon investigating, his urine was positive for proteins with no hematuria and no RBC casts. To conclude the diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome, the range of proteinuria is defined as >_____ mg/m2/hr and urine protein:creatinine ratio of >________.
questions.explanation:
The currently accepted definitions of “nephrotic range proteinuria” include:

• Urine protein: creatinine ratio > 2

• Urine protein > 40 mg/m2/hr

• Urine protein 3+ or 4+ in dipstick test

As a consequence of the large urinary loss of protein, the patient develops hypoalbuminemia (< 2.5 g/dL) and gross edema.

questions.question: It is expected to see all of the following clinical features in a 5-year-old boy with nephrotic syndrome except-
questions.explanation:
Hematuria is not a usual feature of nephrotic syndrome. It is a feature of nephritic syndrome. However, occasionally it is seen in the FSGS variant of nephrotic syndrome as well.

Classic features of nephrotic syndrome:

• Nephrotic range proteinuria ( >40mg/m2/hr urine protein: creatinine ratio >2)

• Hypoalbuminemia (<2.5 g/dL)

• Edema

• Hyperlipidemia (cholesterol > 200 mg/dL)

• Hypercoagulability

questions.question: What is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children?
questions.explanation:
The commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children is minimal change disease. (85% of cases).

The glomeruli appear almost normal on microscopy, hence the name. Immunofluorescence microscopy are negative, and electron microscopy shows effacement of the epithelial cell foot processes.

Treatment: Steroids; 95% of patients respond.

Other options:

• Membranous nephropathy is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in the elderly; it is a rare cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.

• Alport syndrome or hereditary nephritis: All patients have asymptomatic hematuria; progressive proteinuria is common only by the 2nd decade of life and can be severe enough to cause nephrotic syndrome. This nephrotic syndrome is not common in children.

• IgA nephropathy presents more commonly as an acute nephritic syndrome or with asymptomatic hematuria. It presents with nephrotic syndrome quite rarely.

questions.question: A 5-year-old child was brought to the hospital with complaints of progressive swelling around the eyes, abdomen and feet for 2 weeks. On investigating, his urine was positive for 4+ proteinuria with absent hematuria. A spot urine protein: creatinine ratio was reported to be 2.5. His serum albumin was 2.3 g/dL and serum creatinine was 0.5 mg/dL. Serum cholesterol and triglyceride levels were also elevated. A diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome was concluded. Which of the following correctly mentions the aetiology of its most common variant in children?
questions.explanation:
Nephrotic syndrome is concluded as the diagnosis here because of the symptoms of anasarca and proteinuria. A spot urine protein:creatinine ratio >2, low serum albumin levels, and hyperlipidemia marked by high cholesterol and triglyceride levels, further add to this diagnosis. Minimal change disease is the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and constitutes 85% of all paediatric cases. The etiology is due to the flattening of foot processes (podocytes) of epithelial cells (seen on electron microscopy). This finding is marked in the image given below.

• Here, the glomeruli appear normal or show a minimal increase in mesangial cells and matrix.

• It is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.

• Epithelial cells, in conjunction with the basement membrane, allow the filtration of plasma solutes but block the passage of cells and plasma proteins. Hence, this epithelial cell disease, disrupts the filtration barrier, resulting in proteinuria.

• More than 95% of children with minimal change disease respond to corticosteroid therapy.

Causes of epithelial cell injury:

• Minimal change disease

• Membranous nephropathy

• Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

• Class V lupus nephritis

• Diabetic nephropathy

questions.question: Which of the following is not a cause of hypercoagulability in nephrotic syndrome?
options: Vascular stasis due to hemoconcentration and intravascular volume depletion
Increase in hepatic production of fibrinogen
Urinary loss of antithrombin III and protein S
questions.answer: D. Decreased platelet number and aggregability
questions.explanation:
Increased (and not decreased) platelet number and aggregability cause hypercoagulability in nephrotic syndrome.

Hypercoagulability in nephrotic syndrome is due to all of the following factors:

• Vascular stasis due to hemoconcentration and intravascular volume depletion

• Increase in hepatic production of fibrinogen

• Urinary loss of antithrombin III and protein S

• Increased platelet number and aggregability

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy presents with facial oedema that has now progressed to total body swelling involving the face, abdomen, scrotum, and feet. Urinalysis revealed protein 4+ and serum cholesterol was also elevated. What is the initial treatment of choice?
questions.explanation:
The clinical picture and investigations are highly suggestive of minimal change nephrotic syndrome and the initial treatment of choice is corticosteroids such as prednisolone.

Minimal change nephrotic syndrome is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome. It is seen in ages 2-6 years with a clinical picture of nephrotic syndrome, that is, heavy proteinuria, oedema, hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. They may be asymptomatic or can present with peripheral oedema. Renal biopsy is not required for confirmation and treatment can be initiated if the child fits the standard clinical picture of nephrotic syndrome.

They show excellent response to steroid therapy with prednisone or prednisolone. A daily dose of 2mg/kg (max 60mg) for 6 weeks followed by an alternate dose of 1.5mg/kg (max 40mg) for the next 6-8 weeks is recommended.

Alternative drugs used in steroid-dependent patients, frequent relapsers, steroid-resistant patients, and those with severe corticosteroid toxicity are as follows:

• Cyclophosphamide

• Calcineurin inhibitors: Cyclosporine and Tacrolimus

• Mycophenolate

• Levamisole

• Rituximab (chimeric monoclonal antibody against CD20)

questions.question: Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome is defined as failure to achieve remission after _____ weeks of corticosteroid therapy.
questions.explanation:
Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome is defined as failure to achieve remission after 6 weeks of corticosteroid therapy.

According to the latest Indian Society of Pediatric nephrology(ISPN) guidelines, it is defined as the absence of remission despite 6-weeks therapy with prednisolone at daily dose of 60mg/m2

questions.question: Congenital nephrotic syndrome is defined as nephrotic syndrome manifesting ______.
options: At birth or within 3 months of life
At birth or within 6 months of life
At birth or within 1 year of life
questions.answer: B. At birth or within 3 months of life
questions.explanation:
Congenital nephrotic syndrome is defined as nephrotic syndrome manifesting at birth or within 3 months of life.

It may be

• Primary: Due to inherited disorders caused by mutations in NPHS 1, NPHS 2, WT1, or LAMB2.

• Secondary: Due to in utero infections like cytomegalovirus infection, toxoplasmosis, syphilis, HIV infection, hepatitis B virus or hepatitis C virus HCV infection, infantile systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), or mercury exposure.

questions.question: An 11-year-old boy with a chronic hepatitis B infection develops nephrotic syndrome. What would be the most likely pathology encountered in renal biopsy of this child?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario suggests that the pathology would be membranous nephropathy. Membranous nephropathy can be secondarily caused by Hepatitis B infection.

Membranous nephropathy:

Membranous nephropathy is a rare cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.

• It is classified as the primary, idiopathic form, where there is an isolated renal disease, or secondary, where nephropathy is associated with other identifiable systemic diseases or medications

• In children, secondary form is far more common. The most common etiologies of secondary form are systemic lupus erythematosus or chronic infections. Among the latter, chronic hepatitis B infection and congenital syphilis are the best characterized and recognized causes.

questions.question: Finnish-type congenital nephrotic syndrome is caused by a mutation in the _____ gene.
questions.explanation:
Finnish type congenital nephrotic syndrome is a steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome caused by a mutation in the nephrin gene (NPHS 1).

• Affected infants usually present at birth with edema caused by massive proteinuria.

• They are delivered with a large placenta (>25% of the infant’s weight).

• There is severe hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, and hypogammaglobulinemia.

• Prenatal diagnosis can be made by elevated maternal and amniotic α-fetoprotein levels.

questions.question: FSGS is caused by mutations in the _____ gene.
questions.explanation:
• focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is caused by mutation in NPHS2 (podocin) gene.

• Steroid resistant nephrotic syndrome is usually caused by FSGS (in 80% of cases).

• In FSGS, glomeruli show lesions of mesangial cell proliferation and segmental scarring that are both focal (present only in a proportion of glomeruli) and segmental (localized to ≥1 intraglomerular tufts).

• FSGS is associated with a 50% risk for end-stage kidney disease.

questions.question: During her antenatal ward rounds, an intern noticed a USG report indicating the presence of just one kidney in the fetus. Which of the following association would be expected to be seen in the baby?
questions.answer: D. Presence of single umbilical artery
questions.explanation:
The presence of a single umbilical artery can be expected to be seen in the case of a baby with unilateral renal agenesis.

Renal agenesis occurs secondary to a defect of the Wolffian duct, ureteric bud, or metanephric blastema. It is often discovered during the course of an evaluation for other congenital anomalies (VACTERL syndrome). Its incidence is increased in newborns with a single umbilical artery. The contralateral kidney undergoes compensatory hypertrophy. Some children also have contralateral vesicoureteral reﬂux. Most males have an ipsilateral absent vas deferens.

NOTE:

VACTERL syndrome - Vertebral defects, imperforate Anus, Congenital heart disease, Tracheo-Esophageal fistula, Renal and Limb defects

questions.question: A 10-month-old female is brought to the clinic with a 102° F fever for 2 days. The mother says that she also cries during urination. The history is significant for similar episodes in the past which were treated with antibiotics. Urine analysis shows nitrite-positivity and gram-negative bacteria are seen on urine microscopy. Which of the following anomaly is most commonly associated with this child's condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of recurrent urinary tract infection. The most common anomaly associated with this condition in children is vesicoureteral reflux (VUR).

VUR usually is congenital and often familial. It is more common in females. It occurs when the submucosal tunnel between the mucosa and detrusor muscle is short or absent.

The image below shows VUR grading

questions.question: A pediatrician suspects vesicoureteric reflux in a girl with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections. What is the investigation of choice to confirm this condition?
questions.explanation:
Voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) is the investigation of choice for vesicoureteral reflux.

Recurrent febrile urinary tract infections in a child should raise the suspicion of an anatomical defect like vesicoureteric reflux as the cause. Compared to other investigations, a VCUG provides more anatomic information. It can demonstrate:

• Vesicoureteral reflux

• Duplex collecting system

• Ectopic ureter

• Paraureteral (bladder) diverticulum

• Bladder outlet obstruction

• Signs of voiding dysfunction, such as a spinning top urethra

questions.question: Which of the following is the first-line imaging investigation done in a child presenting with an episode of UTI?
questions.explanation:
In a child presenting with an episode of urinary tract infection (UTI), initial imaging should be ultrasonography of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder.

A voiding cystourethrogram is indicated only if the ultrasound study is abnormal, the patient has atypical features or after a recurrent febrile UTI.

DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) scan may be done after 4–6 months of acute infection as it may help to locate and delineate the scarring

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of urinary tract infection in children?
questions.explanation:
Urinary tract infections in children are most commonly caused by the following:

• Escherichia coli (Most common)

• Klebsiella species

• Proteus species

• Staphylococcus saprophyticus

• Enterococcus

• Adenovirus and other viral infections (cause cystitis and gross hematuria)

questions.question: A mother is concerned that her 1-year-old daughter has been having repeated episodes of UTI since birth. The pediatrician ordered a voiding cystourethrogram, which revealed reflux of urine into the upper collecting systems without any dilation. Under which grade of vesicoureteral reflux will this presentation be classified?
questions.explanation:
Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) severity is graded according to the appearance of the urinary tract on a contrast voiding cystourethrogram.

It is classified into 5 grades (Grade I to V):

Grading of vesicoureteral reﬂux:

• Grade I- VUR into a non-dilated ureter

• Grade II- VUR into the upper collecting system without dilation

• Grade III- VUR into the dilated ureter and/or blunting of calyceal fornices.

• Grade IV- VUR into a grossly dilated ureter

• Grade V- Massive VUR, with significant ureteral dilation and tortuosity and loss of the papillary impression.

questions.question: Ashi, a 12-year-old girl presented with features of hematuria, headache, and blurring of vision. Her past history is significant for recurrent UTI. On examination, she was found to have a BP of 150/110 mmHg. Investigations revealed mild renal scarring and urine analysis showed broad casts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Posterior urethral valve with chronic renal failure
Reflux uropathy with chronic renal failure
questions.answer: D. Reflux uropathy with chronic renal failure
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of reflux uropathy with chronic renal failure.

The pathogenesis of vesicoureteral reflux is as follows:

Loss of renal parenchyma and renal scarring reduces renal function significantly. This renal insufficiency leads to renin-mediated hypertension and further progresses to end-stage renal disease.

Reﬂux nephropathy remains a common cause of hypertension in children.

Broad casts or renal failure casts are associated with end-stage renal disease.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of abdominal mass in neonates?
questions.explanation:
Multicystic dysplastic kidney (MCDK) is the most common cause of an abdominal mass in the newborn but is mostly non-palpable at birth.

In most cases, it is discovered incidentally during prenatal sonography. In some patients, the cysts are identified prenatally, but the cysts regress in utero, and no kidney is identified on imaging at birth. MCDK is usually unilateral and generally not inherited, unlike polycystic kidney disease (PKD). Contralateral hydronephrosis is present in 5-10% of patients.

questions.question: Komal, a high school student developed a fever after she came back from a trip with her friends. She also complained about pain while urinating. She says she has been having these episodes frequently for the past few years. Her father and her grandfather are a known case of cystic kidney disease. Her urine analysis is indicative of UTI with hematuria. Renal ultrasound was done and its findings are shown below. Which of the following chromosomes are associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
The presence of multiple cysts seen on the ultrasound(image) along with a positive family history point towards the diagnosis of autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease. Chromosomes 16 and 4 are associated with this condition.

Autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease inheritance:

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is not associated with the lesion seen in the image?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows a horseshoe kidney. It is not associated with the posterior urethral valve.

Horseshoe kidney is the most common congenital anomaly of the kidneys.

Horseshoe kidney is caused due to the fusion of the lower poles of the kidney. The lower border of the kidneys usually lie in front of L3 vertebra due to arrest of ascent.

The common associations of horseshoe kidney are:

• Vesicoureteral reflux

• Wilms tumor

• Multicystic dysplastic kidney

• Turner’s syndrome

questions.question: A 3 yr old male child with left flank pain is diagnosed to have an acute UTI. On USG, the left ureter was found to be duplicated. The most probable site of the opening of ectopic ureter will be?
questions.explanation:
Opening of the ectopic ureter in male (most to least common) :

• Posterior urethra (prostatic) above the external sphincter

• Seminal vesicle

• Prostatic utricle

• Ejaculatory duct

• Vas deferens

questions.question: A newborn is being evaluated for anuria. Imaging reveals renal agenesis and pulmonary hypoplasia. The delivery was complicated due to oligohydramnios. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A newborn infant with anuria, renal agenesis, and pulmonary hypoplasia, with a history of oligohydramnios, is suggestive of Potter's sequence

Potter's sequence is characterized by the triad of:

• Renal agenesis

• Oligohydramnios

• Pulmonary hypoplasia

Option B: Pierre–Robin syndrome: micrognathia, retrognathia, glossoptosis.

Option C: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: It can present with pulmonary hypoplasia but other features like renal agenesis, anuria will not be seen.

Option D: CHARGE syndrome: Coloboma of the eye, Heart anomaly, choanal Atresia, Retardation, Genital and Ear anomalies.

questions.question: Antenatal hydronephrosis due to PUJ obstruction is defined as the anteroposterior diameter of the renal pelvis of more than _____ in the third trimester.
questions.explanation:
Anteroposterior diameter of the renal pelvis of >7 to 7.5 mm in the third trimester denotes antenatal hydronephrosis due to pelvic ureteric junction (PUJ) obstruction.

Definition of antenatal hydronephrosis by anteroposterior diameter:

questions.answer: D. Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease
questions.explanation:
Hepatic and periportal fibrosis is associated with autosomal-recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD)
