questions.question: Ask-Upmark kidney refers to ________
questions.explanation:
The Ask-Upmark kidney is also termed segmental hypoplasia.

Renal segmental hypoplasia:

• Severe segmental renal atrophy with loss of parenchymal elements in small kidneys is commonly known as segmental hypoplasia.

• It refers to small kidneys, usually weighing not more than 35 g.

• The scars are seen as cortical depressions overlying shrunken medullary pyramids and their dilated calyces, and they are characterized histologically by colloid-filled tubular microcysts and a paucity or absence of glomeruli.

• Most patients are 10 years or older at diagnosis and have severe hypertension.

• Nephrectomy usually controls the hypertension.

questions.question: A 20-year-old primigravida was rushed to the OT for an emergency caesarean section. Her pregnancy was unplanned and she did not take folic acid supplementation prior to conception. Moreover, owing to the pandemic led lockdown and her remote residence, she could not adhere to regular antenatal care. The newborn was born with a neural tube defect and immediately shifted to the NICU. What is the least likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Holoprosencephaly is not a neural tube defect (NTD) and hence, it is the least likely diagnosis. Folic acid deficiency, especially in a young primigravida, is a risk factor for the development of NTDs in children, as seen in the given clinical vignette.

NTDs result from the failure of the neural tube to close spontaneously between the 3rd and 4th week of in utero development. These can be detected in antenatal ultrasound scans and subsequently managed for a better prognosis. The major NTDs include the following:

• Spina bifida occulta

• Meningocele

• Myelomeningocele

• Encephalocele

• Anencephaly

• Syringomyelia

• Diastematomyelia (split spinal cord)

• Iniencephaly

In holoprosencephaly, the forebrain fails to develop into two hemispheres due to mutations in the sonic hedgehog gene at the long arm of chromosome 7. It is a developmental disorder of the brain that results from the defective formation of the prosencephalon and the inadequate induction of the forebrain structures. The three types include, alobar, semilobar, and lobar, apart from the middle interhemispheric fusion variant or syntelencephaly.

The image given below shows alobar holoprosencephaly-

questions.question: A 27-year-old pregnant woman underwent second-trimester screening and had an abnormal presence of a biochemical marker. Following this, she went to a tertiary care referral centre for further investigations. An anomaly scan revealed cranial lemon and cerebellar banana signs. What is the abnormal marker present in this condition?
questions.explanation:
In the given clinical scenario, the presence of abnormal sonographic markers, like the lemon and banana sign, is highly suggestive of neural tube defects (NTDs). Acetylcholinesterase is used as a biochemical marker of neural tube defects during the screening tests.

NTDs account for the largest proportion of congenital anomalies of the CNS. The failure of closure of neural tube allows excretion of fetal substances such as α-fetoprotein (AFP) and acetylcholinesterase into the amniotic fluid thereby serving as biochemical markers for NTDs.

The lemon and banana sign, noted on antenatal imaging, are one of the many notable fruits' inspired signs. The banana sign refers to the shape of the cerebellum owing to caudal displacement while the lemon sign refers to the lemon-shaped head resulting from scalloping of the frontal bones. It is seen in fetuses with open neural tube defects.

The image below shows the characteristic lemon sign on ultrasound-

The image below shows the characteristic banana sign on ultrasound-

Note:

Pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A (PAPPA), inhibin A, and human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) are the biochemical markers of trisomy 21 (Down's syndrome).

questions.question: A child is scheduled for myelomeningocele surgery. Until the patient is waiting for surgery, the covering of the sac will be protected by a gauze soaked in______.
questions.explanation:
Until the time of surgery, the sac of myelomeningocele has to be covered with a sterile gauze soaked in normal saline. This is to prevent drying and trauma to the sac. As the normal saline is less irritant to the sac, it is preferred.

Note:

Surgery is done as early as possible (within a day of birth).

questions.question: A 28-year-old pregnant woman was rushed to the casualty of a maternity hospital due to imminent delivery. It resulted in a stillborn baby as shown in the picture below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows an occipital bone defect with retroflexion of the neck and trunk, which is typical of iniencephaly. Inion is the tip of the external occipital protuberance and this defect comes under the spectrum of neural tube defects.

Diastematomyelia (Option A) is a congenital disorder in which a part of the spinal cord is split, usually at the level of the upper lumbar vertebra.

Craniorachischisis (Option B) is the anencephaly associated with a continuous bony defect of the spine and exposure of neural tissue.

Holoprosencephaly (Option D) occurs when the procencephalon fails to develop into two hemispheres.

questions.question: An infant is brought to the OPD with complaints of multiple episodes of vomiting that is more in the morning and relieved when sitting. She has an unusually large head with bulging fontanelles. The image of the child showing a characteristic sign is given below. Which of the following is not a cause of the communicating variant of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The clinical features of frequent vomiting, large head, bulging fontanelles, and a positive sunset sign (as seen in the image) point to a likely diagnosis of hydrocephalus. A vein of Galen malformation can expand to become large and, because of its midline position, obstruct the flow of CSF, thereby causing an obstructive or non-communicating hydrocephalus. Vomiting is more in the morning and becomes better when sitting due to poor absorption of CSF in a lying down position.

Hydrocephalus is not a specific disease; it represents a diverse group of conditions that result from impaired circulation or absorption of CSF.

Causes of hydrocephalus:

Communicating (external/non-obstructive)
Non-communicating (internal/obstructive)

• Achondroplasia (raised ICP due to jugular foramen stenosis)

• Choroid plexus papilloma

• Meningeal malignancy

• Meningitis

• Posthemorrhagic

• Sarcoidosis

• Aqueductal stenosis

• Arnold-Chiari malformation

• Dandy–Walker malformation

• Klippel–Feil syndrome

• Tumours and neurocutaneous disorders (astrocytoma)

• Vein of Galen malformation

questions.question: Shreya, a 2-year-old girl, presented with irritability for 2 days. On examination, macrocephaly, hypotonia and spasticity were present with a positive head transillumination test. She started walking independently at 18 months and became dry by day a month before her 2nd birthday. An MRI-brain revealed cystic expansion of the fourth ventricle and midline cerebellar hypoplasia. What is the most likely diagnosis explaining her obstructive hydrocephalus?
questions.explanation:
The features of hydrocephalus like irritability along with macrocephaly, hypotonia and spasticity indicate a likely diagnosis of Dandy-Walker syndrome. A positive transillumination test is present in this syndrome. The child has developmental delay especially in motor and cognitive milestones because normally children walk independently at 12-13 months and become dry by day around 18 months.

The Dandy-Walker malformation consists of a cystic expansion of the fourth ventricle in the posterior fossa and midline cerebellar hypoplasia. It results from a developmental failure of the roof of the fourth ventricle during embryogenesis. Most of the affected patients have hydrocephalus, agenesis of the posterior cerebellar vermis, and corpus callosum. Brisk tendon reflexes, spasticity, clonus, Babinski sign, cerebellar ataxia, and delayed motor and cognitive milestones are seen in this. Management is by shunting if hydrocephalus is present.

The image below shows a sagittal section of the magnetic resonance tomography scan of a patient with Dandy-Walker syndrome.

questions.question: A 6-month-old baby presented with fever, poor feeding, and frequent vomiting. On examination, the head circumference was 46.5cm with a positive sunset and Macewen sign. Which of the following infections is associated with the most common cause of the underlying neurological disease in this child?
questions.explanation:
Symptoms of poor feeding and frequent vomiting with signs of enlarged head circumference and a positive sunset and Macewen sign(crack-pot resonance) points toward a diagnosis of hydrocephalus. Aqueductal stenosis is the most common cause of hydrocephalus. Out of the above options, mumps infection can cause stenosis of the cerebral aqueduct.

Mumps is associated in a child with aqueductal stenosis because-

• Mumps virus is neurotropic and is thought to enter the CNS via the choroid plexus and infect the choroidal epithelium and ependymal cells.

• CNS complications of mumps include meningitis, meningoencephalitis (most commonly manifests 5 days after the parotitis), transverse myelitis, aqueductal stenosis, and facial palsy.

questions.question: A 9-month-old baby presented with seizures, developmental delay and failure to thrive. Following an MRI, a diagnosis of a neuronal migration disorder was made. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, schizencephaly is a neuronal migration defect. MRI is the study of choice for elucidating schizencephaly and associated malformations.

Neuronal migration is the process during brain development, where the neuronal cells migrate to their proper designated site by various mechanisms, to form the 6-layered cerebral cortex. Any abnormality in the above process leads to neuronal migration defects.

Neuronal migration defect includes the following:

• Schizencephaly: (schiz = split or cleavage) It is the presence of unilateral or bilateral clefts within the cerebral hemispheres. The patient can be severely intellectually challenged, with microcephaly, seizures, and spastic quadriparesis.

The image below shows schizencephaly:

• Lissencephaly (agyria): It is the absence of cerebral convolutions. Rather than the normal 6 layers of the cortex, there may be fewer layers. The child will have developmental delay, microcephaly, and seizures.

The image below shows lissencephaly:

Myelomeningocele (Option B) is a neural tube defect that occurs due to defective closure of the neural tube.

Lhermitte–Duclos disease (Option C) is the cerebellar dysplasia leading to focal enlargement of cerebellum and macrocephaly, cerebellar signs, and seizures.

Plagiocephaly (Option D) is the asymmetry and flattening of the skull of the child, due to extrinsic moulding forces (consistent sleeping on the same side of the head).

questions.question: During a telemedicine consultation, you come across a case of a 9-year-old child with a previously diagnosed autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome known as tuberous sclerosis. Which one of the following is not seen in it?
questions.explanation:
Ependymomas are not seen in tuberous sclerosis. Neurocutaneous syndromes like tuberous sclerosis are a group of disorders with abnormalities in both the integumentary system and the CNS (defect of primitive ectoderm). They include the following:

• Neurofibromatosis

• Tuberous sclerosis

• Sturge–Weber syndrome

• von Hippel–Lindau disease

• Ataxia telangiectasia

Tuberous sclerosis is caused due to mutation of genes coding for hamartin (chromosome 9) and tuberin (chromosome 16), which leads to the formation of hamartomas.

Clinical features:

• CNS

• CNS involvement is the hallmark of tuberous sclerosis.

• Glioneuronal hamartomas (cortical tubers).

• Subependymal nodules are lesions found along the wall of the lateral ventricles, where they undergo calcification.

• Subependymal giant cell astrocytomas (SEGAs) are the characteristic brain tumours. These benign, slow-growing tumours arise in the periventricular area.

• White matter lesions are common and include nodules, cysts, and areas of gliosis and hypomyelination.

• Skin

• Facial angiofibroma (adenoma sebaceum)

• Periungual fibroma

• Shagreen patch

• Confetti skin lesions

• Others

• Renal angiomyolipoma

• Cardiac rhabdomyoma

questions.question: During rounds in the neurology ward, an 11-year-old child is observed with the following lesion on his back. Which of the following characteristic skin manifestation of tuberous sclerosis is depicted in this picture?
questions.explanation:
The lesion seen in the picture depicts a shagreen patch. This is a characteristic skin lesion found in patients with tuberous sclerosis. It consists of a roughened, raised lesion with an orange-peel consistency, located primarily in the lumbosacral region. Shagreen is shark skin used as a decorative material present in the image of the question.

Skin lesions in tuberous sclerosis:

• The typical hypomelanotic ash leaf–type macules on the trunk and extremities are seen in 90% of the patients. It is visualized by the use of a wood ultraviolet lamp.

• Facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum) develop between 4 and 6 years of age; they appear as tiny red nodules over the nose and cheeks and are sometimes confused with acne. Later, they enlarge, coalesce, and assume a fleshy appearance.

• Periungual fibroma are small fibromas or nodules of skin, which form around fingernails or toenails in some adolescent patients.

• Confetti skin lesions are seen less commonly as a minor feature of tuberous sclerosis.

questions.question: A 3-year-old child is rushed to the emergency department because of an episode of fits associated with uprolling of eyes and high fever. Kernig’s sign is negative and there are no post-ictal neurological deficits. There is a history of a similar episode when the child had a fever due to gastroenteritis. Which of the following is false regarding this type of seizures?
options: Likelihood of developing epilepsy is low
Associated with temperature of 38°C or higher
Antipyretics reduce the risk of recurrent febrile convulsions
Absence of having a developmental delay
questions.answer: C. Antipyretics reduce the risk of recurrent febrile convulsions
questions.explanation:
This is a probable case of febrile seizures due to the presence of high fever, no post-ictal deficits and a negative Kernig's sign ruling out meningitis. Antipyretics do not reduce the risk of recurrent febrile seizure, as the seizure often occurs as the temperature is rising or falling abruptly.

Febrile seizures are seizures that-

• Occur between the age of 6 months and 5 years

• Occur at a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher

• Are not due to any CNS infection or any metabolic imbalance

• Occur without a history of prior afebrile seizures

• Occur with no post-ictal neurological deficit.

Types of febrile seizures:

Simple febrile seizures
Complex (atypical) febrile seizures

Occurs within 24 hours of the onset of fever
Can occur at any time during a fever

Generalized seizures
Focal seizures

Duration is <15 min
Prolonged

No recurrence within 24 hrs of seizures
Recurrent

Chances of going into epilepsy 1%
Chances of going into epilepsy 6%

Investigations:

• Lumbar puncture should be performed in the first episode of seizures with fever, for all infants <6 months age (to exclude meningitis).

• EEG and neuroimaging are advised for children with atypical febrile seizures.

Treatment:

Antipyretics and proper hydration. Midazolam or diazepam (rectal) can be used if seizures present.

Prophylaxis:

• Intermittent prophylaxis: If the febrile seizures are 3 or more in 6 months, or 4 or more seizures in 1 year, oral clobazam (1mg/kg/day) for 3 days during the fever episode.

• Continuous prophylaxis: If intermittent prophylaxis fails or in recurrent atypical febrile seizures, sodium valproate and phenobarbitone can be used.

questions.question: Your neighbour, Sheila, frantically knocks on your door to seek help as her toddler had suddenly started convulsing with uprolling of eyes. The child had a high fever and this was his third episode of seizures in 6 months. Post-recovery, Sheila is still anxious and wishes to know the risk factors for such recurrences of febrile seizures. You would explain all of the following except-
questions.explanation:
Early age of onset (age <1 year) is a risk factor for recurrence of febrile seizures. The other risk factors for such recurrences are as follows:

Major:

• Age <1 yr

• Duration of fever <24 hr

• Fever 38-39°C

Minor:

• Family history of febrile seizures

• Family history of epilepsy

• Complex febrile seizure

• Male gender

• Lower serum sodium at the time of presentation

questions.question: A child presents with developmental delay and multiple seizure types. The seizures could not be controlled by an array of drugs. Electroencephalogram (EEG) shows 1-2 Hz spike and slow waves with polyspike bursts in sleep. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A child with features of developmental delay, intractable seizures and an electroencephalogram (EEG) showing 1-2 Hz spike and polyspike bursts in sleep has a likely diagnosis of Lennox–Gastaut syndrome.

Lennox–Gastaut syndrome- Typically starts between the age of 2 and 10 years. Consists of a triad of:

• Developmental delay

• Multiple seizure types (includes atypical absences, myoclonic, astatic, and tonic seizures)

• EEG findings 1-2 Hz spike and slow waves, polyspike bursts in sleep, and a slow background in wakefulness

Patients will have long-term cognitive impairment and intractable seizures despite multiple therapies. The drug of choice for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is valproate. Other drugs used for this condition are clobazam, lamotrigine, rufinamide and topiramate.

Other options:

Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (Janz syndrome)- Typically, it starts in early adolescence (not in childhood) and the EEG usually shows generalized 4-5 Hz polyspike and slow-wave discharges

Landau–Kleffner syndrome- A rare condition characterized by loss of language skills in a previously normal child (not a child with developmental delay)

West syndrome- Starts between the ages of 2 and 12 months and typical EEG picture is called hypsarrhythmia (high-voltage, slow with chaotic background)

Disease
Typical EEG features
Drug of choice

Lennox–Gastaut syndrome
1-2 Hz spike and polyspike bursts in sleep
Valproate

Absence seizures
3 Hz spike and slow-wave (spike and dome pattern)
Ethosuximide

Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
4-5 Hz spike polyspike and slow-wave discharges
Valproate

Hypsarrhythmia (high-voltage waves with chaotic background
Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)

questions.question: Which of the following is true for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome?
options: Constitutes of a single seizure type
Good prognosis and adequate controlled epilepsy
EEG showing slow (<3Hz) spike and wave discharge
questions.answer: D. EEG showing slow (<3Hz) spike and wave discharge
questions.explanation:
Lennox–Gastaut syndrome is associated with 1-2 Hz spike and slow-wave discharges.

• Typically starts between the ages of 2 and 10 years

• Consists of a triad of developmental delay, multiple seizure types (that as a rule includes atypical absence seizures, myoclonic, astatic, and tonic seizures) and specific EEG abnormalities.

• Most are left with long-term cognitive impairment and intractable seizures despite multiple therapies.

• Lennox–Gastaut syndrome has a poor prognosis

questions.question: A concerned kindergarten teacher calls up the mother of one of her students who was having transient lapses of consciousness. The teacher elaborated that the child was having multiple episodes of staring blankly into space for a few seconds before quickly returning to alertness. Following investigations including an EEG, a diagnosis of atypical absence seizures was made. Which of the following is a feature of it?
options: Associated with head drop during seizure
EEG shows 3Hz spike and slow wave pattern
questions.answer: A. Associated with head drop during seizure
questions.explanation:
Atypical absence seizures have associated myoclonic components and tone changes of the head (head drop) and body.

Absence seizures (typical)
Atypical absence seizures

No change in the body tone
Change in the tone of the head (head drop) and body.

Precipitated by hyperventilation
Precipitated by drowsiness

3 Hz spike and slow wave pattern on EEG
1-2 Hz spike and slow wave pattern on EEG

Usually not associated with other syndromes
Associated with Lennox–Gestaut syndrome

questions.question: Harish had a panic attack when he was called to recite a poem on the stage. This was followed by a sudden lapse in consciousness and manifested as a blank stare along with fluttering of eyes. He appeared frozen without any change in the body tone. Which of the following is a characteristic feature of this condition on electroencephalography (EEG)?
options: Waves at the rate of 10/ sec
questions.answer: B. 3 Hz spike and slow wave
questions.explanation:
The features of a lapse of consciousness precipitated by hyperventilation (panic attack), without any change in the tone of the body (head drop), point towards a likely diagnosis of petit mal or typical absence seizures. The electroencephalogram (EEG) in petit mal seizure is associated with a 3 Hz spike and slow-wave discharges.

Features of petit mal seizures (typical absence seizures):

• Starts abruptly in childhood (6 to 8 years)

• Approximately 25% of patients also develop generalized tonic-clonic seizures.

• Characterized by brief lapses of consciousness and sudden discontinuation of activity with staring spell, eye fluttering, or rhythmic movements

• No loss of postural control or incontinence

• No post-ictal confusion.

Hyperventilation for 3-5 min can precipitate the seizures. The drug of choice is ethosuximide.

Image: EEG waveform for an absence seizure- 3 waves per second, with spike and slow-wave pattern

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy was playing at his crèche centre when he suddenly developed rapid jerky movements of both the upper and lower limbs and was rushed to the emergency department. It had been ongoing for the past 10 minutes and the boy had been unresponsive throughout. Which of the following is not useful in the management of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario is that of status epilepticus. This is due to rapid jerky movements causing continuous seizure activity for more than 5 minutes. Carbamazepine is not commonly used in the treatment of status epilepticus.

Status epilepticus is defined as continuous or recurrent seizure activity lasting for more than 5 minutes without regaining consciousness. The image given below depicts the management of this condition in a flowchart-

questions.question: A 15-year-old girl presented with episodes of brief involuntary muscular twitching that causes her to drop her toothbrush or teacup in the morning. Following investigations including an EEG, a diagnosis of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy was made. Which of the following is not a feature of it?
questions.answer: D. EEG shows 1-2 Hz spike waves.
questions.explanation:
In juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, EEG characteristically shows 4-5 Hz polyspike and slow-wave discharges.

Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (Janz syndrome):

• It is the most common generalized epilepsy in young adults ( 12-18 years).

• They are benign generalized myoclonic seizures with a good prognosis.

• They commonly affect the upper limbs more than the lower limbs and sometimes cause the dropping of objects.

• Typically, it starts in early adolescence (12-18 years), with 1 or more of the following manifestations:

• Myoclonic jerks in the morning (“shock-like” contraction of a muscle, that is often repeated), generalized tonic-clonic or clonic seizures upon awakening; and juvenile absences.

• Sleep deprivation, alcohol (in older patients), and photic stimulation provoke seizures.

• The EEG usually shows generalized 4-5 Hz polyspike and slow-wave discharges.

• The drug of choice for juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is valproate. Lamotrigine is also useful.

questions.question: A 7-month-old boy presents with brief episodes of head drops and flexion of the body, followed by tonic extension of arms and legs. These movements last 1 to 2 seconds and occur in several clusters per day, with 15 to 30 spasms per cluster. EEG is given below and is suggestive of infantile spasms. Which of the following is the drug of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
The drug of choice for infantile spasms is adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). The EEG shows a specific type of abnormal chaotic brainwave pattern called hypsarrhythmia. It is characterized by continuous, high-amplitude, asynchronous delta activities with interspersed independent, multiple spikes. Hypsarrhythmia on EEG can occur even between attacks.Excessive corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) production is hypothesized to cause infantile spasms. ACTH administration suppresses CRH secretion and hence controls the seizures.

Infantile spasms (West syndrome)

• Age of onset is 3–8 months of life

• Characterized by salaam spells (sudden dropping of the head or flexion of arms, followed by tonic extension of arms and legs) and hypsarrhythmia on EEG.

• Causes include hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, neurocutaneous syndromes, and idiopathic.

• Drug of choice: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), Vigabatrin.

questions.question: An 8-month old male child presented with delayed motor milestones. He was born at 28 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 1200 grams. A diagnosis of cerebral palsy is made following investigations. An MRI scan of the brain revealed periventricular leukomalacia. Which of the following subtypes of cerebral palsy is most likely in this child?
questions.explanation:
The most likely subtype in this child with delayed motor milestones and a history of prematurity and low birth weight is spastic diplegia. This is because the most common sequelae of periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) is spastic diplegia. PVL is the ischemia of white matter adjacent to the lateral ventricles of the brain.

Cerebral palsy

It is a group of disorders, affecting movement or posture, due to non-progressive disturbances occurring in the developing fetal brain. These could be due to hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. The most common subtype of cerebral palsy is spastic diplegia.

Cerebral palsy subtype
Pathology

Spastic diplegia
Periventricular leukomalacia

Spastic quadriplegia
Parasagittal brain injury

Spastic hemiplegia
Middle cerebral artery territory infarction

Dyskinetic cerebral palsy
Basal ganglia

questions.question: A newborn presented with high-grade fever, poor feeding and incessant cry for the last 2 days. Multiple episodes of vomiting are present as well. On examination, hypotonia is present along with weak reflexes. The patient is admitted and during rounds, subtle lip-smacking seizures are also observed along with a vacant stare. CSF examination shows reduced glucose, increased protein, and increased leukocytes with predominant neutrophils. Which of the following organism is unlikely to cause this condition?
questions.explanation:
The acute features of fever, poor feeding, incessant cry, vomiting and seizures points toward a likely diagnosis of neonatal meningitis. The CSF findings correlate with that of bacterial meningitis due to purulent appearance, increased proteins, decreased glucose and a predominance of polymorphs. Neonatal meningitis is not caused by Neisseria meningitidis because, in neonates, bacteria are often acquired from the maternal vaginal flora.

The common causes of acute bacterial meningitis:

Age group
Organism

Neonates
Group B streptococci, Escherichia coli, Listeria

Infants and children

Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae

Adolescents and young adults
S.pneumoniae, N. meningitidis

questions.question:
During your PICU rotation, you are assigned a bedside case of a child with fever, convulsions, and signs of meningeal irritation. On browsing through his file, you find a lumbar puncture report mentioning the following findings. What is the likely diagnosis?

1000 cells/µL, 90% PMNL

questions.explanation:
Fever, convulsions, and signs of meningeal irritation (nuchal rigidity, Kernig's sign, Brudzinski's signs) in a child, with CSF showing reduced glucose, increased protein, and increased leukocytes levels is a typical presentation of bacterial meningitis.

questions.question: Asif, a young child with previously diagnosed tuberculosis, is brought to your hospital for further management. Examination reveals a characteristic finding as present in the image. What do you expect in the cranial CT of this child?
options: Focal involvement of the temporal lobe
questions.explanation:
A history of tuberculosis along with a positive Kernig's sign (as seen in the image) is suggestive of tubercular meningitis. Cranial computed tomography (CT) in a case of tubercular meningitis shows basal exudates and hydrocephalus. Intracranial tuberculosis can also manifest as ring-enhancing lesions (tuberculoma), but the basal exudates are the most common and characteristic feature of tubercular meningitis.

Tubercular meningitis

It is common between 6 months and 4 years of age and usually spread by the hematogenous route. The gelatinous exudate infiltrates the corticomeningeal blood vessels leading to hydrocephalus.

The three stages are-

• Prodromal stage

• Stage of meningitis

• Stage of coma

CSF study shows reduced sugar level, increased protein level, and lymphocytosis. Treatment includes antitubercular drugs for 12 months and corticosteroids (to reduce neurologic sequelae). TB meningitis is the only indication of steroids in TB.

Other options:

Ring-enhancing lesions are seen in cerebral abscess, neurocysticercosis and tuberculoma(rich focus). Focal involvement of the temporal lobe is seen in herpes simplex encephalitis. Subependymal calcifications are seen in tuberous sclerosis.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common, preventable cause of mental retardation?
questions.explanation:
Congenital hypothyroidism is the most common preventable cause of mental retardation which results from a deficient production of thyroid hormone. It is more common among girls and the prevalence is about 1:3000 to 1:4000 births.

Down's syndrome is the most common overall cause of mental retardation, followed by Fragile X syndrome, which mainly affects boys.

Causes of mental retardation:

Prenatal

Congenital hypothyroidism

Infection (toxoplasma, rubella, CMV, HSV)

Genetic abnormalities

• Trisomy 21

• Fragile X syndrome

• other point mutations and chromosomal abnormalities

Toxins and teratogens

• Alcohol

• Drugs

• Radiation

Inborn errors of metabolism

Perinatal

Hypoxia

Prematurity

Intracranial haemorrhage

Perinatal CNS infection

Postnatal

Acquired brain injury

CNS infection, haemorrhage, malignancy

Severe malnutrition and deprivation

Environmental toxins (lead, mercury)

questions.question: In a 4-month old, term infant with open posterior fontanelle and hypotonia, you suspect congenital hypothyroidism and send thyroid studies. Which of the following is the most common cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Thyroid dysgenesis is the most common cause of permanent congenital hypothyroidism (80–85% of cases) > dyshormonogenesis (15%).

Dysgenesis may involve ectopy, agenesis (absence) or hypoplasia (underdevelopment) of the thyroid gland. Dyshormonogenesis results from a defect in any of the steps in thyroid hormone biosynthesis.

Etiology of congenital hypothyroidism:

Primary hypothyroidism:

• Thyroid dysgenesis

• Thyroid dyshormonogenesis

• Iodine deficiency (endemic goiter)

• Defect in thyroid hormone transport- Mutation in MCT8 (monocarboxylate
transporter 8) gene

• Maternal antibodies- thyrotropin receptor–blocking antibody
(TRBAb)

• Maternal medications- iodides, amiodarone, propylthiouracil, methimazole, radioiodine

Central (hypopituitary) hypothyroidism:

• TSH deficiency- mutation in TSH β-subunit gene

• TRH deficiency- mutation in TRH gene

• TRH unresponsiveness- mutation in TRH receptor gene

• Multiple congenital pituitary hormone deficiencies

*TSH - thyroid-stimulating hormone; TRH - thyroid-releasing hormone

Acquired hypothyroidism can be caused by iodine deficiency, thyroiditis, radiation, histiocytosis, and drugs. The most common cause of acquired hypothyroidism is autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's).

Note: Mutation in PAX-8 gene is associated with congenital hypothyroidism and genitourinary abnormalities such as renal agenesis.

questions.question: You are called to see a 3-day-old, term neonate, who has not passed meconium yet. On clinical examination, there is generalized hypotonia and the abdomen is slightly distended without any evidence of ascites or hepatosplenomegaly. Incidentally, you also note a palpable goitre in this baby. Laboratory investigations reveal low T4 and elevated TSH levels. Which of the following is the most likely cause for this child's condition?
questions.explanation:
A history of decreased activity and late passage of meconium, associated with low T4 and high TSH is suggestive of primary hypothyroidism. In an infant with a palpable goitre, the likely diagnosis is congenital hypothyroidism secondary to thyroid dyshormonogenesis.

The most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism is thyroid dysgenesis but it is not associated with goitre. Thyroid dyshormonogenesis results from the deficiency of one or more enzymes involved in thyroid hormone synthesis/secretion.

Congenital hypothyroidism can be:

Goitrous (Palpable goitre)
Non-goitrous (No palpable goitre)

Thyroid dyshormonogenesis

Iodine deficiency

Placental passage of antithyroid drugs

Thyroid dysgenesis

Thyroid receptor blocking antibodies

Central (hypopituitary) hypothyroidism

questions.question: At how many weeks of gestation does thyroxine secretion begin in a fetus?
questions.explanation:
Thyroxine secretion begins in the fetus at 12 weeks of gestation.

The fetal thyroid arises from an outpouching of the foregut at the base of the tongue (foramen cecum). It migrates to its normal location over the thyroid cartilage by 8-10 wk of gestation. The bilobed shape of the thyroid is recognized by 7 weeks of gestation.

questions.question: An anxious mother has brought a 4-month-old baby with complaints that the baby is not feeding well and is excessively sleepy all the time. Clinical examination reveals jaundice and hypotonia. His picture is provided below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The above picture shows a child with a protuberant abdomen, umbilical hernia, macroglossia, and edematous facies. Also, the infant is sluggish, has jaundice, feeding difficulties, and hypotonia, all of which suggests a diagnosis of congenital hypothyroidism.

Clinical features of congenital hypothyroidism:

• Prolongation of physiologic hyperbilirubinemia- early sign (it is due to delayed maturation of glucuronide conjugation)

• Constipation- usually does not respond to treatment

• Wide open anterior and posterior fontanelles (>0.5 cm) and cranial sutures

• Developmental delay, delayed bone growth, delayed dentition

• Cardiovascular- slow pulse rate, cardiomegaly, asymptomatic pericardial effusion, edema

• Respiratory- macroglossia, feeding difficulties, choking spells, respiratory difficulties

• Haematological- macrocytic anaemia refractory to treatment with haematinics

• Nervous system- hypothermia, hypotonia, slow relaxation of deep tendon reflexes, sluggishness, and somnolence

questions.question: A newborn with abnormal neonatal screening tests was diagnosed with Pendred syndrome. Which of the following is not a feature of this syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Sensorineural hearing loss is present in Pendred syndrome; not conductive hearing loss.

Pendred syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder, caused by a mutation in the gene SLC26A4 on chromosome 7, which codes for pendrin, a chloride–iodide transport protein common to the thyroid gland and the cochlea.

Clinical features include sensorineural hearing loss and goitre with hypothyroidism. It is the most common cause of syndromic deafness. The biochemical reason for hypothyroidism in patients with Pendred syndrome is impaired iodide organification (resulting from a mutation in the Pendrin gene).

questions.question: A 9-day-old infant has elevated TSH level and low T4 level on newborn screening. If this condition is left untreated, which of the following is most likely to be seen in this infant in the first few months of life?
questions.explanation:
Elevated TSH levels and low T4 levels in a 9-day-old infant are suggestive of congenital hypothyroidism. Prolongation of physiologic hyperbilirubinemia is an early sign of congenital hypothyroidism. It is due to delayed maturation of the hepatic glucuronide conjugation system.

Hyperreflexia, hyperirritability and diarrhoea are seen in hyperthyroidism; not hypothyroidism.

Note:

Kocher–Debré–Sémélaigne syndrome: The muscles are usually hypotonic in congenital hypothyroidism. Rarely, hypothyroidism in infancy can be characterized by generalized muscular pseudohypertrophy, myxoedema, short stature and cretinism. Affected older children can have an athletic appearance. Boys are more prone to the development of the syndrome.

questions.question: During a rural health camp, a father brings a dull-looking baby with macroglossia and an umbilical hernia. On enquiry, you find out that the parents were told about a thyroid problem in the child at birth, for which they did not pursue any treatment. Which of the following is least likely to be found in children with the given condition?
questions.answer: A. Abnormal facies due to craniosynostosis
questions.explanation:
A dull-looking face with macroglossia, and umbilical hernia in a child with a thyroid disorder are all indicative of congenital hypothyroidism. Craniosynostosis is not seen in neonatal hypothyroidism. It is seen in hyperthyroidism.

Craniosynostosis refers to the premature fusion of sutures and closure of fontanelles and often results in abnormal, triangular facies. In congenital hypothyroidism, there is delayed closure of the fontanelles. Palpable goitre, though not common, can be seen in cases of untreated thyroid dyshormonogenesis.

questions.question: As part of a quality improvement project undertaken by the maternal and child health services, you are evaluating the current practice of newborn screening and detection rates of hypothyroidism in various community health centres. Which of the following statements is false?
options: Simultaneous measurement of T4 and TSH levels is the ideal method.
The sample is obtained by heel-prick between 1-5 days of life using dried blood spot.
Newborn screening always detects the affected twin in same-sex twins.
Primary TSH, with back up T4 is the most common strategy used.
questions.answer: C. Newborn screening always detects the affected twin in same-sex twins.
questions.explanation:
Newborn screening can fail to detect the affected twin with hypothyroidism.

Discordance for thyroid dysgenesis is the rule in monozygotic twins. The transfusion of euthyroid blood from the unaffected twin normalizes the serum levels of T4 and TSH in the affected twin, resulting in delayed or missed diagnoses. Therefore, a second sample for congenital hypothyroidism screening at 14 days of age should be considered in monozygotic twins.

Neonatal thyroid screening strategies:

• Primarily TSH, backup T4; T4 is measured if TSH level is >20 mU/L

• Primarily T4, backup TSH: TSH is measured only if T4 level is low

• Concomitant T4 and TSH; it is the most sensitive method

Note: the sample is obtained after 24-48 hours, to minimize the false elevation of TSH values due to normal post-delivery neonatal TSH surge.

questions.question: As an intern posted in paediatrics, you are asked to interpret the results of a heel prick test that you performed on a newborn. Which of the following results is suggestive of primary hypothyroidism?
options: Low T4 level and low TSH level
Low T4 level and high TSH level
High T4 level and low TSH level
High T4 level and high TSH level
questions.answer: B. Low T4 level and high TSH level
questions.explanation:
Low T4 and high TSH levels indicate primary hypothyroidism.

Blood specimen for neonatal thyroid screening is obtained by heel prick between 1 and 5 days of life.

Levothyroxine therapy is started immediately after diagnosis, at 10 to 15 µg/kg per day.

questions.question: The image given below depicts an x-ray of the knee in a term baby. Which among the following conditions is associated with it?
questions.explanation:
The deformity shown in the X-ray image is the absence of distal femoral epiphysis, which is a typical radiological feature of congenital hypothyroidism.

X-ray findings in hypothyroidism

• Absence of distal femoral and proximal tibial epiphyses at birth.

• Punctate epiphyseal dysgenesis (multiple foci of ossification)

• Deformity or beaking of the 12th thoracic or 1st or 2nd lumbar vertebra

• X-ray image of the skull shows large fontanels and wide sutures; wormian (intrasutural) bones; and, often, an enlarged and round sella turcica.

Image below: The infant on the left with congenital hypothyroidism demonstrates the absence of the distal femoral and proximal tibial epiphyses, while in the normal infant on the right the distal femoral epiphysis is present:

The image below shows small upper femoral epiphyses:

The image below shows enlarged sella turcica and wormian bones (intrasutural):

questions.question: Ayesha is a 9th standard girl who presented with a neck swelling, which began more than a year ago. Her mother says she is embarrassed about it and always covers her neck with a shawl when she goes to school. Her menstrual cycles have also become irregular as of late. Blood tests reveal slightly elevated TSH levels and the presence of thyroid peroxidase antibodies. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The presence of thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPO-Abs) and elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level in a child with a goitre is suggestive of chronic lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis.

Chronic lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease. Clinical presentation can include goitre, growth retardation, and other features of hypothyroidism. The thyroid is diffusely enlarged, firm, and non-tender.

TSH is moderately elevated and TPO-Abs and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (anti-Tg Abs) can be detected.

The image given below shows goitre due to Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

questions.question: A lady, with a history of a thyroid disorder and three prior abortions, delivered a female neonate prematurely at 34 weeks of gestation. In the newborn infant, tachycardia, irritability, and prominent eyes were noted and neonatal hyperthyroidism was suspected. Which of the following statements is false about the condition?
options: Maternal Graves' disease is the most common cause of neonatal hyperthyroidism
It results from the transplacental passage of maternal stimulatory TSH receptor antibody
Microcephaly and frontal bossing with triangular facies are common clinical findings
Neonatal hyperthyroidism occurs in most infants born to mothers with a history of Graves’ disease
questions.answer: D. Neonatal hyperthyroidism occurs in most infants born to mothers with a history of Graves’ disease
questions.explanation:
Neonatal hyperthyroidism occurs in only about 2% of infants born to mothers with a history of Graves’ disease. But maternal Graves' disease is by far the most common cause of neonatal hyperthyroidism.

Neonatal hyperthyroidism (due to Grave's) results from the transplacental passage of maternal stimulatory thyrotropin/TSH receptor antibody (TSHR-Ab).

Clinical features are as follows:

• Low birth weight (IUGR)

• Premature birth

• Microcephaly

• Frontal bossing and triangular facies

• Warm, moist skin

• Irritability, hyperactivity, restlessness, poor sleep

• Tachycardia

Note:

TSHR-Ab (TSH-R-stimulating antibodies) is another name for TSH-R-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI).

questions.question: A pregnant woman with a past history of Grave's disease has currently completed 36 weeks of gestation. She underwent partial thyroidectomy 10 years back and has remained euthyroid since then. The previous child had craniosynostosis. Which of the following antibodies is most likely to be detected, if a cord blood sampling is done at delivery?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with a history of Graves' disease in the mother and craniosynostosis (neonatal Graves') in the previous child suggests that the fetus is at increased risk of neonatal Grave's disease. Thus, the antibody likely to be found at birth in the cord blood sampling is the TSH receptor stimulating antibody (TRSAb).

Neonatal Graves is caused by the transplacental passage of TRSAbs from a mother with a history of Graves' disease. The mothers can have

• Active Graves' disease

• Graves' in remission

• Prior history of Graves' treated with radioactive ablation or thyroidectomy

TSRAbs bind to the receptor for TSH and stimulate cyclic AMP, leading to thyroid hyperplasia and unregulated overproduction of thyroid hormone.

questions.question: A 4-year-old girl, a known case of celiac disease, presented to the pediatric endocrine clinic with a history of neck swelling, tremor, and weight loss. On evaluation, she was found to have Graves’ disease. Other conditions that need to be screened in this patient include all of the following except __________.
questions.explanation:
Type 2 Diabetes mellitus is not associated with Grave's disease.

Conditions associated with Grave's disease (autoimmune diseases):

• Diabetes mellitus type 1

• Pernicious anaemia

• Celiac disease

• Vitiligo

• Addison disease

• Alopecia areata

• Myasthenia gravis

questions.question: An 11-year-old girl was brought by her parents with complaints of weight loss, increased appetite, and a decline in scholastic performance. Following investigations, a diagnosis of Grave’s disease is made. Which of the following is the drug of choice for initial therapy?
questions.explanation:
Methimazole is the initial drug of choice for treating Grave's disease (hyperthyroidism) in children.

Option A: Propylthiouracil is not recommended in children because it is associated with fatal hepatotoxicity.

Option C: Radioactive iodine is not preferred as the first-line treatment in hyperthyroidism for children.

Option D: Levothyroxine is used to treat hypothyroidism.

questions.question: Your unit chief has asked you to present the case of a teenager, who was admitted for evaluation of mental retardation, deaf-mutism and a gait disturbance. He also has a significant patellar clonus. On general exam, you note a goitre but according to lab reports, he is apparently euthyroid. His pubertal development has also been normal. The most likely diagnosis is _______.
questions.explanation:
The clinical presentation of a euthyroid patient with goitre as well as mental retardation, deaf-mutism, and normal pubertal development points towards neurological endemic cretinism.

Endemic cretinism includes 2 different, but overlapping, syndromes: neurologic type and myxedematous type. It is essentially the same disorder, phenotypically modified by the length and severity of postnatal hypothyroidism. Neurological manifestations are interpreted as reflecting the effects of maternal and fetal hypothyroxinemia, secondary to severe iodine deficiency, on the developing nervous system. Both neurologic and myxedematous type can manifest neurologic symptoms.

Although neurological cretins are euthyroid, linear growth arrest lines in the long bones are often demonstrated radiologically, suggesting previous hypothyroidism.

Option B: Graves disease includes a triad of hyperthyroidism with goitre, ophthalmopathy, and dermopathy (no mental retardation, deafness, or pyramidal signs).

Option C: Pendred Syndrome is caused by a mutation in chloride–iodide transporter in thyroid and cochlea resulting in euthyroid/hypothyroid goitre and sensorineural hearing loss (pyramidal signs like clonus are not seen).

questions.question: During a health outreach program in Sikkim, you come across 3 children from the same family, with goiter. Endemic cretinism was suspected. Which of the following can be a manifestation of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Strabismus and spastic diplegias are among the manifestations of the neurological type of endemic cretinism.

Cretinism is a condition characterized by irreversible abnormalities in intellectual development. Endemic cretinism occurs due to the nutritional deficiency of iodine. It can be neurological cretinism or myxedematous cretinism. It is associated with severe, irreversible mental retardation.

chapters.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia And Related Disorders

questions.question: The parents of a neonate diagnosed with congenital adrenal hyperplasia come with queries about the disease. They have been told that it's an inherited condition and ask you how is it possible for the baby to be affected when neither of the parents are. What is the mode of inheritance of the disease?
questions.explanation:
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia / adrenogenital syndrome follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.

Depending on the enzyme that is deficient, patients will have :

• Mineralocorticoid deficiency (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia) or excess (hypernatremia, hypokalemia)

• Incomplete virilization or precocious puberty in males

• Virilization or sexual infantilism in females

questions.question: A baby delivered at home was born with ambiguous genitalia. The parents could not identify the sex of the child. The baby was diagnosed with congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is this child most likely to have?
questions.explanation:
This child is most likely to have a 21-hydroxylase deficiency as it is the most common enzyme deficiency implicated in congenital adrenal hyperplasia. The second most common is 11 beta-hydroxylase deficiency.

21-hydroxylase enzyme hydroxylates progesterone and 17-hydroxyprogesterone to yield 11-deoxycorticosterone and 11-deoxycortisol, respectively. They help in the synthesis of aldosterone and cortisol. Therefore, the deficiency of this enzyme leads to the deficiencies of aldosterone and cortisol.

Also, the accumulated steroid precursors are diverted into the pathway for androgen (testosterone) production.

Clinical profile in 21-hydroxylase deficiency:

• Aldosterone deficiency: Salt-wasting crises (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, and metabolic acidosis)

• Cortisol deficiency: Hypoglycemia, hyperpigmentation (due to increased ACTH production), weight loss, weakness, anorexia, vomiting, and shock

• Androgens excess: Virilization of females and precocious puberty in males

questions.question: Which of the following types of congenital adrenal hyperplasia is not due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Under virilizing type of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is not caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

Depending on the extent of enzyme deficiency, CAH caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency is broadly classified into classic and non-classic forms:

Classic forms can be of two types - salt-wasting and simple virilizing types.

• Salt-wasting type is the severe form in which both cortisol and aldosterone are deficient, with excess androgen production.

• In the simple virilizing type, there is an impaired synthesis of cortisol and adequate amounts of aldosterone. Here, clinical features are due to the overproduction of androgens.

The non-classic form is characterized by partial 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Cortisol and aldosterone are produced normally, but at the expense of producing excess androgens.

questions.question: A concerned mother brings her 15-day old baby to you with complaints of decreased activity and vomiting. On examination, the baby is hypotensive, has depressed fontanelles and reduced skin turgor. The image of the external genitalia of the baby is shown below. Which electrolyte abnormality can you expect to see in this baby?
questions.explanation:
The image shows ambiguous genitalia. This along with signs of dehydration and hypotension suggest congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Hyperkalemia and hyponatremia (due to mineralocorticoid deficiency) can be seen in this condition.

These babies present at 10–14 days of age with progressive weight loss, weakness, anorexia, vomiting, dehydration, hypoglycemia, and hypotension.

Without treatment, shock, cardiac arrhythmias, and death may occur within days or weeks.

questions.question: Investigation of choice to diagnose congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency is estimation of ____________ levels.
questions.explanation:
17-hydroxyprogesterone levels estimation is the investigation of choice to diagnose CAH due to 21 hydroxylase deficiency. It will be markedly elevated.

Other findings include:

1. Elevated androstenedione and testosterone (in females).

2. Low cortisol and aldosterone.

3. Elevated ACTH levels.

questions.question: You see Sanjay who is a known case of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, on steroid therapy in the ER with vomiting and fever. You administer double the regular dose of steroids. Which drug is being referred to here?
questions.explanation:
Hydrocortisone, which is the mainstay treatment for commonest type of CAH, is the drug referred to in the given clinical scenario.

Double or triple doses are indicated during periods of stress, such as infection or surgery.

Glucocorticoid replacement therapy with hydrocortisone, 15-20 mg/m²/24 h, orally, in 3 divided doses is continued lifelong.

Mineralocorticoid replacement with fludrocortisone is used for patients with the salt-wasting disease. The daily dose of fludrocortisone in infants is higher than that in older children.

questions.question: The autopsy image of a baby who died during the neonatal period is shown below. Parents of the child undergo genetic counseling regarding future pregnancies. When should the mother be started on steroids in a future pregnancy?
options: As soon as pregnancy is diagnosed
After karyotyping and determination of sex of the baby
questions.answer: A. As soon as pregnancy is diagnosed
questions.explanation:
The autopsy image shows a bilaterally enlarged adrenal gland (white arrows) with a history of death during the neonatal period (probably due to shock, cardiac arrhythmias) which is suggestive of CAH in the baby. Mothers with a previously affected child of CAH should be started with steroid therapy as soon as pregnancy is diagnosed. Since it is an autosomal recessive disorder, there is a risk of the subsequent children being affected.

Dexamethasone at 20 μg/kg is started to suppress the secretion of steroids by the fetal adrenals (including adrenal androgens) and prevent the virilization of the external genitals in affected females. Then, chorionic villus biopsy is performed to determine the sex and genotype of the fetus, and therapy is continued only if the fetus is an affected female.

questions.question: You see Sathya, an adolescent in the endocrinology clinic referred by his family physician. He was told by his parents that he was a boy, but he felt differently. As he grew up, he felt increasingly uncomfortable with his identity and this caused him a great deal of sadness and isolation. On examination, he is hypertensive and has genitalia resembling a female phenotype. After karyotyping, you diagnose him with 46XY DSD. Which of the following enzyme deficiency would be in your differential?
questions.explanation:
46XY DSD - a genotypical male with female phenotype- along with hypertension makes the diagnosis of congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 17-hydroxylase deficiency more likely.

Clinical profile in 17-hydroxylase deficiency:

Aldosterone excess: Salt retention, hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and hypertension.

Sex steroid deficiency: In contrast to 11β-hydroxylase deficiency, patients with 17-hydroxylase deficiency are unable to synthesize sex hormones. Affected males are incompletely virilized (male pseudo-hermaphroditism/ ambiguous genitalia 46XY) and there is a failure of sexual development in affected females.

Cortisol deficiency is not manifested, as elevated corticosterone is an active glucocorticoid.

Intersex or DSD means a condition in which development of chromosomal, gonadal, or anatomical sex is atypical. There is a greater incidence of gender dissatisfaction, gender non-conformity, gender fluidity in such individuals.

questions.question: An infant with hypospadias, bifid scrotum presents with signs and symptoms of salt wasting. Lab reports reveal elevated levels of 17-hydroxy pregnenolone and dehydroepiandrosterone. Which of the following deficiency would you suspect in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of incomplete virilization (hypospadias with or without bifid scrotum and cryptorchidism), salt wasting due to cortisol and aldosterone deficiency, and elevated dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and 17 hydroxy pregnenolone levels are suggestive of 3 beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency.

Clinical profile in 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (3β-HSD):

• Aldosterone deficiency- Salt-wasting crises (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, and acidosis)

• Cortisol deficiency- Hypoglycemia, hyperpigmentation (due to increased ACTH production), and shock

• Androgen deficiency- Males are incompletely virilized (male pseudo-hermaphroditism/ambiguous genitalia 46XY/hypogonadism, cryptorchidism)

• Excess DHEA (weak androgen)- Females are mildly virilized (acne, hirsutism).

questions.question: The most common enzyme deficiency leading to childhood hypertension among the following is ______.
questions.explanation:
The most common enzyme deficiency leading to childhood hypertension is 11β-hydroxylase deficiency causing congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH).

Hypertension in CAH is due to 11β-hydroxylase deficiency followed by 17-hydroxylase deficiency.

Cortisol and aldosterone deficiency cannot be manifested because some corticosterone is synthesized from progesterone, and hence, there are no signs of adrenal insufficiency.

21- hydroxylase deficiency causes salt-wasting resulting in hypotension.

questions.question: A boy presents with precocious puberty and hypertension to your OPD. The estimation of ______ will help in the diagnosis of CAH.
questions.explanation:
Precocious puberty in a male with hypertension is suggestive of CAH due to 11β-hydroxylase deficiency. An increase in 11-deoxycortisol levels is diagnostic of the enzyme deficiency.

11β-hydroxlase catalyzes the convertion of deoxycortisol to cortisol. Therefore, 11β-hydroxlase deficiency causes an increase in 11 deoxycortisol levels.

questions.question: On a vacation trip to Hawaii, a father was helping his 7-year-old son change into swimming trunks. He noticed the presence of pubic and axillary hair. He knew it was abnormal and brought the child to the pediatrician. Which of the following is the least likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The presence of pubic and axillary hair in a seven-year-old boy is suggestive of precocious puberty and 17-Hydroxylase deficiency is least likely to cause it.

In 17-hydroxylase deficiency, patients are unable to synthesize sex hormones, and hence the affected males are incompletely virilized and present as phenotypic females (but gonads are usually palpable in the inguinal region or the labia).

In both 21-hydroxylase and 11β-hydroxylase deficiencies, the respective precursors to the hormones are shunted to the androgen synthesis pathway, resulting in all the signs and symptoms of androgen excess, including virilization of female and precocious puberty in males.

questions.question: A postgraduate examines a female baby in late infancy with failure to thrive. The genitalia appears normal. Reports reveal serum sodium of 125 MEq/L and serum K+ of 6.5 MEq/L. Estimation of which of the following hormones will be helpful in the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of failure to thrive in late infancy, normal genitalia, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia suggests aldosterone synthase deficiency. Estimation of aldosterone levels will help in the diagnosis.

Normal genitalia in female children rules out congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) caused by 21-hydroxylase and 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency. Hyponatremia and hyperkalemia rule out CAH due to 17-hydroxylase deficiency and 11β-hydroxylase deficiency.

Infants with aldosterone synthase deficiency may have severe electrolyte abnormalities with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic
acidosis.

Since cortisol synthesis is unaffected, infants rarely become as ill as untreated infants with salt-losing forms of CAH. So some infants escape diagnosis at birth because of normal cortisol levels.

Later in infancy or in early childhood, they may exhibit failure to thrive and poor growth.

Adults often are asymptomatic, although they may develop electrolyte abnormalities when depleted of sodium through procedures such as bowel preparation for a barium enema.

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy presents with obesity and short stature, with signs of abnormal masculinization as shown below. Which statement regarding this condition is false?
options: Most common cause is adrenocortical tumor
Hypertension seen here can occasionally lead to heart failure
Generalized obesity is a common finding in younger children.
questions.answer: A. Most common cause is adrenocortical tumor
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario along with the image showing round face (moon facies), obesity, abnormal masculinization, and purple skin striae are suggestive of Cushing's syndrome. The most common cause of Cushing's syndrome is prolonged exogenous administration of glucocorticoids, not an adrenocortical tumor.

Cushing's syndrome is characterized excess glucocorticoids that can be due to:

• Prolonged exogenous administration of glucocorticoids

• Excess endogenous cortisol secretion:

• In children <7 years: Most often by a functioning adrenocortical tumor

• In children >7 years: Most often by an ACTH–producing pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease)

Important clinical features in children:

• Obesity or weight gain (most common)

• Moon facies

• Purple skin striae

• Abnormal masculinization (acne, bruising, enlargement of the clitoris in girls)

• Pubertal developmental delay and amenorrhea in girls

• Proximal muscle weakness

• Osteoporosis

• Hypertension

• Hyperpigmentation

• Hypokalemic alkalosis

• Hyperglycemia

• Sepsis

questions.question: A high school girl Meenu presents to you with anorexia, vomiting, and muscle weakness for the past few months. On examination, she had the finding shown in the image. Which of the following will not be seen in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Given clinical scenario is suggestive of Addison's disease and hypertension is not seen here.

Addison's disease is a primary adrenal insufficiency due to acquired lesions of the adrenal cortex, which prevent the production of cortisol and, often, aldosterone. Hence, due to mineralocorticoid deficiency, there will be hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension.

The deficiency of cortisol stimulates the production of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). Increased ACTH leads to diffuse hyperpigmentation, including areas not exposed to the sun, such as buccal mucosa and gums.

Addison’s disease is characterized by the following:

• Hyponatremia

• Hyperkalemia

• Hypotension

• Hypoglycemia

• Increased ACTH levels

• Metabolic acidosis

• Hyperpigmentation

ACTH stimulation test (cosyntropin) - Low cortisol levels before and after administration of ACTH are suggestive of primary adrenal insufficiency, Addison's disease.

questions.question: You have been called to see a 10-year-old child in the emergency room with complaints of fever and vomiting for the past three days. On examination the child had tachycardia and there was significant postural hypotension. Upon investigation, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia were present. You suspect adrenal insufficiency. Which of the following is the most likely organism grown in blood culture?
questions.explanation:
The most common infectious etiology for adrenal insufficiency in children is meningococcemia caused by Neisseria meningitidis.

Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome:
Adrenal apoplexy due to fulminant bacterial infection (most common Meningococcus).

Clinical features: Non-specific like fever, rigors, vomiting, headache, disseminated intravascular coagulation (large petechial rashes in the skin and mucous membrane), hypotension, and septic shock

Petechial rashes in meningococcal infection:

Most commons in adrenal insufficiency:

• The most common infectious cause of Addison's disease in India is tuberculosis.

• The most common cause of adrenal insufficiency is the sudden withdrawal of steroids in a patient on long-term steroid therapy.

• The most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in children is congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH).

• The most common antigen against which antibodies are found in Addison's disease is CYP 21 (21-hydroxylase).

questions.question: In the pediatric ward, a resident is evaluating a case of primary adrenal insufficiency who has failure to thrive, recurrent emesis, and hepatosplenomegaly. Bilateral adrenal calcification is noted radiologically. The most likely diagnosis is ______.
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Wolman's disease.

It is a rare lipid disorder caused by a deficiency of lysosomal acid lipase (chromosome 10) that leads to the accumulation of cholesterol esters and triglycerides in most of the visceral organs.

Patients present in the first few weeks of life with failure to thrive, vomiting, abdominal distention, steatorrhea, hepatosplenomegaly, and hyperlipidemia with extensive bilateral calcifications of the adrenal glands.

questions.question: You are evaluating a case of hyperpigmentation. The patient reports having undergone bilateral adrenalectomy a few years back for Cushing's disease. MRI shows an enlargement of the pituitary adenoma. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario of hyperpigmentation, history of bilateral adrenalectomy and MRI showing enlarged pituitary adenoma points to the diagnosis of Nelson's syndrome.

Nelson's syndrome is a rare complication of total bilateral adrenalectomy (TBA). TBA is a procedure used to control hypercortisolism in Cushing's disease (due to ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma) when resection of the primary tumor is not possible.

The loss of feedback inhibition of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis following TBA increases CRH. This leads to stimulation of ACTH-secreting corticotroph cells, causing enlargement of the original pituitary tumor or formation of a new one.

Nelson's syndrome is associated with a clinical triad of:

• Hyperpigmentation

• Excessive ACTH secretion

• Corticotroph adenoma

Screening is done with fasting plasma ACTH levels and MRI brain performed at regular intervals. Prophylactic pituitary irradiation may be recommended to prevent its incidence. The primary treatment is transsphenoidal surgery. Patients will also require life-long glucocorticoid replacement, as they do not produce cortisol.

The use of steroidogenic inhibitors in the treatment of Cushing's disease has decreased the need for bilateral adrenalectomy these days.

Option B: Steele-Richardson-Olszewski syndrome, also known as progressive supranuclear palsy is a neurodegenerative disease. It affects the brainstem and basal ganglia.

Option C: Hamman-Rich syndrome also known as acute interstitial pneumonia, is a rare and severe form of idiopathic interstitial lung disease.

Option D: Job syndrome, also known as hyper-IgE syndrome is an autosomal dominant immunodeficiency disorder. It occurs as a result of STAT3 mutation leading to deficiency in the IL-17 producing T cells. This results in impaired recruitment of neutrophils to sites of infection.

questions.question: Using novel chemiluminescence immunoassay techniques, you measure the hormonal profile of the adrenal gland of a normal fetus. Which of the following would be present in higher concentrations?
questions.explanation:
The fetal adrenal gland produces a maximum amount of DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone).

DHEA and DHEA-S serve as estrogen precursors. The maternal adrenal gland does not produce a sufficient amount of DHEA-S. The fetal adrenal glands are quantitatively the most important source of placental estrogen precursors in pregnancy. During most of gestation, the fetal adrenal gland is almost solely dedicated to the production of dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate DHEAS.

questions.question: A woman has a previous child with congenital adrenal hyperplasia. In the present pregnancy, steroid therapy should be started _______
options: As soon as pregnancy is diagnosed
After karyotyping and determination of sex of the baby
questions.answer: A. As soon as pregnancy is diagnosed
questions.explanation:
Mothers with pregnancies at risk (previously affected child) of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) should be started with steroid therapy as soon as pregnancy is diagnosed.

Dexamethasone 20 μg/kg is started to suppress the secretion of steroids by the fetal adrenals (including adrenal androgens) and prevent the virilization of the external genitals in affected females.

Then, chorionic villus biopsy is performed to determine the sex and genotype of the fetus and therapy is continued only if the fetus is an affected female.

questions.question: You see a newborn with an enlarged clitoris and partially fused labia. You also note features such as frontal bossing, brachycephaly, midface hypoplasia, slender fingers, medial bowing of ulna, and heart abnormalities. Investigation reveals a deficiency of P450 oxidoreductase. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Deficiency of P450 oxidoreductase (POR) along with the given findings are suggestive of Antley-Bixler syndrome.

Features of Antley–Bixler syndrome:

These include deficiencies of 17-hydroxylase and 21-hydroxylase along with other congenital anomalies.

It leads to under virilization of males and virilisation of females via an alternate pathway. Virilization of mother is seen because of decreased placental aromatase activity leading to excess androgens in fetus and mother.

 Congenital anomalies seen are as follows:

• Head and face: Craniosynostosis, brachycephaly, frontal bossing, severe midface hypoplasia, with proptosis and choanal atresia.

• Limbs: Humeroradial synostosis; medial bowing of the ulnas; long, slender fingers, with camptodactyly and anterior bowing of the femurs.

• Malformations of the heart and kidneys.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common tumor associated with growth hormone deficiency in children?
questions.explanation:
The most common tumor associated with growth hormone (GH) deficiency in children is craniopharyngioma.

Growth hormone deficiency can be caused by congenital CNS malformations, genetic defects or acquired neurological insults.

Note:

• Most common cause of GH deficiency: Idiopathic

• Most common infection causing GH deficiency in India: Tuberculosis > Histoplasmosis

• Most common infiltration causing GH deficiency in India: Histiocytosis > Sarcoidosis.

• Trophic hormone failure with pituitary compression or destruction: GH> FSH> LH> TSH> ACTH.

• Most common tumors associated with central diabetes insipidus: Pinealomas, Germinomas

questions.question: Asha was being bullied about her height in school. The concerned parents bring her to the pediatrician who plots the growth chart as shown below. On evaluation, growth hormone levels are found to be high and insulin-like growth factor levels are low. Which among the following could be a cause?
questions.explanation:
The presence of high GH levels and low insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) levels point towards Laron syndrome/dwarfism. It is caused by end-organ resistance to growth hormone(GH insensitivity) due to the GH receptor mutation. It is an autosomal-recessive disorder with clinical features as those seen in pituitary dwarfism.

Here, growth hormone is produced but is unable to act on the target tissues. Thus, the resting and stimulated GH levels are high and IGF-1 levels are low.

In Turner's syndrome (Option A), loss of the short arm of the X chromosome is implicated in dwarfism. The short stature occurs due to a state of GH resistance, relative deficiency, and decreased utilization.

Pituitary dwarfism (Option B) is a condition with GH deficiency.

Maternal deprivation dwarfism (Option D) is due to psychosocial causes such as emotional deprivation and neglect. There is an inadequate response to GH stimulation tests. The mechanism is not fully understood. No history suggestive of disturbed maternal or family relationships rules this out.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common genetic cause for multiple pituitary hormone deficiency?
questions.explanation:
The most common genetic cause for multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies (MPHD)/panhypopituitarism is the mutation of the PROP1 gene.

LHX3 and GLI2 are other genes involved in MPHD.

GNAS1 mutations cause McCune Albright Syndrome.

c-MYC gene is mutated in Burkitt's lymphoma

WT-1 gene is mutated in Wilms tumors.

questions.question: You come across a child with growth hormone deficiency during your ward rounds. Which of the following features would you not expect in this child?
options: History of short stature at birth
questions.answer: A. History of short stature at birth
questions.explanation:
Children with growth hormone deficiency usually have normal growth at birth. Growth retardation (decline in growth velocity) becomes apparent around 1 year of age.

Growth in-utero is dependant on genetic, environmental, nutrition and growth factors. GH levels peak at mid-gestation, increase at birth, and then reduce by 2 weeks of life. At around 6 months of age, GH levels reach pre-pubertal levels and from there on have a major influence on growth. Thus the deficiency becomes apparent after a significant period of GH-dependent growth has occurred.

Characteristic features of growth hormone deficiency (Pituitary Dwarfism):

1. Normal growth at birth with growth retardation becoming apparent around 1 year of age

2. Proportionate short stature

3. Hypoglycemic seizures in newborn

4. Small larynx with a high-pitched voice

5. Small genitalia (micropenis)

6. Delayed skeletal maturation

7. Delayed dentition

8. Delayed puberty (sexual infantilism)

9. Doll-like facial appearance: small, round facies, frontal prominence, depressed nasal bridge (saddle nose), eyes may bulge, underdeveloped mandible and chin, normal head circumference but craniofacial disproportion due to small facies

10. Short neck

11. Normal intelligence.

questions.question: You are evaluating children with short stature on whether they are eligible to receive growth hormone therapy as per FDA guidelines. In which of the following children would you prescribe it?
options: An 8 year old with Laron dwarfism
A neonate diagnosed with congenital hypothyroidism
A 7 year old with Chronic kidney disease
A 6 year old diagnosed with Maternal deprivation dwarfism
questions.answer: C. A 7 year old with Chronic kidney disease
questions.explanation:
Chronic kidney disease is an FDA-approved indication for growth hormone (GH) therapy.

Renal failure is a state of GH resistance. Moderate-to-severe growth retardation in chronic kidney disease is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. GH therapy with recombinant growth hormone has been shown to improve catch-up growth and to allow the child to achieve normal adult height; the final adult height is still significantly below the genetic target.

FDA-approved indications for growth hormone (GH) treatment-

1. GH deficiency

2. Turner's Syndrome

3. Chronic Renal Failure before Transplantation

4. Small for Gestational Age / Short Stature

5. Idiopathic Short Stature

6. Noonan Syndrome

7. Prader-Willi Syndrome

8. AIDS-related wasting

9. Malabsorption associated with the short-bowel syndrome

questions.question: Chotu, a 5-year-old boy is on regular outpatient follow-up for growth hormone deficiency diagnosed 2 weeks back. He is planned for recombinant growth hormone therapy. All of the following are possible side effects except-
questions.explanation:
The use of recombinant growth hormone is associated with the risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus (not type 1 diabetes mellitus).

Other adverse effects:

• Pseudotumor cerebri

• Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

• Gynecomastia

• Worsening of scoliosis

Children who have been treated with rhGH have a higher risk of developing hemorrhagic strokes in adulthood.
Some studies show an increased risk of new neoplasms in cancer survivors.

questions.question: The most common pituitary adenoma diagnosed in childhood is _________.
questions.explanation:
The most commonly diagnosed adenomas during childhood are prolactinoma > corticotropinoma > somatotropinoma.

Note:

Hypothalamic hamartomas that secrete excess gonadotropin-releasing hormone can cause precocious puberty.

questions.question: Akash is the tallest kid in his 5th-grade class. While at a routine visit for a booster immunization, his pediatrician plots his height on a growth chart and finds him to be above 3-SD for his age. Which of the following can be an endocrine cause for his height?
questions.explanation:
McCune–Albright syndrome (endocrine dysfunction affecting multiple glands) is an endocrine cause of tall stature in childhood. The triad of McCune–Albright syndrome is precocious puberty, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, and cafe au lait macules

Causes of childhood tall stature:

Non-endocrine causes
Endocrine causes

Familial (constitutional) tall stature
Excess GH secretion(pituitary gigantism)

Cerebral gigantism (Sotos syndrome)
McCune–Albright syndrome

Marfan syndrome
Precocious puberty

Fragile X syndrome
Hyperthyroidism

Homocystinuria

Klinefelter syndrome(XXY)

XYY syndrome

Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome

questions.question: "Weak giants" are produced by _________.
questions.explanation:
"Weak giants" are due to hyperpituitarism that is most commonly produced by pituitary adenomas.

Hyperpituitarism causes growth hormone (GH) excess, leading to tall stature (giants) with weak muscles. Overproduction of GH results in gigantism in children (before fusion of bone growth plate) and acromegaly in adults.

Clinical features include:

• Gigantism, prognathism (protrusion of jaw), hypertrophy of frontal bones

• Proximal myopathy (though there is muscle hypertrophy, it is weakened due to atrophy of type II muscle fibers)

• Acral enlargement in hands and feet (due to thickening of soft tissues)
