• Visceromegaly: Enlargement of most organs especially the tongue, thyroid, salivary gland, liver, spleen, kidney, and prostate

• Local effects of the adenoma: Headache, visual field defects, raised ICT

Note: Although hypothalamic hamartomas can also produce gigantism, the most common cause of gigantism is pituitary adenomas.

questions.question: A young boy is diagnosed to have central diabetes insipidus. A lesion in which of the following nuclei is likely to cause this condition?
questions.explanation:
Lesions in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus can cause central diabetes insipidus.

These nuclei synthesize vasopressin, a 9-amino-acid peptide with antidiuretic and vascular pressor activity. It is transported to the posterior pituitary via axonal projections, where it is stored for release into the systemic circulation.

Diabetes insipidus (DI) is characterized by pathologic polyuria and polydipsia (>2 L/m²/24 hr or 5 mL/kg/hr). It can result from either:

• Vasopressin deficiency (decreased anti-diuretic hormone production) causes central DI.

• Vasopressin insensitivity at the level of the kidney causes nephrogenic DI.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy was brought by his mother with new-onset nocturnal bedwetting. She also reported, he has been drinking more water for the last 3-4 months. 24-hour urine volume was 4 liters and the urine osmolality was low. ADH assays recorded a value was 0.7 pg/mL. T1 weighted MRI brain indicated an absence of a pituitary bright spot. What is the treatment of choice for his condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of central diabetes insipidus. The treatment of choice is desmopressin. It is a vasopressin analog (V2 receptor agonist). It can be administered intranasally, or subcutaneously.

Option A: Leuprolide is a GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) analog used in the treatment of prostate cancer, breast cancer, and endometriosis.

Option B: Thiazides paradoxically exert an antidiuretic effect in DI but are not the drug of choice. They are generally used in nephrogenic DI.

Option D: Terlipressin is a long-acting analog on vasopressin that acts on V1 receptors of vascular smooth muscle. It is used as a vasopressor in shock and acute variceal bleeding.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy diagnosed with Wolfram syndrome is admitted to the pediatric ward of your hospital. Which of the following features would you expect to find in this child?
questions.explanation:
Optic Atrophy is seen in Wolfram syndrome. The components of the syndrome are represented by the acronym DIDMOAD:

• Diabetes Insipidus

• Diabetes Mellitus (type 1)

• Optic Atrophy

• Neural Deafness

It is caused by mutations of the WFS1 gene.

questions.question: While working in a tertiary care center, a 5-year-old girl presents with polyuria, polydipsia, and nocturnal enuresis for the past 1 year. A water deprivation test is done and shows low urine osmolality on stopping the intake of water. On desmopressin administration, there is a 7% rise in urine osmolality. The treatment of this condition uses all of the following except?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. The treatment includes pharmacological treatment combined with salt restriction and not increased salt intake.

Treatment of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus:

• Adequate water intake along with a low sodium diet

• Thiazide diuretics: Acts by

• Volume contraction and increases the responsiveness of other parts of the tubule

• Increase the AQP2 channels independent of vasopressin

• Potassium-sparing diuretics (triamterene and amiloride): Amiloride is the drug of choice for lithium-induced DI

• Prostaglandin synthesis inhibitor (indomethacin)

questions.question: You are suspecting a case of delayed puberty in a 15-year-old boy. To assess puberty in this patient, what is the first sign you would look for?
questions.explanation:
The first sign of puberty in males is the increase in testicular volume.

In males at 11 to 12 years, the growth of the testis (>4 mL in volume) and thinning of the scrotum occurs, which are the first signs of puberty. This is followed by the pigmentation of the scrotum, growth of the penis, and pubarche.
Growth of testis > pubarche > adrenarche > growth spurt (TPAG).

In females at 10 to 11 years, the breast bud (thelarche) appears, which is the first sign of puberty followed by the appearance of pubic hair (pubarche), growth spurt, and menarche.
Thelarche > pubarche > growth spurt > menarche (TPGM).

questions.question: As an intern, you are currently posted in the Paediatric endocrinology OPD where you see multiple cases of girls having precocious puberty. The condition is defined by the onset of secondary sexual characteristics before the age of_________.
questions.explanation:
Precocious puberty is defined as the onset of secondary sexual characteristics before the age of 8 years in girls and 9 years in boys.

Depending on the primary source of hormonal production, precocious puberty can be classified in the following manner:

Central Precocious Puberty

(Gonadotropin-dependent puberty)

Peripheral Precocious Puberty

(Gonadotropin independent)

Due to the excess secretion of gonadotropins (FSH and LH) from pituitary

Due to excess secretion of testosterone or estrogen from the gonads/adrenals.

Always isosexual (appearance of phenotypically appropriate secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 years in girls and before 9 years in boys).

Can be isosexual or heterosexual (appearance of secondary sex characters of the opposite sex).

Girls

• Idiopathic (most common)

Boys

• CNS pathology (most common)

Girls

• Estrogenic ovarian cysts (isosexual)

• Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) (testosterone increases; heterosexual)

Boys

• CAH (isosexual; most common)

Note:

Central Precocious Puberty(more common) >> Peripheral Precocious Puberty

questions.question: A 6-year-old girl was brought to the OPD by her mother who is concerned about her significant increase in height compared to her classmates in the last 2 years. On examination, the girl shows breast development corresponding to B2 Tanner stage. What is the most common brain lesion causing this condition?
questions.explanation:
Hypothalamic hamartoma, a neuronal migration defect, is the most common cause of organic central precocious puberty. The onset of breast development before the age of 8 years in females and onset of testicular development (>4 mL) before the age of 9 years in males is suggestive of central precocious puberty.

It is a congenital malformation that consists of ectopically located neural tissue characterised by-

• Early-onset of puberty

• Seizures associated with unnatural crying or laughing episodes are known as gelastic seizures.

Tuberculous meningitis, tuberous sclerosis, and astrocytomas can also cause central precocious puberty.

questions.question: A young girl was referred to the paediatrician with stage IV breast development and growth acceleration seen at the age of 5 years. Her estradiol concentrations were elevated. The sagittal MRI of the brain is as shown below. What is the treatment of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
A pedunculated mass in the floor of the 3rd ventricle as shown in the MRI, with elevated levels of estrogen is suggestive of a Hypothalamic Hamartoma, which is the most common brain lesion causing central precocious puberty and is treated with GnRH agonists.

Treatment of Hypothalamic Hamartoma-

• GnRH agonists (depot-forms or implant) are the treatment of choice of tumour-induced Central precocious puberty

• In patients with hypothalamic hamartoma and associated intractable gelastic or psychomotor seizures, stereotactic radiation therapy (Gamma Knife surgery) is more effective and has fewer risks than neurosurgical intervention.

Long-acting formulations of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists are the preparations of choice for the treatment of central precocious puberty as they maintain fairly constant serum concentrations of the drug for weeks or months.

questions.question: A primary school teacher notices bloodstains on the skirt of her second-grade student. She immediately informs her parents and accompanies the child to the doctor on campus. On examination, the 7-year-old girl had blood-stained vaginal discharge, enlarged breasts and areola. Which of the following is not a cause for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Vaginal bleeding with well-developed breasts before the age of 8 years is suggestive of precocious puberty. Prader–Willi syndrome is one of the causes of delayed puberty in girls (not precocious puberty), where there is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

Hypothalamic hamartoma, McCune–Albright syndrome and hypothyroidism are causes of precocious puberty.

Note:

In prolonged hypothyroidism, adolescents typically have delayed puberty. Younger children might present with pseudo-precocious puberty, characterized by breast development and vaginal bleeding in girls and macroorchidism in boys.

Elevated levels of TSH appear to interact with the FSH receptor (specificity spillover), thus inducing FSH-like effects in the absence of LH effects on the gonads. The FSH-like effect suffices to induce estradiol secretion by the ovaries, whereas in males, testicular enlargement occurs without substantial testosterone secretion.

questions.question: An incessantly crying 5-year-old girl is brought to the OPD by her father. You observe that she needs support to walk and her trunk is not symmetrically aligned. There is a history of recurrent fractures in her limbs. She also has blood-stained vaginal discharge from a few days. On examination, the girl appears as shown in the image below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Precocious puberty(vaginal discharge), bony lesions (polyostotic fibrous dysplasia), and cafe au lait spots, as shown in the picture, are features of McCune–Albright syndrome. There is pain due to the multiple bony lesions and repeated fractures may result in incessant crying in the children and may require regular visits to the orthopaedics department.

McCune–Albright syndrome is a classical cause of peripheral precocious puberty caused by a mutation of GNAS1 gene. It affects the bones, skin, and several endocrine tissues.

Fibrous dysplasia of multiple bones (polyostotic) represents a major cause of morbidity in this syndrome. The base of the skull and the proximal femurs are most commonly involved, but any bone can be affected. A CT scan is usually recommended even in absence of deformities. The prognosis is favourable for longevity, but deformities, repeated fractures, pain, and occasional cranial nerve compression may result from the bony lesions.

Cardinal features:

• Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia

• Cafe au lait macules

• Endocrine abnormalities: hyperthyroidism, acromegaly, adrenal adenomas, and autonomous ovarian hyperfunction, leading to precocious puberty

• Predominantly affects girls

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy on examination is found to have genital development corresponding to Tanner stage 1 and his height is below the 3rd Percentile on growth charting. What is the most common cause for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Failure of development of pubertal features by the age of 14 years in male is suggestive of Delayed Puberty.

The most common cause of delayed puberty in males and females is a constitutional delay in growth and puberty. Lack of pubertal changes in boys by the age of 14 years is suggestive of delayed puberty. Delayed puberty is more common in boys than in girls.

questions.question: Breast and papillae appear as a small mound on examination of a young girl. If you are suspecting a case of delayed puberty, it is defined as a lack of development of secondary sexual characters beyond the age of __________.
questions.explanation: Delayed puberty in girls is defined as lack of secondary sexual characteristics by the age of 13 years or absence of menarche by the age of 16 years or within 3 years of pubertal onset.

questions.question: A child presents with features of delayed puberty. On investigating, he has decreased levels of LH, FSH, and testosterone. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This patient has low levels of luteinizing hormone (LH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and testosterone pointing towards hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and Kallman's syndrome is the only condition in the given choices causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

Causes of delayed puberty:

Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Secondary/central)

Hypogonadism is due to the impaired secretion of gonadotropins (FSH and LH) by the pituitary gland and the resultant lack of sex steroid production

• Malnutrition, systemic diseases

• Kallmann (anosmia), Prader–Willi syndrome (mental retardation, obesity, low intelligence)

Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (Primary gonadal failure)

Hypogonadism is due to an impaired response of the gonads to the gonadotropins (FSH and LH), which in turn leads to a lack of sex steroid production and elevated gonadotropin levels (as an attempt of compensation by the body)

• Sex chromosome anomalies (Turner's, Klinefelter's syndrome)

• Androgen insensitivity syndrome

• Ovotesticular dysgenesis

questions.question: All of the following are features of Laurence-Moon-Biedl syndrome except _________.
questions.explanation:
Hypertension is seen in Laurence–Moon–Biedl syndrome.

Laurence–Moon–Bardet–Biedl is an autosomal-recessive disorder of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

Characteristic features:

• Polydactyly

• Obesity

• Retinitis pigmentosa

• Male hypogonadism

• Hypertension

• Mental retardation

questions.question: A female child presents with bilateral inguinal masses, which were thought to be hernias but were found to be testes in the inguinal canals. Which karyotype would you expect to find in the child?
questions.explanation:
Here, this baby girl with bilateral inguinal masses (testis) probably has androgen-insensitivity syndrome, where karyotype is 46,XY.

Androgen-insensitivity syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in the androgen receptor gene that makes XY fetuses insensitive to androgens. The patients phenotypically resemble females because a part of the testosterone is converted to estrogen, which leads to the development of female external genitalia, normal development of breast, and female habitus.

Patients with Klienfelter's syndrome have a karyotype of 47, XXY and can have undescended testis, but they have male external genitalia where the phallus tends to be smaller than average.

Characteristic features:

• Most common forms of male disorders of sexual differentiation (DSD).

• 46 XY male child with female phenotype, present with primary amenorrhoea.

• Normal male gonads, mostly undescended ones, can present as inguinal masses or hernia.

• Here, as testosterone receptors are defective, they do not act on tissues, leading to the absence of secondary sexual characters (absence of pubic hair and axillary hair).

questions.question: An infant was found to have elevated levels of LH. The baby has a 46, XY chromosome pattern on karyotyping and the vagina is short and ends blindly in a pouch. Which of the following is false in the condition suffered by the infant?
questions.answer: B. Internal female genitalia is normal
questions.explanation:
An infant with a 46, XY chromosome pattern and female external genitalia are suggestive of Androgen-insensitivity syndrome(AIS) where there is absent internal female genitalia.

These patients have absent internal female genitalia with normal female external genitalia with the vagina ending blindly, in a pouch and normal male gonads in the form of undescended testis (mostly) which can present as inguinal masses.

In a male child (46, XY), testicular hormones are resistant to receptors, and a part of the testosterone is converted to estrogen leading to the development of female external genitalia and eventually normal development of breast, and female habitus.

Features of Androgen insensitivity syndrome at different age groups-

• In infants, elevated LH levels should suggest the diagnosis of AIS

• Prepubertal females with this disorder are often detected when inguinal masses which prove to be testes

• In older children and adults, amenorrhea is the usual presenting symptom.

Note:

Reifen-Stein syndrome: Males with various forms of ambiguous genitalia and undervirilization (hypogonadism, severe hypospadias, and gynecomastia). They are phenotypically normal-appearing males with infertility.

questions.question: A 31-year-old female delivers a term baby. On examination, it has a micropenis and unpalpable testis. She gives a history of acne from 16 weeks of gestation which worsened throughout pregnancy and was treated after delivery. The baby was diagnosed to have female pseudohermaphroditism. Which of the following statements are right about the given condition?
options: Female external genitalia and male internal genitalia
questions.answer: C. XX genotype, male external genitalia
questions.explanation:
Female pseudohermaphrodites are genectic females (XX genotype) with male external genitalia.

Causes:

• Enzyme deficiencies: 21 hydroxylase, 11 hydroxylase, and 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (HSD) deficiencies

• Maternal androgen excess

Male pseudohermaphrodites are genetic males (XY genotype) with female external genitalia.

Causes:

• Enzyme deficiencies: 17 hydroxylase and 3-beta HSD deficiencies

• Defect in androgen action

True hermaphroditism/ovotesticular dysgenesis: An intersex condition in which an individual is born with ovarian and testicular tissue.

questions.question: Cancer-'The emperor of all maladies spares no one'. Which of the following is the most common childhood malignancy?
questions.explanation:
Leukemias are the most common childhood malignancies. Among these, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common, accounting for about 77% of childhood leukemias.

Most commons in childhood malignancies:

• Second most common malignancy in childhood: Brain tumor

• Third most common malignancy in children: Lymphoma

• Most common solid tumor in children: Brain tumor

questions.question: You are asked to review an article titled, 'Childhood cancers- a menace'. Which of the following statements is wrong and needs to be edited out?
options: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is the most common type of leukemia in children with Down syndrome.
The most common intra-abdominal malignancy is Wilm’s tumor.
The most common extracranial solid malignancy is neuroblastoma.
The most common brain tumors in children are infratentorial.
questions.answer: B. The most common intra-abdominal malignancy is Wilm’s tumor.
questions.explanation:
The most common intraabdominal malignancy in children is neuroblastoma.

• The most common leukemias seen in Down’s syndrome: acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) > acute myeloid leukemia (AML)

• The most common site of a brain tumor in children: Infratentorium

• The most common extra-cranial solid neoplasm in children: Neuroblastoma

• The most common intra-abdominal neoplasm in children: Neuroblastoma

• The most common primary neoplasm of renal tissue in children: Wilm’s tumor

questions.question: What is the most common leukemia you would encounter in a child with the following findings?
questions.explanation:
The image shows a typical Down's facies (flattened nose, flat occiput, low set ears, protruding tongue). The most common leukemia in children with Down syndrome is acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).

Children with Down syndrome are at increased risk of both acute lymphoid leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

10% of neonates with Down's syndrome develop transient leukemia or myeloproliferative disorder. These features usually resolve within the first 3 months of life. However, they require close follow-up, because 20–30% will develop typical leukemia (often acute megakaryocytic leukemia) by 3 years of life.

Note:

• Most common leukemia in Down's syndrome: B-cell Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (overall)

• The most common leukemia in children <3years of age with Down syndrome is acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

• Most common AML in Down's syndrome: M7/megakaryoblastic

questions.question:
Jeevit, a 7-year-old boy brought to you by his mother, complains of bone pain so severe that he cannot sleep. Investigations reveal:

Leukocyte count: 16,000 cells/mm3

Hemoglobin: 6 g/dl

Platelet count: 60,000 cells/mm3

Peripheral smear shows numerous immature blast cells and is suggestive of acute lymphoblastic leukemia

In this age group, which immunophenotype of ALL is most commonly encountered?
questions.explanation:
B-lymphoblastic leukemia(pre-B-ALL) is the most common immunophenotype with TdT+,HLA DR+, CD10+, CD19+, CD20+, CD24+, Cy Ig + , with onset at 1-10 years of age.

The most common type of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in children is B-lymphoblastic leukemia (previously termed pre-B-ALL)

Based on current WHO classification: The most common subtype of ALL is B lymphoblastic leukemia > T lymphoblastic leukemia > Mature B-cell Leukemia (Burkitt leukemia)

The production of symptoms and signs of ALL is a result of the replacement of bone marrow by malignant cells and caused by secondary bone marrow failure. On physical examination, findings of pallor, listlessness, purpuric/petechial skin lesions, or mucous membrane hemorrhage can reflect bone marrow failure. The proliferative nature of the disease may be manifested as lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, or, less often, hepatomegaly. At presentation 75% of patients have leukocyte counts of <20,000/µL; thrombocytopenia is seen in 75% of patients and hepatosplenomegaly in 30–40% of patients. Patients with joint pain may have evidence of joint swelling and effusion. Deep bone pain may be present with marrow involvement, but tenderness will not be elicited.

questions.question:
You are posted in the pediatric hematology department as a first-year postgraduate. All of the following cases you encounter are at an increased risk of developing leukemias except:

Case 1: A 2-year-old child with neurofibromatosis type 1

Case 2: A 4-year-old with Fanconi syndrome

Case 3: A 1-year-old with ataxia-telangiectasia

Case 4: A 3-year-old with severe combined immunodeficiency

Case 5: A 10-month old with pernicious anemia
questions.explanation:
Fanconi’s anemia (not syndrome) predisposes to the development of childhood leukemias eg: B-ALL due to defective DNA repair. Fanconi syndrome is a syndrome of inadequate reabsorption in the proximal renal tubules. Congenital pernicious anemia does not predispose to leukemias.

Factors predisposing to childhood leukemias

• Genetic conditions:

• Fanconi’s anemia

• Bloom syndrome

• Ataxia telangiectasia

• Li-Fraumeni syndrome

• Down syndrome

• Severe combined immunodeficiency

• Neurofibromatosis 1

• Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

• Diamond-Blackfan anemia

• Schwachman diamond syndrome

• Kostmann syndrome

• Environmental factors:

• Ionizing radiation

• Alkylating agents

• Nitrosoureas

• Epipodophyllotoxin

• Benzene exposure

• Advanced maternal age.

questions.question: To diagnose a 5-year-old child with acute lymphoblastic leukemia, a pathologist has to see at least ____ percentage of blast cells in a bone marrow biopsy.
questions.explanation:
The lower cut-off percentage for diagnosing acute lymphoblastic leukemia on bone marrow biopsy is 25%.

Unlike with myeloid leukemias, there is no agreed-upon lower limit for the proportion of blasts required to establish a diagnosis of lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). In general, the diagnosis should be avoided when there are < 20% blasts.

The image below shows numerous lymphoblasts seen on a peripheral smear.

Work-up of ALL:

It is important that all studies necessary to confirm a diagnosis and adequately classify the type of leukemia be performed, including bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, flow cytometry, cytogenetics, and molecular studies. The initial evaluation should also include a CSF examination. If lymphoblasts are found and the CSF leukocyte count is elevated, overt CNS or meningeal leukemia is present. This finding reflects a poorer stage and indicates the need for additional CNS and systemic therapies.

questions.question: A 4-year-old child who was being evaluated for pancytopenia is diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Which of the following findings would indicate a poor prognosis?
options: Minimal residual disease>0.01% at the end of induction therapy
questions.answer: A. Minimal residual disease>0.01% at the end of induction therapy
questions.explanation:
MRD(Minimal residual disease) is a quantitative estimate of the burden of leukemic cells present in marrow. MRD>0.01%at the end of induction suggests a poorer prognosis.

Initial WBC count of <50,000cells/mm3, B-cell immunophenotype and t(12,21) indicate a standard risk(Favourable prognosis)

Risk-directed therapy is the standard of current ALL treatment and accounts for:

• Age at diagnosis

• Initial WBC count

• Immunophenotypic and cytogenetic characteristics of blast populations

• The rapidity of early treatment response (i.e., how quickly the leukemic cells can be cleared from the marrow or peripheral blood)

• Assessment of MRD at the end of induction therapy.

questions.question: A 14-year-old boy is rushed to the casualty due to difficulty in breathing and swelling of the face and neck. Clinically, he has features suggestive of superior vena cava obstruction. Chest X-ray image shows superior mediastinal widening. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is the most likely diagnosis since the chest X-ray shows superior mediastinal widening- indicating an involvement of the thymus gland.

T-ALL accounts for about 15% of childhood ALL cases; it is more common in adolescents - this is the time when the thymus reaches maximum size.

60% of patients with T-ALL present with a mediastinal mass. The mediastinal mass may be asymptomatic and detected only on chest x-ray or may cause cough and dyspnea, particularly on lying flat or with facial swelling and plethora due to vascular compression (superior vena cava syndrome).

B-ALL presents usually between 1-10 years of age perhaps because the number of normal bone marrow pre-B-cells (the cell of origin) is greatest very early in life.

questions.question: A 2-month-old infant with seizures and failure to thrive has cutaneous nodules and hepatosplenomegaly. On investigations, CBC reveals hyperleukocytosis with a leukocyte count of 1,10,000cells/mm3. Peripheral smear and immunophenotyping studies reveal large, irregular lymphoblasts, with a phenotype negative for the CD10 (common ALL antigen) marker. On a cytogenetic study which of the following is most likely to be seen?
questions.explanation:
The above findings are diagnostic of Infantile acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Translocation (4;11) involving the MLL gene is most commonly associated with Infantile leukemia accounts for the very high relapse rate.

2% of cases of leukemia during childhood occur before the age of 1 year and are referred to as infantile leukemia.

Patients often present with hyperleukocytosis and extensive tissue infiltration producing organomegaly. Subcutaneous nodules, known as leukemia cutis, caused by infiltration by leukemic cells are observed more often in infants than in older children.

The leukemic cell morphology is usually that of large, irregular lymphoblasts, with a phenotype negative for the CD10 (common ALL antigen) marker (pro-B), unlike most older children with B-ALL, who are CD10 +. Has a very poor prognosis.

Note:

Infants with AML present with CNS and skin involvement and most commonly have a subtype known as acute myelomonocytic leukemia.

questions.question: A mother has noticed recently that her child refuses to be touched, seems to be in distress, and cries inconsolably. She brings her child to you who was investigated thoroughly and was diagnosed to have acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Which of the following drugs can be used to treat her?
questions.explanation:
L-asparaginase is used in the treatment of acute lymphoid leukaemia (ALL). ALL can present with hepatosplenomegaly, severe joint and bone pains that the kid refuses to be handled.

It is observed that some lymphoid malignancies are unable to synthesize asparagine on their own and must derive it from the bloodstream. L-asparaginase catalyses circulating L-asparagine, thereby inhibiting protein synthesis in the cancer cells.

Treatment of ALL

• Induction: 4 weeks

• L-asparaginase: single dose (side effects: pancreatitis, thrombosis)

• Vincristine: weekly (side effects: neuropathy, SIADH)

• Prednisolone

• Anthracycline

• CNS prophylaxis- intrathecal methotrexate

• Consolidation:

• Methotrexate

• Epipodophyllotoxin

• Cyclophosphamide

• Cytosine-Arabinoside

• Maintenance: 24-36 months

• 6-Mercaptopurine

• Methotrexate

Other options:

• Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used to treat chronic myeloid leukemia and acute lymphoblastic leukemia with t(9;22) BCR-ABL fusion gene.

• Tretinoin is used in acute promyelocytic leukaemia with t(15;17) PML-RARA fusion gene.

• Cladribine is used in hairy cell leukaemia.

questions.question: You are posted in the hematology department as a pathologist. You are asked to report the bone marrow biopsy slide given below, which belongs to a 3-year-old child who is being evaluated for pancytopenia. To make a diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia, what percentage of such cells should you visualize at the least?
questions.explanation:
Diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is confirmed by the presence of more than 20% myeloblast cells (as shown in the image) in the bone marrow.

Flow cytometry and special stains can be used to identify myeloperoxidase-containing cells, which confirms the myelogenous origin of leukemia.

Note:

The diagnosis of acute lymphoid leukemia (ALL) requires the presence of more than 25% blasts in the bone marrow.

questions.question:
A 3-year-old boy was brought to the pediatric OPD with complaints of persistent fever for the past 1 week. His CBC is given below:

Hemoglobin: 5.1 g/dL

Leukocyte count: 1,40,000 cells/mm3

Platelet count: 12,000 cells/mm3

A review of peripheral smear confirms acute myeloid leukemia. Which of the following cytogenetic findings would indicate a poor prognosis for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Monosomy 7 is associated with a poor prognosis in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

The production of symptoms and signs of AML is a result of the replacement of bone marrow by malignant cells and caused by secondary bone marrow failure-pallor, fatigue, exercise intolerance, bruising, oral mucosal bleeding, or epistaxis, as well as fever, which may be caused by infection or the disease.

In addition, patients with AML present with signs and symptoms that are uncommon in Acute lymphoblastic leukemia, including subcutaneous nodules or“blueberry muffin” lesions (especially in infants), infiltration of the gingiva (especially in monocytic subtypes), signs and laboratory findings of disseminated intravascular coagulation (especially indicative of acute promyelocytic leukemia), and discrete masses, known as chloromas or granulocytic sarcomas.

Prognostic implications of chromosomal abnormalities in AML are given below:

Favorable prognosis

• t(8;21); RUNX1-RUNX1T1

• Inv(16) or t(16;16); CBFβ

• NPM1 mutation

• CEBPA mutation

Poor prognosis

• inv(3)

• t(6;9)

• 5q-

• del(7q)

• complex karyotype (≥3 abnormalities)

• Monosomy7

questions.question: A child with a violaceous, raised nodular skin lesion which on biopsy is found to be infiltrated by myeloblasts is likely suffering from which type of Acute myeloid leukemia (AML)?
questions.explanation:
Nodular, violaceous skin lesion infiltrated with myeloblasts is descriptive of Chloroma otherwise known as extramedullary myeloblastoma or granulocytic(myeloid) sarcoma. Myeloid sarcomas are seen in AML subtypes M2, M4, M5a, and M5b.

“Chloroma” was coined due to the peculiar green color of the tumor caused by myeloperoxidase present in tumor cells.

These masses can occur in the absence of apparent bone marrow involvement and typically are associated with t(8;21) translocation. Chloromas also may be seen in the orbit and epidural space.

questions.question: Erythemic myelosis is ______.
questions.explanation:
Erythemic myelosis is AML M6.

Constitute about 1% of AML cases

Two subtypes of AML M6:

• Erythroid or myeloid leukemia: M6a (more common)

• Pure erythroid leukemia: M6b, also called erythemic myelosis (Di Guglielmo disease).

questions.question: A neonate with trisomy 21 has anemia, petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, and no life-threatening complications on examination.CBC reveals high leucocyte count and peripheral smear shows numerous myeloblasts. The genetic makeup of blast cells when studied reveals GATA-1 mutations. At 3 months of age, his CBC counts come back to normal and there are no blast cells in his peripheral smear. As his treating physician, what would you recommend?
questions.explanation:
This infant has a transient myeloproliferative disease, which usually resolves spontaneously in the first 3 months of life, and they require close-follow up because 20–30% will develop typical leukemia (acute megakaryocytic leukemia) by 3 years of life.

Approximately 10% of neonates with Down syndrome develop transient leukemia or myeloproliferative disorder characterized by high leukocyte counts, blast cells in the peripheral blood, and associated anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hepatosplenomegaly. These features usually resolve within the first 3 months of life. Although these neonates can require temporary transfusion support, they do not require chemotherapy unless there is evidence of life-threatening complications.

As only 20-30% of such children develop acute megakaryocytic leukemia a bone marrow transplant would be a drastic step in our case.

questions.question: An 18-month-old child presents to the pediatric OPD with complaints of fever and rashes for the past 1 week after extensive workup gets diagnosed as Juvenile chronic myeloid leukemia. Which of the following findings is not consistent with this baby’s diagnosis?
options: The genetic study may reveal NF-1 mutation
The presence of Philadelphia chromosome on FISH
The bone marrow shows a myelodysplastic pattern with <20% blasts.
The peripheral smear reveals nucleated RBCs
questions.answer: B. The presence of Philadelphia chromosome on FISH
questions.explanation:
Patients with juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia do not have the Philadelphia chromosome.

Formerly termed juvenile chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), it is a clonal proliferation of hematopoietic stem cells that typically affects children younger than 2 years of age. Patients with JMML present with rashes, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and hemorrhagic manifestations.

Patients with this disease do not have the Philadelphia chromosome (the Philadelphia chromosome is characteristic of CML). The peripheral blood smear shows an elevated leukocyte count with increased monocytes, thrombocytopenia, and anemia with the presence of erythroblasts. Bone marrow shows a myelodysplastic pattern, with blasts accounting for <20% of cells. Patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and Noonan syndrome have a predilection for this type of leukemia.

JMML in the setting of Noonan syndrome is unique, with most patients having a spontaneous resolution.

questions.question: The most common non-Hodgkin's lymphoma in children is _____________.
questions.explanation:
Burkitt lymphoma is the most common non-Hodgkin's lymphoma in children under the age of 15 years.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) in adults and adolescents (15-19) years, worldwide.

B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) is the most common childhood malignancy and the most common leukemia in children. (It is not a non-Hodgkin's lymphoma).

questions.question: Which of the following statements best describe the behavior of Non-Hodgkin lymphoma in a 10-year-old child?
options: Is of high grade and aggressive
questions.answer: B. Is of high grade and aggressive
questions.explanation:
In contrast to adult non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL), which is typically indolent, pediatric NHL is usually high-grade and aggressive.

NHL in the pediatric age group has distinct clinical and behavior properties when compared to adults. These include the following:

NHL in adults

NHL in children

Low/intermediate grade

High grade

Dominantly nodal

Extra-nodal

Variable growth fraction

High growth fraction

Poor long-term outcome

Good outcome

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy is brought with complaints of abdominal distension, fatigue, and night sweats for the past 4 months. He also has a 2-month history of postprandial fullness and recurrent non-bilious vomiting. On examination, he is pale, has hepatosplenomegaly and shifting dullness. A CT scan shows mesenteric and retroperitoneal lymph node enlargement. A biopsy specimen of the mesenteric lymph node reveals tumor cells with high mitotic index and starry sky pattern. The cytogenetic study revealed t(8;14).To stage the disease, which of the following systems would you use?
questions.explanation:
Retroperitoneal and mesenteric lymphadenopathy with hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, and short duration of disease, point towards a diagnosis of lymphoid neoplasms.The classic translocation of t(8;14) and starry sky appearance with a high mitotic index on HPE point toward a diagnosis of Burkitt lymphoma. Burkitt’s lymphoma is the most common type of Non-Hodgkin lymphoma worldwide. St Jude system of staging is used for staging childhood non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Disease

System of staging

Hodgkin lymphoma

Ann–Arbor staging

Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma

St Jude(Murphy) staging

Chronic lymphoid leukemia

Rai staging
Binet staging

The current revised staging system used for NHL is the International Pediatric Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma Staging System (IPNHLSS) which reflects our increasing ability to diagnose lower levels of organ involvement with disease. For instance, the older staging system (St. Jude/Murphy classification) did not account for molecular or flow cytometry involvement of bone marrow, which is now reflected in the new system.

questions.question: A lymph node biopsy of a 9-year-old child with cervical lymphadenopathy showed the following picture. The diagnosis is_____.
questions.explanation:
In the picture given above, Reed–Sternberg (RS) cells are seen, which is a pathognomonic feature of Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL).

Reed–Sternberg cells are large and either multinucleated or have a bilobed nucleus (thus resembling an "owl's eye" appearance) with prominent eosinophilic inclusion-like nucleoli. The RS cell is clonal in origin and arises from the germinal center B cells but typically has lost most B-cell gene expression and function.

Hodgkin lymphoma encompasses a group of lymphoid neoplasms that typically arise in a signal node or chain of nodes and spread first to anatomically contiguous sites.

WHO classification of Hodgkin lymphoma includes 5 subtypes namely;

1. Nodular sclerosis

2. Mixed cellularity

3. Lymphocyte-rich

4. Lymphocyte depletion

5. Nodular lymphocyte predominance

questions.question: A 12- year-old female comes to you with a flu-like illness and left supraclavicular swelling of uncertain nature. Her chest X-ray shows left mediastinal enlargement. CT scan of the chest and abdomen reveals the presence of enlarged lymph nodes in the neck, mediastinum, and liver, and an FDG-PET/CT scan shows multiple scattered consolidation lesions involving also the bones. The diagnosis of classical Hodgkin’s lymphoma, nodular sclerosis subtype, is made on cervical lymph node biopsy. According to Ann-Arbor's staging system, how will you stage her disease?
questions.explanation:
The clinical vignette describes Hodgkin’s lymphoma with the involvement of liver and bone marrow, which is classified as Stage 4 according to Ann-Arbor staging.

Ann Arbor Staging of Hodgkin’s Lymphoma

Stage I

Involvement of a single lymph node (I) or Lymphoid structure(eg: spleen, thymus, Waldyer's ring)

Stage II

Involvement of 2 or more lymph node regions on the same side of the diaphragm

Stage III

Involvement of lymph node regions or lymphoid structures on both sides of the diaphragm (III)

Stage IV

Involvement of extranodal site beyond that designated as 'E'

More than one extranodal deposit at any location

Any involvement of liver or bone marrow

A

No symptoms

B

The presence of fever >38°C (100.4°F) for 3 consecutive days

Recurrent drenching night sweats

Unexplained loss of >10% of body weight in the 6 months

E
 Localized, solitary involvement of extra lymphatic tissue, excluding liver and bone marrow

questions.question: Sanctuary sites of acute lymphoblastic leukemia are______.
questions.explanation:
Both CNS and testis are considered as sanctuary sites of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).

• A sanctuary site is an area of the body that is poorly penetrated by pharmacological agents and, therefore, serves as a place in which tumor cells or infectious organisms can escape the effects of drug therapy.

• Early institution of CNS prophylaxis (intrathecal methotrexate) is essential to eradicate these escaped leukemic cells.

• Testicular involvement is rarely evident at diagnosis, testicular involvement can present as painless testicular enlargement.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy presents with pancytopenia and hepatosplenomegaly. Bony tenderness is also present. He is most likely suffering from the following type of ALL_____.
questions.explanation:
B-cell lymphoblastic leukemia (L1)

• This is the most common immunophenotype of acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) in a child between the ages of 1-10 years.

• They present with features of bone marrow failure and organ infiltration such as pancytopenia and hepatosplenomegaly, respectively, so B-cell ALL is the most likely diagnosis.

• Bony tenderness may be present due to sub-periosteal infiltration of lymphoblastic cells.

• T-cell ALL (L2) typically presents in adolescent boys with a large anterior mediastinal mass (thymus or mediastinal lymph nodes), causing respiratory distress or superior vena cava obstruction.

questions.question: Which of the following is the second most common malignancy in childhood?
questions.explanation:
The second most common malignancy in childhood is a brain tumor.

The most common malignancy in childhood is Leukemias.

Brain tumors in childhood:

• Most common solid tumor in children- Brain tumor

• Most common site of a brain tumor in children- Infratentorium

• Most common brain tumor in childhood- Pilocytic astrocytoma

questions.question: The MRI scan of an 11-year-old girl revealed a brain tumor. In which of the following conditions would you do a lumbar puncture for cytological analysis?
questions.explanation:
Germ-cell tumor is an indication for lumbar puncture for cytological analysis of CSF.

Usually, lumbar punctures are contraindicated in intracranial space-occupying lesions with high intracranial pressure as it can lead to brain herniation and death. They are thus delayed until surgery or shunt placement. However, in tumors with a risk of leptomeningeal metastases, lumbar puncture is indicated for cytology.

Tumors where LP is indicated
Tumors where LP is contraindicated

Medulloblastoma or primitive neuroectodermal tumors

Infratentorial tumors

Ependymoma

Supratentorial tumors with midline shift

Germ cell tumors

Tumors with hydrocephalus secondary to CSF obstruction

questions.question: A mother brought her 10-month-old baby to the hospital with sudden onset vomiting. She has also been noticing an alarming increase in the head size of the baby. On examination, significant macrocephaly is seen. MRI reveals a supratentorial tumor. Which of the following tumors is the most likely cause of this child's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Choroid plexus carcinoma is a pediatric supratentorial tumor presenting with macrocephaly and focal neurologic deficits.

Choroid plexus tumors are the most common CNS tumors in children aged less than 1 year. These tumors are intraventricular epithelial neoplasms arising from the choroid plexus.

Children present with signs and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (ICP), whereas infants may present with macrocephaly and focal neurologic deficits.

Medulloblastoma, pilocytic astrocytoma, and ependymoma, are all predominantly infratentorial tumors.

The age-related differences in the primary location of the tumor are given below:

Age
Predominant Site
Examples

< 1 year
Supratentorial
Choroid plexus tumor and teratoma

1 - 10 years
Infratentorial
Juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma and medulloblastoma

> 10 years
Supratentorial
Diffuse astrocytoma

questions.question: Sanam, a 7-year-old kid is suspected to have an ependymoma. Which of the following features on histopathology would favor this diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Perivascular rosettes will be seen on histopathological examination of ependymoma. Other features include ependymal rosettes and monomorphic nuclear morphology.

Ependymomas are tumors derived from the ependymal lining of the ventricular system occurring predominantly in childhood. They are usually non-invasive, extending into the ventricular lumen and/or displacing normal structures, sometimes leading to significant obstructive hydrocephalus.

questions.question: A young child was evaluated for increased ICP. A brain tumor was found on an MRI scan. It was resected and sent for histopathological examination. The slide is shown below. This tumor is found most commonly in the __________.
questions.explanation:
The slide shows perivascular pseudorosettes and ependymal rosettes, characteristic of ependymoma. The most common site of ependymoma in children is the floor of the 4th ventricle. Monomorphic nuclear morphology can also be noted.

Ependymomas are tumors derived from the ependymal lining of the ventricular system, occurring predominantly in childhood. These tumors are usually non-invasive, extending into the ventricular lumen and/or displacing normal structures, sometimes leading to significant obstructive hydrocephalus.

questions.question: A concerned mother brought her daughter to the clinic for evaluation of symptoms that have worsened in the last few weeks. The daughter frequently wakes up at night with severe headaches and vomiting. She has also been having some difficulty walking. On examination, ataxia and multiple cranial nerve palsies are noted. Imaging is suggestive of a brainstem tumor. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The MRI given shows a diffuse, infiltrating pontine lesion. Multiple cranial nerve dysfunctions, cerebellar signs, motor weakness, and features of raised intracranial pressure (ICP) are all strongly suggestive of a pontine glioma.

These are not amenable for surgical resection. The standard approach is radiation therapy. The prognosis is very poor.

questions.question: On your neurology rotation, you come across Ashu, a 5-year-old child who presented with a 6-month history of ataxia, headaches, and vomiting. He was admitted to the ward for further evaluation. MRI scan showed a brain tumor with a combination of solid and cystic components. Biopsy findings of the tumor are shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given slide shows condensed masses of glial filaments occurring in compact areas suggestive of Rosenthal fibers. The clinical features, MRI findings, and histopathology point towards a diagnosis of pilocytic astrocytoma.

Pilocytic astrocytoma is a low-grade astrocytoma tumor. It is the most common type of astrocytoma in children. These are classically found in the cerebellum (infratentorial) and the optic pathway regions.

There is usually a 3-6 month history of limb ataxia, secondary headaches, and vomiting. Mural nodule, a contrast medium enhancing nodule within the wall of a cystic mass is seen on MRI.

The tumor has a low metastatic potential and is rarely invasive.

questions.question: What is the WHO grading for Pilomyxoid astrocytoma?
questions.explanation:
Pilomyxiod astrocytoma falls under WHO Grade II.

Pilomyxoid astrocytoma:

Occurs most commonly in the hypothalamic/optic chiasmic region and carries a high risk of local as well as cerebrospinal spread. This astrocytoma affects young children and infants. It is classified as a WHO grade II tumor.

WHO Grades of brain tumor:

WHO grade
Example

Grade I

Pilocytic astrocytoma

Myxopapillary Ependymoma/subependymoma

Grade II

Diffuse astrocytoma

Pilomyxoid astrocytoma

Papillary/ cellular/Clear-cell ependymoma

Grade III

Anaplastic astrocytoma

Anaplastic ependymoma

Grade IV

Glioblastoma multiforme

Malignant pineoblastoma and medulloblastoma

questions.question: You are a pathology resident who is looking at a slide, showing small round blue cells and Homer-Wright rosettes as shown below. The history you received from the pediatric surgery resident was that the specimen was resected from a 5-year-old child with ataxia. The tumor was present in the midline vermis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and slide are suggestive of Medulloblastoma.

Medulloblastoma is an embryonal CNS tumor, occurring predominantly in the cerebellar vermis that causes ataxia, poor balance, and dysmetria. It may cause obstructive hydrocephalus and often metastasizes extraneurally.

Histopathology shows a tumor composed of small, round, blue cells and is characterized by Homer–Wright rosettes and an immunopositivity for synaptophysin.

Standard treatment for medulloblastomas is surgical resection, with adjuvant craniospinal radiotherapy for those over 3 years of age and chemotherapy.
Prognosis is strongly influenced by surgical resection, the presence of CSF metastases at the time of diagnosis, and the expression of the c-erbB-2 (HER2/neu) oncogene.

Note: Small, round, blue-cell tumors are malignant neoplasms that have a characteristic appearance under the microscope. It consists of sheets of small round cells that stain blue on routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. Examples are:

• Medulloblastoma

• Neuroblastoma

• Retinoblastoma

• Ewing’s sarcoma

• Rhabdomyosarcoma

questions.question: A child is brought to the emergency department by his teacher when he started having abnormal jerking movements during math class. The parents give a history of the child having similar episodes in the past. On the way to the CT room, the child had an episode of seizure and was stabilized with lorazepam. The imaging done is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Calcified cortical mass with a seizure is suggestive of oligodendroglioma.

Oligodendrogliomas are uncommon tumors of childhood. These infiltrating tumors occur predominantly in the cerebral cortex and originate in white matter. Treatment involves surgical resection followed by involved field radiation therapy.

The image below shows histology of oligodendroglioma showing characteristic fried egg appearance and chicken wire capillaries.

Craniopharyngioma is associated with suprasellar calcification. Also, the child may often present with a history of endocrinological and visual complaints.

questions.question: An erythropoietin-secreting brain tumor is detected in a child. His father passed away one year back from end-stage renal cell carcinoma. Family history is significant for VHL mutation. On examination, a fiery red retina is seen. Which of the following is the most likely tumor present in this child?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a cerebellar hemangioblastoma.

Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition. The major neurological features of VHL include cerebellar hemangioblastomas and retinal angiomas.

Cerebellar hemangioblastomas are erythropoietin-secreting tumors, which can lead to polycythemia. It typically appears as a cystic cerebellar lesion with a vascular mural nodule on CT or MRI scan.

Retinal angiomas are small masses of thin-walled capillaries, usually located in the peripheral retina that is fed by large and tortuous arterioles and venules appearing as a fiery red vascular mass. It can lead to retinal detachment and visual loss.

Associations of VHL syndrome include:

• Cystic lesions of kidneys, pancreas, liver, and epididymis

• Renal cell carcinoma (most common cause of death)

• Pheochromocytoma

• Cerebellar hemangioblastoma

• Retinal angioma

questions.question: Akhil, a 15-year-old boy with sun-setting eyes, has a tumor in the pineal region as seen in the MRI. Parinaud syndrome is suspected. Which of the following findings will not be seen in this boy?
options: Convergence retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze
questions.explanation:
Parinaud’s syndrome refers to supranuclear vertical gaze disorder.

Parinaud’s syndrome/dorsal midbrain syndrome is caused by damage to the posterior commissure. Classically, signs of hydrocephalus are seen due to aqueductal stenosis.

Causes:

• Pineal region or midbrain tumors (Most common cause)

• Neurocysticercosis

• Stroke

• Multiple sclerosis

Features include the following:

• Loss of up-gaze (downward gaze is usually preserved)

• Convergence–retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze

• Downward ocular deviation- Setting-sun sign

• Lid retraction- Collier's sign

• Pseudo-Argyll–Robertson pupil- Accommodative paresis ensues and pupils become mid-dilated and show light-near dissociation

• Bilateral papilledema

• Skew deviation

• Pseudoabducens palsy

questions.question: An 8-year-old child is brought to the casualty after a minor accident that occurred when he failed to see a bike coming from sideways. His mother says he is a clumsy child, who sometimes knocks things over accidentally even at home. Visual field examination findings are given below. On imaging, an intracranial mass is seen. The resected specimen shows cholesterol-rich machinery-oil-like fluid. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Patients with adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma present with bitemporal hemianopia (image), and the cystic component of this tumor contains a cholesterol-rich, thick, brownish-yellow fluid that is comparable to "machine oil."

Craniopharyngiomas develop from remnants of the Rathke pouch. Adamantinomatous variant of craniopharyngioma predominates in childhood.

These tumors are usually large and heterogeneous, displaying both solid and cystic components, and occur in the suprasellar region. Patients usually present with headache and visual field abnormalities. These children also have endocrinological abnormalities such as growth failure and delayed sexual maturation due to hypopituitarism (GH deficiency).

These tumors are minimally invasive, adhere to the adjacent brain parenchyma, and engulf normal brain structures. CT may show calcifications associated with the solid and cystic components.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common extracranial solid tumor in the pediatric age group?
questions.explanation:
Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children and the most commonly diagnosed malignancy in infants. It is an embryonal cancer of the peripheral nervous system.

The signs and symptoms depend on the location of the tumor and the extent of the disease. Neuroblastomas originating from the superior cervical ganglion can present with Horner syndrome.

Metastatic disease can cause a variety of signs and symptoms, including the following

• Fever

• Irritability

• Failure to thrive

• Bone pain

• Cytopenia

• Bluish subcutaneous nodules

• Orbital proptosis, and periorbital ecchymoses

Rapid dancing eye movements (opsoclonus), rhythmic jerking of limbs/trunk (myoclonus), and ataxia are characteristic of the opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome (OMA). It is a paraneoplastic syndrome of autoimmune origin with a strong association with neuroblastomas.

Some neuroblastomas may undergo spontaneous regression, whereas some may be unresponsive to therapy and run a very aggressive course.

Neuroblastoma

questions.question: A 5-year-old child presents with rapid dancing eye movements, rhythmic jerking of limbs and poor coordination. You suspect a paraneoplastic syndrome. Which of the following conditions should you look for in this child?
questions.explanation:
Rapid dancing eye movements (opsoclonus), rhythmic jerking of limbs/trunk (myoclonus) and ataxia is characteristic of opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome (OMA). It is a paraneoplastic syndrome of autoimmune origin with a strong association with neuroblastoma.

All children with OMA should undergo investigations for neuroblastoma such as ultrasound followed by CT or MRI of chest and abdomen, bone scans and marrow biopsies. The definitive diagnosis of neuroblastoma is through biopsy which shows small round blue cells.

Other small round blue cell tumours are medulloblastoma, retinoblastoma, Ewing’s sarcoma and rhabdomyosarcoma.

questions.question: In the ophthalmology OPD, you see a 3-year-old child with the following finding. There is no history of trauma. There is no significant family history. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This image shows periorbital ecchymoses and proptosis suggestive of metastases of neuroblastoma (a sign of orbital bone involvement).

Neuroblastomas may develop at any site in the sympathetic nervous system. Metastatic spread is common in children who are diagnosed after 1 year of age. It occurs via local invasion, hematogenous, or lymphatic routes.

Metastatic disease can cause a variety of signs and symptoms, including the following:

• Fever

• Irritability

• Failure to thrive

• Bone pain

• Cytopenia

• Bluish subcutaneous nodules

• Orbital proptosis, and periorbital ecchymoses

questions.question: A 10-month-old infant is diagnosed with neuroblastoma. Which of the following factors is associated with a good prognosis?
questions.explanation:
Hyperdiploidy is associated with a good prognosis in neuroblastoma if the child is younger than 1 year of age at diagnosis.

Bad prognosis in neuroblastoma is seen in cases of:

• Amplification of N-MYC

• Loss of Heterozygosiy of 1p, 11 q ,14q

• Gain of 17q

• TrkB expression

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy presents with a 2-month history of an enlarging scalp lesion. There is no history of trauma to the head or scalp. The child is otherwise healthy and investigations are normal. X-ray of the head is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with the x-ray image showing a punched-out lytic lesion is suggestive of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH).

LCH is a rare histiocytic disorder characterized by single or multiple osteolytic bone lesions that can infiltrate nearly every organ, most notably the skin (of the scalp), lungs, thymus, liver, spleen, bone marrow, or the central nervous system.

LCH is so named because of its resemblance to the Langerhan’s cells, which are specialized dendritic cells found in the skin and mucosa.

questions.question: A 12-year-old child is brought with 4 small, purplish, rubbery lesions on his back and arms. On examination, you note inguinal freckling and nodules on the iris as shown below. Which chromosome is involved in the syndrome described in this child?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of neurofibromatosis type 1. The NF1 gene on chromosome 17q11 is involved. It is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome.

It is diagnosed when at least 2 of the following 7 criteria are met:

1. 6 or more cafe-au-lait macules

1. >5mm prepuberty

2. >15mm post-puberty

2. Skin-fold freckling- axillary and inguinal

3. 2 or more iris lisch nodules (image)

4. 2 or more neurofibromas or 1 plexiform neurofibroma (purplish, rubbery lesions)

5. Osseous lesions

1. Osseous dysplasia

2. Cortical thinning of long bones without a pseudoarthrosis

6. Low-grade astrocytomas like optic gliomas

7. 1st degree relative with diagnosed NF-1

questions.question: Vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, and spinal cord ependymomas are the CNS manifestations of __________.
questions.explanation:
Vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, and spinal cord ependymomas are the CNS manifestations of neurofibromatosis type 2

It is an autosomal-dominant neurocutaneous syndrome, which occurs due to a mutation in the NF2 gene on chromosome 22q12.

von Hippel–Lindau syndrome is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome, which occurs due to a mutation in the VHL gene on chromosome 3p25-26. The CNS manifestation is usually a hemangioblastoma.

Turcot syndrome is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome, which occurs due to a mutation in the APC gene on chromosome 5q21. The CNS manifestation is a medulloblastoma.

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy presented with focal seizures involving the right side of his body. On investigations, a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma is found. Which of the following syndromes is most likely to be associated with this?
questions.explanation:
Subependymal giant-cell astrocytoma is a characteristic CNS finding in tuberous sclerosis.

questions.question: What is the most common intraocular tumor diagnosed in the pediatric age group?
questions.explanation: Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular tumor of the pediatric age group. It is an embryonal malignancy of the retina.

questions.question: James was brought by his mother for evaluation of a squint she noticed. On examination, the given finding was observed. Investigations revealed retinoblastoma with a germline RB1 gene mutation. The secondary malignancy most likely to develop in him is:
questions.explanation:
Children with germline RB1 mutations are at significant risk for the development of secondary malignancies, especially

• Osteosarcoma (Most common)

• Soft tissue sarcomas

• Malignant melanoma

The risk of secondary malignancies is further increased by the use of radiation therapy.

A pineoblastoma occurring in a child with bilateral hereditary retinoblastoma is called 'trilateral retinoblastoma'.

The image shows leukocoria, a white pupillary reflex. It may be seen in the following conditions:

• Congenital cataract

• Retinoblastoma

• Retinopathy of prematurity (retrolental fibroplasia)

• Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous

• Coats disease

• Toxocara endophthalmitis

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy presented with an abdominal mass. On examination, the mass is firm, smooth, non-tender, and does not cross the mid-line. The boy is also found to have moderate hypertension. Urinalysis reveals microscopic haematuria. Wilms tumor is suspected. This condition can be associated with all of the following except ___________.
questions.explanation:
Polycystic kidneys are not associated with Wilm's tumor.

Wilms tumor (WT), also known as nephroblastoma, is the most common primary malignant renal tumor of childhood.

Polycystic kidney disease can also present with an abdominal mass, hypertension, and hematuria. However, there will be multiple irregular cysts on ultrasound and is not associated with Wilms tumor.

questions.question: You are assisting on a left partial nephrectomy in a child with Wilms tumor. Intraoperatively, a small mass is noted on the right kidney as well. Frozen section reveals it to be a Wilms tumor. What is the stage of Wilm's tumor in this child?
questions.explanation:
Wilms tumor with involvement of both kidneys is stage 5.

Children’s Oncology Group (COG) Staging System

Stage I

Tumor confined to the kidney and completely resected with negative lymph nodes.

Stage II

Tumor extends beyond the kidney but is completely resected with negative margins and lymph nodes.

Stage III

Residual tumor present following surgery confined to the abdomen, including gross or microscopic tumor.

Stage IV

Hematogenous metastases (lung, liver, bone, brain, etc.)

or lymph node metastases outside the abdominopelvic region

Stage V

Metastasis to opposite kidney (bilateral renal involvement)

questions.question: While posted in the pediatric oncology ward, you come across a case of metastatic triphasic nephroblastoma in a 4-year-old. What is the most common site for metastasis of this tumor?
questions.explanation:
The most common sites for metastases of nephroblastoma or Wilms tumor are the following:

• Lungs (Most common)

• Regional lymph nodes

• Liver

The triphasic components visualized on histopathology are-

1. Malignant small round (blue) cells (blastemal component).

2. Tubular structures/rosettes (epithelial component).

3. Loose pauci-cellular stroma with spindle cells (stromal component)

questions.question: What is the most important determinant of prognosis in a child diagnosed with Wilm's tumor?
options: Loss of heterozygosity of chromosome 1 p
questions.explanation:
Histology is the most important determinant of prognosis in Wilm's Tumor. The absence of anaplasia is considered a favorable histological finding.

Other prognostic factors for risk-adapted therapy include

• Age

• Stage

• Tumor weight

• Loss of heterozygosity at chromosomes 1p and 16q.

questions.question: A 5-year-old child comes with abdominal distension, a palpable mass, and gross hematuria. A biopsy of the mass shows the following picture. Which of the following paraneoplastic syndromes in not associated with this tumor?
questions.explanation:
The histopathological image shows the characteristic triphasic components of Wilm's tumor.

Hypertrophic primary osteoarthropathy is not a paraneoplastic syndrome of Wilm's tumor.

Several distinct paraneoplastic syndromes have been reported in Wilm's tumor. They are as follows:

• Hypertension

• Erythrocytosis/Polycythemia

• Hypercalcemia

• Cushing syndrome

• Acquired von Willebrand disease

Bleeding may occur as a paraneoplastic syndrome in Wilm's tumor. It is due to acquired deficiency of von Willebrand factor or factor VII deficiency.

The triphasic components visualized on histopathology are-

1. Malignant small round (blue) cells (blastemal component).

2. Tubular structures/rosettes (epithelial component).

3. Loose pauci-cellular stroma with spindle cells (stromal component)

questions.question: The most common soft tissue sarcoma in the pediatric age group is______.
questions.explanation:
Rhabdomyosarcoma, a tumor of striated skeletal muscle, is the most common pediatric soft tissue sarcoma.

The most common sites are- head and neck (25%) > genitourinary tract (24%) > extremities (19%) > orbit (9%).

questions.question: A 4-year-old girl presents with the lesion shown in this picture. The diagnosis is_____.
questions.explanation:
The lesion seen in the picture is sarcoma botryoides

Vaginal rhabdomyosarcoma may manifest as a grape-like mass of tumor tissue bulging through the vaginal orifice, known as sarcoma botryoides.

questions.question: The precursor lesion of Wilm's tumor is _______.
questions.explanation:
• Wilms tumor is derived from foci of incompletely differentiated/undifferentiated renal mesenchyme called nephrogenic rests.

• Nephrogenic rests usually regress or differentiate, but those that persist can become malignant.

• Nephrogenic rests that persist abnormally in the kidneys into postnatal life are seen in 1% of children in the general population, but are seen in up to 90% of children who develop or have a family history of Wilms tumor.

questions.question: The term “trilateral retinoblastoma” refers to bilateral retinoblastoma + ___________.
questions.explanation:
A pineoblastoma occurring in a child with bilateral hereditary retinoblastoma is called “trilateral retinoblastoma.”

In hereditary retinoblastoma (having spontaneous germline RB1 mutation), second malignancies are a major concern. The most common second malignancy is osteosarcoma; other second neoplasms include rhabdomyosarcoma and melanoma.

questions.question: Tumor which may undergo spontaneous regression is ______.
questions.explanation: Neuroblastoma is an embryonal cancer of the peripheral sympathetic nervous system with heterogeneous presentation and prognosis; some tumors may undergo spontaneous regression, whereas some may be unresponsive to therapy and run a very aggressive course.

questions.question: Which of the following pediatric tumors is called a “triphasic" blastoma?
questions.explanation:
• The classic nephroblastoma, aka Wilms tumor, is a mixed tumor (more than one neoplastic cell type) derived from one germ-cell layer (examples: Wilms tumor and pleomorphic adenoma of salivary gland).

• Histologically, it is made up of the classic "triphasic" combination (recapitulating stages of normal renal development) of

• Stromal

• Epithelial, and

• Blast cells

questions.question: Which of the following is the predominant site of hematopoiesis in a 20-weeks old fetus?
questions.explanation:
The liver is the predominant site of hematopoiesis in the fetus during mid-pregnancy.

Sites of hematopoiesis:

• 2–6 weeks- yolk sac (mesoblastic phase)

• 8–24 weeks- liver (hepatic phase)

• 28 weeks onwards- bone marrow (myeloid phase)

Note:

There is some overlap between the different phases of hematopoiesis. The ranges given above refer to the predominant site of hematopoiesis.

questions.question: Electrophoresis and globin gene sequencing are performed on a normal embryo's blood sample as a part of hematology research. Which of the following type of hemoglobin is likely to be present?
questions.explanation:
Hb Portland is likely to be present as it is embryonic hemoglobin.

Gower-I (ζ2ε2), Gower-II (α2ε2), and Hb Portland (ζ2γ2) are called embryonic hemoglobins and are seen at 8 weeks of intrauterine life.

HbM Iwate (option A) and Hb Auckland (option C) and HbM Boston (option D) result from globin mutations that stabilize iron in the ferric state, leading to congenital methemoglobinemia.

questions.question: When does hemoglobin synthesis switch from HbF to HbA?
questions.answer: C. At 38 weeks of intrauterine life

Hemoglobin synthesis switches from HbF to HbA at 38 weeks of intrauterine life.
