questions.question: Hemoglobin fractions were analyzed in a neonate with a family history of sickle cell disease. The test shows elevated levels of fetal hemoglobin (HbF). Which of the following is true about HbF?
options: HbF accounts for 100% of the total hemoglobin at term.
HbF is resistant to alkali denaturation.
HbF has lower affinity for oxygen than HbA.
HbF has higher affinity for 2,3 bisphosphoglycerate than HbA.
questions.answer: B. HbF is resistant to alkali denaturation.
questions.explanation:
HbF is resistant to alkali denaturation.

Elevated levels of HbF are seen in sickle cell disease and β-thalassemia, where there is a mutation of the β globin gene. Increased HbF levels persist in childhood and later.

Properties of fetal hemoglobin (HbF)

• HbF is resistant to alkali denaturation.

• This property forms the basis of the alkali denaturation test (or Apt test) to detect the presence of fetal blood in maternal circulation in suspected feto-maternal hemorrhage.

• The Kleihauer–Betke test (or acid elution test) is used to quantitate the amount of feto-maternal hemorrhage to calculate the dosage of anti-D required in Rh-negative mothers.

• HBF accounts for 70% of the hemoglobin at term.

• Increased HbF can be seen in hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin, sickle cell anemia, beta-thalassemia, HbC disease, and HbE disease

• HbF has a higher affinity for oxygen.

• This allows for gas exchange from maternal circulation by binding to oxygen at a relatively low oxygen tension in the maternal blood supplying the chorion.

• HbF has lower affinity for 2,3 bisphosphoglycerate (BPG) than HbA.

• Lack of interaction between HbF and 2,3 BPG increases the affinity of HbF to oxygen.

questions.question: You are measuring the life span of RBCs in a normal neonate using chromium-labeled erythrocyte studies as a part of a research project under the clinical hematology department. What would be the result?
questions.explanation:
The lifespan of neonatal RBCs is 60-90 days.

The short lifespan of neonatal RBCs is the cause for rapid fall in hematocrit immediately after birth. The highest hematocrit during a person’s lifetime occurs at birth, and the lowest occurs about 10 weeks later.

The lifespan of RBCs in preterm infants is 35-50 days.

The average lifespan of RBCs in adults is 120 days.

questions.question: A concerned mother brings her preschool child to you. She states that her child was fine until yesterday night and now is covered with bruises and purple dots, which she had noticed while changing his clothes in the morning. She informs you that one month back, her child had a cough and cold. Findings on physical examination are normal, other than petechiae and purpura. Which of the following is most likely to be seen while investigating this child?
questions.explanation:
An otherwise well-baby with acute onset of petechiae and purpura with a preceding history of viral infection 1 to 4 weeks prior to the onset of thrombocytopenia is a classical presentation of (autoimmune) idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura. Prolonged bleeding time is a feature of ITP.

The most common cause of acute onset of thrombocytopenia in an otherwise well-child is (autoimmune) idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

ITP is a bleeding disorder and has prolonged bleeding time, low platelet count, and normal coagulation profile (prothrombin time [PT] and activated partial thromboplastin time [aPTT]).

ITP has an acute presentation with a self-limited course in children.

Features of ITP:

• Commonly affects children between 1-4 years

• Preceded by a viral infection

• Mucocutaneous bleeding

• Ecchymoses and petechiae

• Wet purpura (blood blisters in the mouth)

• Retinal hemorrhages

• Bleeding into the CNS, which may be life-threatening

• Hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy, fever, jaundice are absent

• Resolves spontaneously in 80% of the cases in 4-6 weeks.

Laboratory features of ITP:

• Thrombocytopenia (commonly <20,000/μL)

• Normal/Increased megakaryocytes in bone marrow

• Prolonged bleeding time

• Normal tests for coagulation (PT/aPTT/INR)

• Eosinophilia and lymphocytosis common

• Peripheral smear is normal

• Bone marrow biopsy shows megakaryocytes

questions.question: A pediatrician sees a child in the OPD. He has bruising, petechiae, and occasional minor epistaxis, which has very little interference with his daily activities. Based on further workup, he diagnoses the child as a case of mild ITP. How will he manage this child?
options: A single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin
questions.answer: D. Education, counseling and watchful expectancy
questions.explanation:
Other than education, counseling, and watchful expectancy, no therapy is needed for patients with mild ITP.

Classification system for ITP:

1. No symptoms.

2. Mild symptoms- bruising and petechiae, and occasional minor epistaxis which has very little interference with daily living.

3. Moderate symptoms- more severe skin and mucosal lesions, more troublesome epistaxis, and menorrhagia.

4. Severe symptoms- bleeding episodes - menorrhagia, epistaxis, and melena - requiring transfusions or hospitalization, symptoms interfering seriously with quality of life.

Treatment of ITP:

• Mild to moderate bleeding symptoms- watchful expectancy, education, and counseling.

• Platelet count < 30,000 + risk factors for bleeding (antiplatelet drugs/anticoagulants or concomitant bleeding disorders)- oral glucocorticoids/ intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or IV anti-D

• Severe bleeding symptoms- IV methylprednisolone ± IVIG or IV anti-D

• Life-threatening bleeding (eg. intracranial hemorrhage)- platelet transfusion + IV methylprednisolone + IVIG or IV anti-D

Note:

The role of splenectomy in ITP should be reserved for 2 circumstances:

1. The older child (≥4 yr) with severe ITP that has lasted >1 year (chronic ITP) and whose symptoms are not easily controlled with therapy

2. When life-threatening hemorrhage (ICH) complicates acute ITP and the platelet count cannot be corrected rapidly with transfusion of platelets and administration of IVIG and corticosteroids.

questions.question: Veena, an adolescent girl has had recurrent episodes of bleeding from her nose and gums. She also gives a history of heavy menstrual bleeding and repeated blood transfusions. Her bleeding time is deranged and flow cytometry reveals markedly decreased CD41 and CD61 expression. A defect in which of the following is most likely seen in her?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Glanzmann's thrombasthenia which is characterized by defective platelet aggregation.

Decreased CD41 (GPIIb) and CD61 (GPIIIa) expression are diagnostic of Glanzmann's thrombasthenia. Bleeding in Glanzmann thrombasthenia is quite severe and is typically mucocutaneous, including epistaxis, gingival, and GI bleeding.

Bernard-Soulier syndrome and Glanzmann thrombasthenia are severe congenital disorders of platelet function. Patients usually present with petechiae and purpura at birth. The diagnosis is confirmed by flow cytometric analysis of the patient’s platelet glycoproteins.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common congenital bleeding disorder?
questions.explanation:
Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the most common congenital bleeding disorder.

VWD is thought to affect approximately 0.1- 1% of the population. It is due to abnormal von Willebrand factor (VWF).

VWF is an adhesive protein that acts as a bridge between subendothelial collagen and platelets. It also binds and protects the circulating factor VIII from rapid clearance in circulation.

Von Willebrand disease is mostly inherited as an autosomal dominant trait (rarely autosomal recessive). The types of disease include quantitatively deficient vWF (partial = type 1 or absolute = type 3) or qualitatively abnormal vWF (type 2 = dysproteinemia). The majority (~ 80%) have type 1 disease.

Hemophilia A (factor 8 deficiency) occurs in 1 in 5,000 males. Hemophilia B (factor 9 deficiency) occurs in approximately 1 in 25,000 males.

questions.question: Shortly after birth through normal vaginal delivery, a neonate develops petechiae and purpura. You suspect bleeding disorder and send samples for further workup. A prolonged bleeding time, normal platelet count, normal aPTT is seen along with large platelets in the peripheral smear. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Bernard–Soulier syndrome is the likely diagnosis in the given clinical scenario.

The presence of petechiae and purpura at birth, especially after vaginal delivery, along with prolonged bleeding time, normal platelet count, normal aPTT are seen in qualitative platelet defect disorders like Bernard-Soulier syndrome and Glanzmann's thrombasthenia.

The presence of large platelets rules out Glanzmann's thrombasthenia. Evans syndrome is an autoimmune hemolytic disorder with thrombocytopenia. Von Willebrand's disease doesn't usually manifest at birth.

Bernard–Soulier syndrome is an autosomal recessive functional/qualitative platelet disorder. It is characterized by the deficiency of Gp Ib-IX receptor causing defective platelet adhesion. It is due to genetic mutations in the genes forming the GPIb complex of glycoproteins Ibα, Ibβ, V, and IX.

Laboratory parameters:

• Normal platelet count (or mild thrombocytopenia)

• Large platelets (megathrombocytes) with dense granules

• Bleeding time abnormally prolonged

• Platelet aggregation tests are normal (with collagen, adenosine diphosphate [ADP], epinephrine)

• Ristocetin aggregation test is abnormal/no response

• von Willebrand factor (vWF) levels are normal.

questions.question: A panicked father brings his adopted daughter to your OPD with complaints of bleeding gums. Hematological investigations reveal a normal platelet count and a prolonged bleeding time. The ristocetin-aggregation test was abnormal. Which of the following would you include in your differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The ristocetin-aggregation test is abnormal in both von Willebrand disease and Bernard–Soulier syndrome.

All of the above diseases are inherited bleeding disorders affecting platelet function. Hence, there is prolonged bleeding time but platelet levels are not significantly affected.

Platelet aggregation tests use a panel of platelet agonists (adenosine diphosphate [ADP], epinephrine, collagen, and ristocetin) to measure platelet activation and aggregation in vitro.

Ristocetin induces the binding of VWF to platelets and agglutinates platelets.

Bernard-Soulier syndrome, a severe congenital platelet function disorder, is caused by an absence or severe deficiency of the VWF receptor on the platelet membrane. Hence, in Bernard–Soulier syndrome, no response (or no aggregation) is seen with ristocetin.

The ristocetin-aggregation test is also abnormal in von Willebrand disease. However, it normalizes after the addition of normal plasma (which contains vWF) since there is no defect in binding receptors.

questions.question: An ENT surgeon refers a child who had developed prolonged bleeding post-tonsillectomy to the hematology department for evaluation. Workup revealed a qualitative defect in the von Willebrand factor. Which of the following disease is more likely in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of von Willebrand disease (VWD) and a qualitative defect in von Willebrand factor (VWF) is seen in type 2 VWD.

Features of VWD:

• Most common type is Type 1

• Most severe type is Type 3

• Most common inheritance: Autosomal dominant

• Type 1- partial quantitative deficiency of VWF

• Type 2- qualitative deficiency of VWF

• Type 3- complete quantitative deficiency of VWF

There is no type 4 VWD.

questions.explanation:
von Willebrand disease associated with thrombocytopenia is Type 2B.

questions.question: A pediatric resident administers 0.5-1 mg of phytonadione intramuscularly to all newborn infants in the ward. Deficiency of which of the following factors is prevented by this medication?
questions.explanation:
Intramuscular injection of 0.5-1 mg of phytonadione is given to all newborn infants because it prevents the deficiency of factor VII that occurs transiently after birth.

Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn is caused by a transient deficiency of vitamin K–dependent factors, factors II, VII, IX, and X.

Causes include:

• Lack of free vitamin K from the mother

• Absence of the bacterial intestinal flora normally responsible for the synthesis of vitamin K.

It is responsive to and prevented by vitamin K therapy (0.5-1 mg of phytonadione).

questions.question: The most common bleeding manifestation seen in severe hemophilia is _____________.
questions.explanation:
Recurrent hemarthrosis is the most common bleeding manifestation of severe hemophilia.

Hemophilia is said to be severe when the residual activity of factor VIII is <1%.

Clinical features of hemophilia:

• Clinically, hemophilia A and B are indistinguishable.

• It presents early in life- bleeding after circumcision or when beginning to walk or crawl.

• Most common bleeding manifestation in severe hemophilia is recurrent hemarthrosis and the most common joint affected is the knee.

• Acute hemarthrosis- local pain, swelling, and erythema; muscle contractures due to fixed positioning.

• Chronic hemarthrosis- synovial thickening and synovitis in response to intraarticular blood.

• Muscle hematomas can lead to compartment syndromes.

• Hematuria is common but self-limited.

• Life-threatening bleeding- bleeding to oropharyngeal spaces, CNS, and retroperitoneum.

questions.question: Which of the following factor deficiencies are matched to the correct disease?
questions.answer: D. Factor XI deficiency - Hemophilia C
questions.explanation:
The correct match is factor XI deficiency and hemophilia C.

Clotting factor deficiencies and associated disorders:

Factor V— parahemophilia
Factor VIII— classic hemophilia, hemophilia A
Factor IX— Christmas disease, hemophilia B
Factor X— Stuart-Prower disease
Factor XI— hemophilia C

questions.question: Dinesh, a 2-year-old boy presented with a painful left ankle swelling and difficulty walking. In the past, he had presented with significant hematomas at immunization sites. On investigation, he was found to have haemophilia A. What is the treatment of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The treatment of choice for hemophilia A is factor replacement therapy with factor VIII concentrate.

Cryoprecipitate is used when factor concentrates are not available. Each bag of cryoprecipitate contains 80 IU of factor VIII.

questions.question: A grandmother has noticed that her granddaughter's umbilical stump hasn't fallen off even after 4 weeks. On examination, the pediatrician notices mild bruising. Which of the following clotting factor deficiencies should he suspect?
questions.explanation:
Delayed separation of the umbilical stump beyond 4 weeks is a characteristic finding seen in factor XIII deficiency. However, these findings can also be seen in septicemia or local infections.

Factor XIII is responsible for the crosslinking of fibrin to stabilize the fibrin clot, symptoms of delayed hemorrhage are secondary to the instability of the clot. Typically, patients have trauma one day and then have a bruise or hematoma the next day.

Results of the usual screening tests for hemostasis are normal in patients with factor XIII deficiency. Screening tests for factor XIII deficiency are based on the observation that there is increased solubility of the clot because of the failure of cross-linking.

questions.question: As a part of the Anemia Mukt Bharat program, you screen preschool children for anemia. What Hb values would prompt you to diagnose anemia in this age group?
questions.explanation:
Anaemia in a preschool child is defined as a hemoglobin level of <11 g/dL.

Preschool age is defined as 2 to 5 years.

WHO cut-offs for the diagnosis of anaemia:

questions.question: A 7-year-old child is brought to the pediatric OPD by his parents with complaints of excessive sleepiness, and poor scholastic performance. On examination, the child has pallor involving the tongue, conjunctiva, and nail beds. A flow murmur is heard upon auscultation. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the underlying disease?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical signs and symptoms are suggestive of anemia. Acquired hypoproliferative anemia, is the most common cause of anemia in children among the given options.

Iron-deficiency anemia (which is classified as an acquired hypoproliferative anemia) is the most common cause of anemia in children and adults worldwide. Iron deficiency is also the most common nutrient deficiency worldwide.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding iron?
options: Breast milk has higher iron content than cow's milk.
Cow's milk has higher oral bio-availability of iron than breast milk.
Introduction of cow's milk at 5 months of age decreases the risk of iron deficiency.
Cow's milk protein can cause chronic intestinal blood loss in infants.
questions.answer: D. Cow's milk protein can cause chronic intestinal blood loss in infants.
questions.explanation:
Exposure to whole cow’s milk protein can cause chronic intestinal blood loss in infants. Therefore, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends delaying the introduction of cow's milk in infancy and limiting it to <700 mL/day.

Both cow's milk and breast milk have the same iron content (≈0.1mg/dL).

The bioavailability of breast milk iron is 2-3 times higher than cow's milk iron.

Exclusive breastfeeding until 6 months of age and complementary feeding with iron-rich foods thereafter reduces the risk of iron-deficiency anemia in infants.

questions.question: An 8-year-old child who has been recently diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia is started on iron therapy. What is the earliest hematological response that you would expect to see following treatment?
questions.explanation:
Bone marrow erythroid hyperplasia is the earliest hematological response observed following iron therapy in iron-deficiency anemia.

Responses to iron therapy in iron deficiency anemia:

12 to 24 h

36 to 48 h

48 to 72 h (peaks at 5-7 days)

questions.question: A child who was diagnosed 3 months back with iron deficiency anemia presents with low hemoglobin despite being on oral iron therapy. What is the most likely cause for the non-responsiveness that you should consider in your differential?
options: Occult blood loss from parasitic infestations.
questions.explanation:
Poor compliance is the most likely cause of non-responsiveness to oral iron therapy.

Differential diagnosis of microcytic anemia that fails to respond to oral iron:

1. Poor compliance (most common cause)

2. Incorrect dose or formulation

3. Malabsorption of administered iron

4. Ongoing blood loss, including gastrointestinal, menstrual, and pulmonary

5. Concurrent infection or inflammatory disorder

6. Concurrent vitamin B12 or folate deficiency

7. Diagnosis other than iron deficiency

• Thalassemias

• Hemoglobins C and E disorders

• Anemia of chronic disease

• Lead poisoning

• Sickle thalassemias, hemoglobin SC disease

• Iron refractory iron-deficiency anemia (IRIDA)

questions.question: Which of the following tests can be used to screen a newborn with a family history of sickle cell disease?
questions.explanation:
High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is used to screen a newborn with a family history of sickle cell disease.

Option A: Hemoglobin electrophoresis is the confirmatory test for sickle cell anemia

Option C: Heel-prick Guthrie test is the neonatal screening test for phenylketonuria.

Option D: Tandem mass spectrometry is being used for neonatal screening of inherited metabolic disorders.

questions.question:
Ravi, an adolescent with sickle cell disease presents to the emergency room with chest pain and respiratory distress. Pulse oximeter shows 85% saturation in room air. Chest X-ray shows new radiodensities. Sputum and blood culture showed no growth. Which of the following are used in the management of this condition?

1. Macrolide antibiotics

2. Incentive spirometry

3. Blood transfusion

4. Third-generation cephalosporins

5. Supplemental oxygen
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute chest syndrome and all of the above are used in the management.

Acute chest syndrome (ACS) refers to a life-threatening pulmonary complication of sickle cell disease. It is diagnosed with the presence of a new radiodensity on chest radiography with any 2 of the following:

1. Fever

2. Respiratory distress

3. Hypoxia

4. Cough

5. Chest pain

In this case, the child with sickle cell anemia satisfies the above criteria. He presented with chest pain and respiratory distress and his chest X-ray image shows new radiodensities.

Most patients with ACS do not have a single identifiable cause. Infection is the most well-known etiology, yet only 30% of ACS episodes will have positive sputum or bronchoalveolar culture. The most common bacterial pathogens implicated are S. pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydia spp.

Oxygen should be supplemented to all patients who demonstrate hypoxia.

Blood transfusion is the only method to abort a rapidly progressing episode of ACS.

Because of the clinical overlap between pneumonia and ACS, all episodes should be treated promptly with antimicrobial therapy, including at least a macrolide and possibly a third-generation cephalosporin.

Regular use of an incentive spirometer at 10-12 breaths every 2 hours can significantly reduce the frequency of subsequent acute chest pain episodes.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy who is a known case of sickle cell disease presents with acute chest syndrome. Which of the following is the drug of choice to reduce such painful crises in the future?
questions.explanation:
Hydroxyurea is the drug of choice for reducing painful crises in sickle cell anemia.

Hydroxyurea is a myelosuppressive agent that is effective in reducing the frequency of painful episodes like dactylitis and acute chest syndrome, decreasing the rate of hospitalization, and requirement for blood transfusion. It is safe and well-tolerated in children and infants.

Option A: Hydrocodone (opioid) is used in the treatment of pain crisis in sickle cell anemia.

Option C: Corticosteroids is one of the first-line therapies for acute idiopathic thrombocytic purpura (ITP) with risk factors for bleeding.

Option D: Ruxolitinib is the drug of choice for the treatment of polycythemia vera.

questions.question: Kevin and Anita both have sickle cell traits. They are devastated when they find out both their children have sickle cell anemia. Kirti is an active 9-year-old. Kamal is her 3-month-old brother. Which of the following prophylactic measures would you not recommend to them?
options: Oral penicillin prophylaxis up to 5 years of age in Kamal
Annual transcranial Doppler ultrasound for Kirti upto age 16
Annual ophthalmology screening from the age of 10 years in both
Hydroxyurea prophylaxis regardless of disease severity or symptoms in both
questions.answer: D. Hydroxyurea prophylaxis regardless of disease severity or symptoms in both
questions.explanation:
Hydroxyurea prophylaxis regardless of disease severity is recommended in children over 9 months of age. Hydroxyurea can be considered for use in infants between six and nine months with symptomatic disease.

Oral penicillin VK is recommended until at least 5 years of age. It is continued beyond 5 years of age in children with a history of pneumococcal infection. Erythromycin ethyl succinate is used if the patient is allergic to penicillin. Pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccinations are administered because of the risk of functional asplenia.

Transcranial Doppler ultrasound is recommended, starting at age of 2 years. This has lead to a decrease in the prevalence of overt stroke among children with sickle cell anemia. Screening should occur annually from age 2-16.

Annual ophthalmology screening should commence from the age of 10 years to screen for retinopathy.

questions.question: Which of the following is responsible for the most common cause of congenital hemolytic anemia due to an enzyme deficiency?
options: Deficiency of an enzyme in glycolysis pathway
Deficiency of an enzyme in Hexose monophosphate pathway
Deficiency of an enzyme in Kreb's cycle
Deficiency of an enzymes in fructose metabolism pathway
questions.answer: B. Deficiency of an enzyme in Hexose monophosphate pathway
questions.explanation:
Deficiency of an enzyme in the hexose monophosphate pathway ie., glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency(G6PD Deficiency), is the most common cause of congenital hemolytic anemia due to an enzyme deficiency

Most common enzymopathies causing hemolytic anemia (in order of most common to least):

1. Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PD)

2. Pyruvate kinase deficiency

3. 5' nucleotidase deficiency

questions.question: Which of the following is not a cause of non-immune hydrops fetalis?
questions.explanation:
Rh incompatibility causes immune hydrops fetalis, whereas alpha-thalassemia, parvovirus B19 infection, and twin-twin transfusion syndrome cause non-immune hydrops fetalis.

Hydrops fetalis refers to the abnormal fluid collections in fetal soft tissues and serous cavities. Edema, signs of heart failure, and profound intra-uterine anemia are the presenting features in the fetus. Other clinical features include marked hepatosplenomegaly, retardation in brain growth, hydrocephaly, urogenital and cardiovascular deformities, and extramedullary erythropoiesis.

Non-immune hydrops fetalis (NIHF) comprises the subgroup of cases not caused by red cell alloimmunization (e.g., Rh(D), Kell)

Bart's hydrops fetalis (alpha-thalassemia) is caused by the deletion or inactivation of all four alpha-globin alleles, leading to a severe deficiency in alpha-globin chains of Hb and to the production of gamma-4 tetramers (Hb Bart). Hb Bart tetramers have an extremely high oxygen affinity and are incapable of effective tissue oxygen delivery.

Parvovirus B19 infection can cause fetal anemia, non-immune fetal hydrops, and fetal death.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about abnormal hemoglobins and their mechanisms is true?
options: HbS is due to substitution of lysine for glutamine in the 6th position of the beta-globin gene.
HbH is the deletion of three alpha-globin genes.
Hb Bart is the deletion of all four beta-globin genes.
HbC is due to substitution of valine for lysine in the 6th position of the beta-globin gene.
questions.answer: B. HbH is the deletion of three alpha-globin genes.
questions.explanation:
HbH is the deletion of three alpha globin chains.

HbS is due to the substitution of valine for glutamic acid in the 6th position of the beta-globin gene (option A).

Hb Bart is the deletion of all four alpha-globin genes. (There are only 2 beta-globin genes) (option C)

HbC is due to the substitution of lysine for glutamic acid in the 6th position of the beta-globin gene (option D).

questions.question: A 5-year-old child presented with pallor, massive hepatosplenomegaly, and hemolytic facies. Which of the following is the most likely iron profile in this patient?
options: Iron - low, Ferritin - low, TIBC-high, TSAT-low
Iron - high, Ferritin - normal, TIBC-normal, TSAT-normal
Iron - low, Ferritin - high, TIBC-low, TSAT-low
Iron - low, Ferritin - low, TIBC-low, TSAT-low
questions.answer: B. Iron - high, Ferritin - normal, TIBC-normal, TSAT-normal
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of thalassemia and the most likely iron profile is iron - normal/high, ferritin - normal, total iron - binding capacity (TIBC) - normal, and transferrin saturation (TSAT) - normal.

Iron- low, ferritin-low, TIBC-high, TSAT-low is seen in iron-deficiency anemia.

Iron-low, ferritin-high, TIBC-low, TSAT-low is seen in anemia of chronic disease.

questions.question: A toddler presented with progressive pallor and abdominal distention. On investigations, he had low hemoglobin. Which of the following red cell indices can be used to distinguish thalassemia from iron deficiency anemia?
options: Mean corpuscular volume/ Red blood cell count
questions.answer: C. Mean corpuscular volume/ Red blood cell count
questions.explanation:
Mean corpuscular volume/ Red blood cell count (MCV/RBC) also known as Mentzer index can be used to distinguish thalassemia from iron-deficiency anemia (IDA).

MCV (mean corpuscular volume) and MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin) are low in both IDA and thalassemia. RBC count may be normal in thalassemia, whereas it is reduced in IDA. A lower RBC count in IDA means the denominator is smaller, yielding a greater MCV/RBC ratio.

Mentzer index is:

• More than 13 in iron-deficiency anemia

• Less than 13 in thalassemia

questions.question: You see a child in the hematology unit who has developed anemia which is progressive along with cardiac decompensation requiring transfusion. He is in the latter half of infancy. You suspect transfusion-dependent thalassemia. Which of the following electrophoresis pattern is seen here?
questions.explanation:
HbA=0%, HbA2=5%, HbF=95% is seen on hemoglobin electrophoresis in transfusion-dependent thalassemia.

Given clinical picture where the child becomes symptomatic during the second 6 months of life requiring transfusion is suggestive of beta-thalassemia major or transfusion-dependent thalassemia.

• Normal pattern- HbA=95%, HbA2=3.5%, HbF =1.5%

• Beta-thalassemia trait- HbA=90%, HbA2=5%, HbF=5%

• Beta-thalassemia intermedia- HbA=45%, HbA2=5%, HbF=50%

Alpha- and beta-thalassemia are inherited disorders in which there is reduced production of alpha-globin or beta-globin chains, respectively. This leads to precipitation of the excess (unpaired) chains, interfering with red blood cell (RBC) production and survival.Disease severity is inversely correlated with the number of functioning globin chains.Each individual carries 2 beta-chain genes and 4 alpha-chain genes.

questions.question: You are given the following x-ray in the viva session. Which of the following is the likely reason behind this abnormal appearance?
questions.explanation:
Crew-cut or hair-on-end appearance on X-ray imaging of the skull is due to extramedullary hematopoiesis, which is seen in thalassemia.

Ineffective erythropoiesis leads to extramedullary hematopoiesis, which causes the widening of the diploic space, thereby causing the thickening of trabeculae. This results in the classical crew-cut or hair-on-end appearance on x-ray imaging of the skull. Extramedullary hematopoiesis also leads to hepatosplenomegaly and enlarged and distorted bony prominences over the face, leading to the characteristic chipmunk facies in thalassemia.

questions.question: You are evaluating a 4-year-old child with ß-thalassemia major. He has been on chronic transfusion therapy since the age of 1 year. He has developed transfusion-induced iron overload. The child has an increased risk of developing which of the following infections?
questions.explanation:
Thalassemic children with transfusion-induced iron overload are at an increased risk of infections with Yersinia enterocolitica.

Iron excess immunologically compromises the host and greatly enhances yersinial growth.

Streptococcus pneumoniae (option A), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (option B), and Chlamydia species (option D) are the common organisms causing infections that predispose to acute chest syndrome in sickle cell anemia.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about Diamond Blackfan Anemia?
options: Short stature, craniofacial abnormalities, and triphalangeal thumb are common features.
Peripheral smear shows microcytic hypochromic anemia.
Bone marrow failure includes erythroid, myeloid and megakaryocytic lineages.
questions.answer: A. Short stature, craniofacial abnormalities, and triphalangeal thumb are common features.
questions.explanation:
Short stature, craniofacial abnormalities, and triphalangeal thumb are common features is the true statement regarding Diamond–Blackfan anemia (DBA).

Features of DBA (congenital hypoplastic anemia):

• Autosomal dominant inheritance.

• Macrocytosis without hypersegmented neutrophils or other megaloblastic features.

• Reticulocytopenia.

• Absent RBC precursors in the otherwise normally cellular bone marrow. Other lineages are unaffected.

• Craniofacial anomaly is the most common congenital anomaly seeen.

• Hypertelorism, snub nose, and high-arched palate seen.

• Thumb abnormalities- flattening of the thenar eminence and triphalangeal thumb

• Short stature

Treatment: Corticosteroids, chronic red cell transfusions, and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

Image showing triphalangeal thumb:

questions.question: You see a neonate undergoing phototherapy for hyperbilirubinemia. Blood workup revealed the presence of a hemolytic picture along with spherocytes and polychromatophilic reticulocytes. MCV is low normal along with elevated MCHC. There was a similar history of hemolytic anemia in the mother. The pedigree analysis points towards an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance. The most likely genetic mutation seen in this case is?
questions.explanation:
The Ankyrin gene mutation is the most likely genetic mutation seen in the given case of autosomal-dominant hereditary spherocytosis (HS).

Hemolytic manifestation causing indirect hyperbilirubinemia requiring phototherapy or blood transfusion in infancy with positive family history and typical laboratory findings is suggestive of HS.

History of blood transfusions in later life and not infancy is used to classify the severity of the disease.

• Most common mode of inheritance of HS- autosomal dominant

• Most common gene mutation in autosomal-dominant HS- ankyrin > Band 3

• Most common gene mutation in autosomal-recessive HS- spectrin

• Most severe form of HS- spectrin (recessive)

Classification of the severity of HS is based on the requirement of blood transfusion in later life and not during infancy.

questions.question: An 11-year-old child, born out of consanguineous marriage developed signs and symptoms of hemolytic anemia and progressive ataxia. He is a known case of retinitis pigmentosa and also had symptoms of fat malabsorption. A peripheral smear of the child is shown. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical features along with the peripheral smear showing acanthocytes make the diagnosis of abetalipoproteinemia more likely.

Abetalipoproteinemia is an autosomal recessive hemolytic disorder in which acanthocytosis is associated with fat malabsorption, progressive ataxia, and retinitis pigmentosa.

Acanthocytes or spur cells are spiculated red cells with a few projections of varying size and surface distribution. The most significant associations include abetalipoproteinemia and severe liver disease.

Note: Do not confuse acanthocytes with echinocytes or burr cells. They appear with multiple small projections that are uniformly distributed on the red cell surface. It is a universal feature of uremia.

Image: The peripheral smear below shows regularly spaced, smoothly rounded crenulations, which are characteristic of a burr cell.

Peripheral smear in other options:

Hemolytic uremic syndrome (option A); Numerous schistocytes and nucleated RBCs with extremely low platelets:

Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (option B); bite cells or degmacytes or blister cells. In G6PD deficiency uncontrolled oxidative stress causes hemoglobin to denature and form Heinz bodies. Bite cells result from the removal of Heinz bodies by macrophages in the spleen.

The image below shows bite cells represented by blue arrows, black arrows represent burr cells:

Hereditary stomatocytosis (option C); Numerous stomatocytes (Uniconcave cup with mouth-shaped area of central pallor), caused by missense mutation in band 3 or AEP

questions.question: A 12-year-old child is receiving iron and folic acid supplements under the Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation (WIFS) Programme. Which of the following is true about this program?
options: It was launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
It is meant exclusively for adolescent school girls between 10-19 years of age.
It exclusively covers government schools in rural India.
It recommends that administration of 50 mg of elemental iron.
questions.answer: A. It was launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
questions.explanation:
Weekly Iron Folic acid Supplementation (WIFS) was launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is the true statement among the given options.

Salient features of Weekly Iron Folic acid Supplementation (WIFS):

i. Objective of Weekly Iron Folic acid Supplementation (WIFS): To reduce the prevalence and severity of anemia in the adolescent population (10-19 years).

ii. Target groups

• School-going adolescent girls and boys in 6th to 12th class enrolled in government/government-aided/municipal schools

• Out-of-school adolescent girls

iii. Intervention

• Administration of supervised weekly iron-folic acid supplements of 60 mg elemental iron and 500 μg folic acid by using a fixed-day approach

• Screening of target groups for moderate/severe anemia and referring these cases to an appropriate health facility

• Biannual de-worming (albendazole 400 mg), six months apart, for the control of helminthic infestation

• Information and counseling for improving dietary intake and for taking actions for prevention of intestinal worm infestation

questions.question: A toddler is brought by his mother with complaints of poor feeding, lethargy, and chronic diarrhea for the past 4 months. Upon clinical examination, the child has pale conjunctiva and is tachycardic. Blood workup reveals low hemoglobin and smear shows macrocytosis, anisopoikilocytosis, and large neutrophils with hyper-segmented nuclei. Serum homocysteine levels are elevated and methylmalonate levels are normal. Bone marrow shows erythroid hyperplasia. Which of the following is true about this condition?
options: Lactate dehydrogenase levels in serum is low.
Folate-deficient mother's give birth to infants with folate deficiency.
Methylenetetrahydrofolate (MTHFR) deficiency is associated with megaloblastic anemia.
Goat’s milk fed infants are more likely to develop this disease
questions.answer: D. Goat’s milk fed infants are more likely to develop this disease
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario along with the megaloblastic picture elevated homocysteine levels, and normal methylmalonate levels are suggestive of folate deficiency anemia.

Goat’s milk is deficient in folate. So goat milk-fed infants are likely to develop folate deficiency anemia. Human breast milk, infant formulas, and pasteurized cow’s milk provide adequate amounts of folic acid.

In folate deficiency anemia, lactate dehydrogenase levels in serum are elevated. Folate-deficient mothers do not give birth to infants with folate deficiency because there is a selective transfer of folate to the fetus via the placental folate receptors.

Methylenetetrahydrofolate (MTHFR) deficiency is the most common inborn error of folate metabolism, and severe cases can produce neurologic and vascular complications; there is no associated megaloblastic anemia.

Malnutrition is the most common cause of folate deficiency in children.

Note: Both homocysteine and methylmalonate levels are elevated in B12 deficiency anemia.

questions.question: A child presents with megaloblastic anemia that is unresponsive to vitamin C, vitamin B12, and folic acid, but responsive to uridine. What do you suspect?
questions.explanation:
Orotic aciduria is to be suspected in this child. Megaloblastic anemia that is responsive to uridine is consistent with orotic aciduria.

Orotic aciduria is a rare inborn error of metabolism in children. A defect in the pyrimidine synthesis pathway results in the failure of conversion of orotic acid to uridine.

Supplementation of vitamin B12, folate, and vitamin C rules out the more common nutritional causes of megaloblastic anemia.

Thiamine deficiency (option A) and anemia due to liver disease (option B) do not respond to uridine.

Pernicious anemia (Option C) responds to treatment with vitamin B12.

questions.question: A 3-year-old child is brought to the clinic because of walking difficulties. His mother says he has always walked on his toes and walks by tilting side-to-side. He also has progressive muscle weakness. There is no history of trauma, fever, or rash. On examination, calf hypertrophy with atrophied thigh muscles is noted as shown below. There is no tenderness on palpation. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The finding of enlarged calf muscles and atrophied thigh muscles with a history of muscle weakness and waddling gait are suggestive of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD).

Duchenne muscular dystrophy is the most common hereditary neuromuscular disease. It is an X-linked recessive disorder. In DMD, pseudohypertrophy of the calf muscles which occurs due to muscle enlargement by the infiltration of fat. It is paradoxically weak, unlike the muscle that enlarges due to hypertrophy. Pseudohypertrophy of calf muscles is the characteristic feature of DMD, whereas the other 3 conditions mentioned in the options do not have this feature.

Clinical features:

1. Progressive weakness with developmental delay

2. Pseudohypertrophy of calves

3. Wasting of thigh muscles

4. Characteristic Trendelenburg gait or hip waddle.

5. Gower’s sign

6. Dilated cardiomyopathy

Diagnosis:

1. Elevated serum creatine kinase levels

2. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis for dystrophin gene

3. If PCR is normal, but clinical suspicion is high, muscle biopsy with dystrophin immunocytochemistry is done.

Treatment includes supportive management for cardiac decompensation, nutritional management, physiotherapy, and glucocorticoids. Death usually occurs by 18 to 20 years of age due to respiratory failure, intractable heart failure, pneumonia, or aspiration.

Note- The FDA has approved Vamorolone, a novel corticosteroid for the treatment of DMD. The drug offers enhanced anti-inflammatory properties and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism as well. It is potentially a safer and more effective alternative to glucocorticoids.

Other options:

Option B: Myotonic dystrophy presents with distal muscle weakness, proximal muscle involvement is very late.

Option C: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), type 1 (which is most common) presents in infancy. Death occurs early.

Option D: Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy presents with predominant involvement of scapular and humeral muscles. The given question describes the involvement of lower limb muscles. Hence, Emery–Dreifuss dystrophy, in this case, is less likely.

questions.question: The image below shows the model of a skeletal muscle fiber. Which of the following structures is affected in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
questions.explanation:
The structure marked as B in the image represents dystrophin protein (a sarcolemmal protein), which is absent in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) due to a mutation in the dystrophin gene.

This gene is located on the short arm of chromosome X near the p21 locus (Xp21). Lack of dystrophin leads to cellular instability, which leads to progressive leakage of intracellular components.

questions.question: Abhi, a young boy is being evaluated in the ward for proximal muscle weakness. Waddling gait and Gowers sign are observed in this child. Genetic analysis confirms the diagnosis as Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Which of the following is false regarding this patient's condition?
options: It is less severe than Becker's dystrophy
Tendon reflexes are lost after age 6
Gene affected is the largest gene in humans
questions.answer: A. It is less severe than Becker's dystrophy
questions.explanation:
Duchenne muscular dystrophy is more severe than Becker’s dystrophy. In DMD, tendon reflexes are lost after age 6.

Becker’s dystrophy is similar to Duchenne muscular dystrophy with a genetic defect at the same locus (Xp21) but clinically less severe. Gene affected in both is dystrophin, which is the largest gene in humans.

Important differences between Duchenne and Becker’s muscular dystrophy:

Duchenne's dystrophy
Becker's dystrophy

Onset
Age: 2–3 years
Age: 5–15 years

Weakness
Progressive
Variable

Intellectual impairment
Common
Uncommon

Prognosis
Wheelchair dependant by adolescence
Ambulatory till early adult life

Death
By the age of 18–20 years
By 40s or 50s

questions.question:
You observe a six-year-old child in the ward and notice the following. Which of the following are true regarding this sign?

1. It is due to distal muscle weakness

2. It is pathognomonic of Duchenne muscular dystrophy

3. It can be seen in Dermatomyositis

4. It is seen only in children older than 5 years

5. It can be seen in Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy
questions.explanation:
The image shows the Gowers sign. Patients use their hands to “climb up” their legs when asked to rise from a prone position to compensate for proximal lower-extremity weakness. An early Gowers sign is often evident by age of 3 years and is fully expressed by age of 5 or 6 years.

This maneuver can be seen in patients with:

• Duchenne muscular dystrophy

• Becker's muscular dystrophy

• Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy

• Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy

• Polymyositis

• Dermatomyositis

questions.question: A concerned mother brought her son to the clinic because of difficulty writing in school. She also says that his eyes remain partially open when he sleeps. There is no history of trauma or surgery. On examination, he has asymmetric wrist and finger weakness. The mouth appears puckered and rounded, deltoid muscles are flattened and the following finding is observed. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The image shows winging of the scapula, which when combined with this patient's features are suggestive of facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy.

Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy is an autosomal dominant condition that generally presents with asymmetric weakness in facial and shoulder girdle muscles. Occasionally, finger and wrist weakness is the first symptom.

The mouth is rounded and appears puckered because of the protruding lips. Upper facial weakness will manifest as an inability to close the eyes completely in sleep. Scapular winging is prominent, even in infants. Flattening or even concavity of the deltoid contour is seen, and the biceps and triceps brachii muscles are wasted and weak. Eventually, proximal muscles get involved and undergo atrophy, and Gowers sign & Trendelenburg gait appear. Lumbar lordosis, foot drop, and kyphoscoliosis are common complications.

Treatment includes orthopedic measures for scoliosis and foot drop, surgical intervention for scapular deformity. Physiotherapy has no value.

Other options:

Long thoracic nerve palsy: No history of trauma or surgery rules out this diagnosis.

Klippel-Feil syndrome: Classic triad of Klippel–Feil syndrome (congenital musculoskeletal condition)

• low posterior hairline

• short neck

• decreased cervical range of motion

Myotonic dystrophy patients have a characteristic V-shaped upper lip, a history of myotonia, and progressive weakness.

questions.question: Rekha brought her 5-day-old infant to the clinic because of feeding difficulties. She says he does not latch properly. Her antenatal history is significant for polyhydramnios and decreased fetal movements. On examination, hypotonia and hyporeflexia are noted in the baby. which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, only Spinal muscular atrophy presents in infancy. The rest present in late childhood.

Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a degenerative disease of motor neurons, that is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. It usually starts in infancy with hypotonia, hyporeflexia, and thin muscle mass (atrophy). Polyhydramnios may be present prenatally due to weakness in swallowing.

Diagnosis is done by genetic testing for SMN gene mutation. Muscle biopsy is done for cases with negative genetic testing and strong clinical suspicion. The muscle biopsy in infancy shows a characteristic pattern of perinatal denervation that is unlike that of a mature muscle. Groups of giant type I fibers are mixed with fascicles of severely atrophic fibers.

Treatment is symptomatic and supportive.

Recent updates:

• Nusinersen is an antisense oligonucleotide approved by the FDA for treating SMA. It is administered intrathecally.

• Risdiplam (first oral drug) has been approved by FDA to treat infants >2 months of age with SMA. It is an oral splicing modifier that corrects the splicing defect of SMN2, which leads to increased levels of full-length SMN protein.

questions.question: Pinky, a high school girl, has difficulty in combing her hair and climbing up stairs since 6 months. On examination, Gower sign is positive and maculopapular rash present over MCP joints. What is the next appropriate investigation to be done?
questions.explanation:
A maculopapular rash over the metacarpophalangeal joints is indicative of Gottron papules in a child with proximal muscle weakness is suggestive of juvenile dermatomyositis. As it is an inflammatory myopathy, the next investigation is serum creatine kinase.

Though the gold standard investigation is a muscle biopsy, it is indicated only when the diagnosis is in doubt or when grading of the disease severity is required. Nerve conduction studies are usually normal unless associated with severe muscle necrosis and atrophy. Electromyography would show the characteristic signs of myopathy and muscle fiber necrosis but is preferably performed in a specialized center.

questions.question: A 1-day-old girl is being evaluated for decreased muscle tone. On examination, thin cheeks, high arched palate, inverted V-shaped upper lip, and a narrow head are observed. Facial muscle wasting is prominent. She has a club foot deformity. Her mother has a history of delayed relaxation of hand muscles after opening doors. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The patient's clinical features along with the history of myotonia in the mother are suggestive of Myotonic dystrophy. Facial weakness, inverted V-shaped upper lip, and loss of muscle mass in the temporal fossae are characteristic of myotonic muscular dystrophy.

A severe congenital form of myotonic dystrophy appears in infants born to mothers with symptomatic myotonic dystrophy. It is inherited as an autosomal-dominant trait. Clinical features include:

• Skeletal deformities (clubfoot deformities alone or congenital contractures involving many joints and can even include the cervical spine).

• Generalized hypotonia and weakness at birth

• Facial wasting and weakness

• Inverted V-shaped upper lip

• Loss of muscle mass in the temporal fossa

Infants can require gavage feeding or ventilator support for respiratory muscle weakness or apnea.

Other Options:

Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), type 1 (which is most common) presents in infancy with hypotonia but has no facial features that are present in this child.

In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the baby appears normal at birth and the facial features present in this child are not seen.

Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy presents with predominant involvement of scapular and humeral muscles. The given scenario makes this diagnosis less likely.

questions.question: A small baby who was being evaluated for multiple bone fractures with minor trauma is found to have brittle bone disease. Which of the following is false regarding this disease?
options: It is caused by defects in type 2 collagen.
Blue sclerae and deafness may be associated.
Biphosphonates are useful in the treatment.
questions.answer: A. It is caused by defects in type 2 collagen.
questions.explanation:
Brittle bone disease is another name for osteogenesis imperfecta (OI). It is due to defects in type 1 collagen, not type 2 collagen.

There are 12 types of OI, with type 1 being the most common. Triad of fragile bones, blue sclera, and deafness is known as van der Hoeve syndrome. Treatment includes bisphosphonate therapy and orthopedic rehabilitation.

questions.question: All of the following are radiological signs of scurvy except _________.
questions.explanation:
White line of Frankel, ground-glass appearance, and zone of rarefaction are the radiological signs seen in scurvy.

Radiological signs in scurvy includes:

• White line of Frankel: calcified cartilage at metaphyses

• Trummerfeld zone: lucent metaphyseal band underlying Frankel line

• Pelkan spur: lateral prolongation of the white line, which is present at the cortical ends

• Wimberger ring sign: circular, opaque radiologic shadow surrounding epiphyseal centers of ossification

questions.question: A 6-month-old infant presents with anemia and hepatosplenomegaly. X-ray imaging done as a part of the skeletal survey showed the following image. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Anemia and hepatosplenomegaly in an infant with the X-ray image showing dense bones, and bone within the bone appearance is suggestive of osteopetrosis.

Osteopetrosis/Marble bone disease/Albers–Schönberg disease

It is a disorder involving defective bone resorption due to mutation of CLCN7 in osteoclasts.

Clinical features include macrocephaly, developmental delay, anemia (reduced bone marrow cavity), and hepatosplenomegaly (compensatory extramedullary hematopoiesis). Low serum calcium and phosphorus levels with elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) and normal vitamin D levels are observed. Radiological features include diffuse bone sclerosis with clubbing of metaphyses. Bone within the bone appearance and "sandwich" appearance of the vertebral bodies can be seen (image). Treatment is symptomatic. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation can be done in severe cases.

Achondroplasia usually presents with pulmonary symptoms like dyspnea, obstructive sleep apnea, and recurrent infections.

In both scurvy and osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), the child cries on touching. On radiography, certain typical features are seen in scurvy, while multiple fractures are seen in OI.

questions.question: Most common rheumatic disease in children is _______.
questions.explanation:
The most common rheumatic disease in children is juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA).

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis represents a heterogeneous group of chronic disorders characterized by

• Arthritis* in ≥1 joint

• Age at onset: <16 years

• Duration of disease: ≥6 weeks

*Arthritis clinically defined as swelling or effusion, or the presence of 2 or more of the following signs:

• limitation of range of motion

• tenderness or pain on motion

• increased heat

questions.question: You are evaluating JIA patients in a pediatric rheumatology clinic. As per the ILAR criteria, which of the following patients would you not include under JIA?
options: A 18-year-old with RF negative Polyarthritis first diagnosed 3 years back
questions.answer: D. A 14-year-old female with Reactive arthritis
questions.explanation:
Reactive arthritis is not a subtype of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis(JIA) so you would not include this subset of patients under your evaluation.

ILAR (International League of Associations for Rheumatology) defines JIA as arthritis of one or more joints with onset below 16 years of age and persisting for at least 6 weeks.

The subtypes of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA):-

1. Oligoarthritis (4 or lesser joints) (Most common type)

2. Polyarthritis (5 or more joints)

1. RF Positive

2. RF Negative

3. Systemic JIA

4. Psoriatic arthritis

5. Enthesitis-related arthritis

6. Undifferentiated

questions.question: Mohit is brought to the pediatrician by his mother because of red-eye. He complains of blurring of vision and on examination, the pupil appears as shown in the picture. Which of the following subtype of JIA is associated with the highest risk for the ophthalmic complication noted in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The patient has red-eye and the blurring of vision along with the finding of the irregular pupil, which is suggestive of uveitis. ANA-positive oligoarthritis is associated with the highest risk for uveitis in patients with Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis.

The presence of a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) confers increased risk for uveitis in children with JIA and requires periodic slit-lamp examination every 3 months.

questions.question: A worried mother brings her 4-year-old girl who has been complaining about pain in the joints of arms and legs for 2 months. On examination, multiple nodules over the bony prominences suggestive of rheumatoid nodules are noted. On investigation, RA-factor was found positive pointing to the diagnosis of RF-positive polyarthritis. Which of the following complication is not likely to occur in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Ankylosis is not seen in patients with RF-positive Polyarthritis.

Polyarthritis is characterized by inflammation of ≥5 joints in both upper and lower extremities. Rheumatoid factor (RF)–positive polyarthritis resembles the characteristic symmetric presentation of adult rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatoid nodules on the extensor surfaces of the elbows, spine, and over the Achilles tendons are associated with a more severe course and almost exclusively occur in RF-positive individuals.

Complications may include:

• Micrognathia (due to chronic temporomandibular joint disease)

• Cervical spine involvement, manifesting as decreased neck extension, occurs with a risk of atlantoaxial subluxation and neurologic sequelae.

• Hip disease may be subtle, with findings of erosion.

questions.question: Which of the following is false regarding systemic Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis?
questions.explanation:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) factor is negative in systemic JIA. It is positive in a subtype of polyarthritic type of JIA.

Systemic JIA is characterized by a fever of at least 2 weeks and Arthritis in 1 or more joints + at least one of

• Evanescent erythematous rash

• Prominent visceral involvement, including hepatosplenomegaly

• Generalized lymphadenopathy

• Serositis

questions.question: Anuj, a school-going kid has been brought to the pediatric OPD by his mother with complaints of fever for 3 weeks. She says her son has been skipping school because of the fever but in the evening he gets better and plays with his siblings. She also noticed a rash that appears along with fever and disappears spontaneously. He has a history of joint pain on and off since pre-school. On examination, generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are noted along with an evanescent erythematous rash on the trunk. Which of the following characteristically defines the fever associated with this child's condition?
questions.explanation:
The patient has clinical features of systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA), which is associated with quotidian fever. Quotidian fever - fever that rises to 39°C (102.2°F) once a day and returns to 37°C (98.6°F) between fever peaks

Systemic JIA is characterized by a fever of at least 2 weeks and Arthritis in 1 or more joints + at least one of

1. Evanescent erythematous rash that is non-pruritic and migratory with lesions lasting<1 hr.

2. Prominent visceral involvement, including hepatosplenomegaly

3. Generalized lymphadenopathy

4. Serositis

questions.question: Aarav is a known case of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA). He is referred to a Rheumatology specialist center from a local hospital, when his condition started deteriorating on steroid treatment. On examination, the patient has lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and purpura along with the acute onset of high spiking fevers. Vitals show persistent hypotension (85/45 mmHg), tachycardia (160/min), and oliguria. He was urgently admitted into the PICU. The resident physician is confused between macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) and JIA flare-up. Which of the following is best suited to distinguish these two?
questions.explanation:
Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) is characterized by all of the listed features. However, the diagnosis is confirmed by bone marrow biopsy demonstrating hemophagocytosis and is the best test to distinguish MAS from a flare-up of JIA.

MAS is a rare but potentially fatal complication of systemic JIA. It is characterized by an uncontrolled activation and proliferation of T lymphocytes and macrophages. It is the result of a cytokine storm that leads to a dysregulated inflammatory activation of the immune system, with rapid progression to multiorgan failure if not promptly diagnosed and properly treated. It is characterized by the following:

• Macrophage hemophagocytosis in the bone marrow

• Hypofibrinogenemia (paradoxical fall in erythrocyte sedimentation rate [ESR])

• Hypertriglyceridemia

• Extreme hyperferritinemia

• Fever >38.5°C

• Splenomegaly

• Cytopenia affecting at least two of three cell lineages

Treatment usually includes high-dose corticosteroids and immunosuppressive agents in refractory cases.

questions.question: A mother brought her 12-day old baby to the OPD due to the rash shown in the picture for the last 5 days. The mother says the rash gets worse in the sun. The infant was born at home and she never had a prenatal check-up. She herself has a history of joint pains and a facial rash which she says is "no big deal". On examination, Vitals are normal for the baby. A subsequent ECG shows P wave rate 120/min and R wave rate at 70/min with no relation between the two. Which of the following antibodies will be used to diagnose this baby's condition?
questions.explanation:
The baby has raccoon eyes (periorbital rash) with complete heart block (P-R dissociation) suggestive of neonatal lupus erythematosus (NLE). Anti-Ro antibodies are used to diagnose neonatal lupus.

Neonatal Lupus Erythematosus(NLE):

NLE is not an autoimmune condition. It occurs when maternal autoantibodies enter the fetal circulation (passive transfer). The antibodies responsible for this condition are anti-Ro antibody (anti-SSA) and anti-La antibody (anti-SSB).

The periorbital rash typically appears within 6 weeks of life and lasts 3-4 months. However, it can be present at birth. Infants may also have cytopenias and hepatitis, but the most feared complication is congenital heart block. Cardiomyopathy is seen in the most severe cases. The noncardiac manifestations of neonatal lupus are usually reversible, whereas congenital heart block is permanent. Conduction system abnormalities can be detected in utero by fetal echocardiogram beginning at 16 weeks of gestational age.

Fluorinated corticosteroids seem to improve cases of hydrops. Significant conduction system abnormalities after birth are treated with cardiac pacing and occasionally intravenous immunoglobulin and steroids, while severe cardiomyopathy may require cardiac transplantation. Transient, noncardiac manifestations are conservatively managed, with topical steroids used occasionally to treat the rash.

Other options:

Anti-Jo antibodies are a type of myositis-specific antibodies. These are not related to neonatal lupus.

Anti-dsDNA antibodies are specific for SLE (Systemic Lupus erythematosus).

Anti-histone antibodies are present in Drug-induced SLE.

Note:

SS in SSA and SSB stands for Sjögren's syndrome-related. Anti-SSA and anti SSB are antinuclear antibodies and are mainly found in patients with SLE and Sjögren's syndrome.

questions.question: Vikas, a high school student is observed to have an indented 'en coup de sabre' lesion as shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
En coup de sabre lesion is seen in juvenile localized scleroderma (morphea).

It appears as an indented, vertical, colourless, line of skin on the forehead. The indentation looks as though the person may have been struck (coup) by a sword (sabre). This lesion involves the scalp and/or face and often extend into the central nervous system, resulting in neurologic sequelae such as seizures and headaches.

questions.question: Pinky, a small child with Kawasaki disease is admitted to the ward for treatment. Which of the following feature would you not expect to see in her?
questions.explanation:
Purulent conjunctivitis is not a feature of Kawasaki disease. Bilateral nonexudative conjunctival infection with limbal sparing is characteristically seen in Kawasaki disease.

Kawasaki disease is also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome and is commonly seen in children between 3 months to 5 years of age.

questions.question: A worried father brought her 5-year-old son to the pediatrician with a history of fever, rash, irritability, and poor feeding. A few days back, he developed perianal desquamation and non-purulent conjunctivitis with edema of the hands and feet. He has been up to date with his immunization. Tongue findings are shown in the image. Which of the following is not likely to occur in the child?
questions.explanation:
The above clinical features are suggestive of Kawasaki disease. Thrombocytosis is a characteristic finding in Kawasaki disease and commonly occurs in the second week.

Important laboratory findings of Kawasaki disease are anemia, elevated ESR, and CRP. Major complications of Kawasaki disease are arteritis and aneurysms of coronary vessels, myocarditis, myocardial infarction, and pericarditis.

questions.question: Nisha presents to the clinic with clinical features suggestive of Kawasaki disease. She was admitted to the ward for treatment. Which of the following is the treatment of choice for this disease?
questions.explanation: Treatment of choice in Kawaski disease is IV immunoglobulins. IV immunoglobulins along with aspirin have proven beneficial in preventing coronary artery abnormalities.

questions.question: Who among the following children with Kawasaki’s disease is at greatest risk for coronary aneurysms?
options: 8 year-old girl with 6 days of high fever and strawberry tongue
5-year-old boy with 8 days of fever and CSF pleocytosis
2-year-old girl with IVIG treatment at 7th day of fever
11-year-old boy with 15 days of fever and low PCV
questions.answer: D. 11-year-old boy with 15 days of fever and low PCV
questions.explanation:
An 11-year-old boy with 15 days of fever and low PCV is at the greatest risk for coronary aneurysms.

Risk factors for coronary aneurysms in Kawasaki's disease:

• Age younger than 1 year or older than 9 years

• Male sex

• Fever ≥14 days

• Hematocrit(PCV) <35 percent

• Serum sodium concentration <135 mEq/L

• White blood cell count >12,000/mm3

• Elevated ESR and CRP

Administration of IVIG during the first 10 days of illness reduces the prevalence of coronary aneurysms fivefold.

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy comes to the clinic complaining about recurrent painful oral ulcers as shown in the picture. He also experiences repeated episodes of eye redness and pain which subsides with medication. On examination, similar ulcers are seen on his genitals. Behçet disease is suspected. Which of the following feature would you not expect to see in this patient?
options: Tender red nodules on the legs
questions.explanation:
Behcet disease is not associated with nail fold capillary abnormalities which is typically seen in systemic sclerosis.

Behcet disease is a neutrophilic vasculitis affecting small- to medium-sized vessels that classically presents as a clinical triad of recurrent oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. Other skin findings include erythema nodosa (red tender nodules on legs) and positive pathergy test (Pustular reaction, 24-48 hrs after sterile needle puncture or normal saline injection).

There can also be gastrointestinal and pulmonary manifestations, with disease mortality related to severe neurologic involvement or rupture of vascular aneurysms. Dural sinus thrombosis is the most common CNS manifestation in children. Pulmonary aneurysms are the most severe feature of pediatric BD.

It is associated with HLA subtype B51. T helper 17(Th17) cells play an important contribution in the recruitment of neutrophils, which will later infiltrate into the vessel wall.
